News.title: Man jailed for killing former partner days after his release
News.content:
When he was arrested on suspicion of Nurse's murder, Sabat claimed he had killed before and was planning a "murder spree".

He told officers: "I'm a murderer, I don't want to come back out, I wanna go to jail... I've been let out a week.

"Let me back... I'm happy in there, I've done wrong. I killed before and got away with it.

"I've murdered three people so far. I'm gonna go on a murder spree."

Outlining the facts of the case, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat and Nurse had been in a relationship and had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father.

Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Nurse's children visited her and on returning home, told their father her "friend or cousin" had been there.

On 22 October, Nurse told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave. Another neighbour saw her in the street shouting: "Get out of my house."

Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim's home, the court heard.

Nurse was last seen on CCTV on 25 October. Her children tried to visit the following day but got no response when they knocked on her door.

Her family raised concerns on 27 October and paramedics entered the flat, where the defendant, armed with a knife, charged at a paramedic, the court heard.

The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called, Farrelly said.

Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used Tasers as they detained Sabat.

Farrelly said officers found Nurse on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A post-mortem examination found she had sustained about eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands.

News.title: Watch: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
News.content:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off earlier this week in Lens.

Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said he had requested the pause until the facts of the incident had been "clarified".

Rights groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers who have been protesting against old buildings, a lack of teachers and overcrowded classrooms all week.

Police unions have said they need non-lethal options such as stun grenades to protect officers in these increasingly violent situations.

More on this story.

News.title: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed
News.content:
Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle.

Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks.

But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which paved the way for others to appeal.

The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis.

Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him.

The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals.

Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years.

"Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said.

"I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well."

Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with his life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable".

Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday.

News.title: Man admits sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a woman who had been drugged and raped by her husband without her knowledge for more than 20 years.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, is accused of inviting 13 other men to abuse her at their family home in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester.

Sean Peers, 38, was due to stand trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court earlier but admitted one count of assault by penetration on 15 September 2024.

The husband, who has already pleaded guilty to 60 offences against his wife, also admitted a fresh charge of rape and one of sexual assault. Both offences happened last summer.

One of the men accused of joining in the abuse, Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee in Scotland, has already pleaded guilty to various offences.

There are a further 11 men due to stand trial who have denied abusing the same woman between 2018 to November 2025.

Peers, from Stockport, was granted conditional bail until sentence, which will take place at the conclusion of the trial involving the other men.

The husband, who is no longer part of the trial as a defendant, will also be sentenced at the conclusion of the case and has been remanded in custody.

News.title: Five arrested for inciting racial hatred outside Jewish group's headquarters, says Met
News.content:
Five people have been arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London, the Metropolitan Police said.

The force said they were detained when a "spontaneous protest" was staged outside the Camden headquarters of the UK's largest Jewish community group.

Elsewhere, two people were arrested at a larger student pro-Palestinian protest in central London - one for breach of conditions and a second for common assault.

The arrests came as a number of student pro-Palestinian protests were taking place in London three years on from the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken as hostages by the militant group.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

Footage from the demonstration outside the Board of Deputies' Camden office showed a few dozen protesters, several of whom were wearing face coverings.

In a statement following the arrests, the Board of Deputies said the group "would not be threatened or intimidated" and thanked police for their "swift" response.

Slogans "calling for intifada" were chanted during the protest, according to the Met. The five arrested remain in custody.

The term intifada came into popular use during the Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1987.

Jewish groups have described the term as a call for violence against Jewish people. Pro-Palestinian groups have said it is a call for peaceful resistance to Israel's occupation.

The Board of Deputies is set to hold a vigil in Richmond Terrace, near Whitehall in central London, later on Wednesday.

Separately, two people were arrested at a student pro-Palestinian march, which went from Lincoln's Inn Fields to Russell Square and was attended by around 100 people.

The Met said it ended ahead of a police-enforced dispersal time, which was imposed when organisers rejected calls to move it from 7 October.

Counter-demonstrators carrying Israeli flags also gathered in Russell Square. There were some minor scuffles between the two groups.

Pro-Palestinian protesters were heard chanting "Zionists not welcome here" and "free Palestine from the river to the sea".

Some use the chant as a call for Palestinian control of all land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, including Israel.

Critics say the slogan is a call for the destruction of the state of Israel.

That interpretation is disputed by pro-Palestinian activists, who say that most people chanting it are calling for an end to Israel's occupation of the West Bank and blockade of Gaza, not the destruction of Israel itself.

News.title: Widdecombe suspect accused of trying to break into Farage's home
News.content:
The man accused of murdering the former MP Ann Widdecombe in July has appeared in court faced with a new allegation of preparing terrorist acts, including trying to break into the home of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said Joshua Kerry, 28, is alleged to have carried out online reconnaissance of "prominent people and institutions... including identifying the home address of Nigel Farage".

The prosecutor later told Westminster Magistrates' Court that damage was found on the doorframe at Farage's home address, adding: "the inference is that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house".

Kerry was accompanied by four custody officers in the dock and was remanded in custody to appear at the Old Bailey on Friday.

Kerry appeared in person the court. With a thick beard and wearing a grey sweatshirt and trousers, he spoke only to confirm his address in Rotherham and his date of birth.

He was told he faced a new charge of preparing terrorist acts between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026 by carrying out research on targets and travelling to, and attempting to gain entry to, the home of Nigel Farage.

The court heard that in April 2025 Nigel Farage's partner found that damage had been caused to their main front door at their house and a bottle of lighter fluid was found in the porch.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s. She became a member of Reform UK in 2019.

News.title: Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs
News.content:
Royal Mail has announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027 as it battles competition and falling demand for letter deliveries.

The cuts at the postal service will represent about 2% of the 131,000-strong workforce.

However, frontline postal workers - posties and drivers - are not part of the proposed restructuring.

Royal Mail said the workforce reduction, designed to improve efficiency, would be achieved through voluntary redundancies and people choosing to leave the company.

It said the cuts would make it more efficient.

"These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers," said chief executive Alistair Cochrane.

He added that the job cuts "will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues".

Royal Mail said it was in formal consultation with its unions, the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite CMA, over the plans.

The CWU said despite reassurances that there would be no compulsory redundancies, the announcement was "further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community".

"We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution," deputy general secretary Martin Walsh told the BBC.

Unite said Royal Mail, regulator Ofcom, and the government had "failed to address the serious problems facing Royal Mail, especially high competition from gig economy postal services".

The union said the cuts would not improve Royal Mail's quality of service.

Royal Mail has been struggling to meet its delivery targets for first and second class post, and has been fined by the regulator for missing targets in recent years.

Just over 75% of first class letters were delivered on time in the year to the end of March, far off its target of 93%.

Fewer people are sending letters, and the company has repeatedly said that its Universal Service Obligation (USO) â a legal requirement to deliver letters six days a week to every address in the UK â is outdated and needs reform.

Royal Mail, which is a separate from the Post Office, has faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries.

In March, postal workers across the UK told the BBC they were being asked to move or hide mail from senior bosses to make it look like delivery targets were being met.

This year, more than 100 MPs have written to regulator Ofcom and the business secretary asking for something to be done about the poor service their constituents say they are receiving.

The firm has said it is investing Â£500m over the next five years as part of its improvement plan.

Royal Mail is owned by Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky's EP Group, after his takeover was approved by shareholders at the end of April last year.

Kretinsky has previously said he will not walk away from the requirement to deliver letters throughout the UK six days a week, as long as he is running the service.

News.title: Husband appears in court accused of GP's murder
News.content:
The husband of a GP has appeared in court charged with her murder after she was found dead at home.

The body of 45-year-old GP Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill in Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.

Mark Cain, 45, also of Fern Hill, was charged with her murder on Tuesday.

He appeared in a black sweatshirt at Norwich Magistrates' Court, where he spoke only to confirm his age, name and address. He was not asked to enter a plea and is due back in court on Thursday.

Prosecutor Jacqui Hanlon told the court the ambulance service contacted the police at 02:25 BST on Sunday.

She said Terry was "found in an upstairs bedroom not breathing, not conscious".

She said a post-mortem examination "noted blunt force injury to the right side of her head had been inflicted, also an injury that could be suggestive of compression of the neck".

District judge Matthew Bone remanded the defendant in custody to appear at King's Lynn Crown Court on Thursday.

News.title: Jaguar unveils new electric car after 'woke' ridicule
News.content:
Jaguar has revealed its new electric car two years after its controversial rebranding sparked a backlash with the firm accused of going "woke".

The unveiling of the all-electric Type 01 is a gamble for parent company JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.

The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.

But it comes at a hefty price tag with a minimum cost of Â£130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US.

The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.

The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".

However, the unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions on social media.

"Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design.

Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that the new design was an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looked like a hearse and lacked any "memorable Jaguar flourish".

But car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 looked "incredible" and made him "proud to be British".

"Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X.

Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising".

"If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC.

But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular, he added.

News.title: Neglect case childminder was 'master manipulator', say parents
News.content:
Parents whose children were cared for by a childminder who has admitted neglect charges have described her as a "master manipulator".

Amanda Mathewson had been looking after many more children than she was allowed to - and at one stage left 27 youngsters alone and unsupervised at her home in Dunfermline.

Families told BBC Scotland that the 55-year-old had been "loved and trusted" in the community before her crimes came to light.

And they said it had been "incredibly traumatic" to learn that their children had not been getting cared for properly.

Mathewson pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court on Tuesday to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health. She will be sentenced next month.

Mathewson has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, providing services at her home for children under the age of 16.

One parent said she was regarded as "one of the best in the area".

"She was loved and trusted throughout the community," they told the BBC.

"Building an apparently unshakeable reputation as friendly, caring and trustworthy with the adults she encountered outside her home was part of how she concealed what was happening."

News.title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
News.content:
Young performer Skye Newman faced what must have seemed like a very unusual X-Factor style panel - King Charles, Sir Elton, his husband David Furnish and Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook.

The music workshop was part of a project between Apple and the King's Trust Creative Labs, and is the latest link-up between the royals and the Californian tech giant.

Last year, the King revealed a playlist of 17 of his favourite tracks, which was issued on Apple Music.

The King didn't include Sir Elton John in any of those choices - but the pop star has been a long-time supporter of the King's Trust charity, which was previously known as the Prince's Trust.

Now in its 50th year, the charity was set up to give opportunities to deprived and marginalised young people - and has so far helped 1.3 million people across the UK.

The tie-up with Apple shows the changing demands for work skills, including using the latest technology for young people wanting to build careers in the music and creative industries.

There was also a royal link with Battersea Power Station - as that had once provided the electricity for Buckingham Palace.

In the power station's control room, the link to the Palace had been discreetly labelled as "Carnaby Street", in case any intruders had ever been tempted to switch off the Palace lights.

News.title: 'It's torture and torment without answers' - dad of teen killed in blast
News.content:
Leona Harper's coat still hangs in the hallway of her family home.

The soil from the pitch of the last game she played is still on her rugby boots.

Her bedroom remains untouched.

Four years on from the Creeslough explosion that claimed the 14-year-old schoolgirl's life, along with nine others, her father says their family remains "desperate for answers" about the events of that day.

The blast happened at a service station in the County Donegal village on 7 October 2022.

No official explanation has been given for the cause of the explosion, and no one has been charged in connection with the blast despite a number of arrests.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) sent a second file to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) in April which is in addition to the primary file it forwarded to prosecutors last September.

A commemoration service will be held on Wednesday in Creeslough for the 10 victims of the explosion.

News.title: 'Dad dragged me out of bed by my hair to work' - rural abuse victims want more support
News.content:
Warning: This story contains content that some readers might find distressing

Growing up on a farm, Tracy Lewis loved being around its animals but said the physical and emotional abuse from her farmer father was "torture".

When she was eight, she recalled her dad pulling her out of bed by her hair to go lambing as her mum told her "you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die".

Tracy, now 48 and a farmer herself, and other domestic abuse survivors are calling on governments to better support victims in rural areas.

The UK government said it was working to address disparities while the Welsh government said challenges will be considered in its next national strategy.

Tracy's family have given their permission to the BBC for her to share her story.

"I remember my father pulled me out of bed by my hair to go and lamb a ewe," she recalled of her childhood in mid Wales.

"I walked past the bathroom and my mum's face had blood all over it and her nose was squashed, she'd been crying. She said to me, you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die."

News.title: The Neet hotspots in England where thousands of young people are out of work
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Urban areas account for the majority of young people in England who are not in employment, education or training (Neet), new findings show.

A study by the Centre for Cities reveals that over a third of these people are concentrated within the nation's nine biggest cities.

Highlighting "stark differences" across regions, the research notes that youth in certain locations are over three times as likely to fall into this category compared to others.

London recorded the highest total figure at an estimated 117,100—representing one in six across England—with Birmingham and Manchester following at 45,000 and 37,700 respectively.

In terms of local proportions, Blackpool registered the highest share at 21 per cent, followed by Doncaster, Bradford, Middlesbrough and Barnsley, which all stood at 17 per cent.

Conversely, York recorded the lowest rate at 6 per cent, followed by Nottingham on 8 per cent, with Bristol, Brighton and Portsmouth each at 9 per cent.

open image in gallery London has around one in six of all Neets in England, according to the research ( PA Archive )

Rob Johnson, senior analyst at the Centre for Cities, said: “Getting young people into work or training is a national challenge that will be won or lost in England’s cities.

“In places like Birmingham, the scale of the problem is striking, with 45,000 out of education or training.

“In other places like Blackpool, the actual number is small but the proportion of young people affected is very high.

“This shows there can’t be a single national solution. Stronger local economies are essential.

“Interventions will only get us so far if areas lack jobs or training places.

“Mayors need the powers to tackle the barriers that young people face, whether that’s skills, training, or the ability to actually get to jobs and courses from where they live.”

open image in gallery London has the largest number of Neets, an estimated 117,100, or one in six of all Neets in England, said the report, followed by Birmingham (45,000) and Manchester (37,700) ( Getty )

The number of young considered Neet currently hovers around the one million mark, recording a slight fall between April and June from 1.01 million to 981,000.

The government has indicated that it will take further action to tackle the UK’s Neet crisis following the publication of a review into youth unemployment by Alan Milburn later this year.

Delivering his interim report earlier this year, the former Labour health minister said that young people were being “abandoned” to a life on welfare. The current system presents a “perverse choice” his report found, with those on health benefits able to find a “higher income, less hassle and lower risk” than if they took up work.

Reacting to his comments, several charities and campaigners have urged the government not to pursue changes to the welfare system which would see health benefits cut only for young claimants.

News.title: Everything we know about how exercise fights the effects of cancer
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It’s well known that people’s overall lifestyle affects their risk of developing cancer.

The disease has been tied to what we eat and drink, the air we breathe and even how much sun we’re exposed to.

And cancer touches the majority of Americans, with over two million expected to be diagnosed with cancer this year, according to the American Cancer Society.

But increasing research conducted over the last few decades shows how fitness can curtail cancer risk – and even help keep cancer from coming back.

One trial last year showed that colon cancer patients who participated in an exercise program over three years were less likely to see their cancers recur and had increased survival. That’s because exercise appears to increase the activity of cancer-fighting immune cells.

open image in gallery Doing yoga and other low-impact exercise is enough to make a positive difference for people with cancer. Years of research shows fitness can improve quality of life for the patients ( AFP via Getty Images )

Exercise has also been shown to lessen inflammation and insulin, which are linked to some cancers, according to The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

“If we had a drug with this magnitude of benefit, it would immediately become standard of care and funded” by insurance companies, Dr. Christopher Booth, an oncologist and professor at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, told The New York Times on Tuesday.

While more research is needed to understand the processes in the body that occur when cancer patients exercise, the overall evidence supports the benefits of exercise for people battling the disease, experts say.

“The science shows that exercising during cancer treatment eases fatigue, anxiety and depression while improving quality of life and physical function,” Karen Basen-Engquist, director of MD Anderson’s Center for Energy Balance in Cancer Prevention and Survivorship, explained.

So how much is enough to see these benefits?

Cancer patients of all ages should get around 30 minutes of daily exercise – including resistance training and aerobic exercise, according to most guidance.

That’s the same recommendation as for people without cancer. Fortunately, the 30-minutes of exercise doesn’t have to be a high-impact workout.

Walking, in particular, has shown results, leading to higher quality of life and lower fatigue in patients, a study of more than 1,700 patients with colorectal cancer found.

And calming yoga can help with sleep, anxiety and mood, according to the University of Rochester Medicine.

open image in gallery Just walking has been proven to lower fatigue in patients with colorectal cancer ( Getty Images )

Exercise can also fight groggy “chemo brain” by improving blood flow, reducing inflammation and leading to brain changes that support learning and memory.

Exercising for up to 150 minutes a week before getting chemotherapy was shown to keep cognitive impairment associated with treatment at bay, according to a 2021 study of breast cancer patients.

For breast cancer patients, exercise may also lower the risk of lymphedema – swelling in the arms and legs – and other complications that people tend to experience after breast cancer treatment, according to the Mayo Clinic.

"There are a lot of training regimens that have shown to have a myriad of positive outcomes for patients with breast cancer," Dr. Andrea L. Cheville, a physiatrist at Mayo Clinic, said in February.

News.title: Here’s how to get discounted fuel at more than 500 supermarkets this October
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

More than 500 supermarkets are offering cut price fuel this month, as prices hit a record high.

But savvy shoppers will be able to get 8p a litre off in a deal running until October 18. The deal is available to Tesco customers who spend £60 or more in a single transaction, without the need for a Clubcard, but it needs to be claimed in-store.

Customers who spend the required amount will be able to redeem their fuel coupon by Sunday 25 October by scanning it at the petrol station till. However, it can’t be used at pay-at-pump services.

The maximum discount is £8, and as the average person fills up 35 to 45 litres of fuel, most people will likely save about £2.80 to £3.60, according to the Money Saving Expert website.

Petrol station at the Asda store in Leyton, east London (Sean Dempsey/PA) ( PA Archive )

It adds that the £60 minimum spend at Tesco excludes: lottery products, e-top up, savings stamps, postage stamps, carrier bags, prescription medicines, infant milk formula, and purchases made at any café, tobacco kiosk, opticians, phone store, concessions, Travel Money, Tesco Bank, and Tesco Whoosh.

Tesco’s isn’t the only supermarket to launch a fuel offer, Asda announced an offer for 5p a litre off fuel when customers spend £40 or more in a single transaction in-store.

This deal runs from September 23 until October 14 at 262 participating Asda and Asda Express sites offering Asda-branded fuel.

It comes as fuel prices hit a record high in the UK. Fuel analysis by the RAC last week showed that diesel has risen to a record of 200.01p a litre. The previous record high was 199.09p, set in June 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

This means the cost of filling up an average family car now stands at £110, according to the motoring group – close to £32 more than at the start of the United States’ war with Iran in February.

The RAC’s head of policy, Simon Williams, said that it was a threshold that ‘no-one wanted to cross’.

“This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders. In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”

Petrol prices have also been on the rise, with a litre of unleaded now standing at 174.71p on average, around 42p more than at the start of the conflict. It means that the cost to fill an average-sized petrol car now stands at £96 overall.

News.title: Princess found stolen engagement ring in UK auction house catalogue, court told
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A Jordanian princess discovered her stolen jewellery, including her one-of-a-kind engagement ring, on sale at a Canterbury auction house, a court heard.

Princess Firyal Irshaid, 81, had left the UK during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, during which her beloved jewellery collection was taken from her Belgravia home and put up for sale.

Her housekeeper, Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, is now on trial at Southwark Crown Court, accused of using her access to carry out the thefts.

Princess Firyal told jurors on Wednesday that she had discovered her possessions had been stolen when her engagement ring was pictured on the front of an auction house catalogue.

She said her friend, Pierre Jeannet, a partner in high-end jewellery maker JAR who had crafted the ring, called on November 21 2020.

“He asked: ‘Are you selling your jewellery?’ And I said: ‘No, what are you talking about?’”, she told the court.

“He told me my ring, made specially for my engagement, was on the cover of a catalogue in an auction house.”

Princess Firyal married Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, in 1964, in a marriage which lasted for 14 years.

open image in gallery Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao worked as the princess’s housekeeper for 11 years ( PA )

Taborda Henao, also known as Lina, worked as the princess’s housekeeper for 11 years, and is accused of stealing jewellery while looking after the Belgravia home in 2020.

Her nephew, Julian Ramirez, is said to have acted as a “key conduit for the sale of stolen property”, and transferred £17,835 to Taborda Henao between June 23 2019 and November 28 2020.

Princess Firyal said that, once alerted to the sale, she obtained copies of the catalogue at Canterbury Auction Galleries and set about proving that she was the true owner of the jewels.

She said the engagement ring, which had been chosen to headline the catalogue, was made specially for her by JAR and was “the only one like it in the world”.

She obtained catalogues from three past sales, in March, May and August 2020 and found more of her property had been sold, but said the auction house managing director, David Parker, was “dismissive” when she first called up to say what had happened.

“I told them who I am, told them I own the pieces,” she said. “He was so disrespectful and dismissive.”

Jurors heard the princess used documents she could get hold of in Jordan, including bills of sale, catalogue images, a photograph of her wearing a pair of earrings that had been stolen, and a picture of a bracelet at her home, to prove she was the real owner.

open image in gallery The 71-year-old housekeeper is now on trial at Southwark Crown Court ( Getty/iStock )

Talking about her jewellery collection, Princess Firyal said it is her “love” as a longtime collector.

“I understand fine art, I love it, and I know I will invest well,” she said.

“Every room I live in has jewellery everywhere, in cupboards, but they are open.

“Most of the time it’s on the counter, what I was wearing that week.

“It was not hidden; anyone could come and take what they wanted – if they mean to.”

Princess Firyal told the court she left her UK home in mid-March 2020, at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, after getting a phone call from her son giving her three hours to pack and get to the airport.

“It was the last plane leaving before they shut the airport in Jordan,” she said.

“There was no chance I was going to miss it. I didn’t want to be here alone; I had no family.”

Taborda Henao was the only staff member left behind, and she told the court that when security guards are on duty, they are strictly only allowed outside the property.

Jurors have heard the princess agreed for Taborda Henao’s sister, Ramirez’s mother, to move into the property during the early stages of the pandemic, and then agreed to pay her a salary.

“I thought it was odd, but I accepted it”, she said, adding that she was told later in 2020 that the sister had fallen ill and left.

She told the court she did not know Ramirez’s name until she was “told by the police who had consigned my jewellery to the auction house”.

During a search of Taborda Henao’s Fulham home, police found the princess’s wedding ring, a pair of earrings, and a jewelled metal necklace.

Ramirez is believed to have flown to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail.

Taborda Henao denies theft by an employee. The trial continues.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect accused of trying to break into Nigel Farage’s home in ‘terror plot’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A man charged with the murder of Ann Widdecombe is also accused of trying to break into Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in an alleged terror plot, a court heard.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with preparing acts of terrorism, including against Mr Farage, between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026.

Westminster Magistrates’ Court heard Mr Kerry allegedly carried out online reconnaissance on prominent people and institutions, including identifying the home address of Mr Farage.

He is accused of travelling to the address and trying to gain entry on 19 April last year.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik told the court that the politician’s partner returned home the following day to find part of the wooden door frame hanging off and a bottle of lighter fluid on the porch.

open image in gallery Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court ( Supplied )

Forensic examination discovered a tool mark, “the inference being that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house”, Mr Malik said.

Mr Kerry is also accused of targeting Reform UK spokeswoman Ms Widdecombe at her home in Haytor, Devon. The 78-year-old former prisons minister was killed on 8 July after she was struck over the head 21 times with a hammer.

Appearing wearing a grey prison issue tracksuit, he spoke only to confirm his identity during the brief hearing.

Chief magistrate Paul Goldspring remanded him in custody to appear the Old Bailey on Friday, telling the defendant: “Mr Kerry, the terrorism charge which you face is indictable only which means I must send it to the crown court.”

open image in gallery Mr Kerry spoke only to confirm his identity during the brief hearing ( PA )

Announcing the fresh charges last week, Counter Terrorism Policing said Mr Kerry, of Byrley Road, Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, contrary to section 5(1)(a) of the Terrorism Act 2006.

Senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time.

“The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counter Terrorism Policing network.

“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”

News.title: The forgotten 2,000-year-old tradition that keeps you warm in cold weather
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

On winter mornings in Harbin, where the air outside could freeze your eyelashes, I would wake up on a bed of warm earth.

Harbin, where I grew up, is in northeast China. Winter temperatures regularly dip to -30°C and in January even the warmest days rarely go above -10°C. With about 6 million residents today, Harbin is easily the largest city in the world to experience such consistent cold.

Keeping warm in such temperatures is something I’ve thought about all my life. Long before electric air conditioning and district heating, people in the region survived harsh winters using methods entirely different from the radiators and gas boilers that dominate European homes today.

Now, as a researcher in architecture and construction at a British university, I’m struck by how much we can learn from those traditional systems in the UK.

Energy bills are still too high, and millions are struggling to heat their homes, while climate change is expected to make winters more volatile. We need efficient, low-energy ways to stay warm that don’t rely on heating an entire home with fossil fuels.

Some of the answers may lie in the methods I grew up with.

A warm bed made of earth

My earliest memories of winter involve waking up on a “kang” – a heated platform-bed made of earth bricks that has been used in northern China for at least 2,000 years. The kang is less a piece of furniture and more a part of the building itself: a thick, raised slab connected to the family stove in the kitchen. When the stove is lit for cooking, hot air travels through passages running beneath the kang, warming its entire mass.

open image in gallery A traditional Chinese kang bed-stove ( Google Gemini, CC BY-SA )

To a child, the kang felt magical: a warm, radiant surface that stayed hot all night long. But as an adult – and now an academic expert – I can appreciate what a remarkably efficient piece of engineering it is.

Unlike central heating, which works by warming the air in every room, only the kang (that is, the bed surface) is heated. The room itself may be cold, but people warm themselves by laying or sitting on the platform with thick blankets. Once warmed, its hundreds of kilograms of compacted earth slowly release heat over many hours. There are no radiators, no need for any pumps, and no unnecessary heating of empty rooms. And since much of the initial heat was generated by fires we’d need for cooking anyway, we saved on fuel.

open image in gallery Each winter the river freezes in Harbin, China ( AP )

Maintaining the kang was a family undertaking. My father – a secondary school Chinese literature teacher, not an engineer – became an expert at constructing the kang. Carefully building layers of coal around the fire to keep it alive over the night would be my mum’s job. Looking back, I realise how much skill and labour was involved, and how much trust families placed in a system that required good ventilation to avoid carbon monoxide risks.

But for all its drawbacks, the kang delivered something modern heating systems still struggle to deliver: long-lasting warmth with very little fuel.

Similar approaches across East Asia

Across East Asia, approaches to keeping warm in cold weather evolved around similar principles: keep heat close to the body, and heat only the spaces that matter.

About the author Yangang Xing is an Associate Professor in the School of Architecture Design and the Built Environment at Nottingham Trent University. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

In Korea, the ancient ondol system also channels warm air beneath thick floors, turning the entire floor into a heated surface. Japan developed the kotatsu, a low table covered by a heavy blanket with a small heater underneath to keep your legs warm. They can be a bit costly, but they’re one of the most popular items in Japanese homes.

Clothing was also very important. Each winter my mum would make me a brand new thick padded coat, stuffing it with newly fluffed cotton. It’s one of my loveliest memories.

Europe had similar ideas – then forgot them

Europe once had similar approaches to heating. Ancient Romans heated buildings using hypocausts, for instance, which circulated hot air under floors. Medieval households hung heavy tapestries on walls to reduce drafts, and many cultures used soft cushions, heated rugs or enclosed sleeping areas to conserve warmth.

The spread of modern central heating in the 20th century replaced these approaches with a more energy-intensive pattern: heating entire buildings to a uniform temperature, even when only one person is home. When energy was cheap, this model worked, even despite most European homes (especially those in the UK) being poorly insulated by global standards.

But now that energy is expensive again, tens of millions of Europeans are unable to keep their homes adequately warm. New technologies like heat pumps and renewable energy will help – but they work best when the buildings they heat are already efficient, allowing for lower set point for heating, and higher set points for cooling.

This highlights why traditional approaches to warming homes still have something to teach us. The kang and similar systems show that comfort doesn’t always come from consuming more energy – but from designing warmth more intelligently.

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.

News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Russia’s plague shouldn’t scare us – its secretive bioweapons should
News.content:
The facts about the laboratory accident in Russia are scant.

A lab technician at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Siberia is dead, 200 people have been quarantined, and the state security services are saying “nothing to see here, folks”.

Denials from the country that has run a covert biological weapons programme since the Cold War have done nothing to quieten speculation about what is really going on in the vast Siberian tundra.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, demanded on Tuesday that Russia be “transparent” about the situation, which he said Washington was monitoring “very closely”.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Mr Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.

A death from plague is a tragedy, but should not be something we need to worry about. We have moved on from the Middle Ages, when the Black Death laid waste to much of Europe.

It’s treatable with antibiotics and does not spread as fast as diseases like Covid. Its replication or R number does not get above 1.5 – measles, for example, has an R number of 12 to 18.

News.title: Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first
News.content:
One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

News.title: UK not prepared for food shortages, experts warn
News.content:
Britain has no way to feed its population of 66 million people in a crisis, a letter addressed to the Prime Minister has warned.

Climate change, cyber-attacks, geopolitical shifts, and energy shocks could put Britain’s food supply at great risk – and the UK is “complacent”, the letter says.

The document was delivered to Andy Burnham on Monday and was signed by 180 experts including academics, farmers, local council leaders, and foodbank workers.

Britain’s food supply is now heavily globalised, with roughly 45-50 per cent of food imported from countries like Spain, the Netherlands and France, as well as South Africa, Columbia and Brazil.

The system provides a cheap and constant supply of food – seasonal or not – but if international supply chains are disrupted, the UK’s home production is “woefully inadequate in [being able to produce] many different food types” , the letter argues.

It adds that “international food supplies can be weaponised”.

Crucially, the UK operates a ‘just-in-time’ food system – meaning hardly any food is stocked and stored in reserves, but is constantly moving from farms and ports directly to supermarket and wholesale shelves when needed.

“When you go to a supermarket and check out, you think, well, ‘it’s adding up the bill’ – it is, but what it’s also doing is reordering,” Tim Lang, emeritus professor of food policy at City University, a signatory of the letter and author of the Just in Case report – a major review that analysed the UK’s food system for the National Preparedness Commission, previously told The Telegraph.

Sports.title: Verstappen: F1 'less stressful' without Horner
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says the Formula 1 paddock is "less stressful" following Christian Horner's exit because "it is not nice when you constantly have tension between people".

Verstappen, who secured his first victory of the season, and the 72nd of his career, at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, won all four of his world championships at Red Bull while Horner was at the helm as team principal.

Horner has been consistently linked with a return to the sport, saying he has "unfinished business" and that leading Ferrari would be a "dream".

Any comeback could see him spar with fellow bosses Toto Wolff (Mercedes) and Zak Brown (McLaren) once again.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jacques Villeneuve comments on the likelihood of Horner joining Ferrari following his comments that working with the team would be a 'dream role'

In an interview with the Press Association, Verstappen said: "To be honest, I like to see people get on. It is not nice when you constantly have tension between people.

"Of course, from the outside, people like it, but honestly between the teams, it is better when you have just a friendly relationship.

"It is not as spicy, but I obviously quite like how things are going at the moment with everyone's behaviour, let's put it like that.

"It is less stressful. We are all leading a stressful life and when you can take a bit of stress out at times, it is good."

On Horner's potential return, Verstappen said: "He has shown he did a good job. Of course, people spread a lot of rumours and I don't know how much of that is true.

"I don't want to sound rude, but it is also not my problem or concern. He wants to come back and if there is a good opportunity I am sure he will but I don't know where that is going to be."

Image: Horner left Red Bull in 2025

Verstappen: Rebuilding Red Bull is what's driving me

Verstappen recently signed a new four-year deal at Red Bull having spoken with other teams including McLaren - but did he fancy a switch to Ferrari?

The Dutchman said: "I only want to win.

"I am not a nostalgic type. Do I have a lot of respect for the [Ferrari] brand? Absolutely. But if that means you then commit yourself, and you are driving P5 or P6, what's the point?

"I am very performance-driven, and I have won a lot with this team already. It is a second family at Red Bull, and the challenge of rebuilding is what's driving me."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Verstappen jokes about getting Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar on his private jet

Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso has penned a deal to stay in F1 beyond his 46th birthday but Verstappen, 29, does not expect to still be around at that age.

"Staying here until then would mean I have dedicated more than half of my life to Formula 1, and that is probably a bit too much," he added.

"I have extended for a few more years, and then I will look again and say to myself, 'can I commit 100 per cent?' If not, or there are other fun things around that deserves more time, then maybe I don't continue.

"I also want to spend more time at home and see the kids growing up."

Sports.title: Pettersen to make golf comeback - and it may not be a one-off
Sports.content:
Suzann Pettersen is making a second return to professional golf since her retirement in 2019 with an appearance at this week's Aramco Korea Championship - and it may not be a one-off.

The Norwegian, 45, retired on the spot seven years ago after sinking the winning putt for Team Europe in the Solheim Cup at Gleneagles.

Pettersen played in the Aramco Team Series event in Jeddah in 2022 and will now tee it up again in Asia, with the two-time major winner having more time on her hands as her children get older.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Pettersen's winning putt at the 2019 Solheim Cup at Gleneagles

She said: "Obviously, I've been playing and practising quite a bit at home. Nothing close to playing competitions. I'm curious just to see where my game is at.

"Coming here to Korea feels quite a long way to come to test your game, but I might as well just get the gloves off. I have nothing to prove to myself. I'm just doing this because I love the game."

Pettersen, who is eligible for the Legends of the LPGA and soon the women's senior major championships, added: "I'm not going to come back and play a full schedule ever. That's being very honest.

"I could ideally see myself playing five or six events a year.

"I want to keep the game going in my body, so I don't have to pick it up in another three years, and then it's going to be even harder.

Image: Pettersen was the first player to win the Evian Championship after it was elevated to a major in 2013

"The clubs are the same. I have the same irons. I haven't changed much since last time I hit a professional golf shot, so we'll see how this goes."

"I think [the players] are all thinking 'what the heck are you doing?'"

Pettersen will play alongside Alexandra Försterling and Emily Kristine Pedersen in the opening round at New Korea Country Club.

Since stepping back as a player, Pettersen has presided over two Solheim Cup campaigns as captain - a trophy-retaining 14-14 draw in Spain in 2023 and then a 15½-12½ defeat in the States a year later.

Sports.title: World Cup criticism still stings Tuchel despite Nations League positives
Sports.content:
The Wembley crowd was in party mood and the fans sang Thomas Tuchel's name. Three straight wins without conceding, Harry Kane feted as England's greatest ever servant, a Nations League quarter-final all-but guaranteed.

Some 83 days after England succumbed to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final, we'd moved on.

And then Tuchel showed that he hasn't, and revealed his underlying bitterness and hurt.

The England boss is clearly still smarting from the vociferous criticism that came at him from all angles following the World Cup exit. And now, when all had been forgotten, if not forgiven, it was Tuchel who brought the subject back up.

He'd made it very clear at the start of this extended international break that he wanted to look forward rather than back. We know that he'd had clear-the-air talks with the England players who had lingering anger at his public criticism of them and their sub-standard 'DNA', but Tuchel stressed it is now all about the bright new future, with an assault on the Nations League trophy and, ultimately, the Euros in two years' time.

But, feeling re-emboldened after a very positive autumn for his England team, he bit back at those pesky journalists who'd dared to question whether he got the tactics wrong when 1-0 up and close to reaching a first World Cup final in 60 years.

Asked whether he'd seen an improvement in mood, confidence and momentum since the end of the World Cup, he replied: "Yeah, I do. It's necessary to move on and I can only repeat: we didn't go out in the group stage. It often feels like that. But we didn't."

A follow-up question asked him whether he felt the scrutiny and assessment of England's World Cup exit had been too harsh, and Tuchel's response was pointed and said with a scornful tone and a stern expression.

"In between, it felt a little bit like it, yeah. (Why?) Why? Were you in the press conference before the France game? (Me? No, I wasn't there.) Yeah. You would have known why."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at Thomas Tuchel's frosty response to a reporter, over England's World Cup exit reaction earlier this year.

The tense exchange came after a three-week camp where sources had told Sky Sports News just how positive the mood had been, and how optimistic the players and staff are about what lies ahead. Tuchel and the squad were as one again, the "Brotherhood" Tuchel craved, back together again.

And yet the image that Tuchel portrayed to the outside world, whenever the cameras were on him at training or in the regular news conferences that came with four games in 11 days, was one of a brooding malaise.

I'm told the England boss became aware of his less-than-positive demeanour and made a conscious effort to change for the latter stages of the camp, and in fact the Tuchel on the touchline at Wembley on Tuesday night was back to his animated, tactile, positive self.

Until the post-match news conference. Where it looked the opposite. And it was very surprising that the England boss decided to take that tack.

Satisfaction and clarity from latest camp

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rob Dorsett and James Green give their England player ratings following their 3-0 win over Czech Republic.

That media moment aside, Tuchel can look back on this extended international break with a lot of satisfaction. He engineered by far the best performance and result of his tenure with the 7-0 obliteration of Croatia on Saturday, and he has what he would call "proof of concept", in the sense that England showed an energy, a ravenousness for the ball, and a relentless attacking intent which the England boss has been calling for from the moment he took over.

Even the defeat to Spain in the opening game came with a great deal of positives, with England matching their opponents in many areas, and they were perhaps a slipped penalty kick away from victory over the world champions.

Most impressive was England's front four, who Bukayo Saka told me is the best in the world when they are on song. Kane told us there is a new freedom and fluidity in the way they play together which brings out the best of all of them, and makes it much more challenging for opposing defences. When he drops deep, others (often Jude Bellingham) run beyond him to fill the void; when Bellingham goes wide to exploit space, Anthony Gordon or Saka will drift inside. Tuchel's assistant, Anthony Barry, described it by saying they'd let Bellingham "out of a cage" and that they were reaping the rewards.

A number of new players put their hands up to be England regulars too. Alex Scott was name-checked by Barry as someone who is already considered part of the inner sanctum, and Lewis Hall showed that he is probably first choice left-back now, after some hugely impressive performances throughout. Trent Alexander-Arnold, too, reminded everyone of his world class ball skills - whether he did enough to impress Tuchel for a regular return to the England fold remains to be seen, when all of the other injured right backs are available again.

It felt like there is more clarity too on some of those players on the England fringes, and who missed this camp. Cole Palmer was given some Tuchel tough love, when the German coach said he'd missed too many opportunities to be in camp. Phil Foden wasn't mentioned at all, after he'd been overlooked in the original squad selection. Harry Maguire likewise, after voicing his frustration at being left out of the World Cup squad.

You also get the feeling that, in the debate around who will ultimately replace Kane as England's No 9, Bellingham is looking more and more likely. It was noticeable that the Real Madrid master often filled in there in this camp, rather than Tuchel turning to Dominic Calvert-Lewin on the bench.

Tuchel now has a month-and-a-half to reflect. He can be very pleased with the direction of travel. But the next stern test is as tough as it gets: Spain away, in November.

Sports.title: How does Arteta turn champions into serial winners?
Sports.content:
When Mikel Arteta signed his last Arsenal contract in September 2024, his quest to bring major silverware back to the club was ongoing. Two years later, he signs his new one after leading them to a long-awaited Premier League title.

His task now is to turn champions into serial winners.

Arteta has overseen a total transformation of the club since his appointment in 2019. Arsenal, 10th in the Premier League table when he took over, were in a state of drift. Now, they are re-established among Europe's elite, unrecognisable in all departments.

Arteta has joined a select group of 13 managers to have won the Premier League. He now has the chance to join an even smaller group, made up of only Sir Alex Ferguson, Pep Guardiola, Jose Mourinho and Arsene Wenger, by winning it more than once.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Kaveh Solhekol and Gary Cotterill provide the latest on Mikel Arteta's Arsenal future as he is expected to sign a new contract

Securing a first Champions League, after guiding Arsenal to only their second final last term, is another chance for immortality.

His new contract, described as an "utmost priority" by co-chair Josh Kroenke in May, reflects the club's belief that they are in the best possible hands. It also gives Arteta the chance to get closer to Guardiola's longevity at Manchester City.

The club feel the departure of Arteta's old mentor from City, coupled with instability there and elsewhere, presents an opportunity to capitalise. Arsenal are in their "win window", to quote Kroenke. "We think we have a chance here to dominate," he said in May.

The group look well-set to build on their success. But Arteta, the rookie head coach-turned elite manager whose work other clubs now strive to emulate, might be Arsenal's biggest asset of all, which is why the news of his new deal is so significant.

Image: Mikel Arteta poses with the Premier League trophy in May

Who better to nurture the culture which has underpinned their success than the man who painstakingly implemented it?

Arteta ensures stability, allowing Arsenal to operate from a position of strength. "Getting the foundations in place is usually the hardest part of the journey," added Kroenke.

His tenure has been a story of steady improvement, both domestically, where Arsenal have ended a 22-year wait for the title, and in Europe, where they have gone from Champions League quarter-finalists, to semi-finalists, to runners-up in three years.

But there is work to do to sustain the trajectory.

Their defeat to Brighton highlighted room for improvement. It felt like a slap in the face to Arsenal, largely because it was so uncharacteristic. Arteta's side, defined by their steeliness, hadn't lost a Premier League game by a margin of three goals since 2023.

Arteta will hope to use the result as a wake-up call, and a reminder to his players that there can be no room for complacency in their efforts to retain their crown. "This is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher explains why he believes Mikel Arteta has become the Sir Alex Ferguson of today's Premier League

He might even come to be grateful for it.

Arsenal went into the season as most people's favourites to win the title. But only a handful of sides have gone back-to-back in the Premier League era. Arsenal haven't managed it since the 1930s. History shows the enormity of the task ahead of them.

Part of the challenge for Arteta is to continue evolving the team.

Heavily impacted by injuries to their best attacking players for a second consecutive season last term, Arsenal leaned into their defensive and set-piece prowess to get over the line in the title race. They remain a formidable outfit on both fronts.

Clearly, there is still work to do in the transfer market to bring their attack up to the same level. For now, though, Arteta must get more from what he has, helped, at least, by a far clearer injury list.

Image: Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard struggled with injuries in the last two seasons

It is worth noting that the last time he had Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Bukayo Saka fit for a full season, in 2023/24, Arsenal broke a club record for goals. The trio, together again at last, scored 10 goals in their first seven games of the campaign.

More broadly, there have been signs of a return to a more possession-orientated playing style, and a greater desire to control games with the ball rather than without it.

It is of course still early in the campaign to make definitive judgements. But Arsenal's numbers are up for possession, passes and passes in the final third compared to last season.

Sports.title: 'We want a winning era' - Arteta signs new Arsenal contract
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has signed a new long-term contract to extend his stay at Arsenal.

The 44-year-old's existing contract with the Premier League champions, signed in September 2024, was due to expire next summer.

But the Spaniard, who was appointed in 2019, has committed his future to the club until June 2030.

Arteta has transformed Arsenal's fortunes during his tenure and guided the club to their first Premier League title in 22 years last season following three straight second-place finishes.

He also led the Gunners to only their second Champions League final, which they lost on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain. He has also won an FA Cup and three Community Shields.

Image: Mikel Arteta poses with the Premier League trophy at the end of last season

"It's a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal," Arteta said in a statement.

"This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue.

"We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Nick Wright discusses Mikel Arteta's transformation of Arsenal since he took over at the club in December 2019, turning them into Premier League champions for the first time in over 20 years.

"I'm extremely grateful to Stan and Josh for their trust and support, and feel honoured to be leading this club through such a special period in its 140-year history.

"This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine - and ours - in return."

Meanwhile, Arsenal chief executive Richard Garlick said: "This is an important time in Arsenal Football Club's history. We want to create a winning era together with Mikel.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Sam Blitz discusses Mikel Arteta's five-stage plan for Arsenal and where the Spaniard currently is on the ladder and how he creates a 'dynasty' with the Gunners.

"We will continue to work hard together as we aim to fulfil our long-term ambitions for the club and our supporters.

"Mikel has the belief, determination and the understanding of what it takes to build something remarkable and enduring here, and we are excited to continue that journey together."

Only four managers - Sir Alex Ferguson, Pep Guardiola, Jose Mourinho and Arsene Wenger - have won the Premier League title more than once.

So can Arteta join the esteemed list? His new contract gives him a chance to build an Arsenal dynasty. Sky Sports' Nick Wright assesses his chances of doing it.

Image: Mikel Arteta took over as Arsenal head coach in 2019

Sky Sports News reporter Gary Cotterill:

"Arsene Wenger certainly got off to a faster start, didn't he? But Arteta has got the time to do it.

Sports.title: ‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.

The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more £20m a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait to be crowned champions after three successive runners-up finishes.

Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. After losing the Champions League final last season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” said Arteta. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”

Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.

“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.

“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”
