Arsenal confirmed this week that they have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. His side face Leeds on Saturday as they attempt to bounce back from a surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton before the international break that ended the champions’ 100% start to the new campaign.

Sports.title: Robertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questions
Sports.content:
What is the general situation after four games?

Scotland are staring at a third-place finish in Group B1 of the Nations League, which will have repercussions for their seeding in Euro 2028 qualifying. More striking, though, was the general standard of performance over Sébastien Pocognoli’s first four games as manager.

Scotland were dismal for a half in Slovenia before a decent but scoreless recovery. They capitulated after an early sending off against Switzerland, failing to register a shot on target in a meek 3-0 loss. North Macedonia were as poor an international team as Scotland have faced in recent times, rendering the 2-0 win a Skopje worthy of little more than a shoulder shrug. Pocognoli’s men rounded off this extended window by being played off the Hampden Park pitch by Slovenia. Andy Robertson, the captain, strikingly questioned the attitude of his teammates. There has been no new manager bounce.

Pocognoli was given only a two-year contract, which was odd given the pedestal he was placed on by the Scottish Football Association when hired in August. The likelihood remains host-nation status will secure the Scots a place in the next Euros, but the country cannot arrive at the event under the cover of darkness. The alarming nature of the performance against Slovenia – it really had no redeeming qualities – places a huge emphasis on November’s fixtures.

Are Scotland suited to the way Pocognoli wants to play?

It does not look that way. The manager deploys a three-man backline as routine, with an emphasis on pressing high and wing backs being crucial to attacking phases. Scotland do not have an obvious two-man central defensive pairing, meaning they most definitely struggle when the number is increased by one. Time and again, they leave far too much space in behind and look woefully exposed. Counterattacks bypass Scotland’s midfield all too easily. Pocognoli’s Scotland are a dream to play against.

Success for the Scots under Steve Clarke came from being well-drilled, compact and difficult to beat. Unsexy perhaps, but effective. Playing with gay abandon is all well and good when having a level of security Scotland simply do not possess currently. Scotland allowed Slovenia to be just as menacing as Morocco and Brazil, top-quality opposition they faced at the World Cup. Pocognoli’s desired methods may be impossible to implement without day-to-day involvement with players. Ideology is fine when club football permits an overhaul of personnel.

When Scotland switched to a defensive four in the closing stages of the Slovenia clash, players appeared generally confused. This was a bad look for Pocognoli, who has insisted he is “flexible” in a tactical sense and disputed having a touchline row with Robertson. Scott McTominay’s return for the next set of fixtures would provide an iota of hope, were it obvious where the Napoli man fits in. The setup as is will not maximise the abilities of McTominay, John McGinn, Ryan Christie and Billy Gilmour.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli consoles Billy Gilmour after Scotland’s feeble defeat at home against Slovenia on Tuesday. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

Didn’t fans want a revolution?

A reality is Scotland have qualified for three of the last four major tournaments. Noise directed towards Clarke underappreciated the scale of his work. That said, after seven years, Clarke’s tenure had run its course.

The obvious move at that point was to turn towards a coach who had succeeded in tournament football with a similarly sized nation. With the level of available talent dropping or ageing, there was also a requirement for pragmatism and realism. Instead, Scottish FA officials spoke of a data-led search for Clarke’s successor, which led them to a coach who had never managed in international football before. Trying to be too smart by half? This team was not fundamentally broken, it just needed to progress.

Nobody of sane mind should insist upon Scotland morphing into the Ajax team of the 1970’s. The baseline, created by Clarke, is now tournament participation. This summer’s World Cup was the latest example of how finals involvement positively alters attitudes within and outside Scottish football to an unparalleled level. That is the important thing. The rest is fluff.

There were 34,000 at Hampden for Slovenia’s visit; hardly disastrous in broader Nations League context but almost 20,000 short of capacity. The public are yet to buy into Pocognoli and the blue-sky vision sold by his employers.

How does Pocognoli handle Ben Gannon-Doak?

Some in Scotland would have us believe Gannon-Doak is the tartan equivalent of a young Ryan Giggs. The truth is that at 20 Gannon-Doak is a player who is lightly raced at club level and, at this point, looks unlikely to make a first-team impact at Bournemouth. He has searing pace and a directness that scares defenders, which is offset by woeful decision making. Whether these shortcomings can he improved upon very much remains to be seen.

What is clear is that Gannon-Doak cannot operate as a right wing-back for Scotland against credible opposition. Deploying him there also denies a start to Aaron Hickey, who is undeniably one of Scotland’s best players. Gannon-Doak is a winger (as are Josh McPake and Findlay Curtis). Pocognoli’s first-choice method does not involve wingers. Something has to give.

View image in fullscreen Ben Gannon-Doak, pictured holding off Slovenia’s Erik Janza, is not a wingback. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

What is the wider scenario that Pocognoli is part of?

The Scottish FA suddenly has a chief football officer in Craig Mulholland, and a head of strategy, operations and performance in Graeme Mathie. The latter was plucked from the Scottish second tier and the former was present in the dressing room during Scotland’s Nations League fixtures. The move to insert this level of middle management carrying wishy-washy job descriptions is strange, not least when neither of the individuals in question can provide working examples of markedly improving the big picture with an equivalent nation. Meanwhile, the new Scotland Under-21 manager, Tony Docherty, who is fielding teams in the same formation as Pocognoli, last took charge of a plummeting Ross County.

Scottish football in general has a reluctance to let others mark its homework. Those in high office, typically very pleased with themselves, fail to convince on umpteen levels. Scotland have to work far, far harder at sourcing and delivering resource for the men’s A team. Six starters against Slovenia were 30 or older. Clarke could be obstinate but there was no raft of exciting footballers that he chose to ignore.

There is no question of the Scottish FA becoming anxious towards Pocognoli. Indeed, as was the case with Clarke, they seem beholden to him. If this goes wrong, however, there will be significant questions to be answered about a chosen direction of travel.

Sports.title: Portuguese authorities took 83 days to tell Rui Pinto his witness protection was ending
Sports.content:
Portuguese authorities kept Rui Pinto in the dark for almost three months about their decision to end his status as a protected witness and notified the Manchester City whistleblower 10 days before it was due to expire, it can be revealed.

According to documents seen by the Guardian, the special security programmes commission (CPES), which oversees Portugal’s witness protection programme, met on 8 and 9 July to discuss Pinto’s case. It concluded that the threat level against him was low and that the special protection measures were no longer warranted.

Yet it was not until 30 September that Pinto, who has been a protected witness since 2020 after agreeing to grant Portuguese authorities access to millions of files gathered before his arrest, was informed of the decision – 83 days after it had been made.

With 10 days’ notice, Pinto was left with little time to address a number of immediate issues. He needs to find somewhere safe to live and establish a way of supporting himself in a new location, while avoiding contact with family members.

The Guardian contacted the CPES on two occasions seeking details of the criteria and evidence used to determine that Pinto’s protection should be withdrawn. On Wednesday, the commission was also asked to explain the 83-day gap between its decision and the notification. None of the inquiries received a response.

On 30 September, the day Pinto was informed his protected-witness status was coming to an end, the Premier League’s guilty verdict against City, which had been confirmed 24 hours earlier, was dominating headlines around the world. The authorities stood by the decision reached nearly three months earlier despite protestations from Pinto and his lawyers that he fears for his life.

Pinto entered Portugal’s protection programme after cooperating with the country’s justice authorities. His revelations have subsequently been used by judicial, tax and sporting authorities across Europe, including the Premier League’s investigation into City’s alleged financial irregularities. Pinto’s lawyers argue that the authorities should take into account his cooperation with the justice system and the continuing risks associated with his disclosures before ending his protection.

Mounting pressure appears to have prompted a rethink. Last Saturday Portugal’s justice minister, Rita Alarcão Júdice, was questioned by journalists about the decision. She said the authorities would review Pinto’s case and promised to respond by Saturday, the date on which his protection is due to end.

“I have received various requests and we are examining them very carefully,” Júdice said. “If there has been any irregularity, or if any procedure was not handled as it should have been, that will, of course, be taken into consideration.”

The Guardian understands that, as it first reported, Pinto remains willing to cooperate with British authorities in the City case and in other investigations stemming from his findings. He handed over millions of documents to investigators in France, which can now be shared with other nations – including the UK – under international cooperation and bilateral ties.

Pinto’s lawyer, Francisco Teixeira da Mota, told the Guardian an appeal against the decision would be filed this week. “The most shocking thing is the fact that he wasn’t heard before the decision was made,” he said. “It’s something that goes against the European court of human rights.”

In a press release last week, Pinto’s defence team called the decision “an act of state terrorism”. Their outrage has intensified after they learnedtheir client had been kept in the dark for almost three months. “It says a lot,” Da Mota added.

Sports.title: ‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plans
Sports.content:
It was on the Portman Road pitch, bathed in bright early May light while immersed in the relief and joy of a third promotion in five years, that Kieran McKenna realised the moment was right. The thought had flickered earlier in the season that this might be his final campaign at Ipswich, only to be pushed into the subconscious by the Championship’s remorseless grind. “But standing out there, I felt this was probably time,” he says of those moments after QPR had been swept aside and a return to the Premier League assured. “Another big victory, a full stadium, in front of my family and the fans. It was an amazing way to go out on a high.”

Five months later McKenna has no regrets about electing to cut things short while the going was so good. The golf bag lying outside his garage speaks of a man enjoying the break and, more pertinently, of something bigger. His son has recently become interested in the sport and sharing those moments with loved ones, whether out on the greens or spending part of the summer travelling along the East Anglian coastline in a camper van, were among the biggest reasons to pause a soaring career. At 40, McKenna had spent two decades immersed in coaching; it was time to appreciate life’s essentials while continuing professional development at his own speed.

He had, as usual, been linked with moves away but the idea of a voluntary career break was hard for many to fathom when the decision was finalised in June. “For people on the outside it’s maybe a bit more difficult,” he says. “But those who know my path and my values, the ones closest to me who know me really well, I think they understood why I wanted to step out and what the benefits were of having a period like this.”

Not everyone in football saw it that way: the phone has rung with proposals for his next move but McKenna says those overtures arrived “too soon, especially given the way I left Ipswich”. Leaving through the front door, a luxury rarely afforded, made him proud and there is no desperation to leap back into the fray. “I’m certainly in no rush,” he says. “I’m enjoying the time I’m having and hopefully an opportunity will come along that’s right. I have an idea what that would feel like but football doesn’t always follow your plan.”

Since early September he has dipped his toe back in. That has involved tuning back into the process of watching and assessing games, while travelling to spend time with Bayern Munich, the Wigan Warriors rugby team and Colorado Rapids, who are managed by his friend Matt Wells. He has been working on foreign languages, topping up an already competent level of Spanish. This week he is visiting clubs in Spain and, next Wednesday, he will begin work as a technical observer for Uefa when Shakhtar Donetsk play AEK Athens at Stamford Bridge. “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge,” he says.

View image in fullscreen McKenna basks in Ipswich’s promotion in May. ‘All we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them,’ he says. Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters

More than once McKenna repeats an assertion he made after promotion in May: that 2025-26 was the hardest of his four-and-a-half seasons at Ipswich, during which he masterminded a dizzying rise from League One to the top flight that marked him among football’s hottest managerial properties. The pressure was heightened last season: Ipswich had gone down and were expected to bounce back, even though the remarkably close-knit core who had propelled them through the divisions were drifting away. In effect, he took two different teams to the top.

“You can see how it could really have gone in two distinct directions,” he says, making a comparison with the fall Luton experienced after a brief reacquaintance with the elite. “We had the feeling internally that if we didn’t work really hard to pull everyone together then it could have gone in a negative way.”

McKenna pulled them over the line and reached the end of his own journey. Along the way he had come close to departing more than once but jumping ship earlier would have jarred. “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really,” he says. “But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.”

The hardest aspect of his final day, he explains, was looking down a camera and addressing the supporters with a five-minute speech in which he did not attempt to suppress his emotion. He reels off a list of coaching staff and other colleagues with whom the goodbyes were touching, meaningful, joyful. Many of the friendships, particularly with members of the “really, really special team” that he led to those successive promotions, will be lifelong. The night before this interview, he spent most of a journey back from London speaking to one of them.

View image in fullscreen Kieran McKenna acclimatising to the Premier League in 2024. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

He laughs off the idea he would have relished getting his hands on the £200m summer transfer spend – not to mention a new training ground whose design he influenced – that appears to have given his successor, Gary O’Neil, a better shot at survival. If anything, he suggests, it shows the club have begun their own new chapter. McKenna also emphasises the thought of potential reputational damage from a second relegation did not factor into his decision to quit. “It wasn’t about the thought of a worst-case scenario or what could go wrong,” he says.

It was about prioritising life where we meet, in the family’s home a brisk half-hour walk from Portman Road. He and his wife chose to stay in Ipswich, where their two children attend school, having become more than mere itinerants passing through. It so happens Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson kept homes nearby after moving upwards. McKenna has hero status here too, in these unassuming yet football-crazed surroundings. Although he keeps a low profile and locations for socialising are chosen judiciously, the overwhelming affection of a town and county often rear up.

“Everyone is respectful; all we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them, their family and their friends, and wishing me the best,” he says. “Moving down here together, going all in, making ourselves part of this community, it’s been another of the really positive things. It’s a little bit different living in the area where you were managing but it’s the right thing for us at this time.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Has muscle memory ever taken him on an early-morning drive to the training ground? “You’d think it might, but it’s just a different life. You’re not setting the alarm for 5.30am and driving there in the dark. You’re getting up with the kids and having breakfast with them, and you’re around when they go to bed. Although the geography is the same, the life is different.”

He does not think such a heady half-decade, in which a talent honed at Tottenham and Manchester United blossomed gloriously, has changed a grounded personality honed in rural County Fermanagh. “I probably feel about 20 years older,” he says. “But my friends at home were telling me in the summer that I haven’t changed since I was 10. I couldn’t have arrived at Ipswich with a better background as a coach but, on the other hand, if you’d given me a list of the things I’d have to deal with in the next five years I really wouldn’t have believed it. After going through so many things you’re wiser for the experience.”

Nonetheless the fact remains: taking a breather when the world is your oyster feels vanishingly rare in football management. Maybe everyone should do it. “But what’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago,” he says. “It’s been a massive body of work. You leave United, pick your bags up, get in the car and five-and-a-half hours later you’re in Ipswich. At 35 you’re leaving your family behind, checking into a hotel 10 days before Christmas; you absolutely throw yourself into the job for the next four and a half years and the family do the same. I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role.”

View image in fullscreen McKenna says his two decades in coaching have taken a toll. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

So what would that next iteration of McKenna’s career look like, in a perfect world? He has been linked with any potential vacancies at Celtic and his old employers Spurs; his name will be circling once the season’s sackings start, although Ipswich will be owed a sizeable fee for any role he takes this year.

“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games,” he says. “But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable. It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.”

The chance will surely arise soon; it does not take a giant leap to imagine McKenna in a Champions League dugout in the next few years if the stars align. Until then the self-growth will continue and there will always be dispatches from Portman Road, where his brother and children are regulars. McKenna would rather look forward and will not beat that path for now. “I think that’ll be some way down the line,” he says. “They’re cracking on with the season. There’s nothing that can lessen my pride and love for everything we’ve been through. Hopefully I’ll be back in the stadium as an old hand, and some of the people will remember the times we had.”

They are unlikely to forget; McKenna’s aim is that, by then, at least one other set of supporters will have felt the magic too.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo: the extraordinary eight points he says Jorge Jesus agreed to make
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on Tuesday that the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, had agreed to make eight points relating to him in a press conference before the team’s game in Denmark last week.

Ronaldo said he had approved a document listing the points after a video meeting involving him, Jesus, his adviser Tiago Craveiro and his club Al-Nassr’s sporting director, Simão Coutinho.

The meeting, according to Ronaldo, was at “the coach’s request” and he said the document was then “delivered to the coach, as he had requested”.

Ronaldo said Jesus’s failure to make the points in the press conference constituted “the second time he had broken his word to me” and that he then “decided to leave the camp without waiting for any further breach of word”.

Ronaldo’s statement included reference to his failure to salute Portugal’s fans after the game in Norway during which he warmed up extensively but was not brought on. He said:

“The notes I validated were the following: ‘I think it is important, also because it is the truth, to clarify a few things before talking about Denmark:

1. I myself, and no one else, proposed to Cristiano a plan for him this sporting season with the national team. It was a long and very good conversation.

2. I know how much he lives and loves the national team and the weight he has in the world, and even more the weight and the positive influence he has had on the national team for 24 consecutive years.

3. The plan I proposed to Cristiano was accepted.

4. He never questioned my options. He was exemplary, loyal and professional.

5. The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

6. I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.

7. To close the subject: I want Cristiano in the national team. In fact I do not want him a little, I want him a lot. Fortunately he also believes in me. He believed at Al-Nassr and he does here as well.

8. About not greeting the fans. We have already spoken about that. Someone who has played more than 230 matches for the national team does not receive lessons from me on love for Portugal. It was a moment of frustration that erases nothing. He is the player who gives the most autographs, takes the most selfies, and shows the most affection to the fans. Let us not invent problems where they do not exist. When we are not happy we react.”

Ronaldo’s statement then said: “That was all. None of these notes, therefore, said that the coach should even apologise to me.”

Reflecting on Jesus’s conduct in the press conference Ronaldo said: “I heard expressions and an aggressiveness that I do not believe I deserved, an attitude of ‘I want, I can and I command’ that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi describes ending Argentina career as his ‘saddest day’ in football
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the “saddest day of my career” after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin.

Messi, who scored and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and teammates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina.

“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the stadium “Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here.

“Not coming any more is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”

Messi said that returning to the Monumental – where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup – was bittersweet. “Now I’m here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you. But now I’ll be on that side [with the fans], supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united.”

View image in fullscreen Drones create the shape of Lionel Messi above the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires. Photograph: Tobias Skarlovnik/Getty Images

Messi said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where they battled through to the final only to lose to Spain.

He said the emotional rollercoaster of that tournament – which included a 2-1 defeat of Argentina’s bitter rivals England in the semi-final – had taken a toll. “Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again. In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big.

“We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close.”

Sports.title: Why are so many British footballers playing in Serie A?
Sports.content:
What do Jimmy Greaves, Ray Wilkins, David Beckham, Paul Gascoigne and Kyle Walker have in common? They all made more than 50 appearances for England as well as playing for Italian clubs. While they are household names, the first Englishman to represent an Italian club is less familiar.

Former soldier Charles Adcock moved to Padova just after the second world war having been spotted playing for the British army. By a strange quirk of fate Adcock never played league football in his own country. After spending a handful of years in Italy, he returned to England in 1953 where he played for non-league Peterborough United.

View image in fullscreen Charles Adcock in Padova colours.

In the 80 years after Adcock’s move, more than 50 English players have played in Serie A. There are more English players with Italian clubs this season than ever before. Of the 21 British players with Italian clubs, the majority are English, led by internationals such as John Stones and Djed Spence who moved to Inter after the World Cup. So, why the sudden influx of players from England?

There was a wave of high-profile English players in Serie A in the 1980s, such as the first £1m player, Trevor Francis, who joined Sampdoria in 1982. He came up against Mark Hateley and Wilkins, who both spent three seasons at Milan in the mid-1980s.

View image in fullscreen Trevor Francis takes on Diego Maradona while playing for Sampdoria against Napoli. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Gascoigne was the big English star in Italy in the 1990s and he was joined by journeymen such as Franz Carr and Danny Dichio. At any time throughout those two decades, only a handful of Englishmen played in Serie A compared to the 15 who are now with Italian clubs.

The fortunes of those English émigrés were followed by fans back home on Gazzetta Football Italia, hosted by James Richardson. Nowadays, the main coverage of Serie A is on TNT, headed up by commentator Adam Summerton.

View image in fullscreen Mark Hateley and Ray Wilkins playing for Milan in 1984. Photograph: David Cannon/Getty Images

“It’s multifaceted,” says Summerton of the British invasion. “It starts with the trailblazers. Someone like Liam Henderson, who’s been in Italy since 2018. Chris Smalling was another in 2019.” Smalling spent five years at Roma and was the player of the match when they won the inaugural Conference League final in 2022 under José Mourinho.

“Italian sporting directors have said how they really value the hard work, professionalism and tenacity of Scottish players in particular,” Summerton says. “They have also developed a reputation for being good in the dressing room – that’s really appealing when you’re building a team.”

View image in fullscreen The Scottish midfielder Liam Henderson has played for Hellas Verona, Empoli, Lecce, Palermo and Sampdoria. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images

Summerton also believes attitudes have changed to British players. The new intake are more rounded characters who actively enjoy the different culture. “The world has become a smaller place, and the modern player seems more likely to see opportunity rather than difficulty in the challenges that come with playing abroad. Players often talk about becoming more mature and more rounded for the experience, both as people and players,” Summerton says.

“Many are aiming to embrace culture, language and even food. Scott McTominay’s appreciation of Neapolitan tomatoes has become well-known. The majority are having good experiences, that will naturally lead to others wanting to try it too.”

Scottish players have improved the perception of British football in Italy. Lewis Ferguson, who moved to Bologna in 2022, was voted Serie A midfielder of the season in 2023-24 and was the club’s captain when they beat Milan in the Coppa Italia final last year. Following on from Ferguson’s success, McTominay joined Napoli and won the Serie A player of the season award as the club won the league title.

Another factor is that the players appreciate the rich traditions of Italian football. “Fikayo Tomori has talked about looking at the Milan badge on his tracksuit every day and taking such pride playing for the great Milan,” Summerton says. Tomori also made a concerted effort to learn the language and was soon conducting interviews in Italian after joining the club in 2020. This runs against the notion that British players are reluctant to assimilate.

View image in fullscreen Napoli fans fly a Scott McTominay flag in the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters

Furthermore, coaching at Premier League academies has advanced to the extent that they are producing technically adept players who suit Serie A. One example is Omari Hutchinson, who was part of Chelsea’s academy and has just moved to Milan on loan from Nottingham Forest.

Hutchinson’s move also points to the more prosaic issue of the economic imbalance between the Premier League and its European counterparts. “Good players who might be on the fringes of a Premier League side see Italy as a chance to be a more important player in a big league with a big-name club,” Summerton says.

View image in fullscreen Curtis Jones joined Inter from Liverpool in the summer. Photograph: Chris Ricco/Getty Images

The English invasion is best summed up by Inter, who signed Curtis Jones from Liverpool this summer to join Spence and Stones. Prior to their arrival, the club had only signed three English players in their history: Gerry Hitchens in 1961, Paul Ince in 1995 and Ashley Young in 2020. Stones swapped Manchester for Milan in the summer and his delight at joining such a football institution as Inter was clear. “I have so many emotions. I’m really happy, proud and excited. I couldn’t imagine a better place to do it.”

Who does Summerton think will make the best impression this season? “The early signs from Jones are good,” he says. “He’s a profile of player that Cristian Chivu, the Inter coach, really wanted.” His performance for Liverpool against Inter in the Champions League last season sowed the seed.

View image in fullscreen Trevoh Chalobah is playing in the Champions League for Como this season. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Uefa/Getty Images

“I’m also really excited for Trevoh Chalobah,” says Summerton. “He’s walked into one of the most exciting projects in world football right now at Como. Cesc Fàbregas is doing tremendous work there. He has started the season really well and they are already strong defensively.”

Chalobah knows what to expect from Fàbregas, having trained together at Chelsea. “I remember how demanding he was with the younger players,” says the centre-back. “I know him really well.” Working with a legend of the game at an ambitious club is appealing for Chalobah. And, as Summerton points out: “He gets to live next to Lake Como and play Champions League football too. There’s a lot to like.”

Sports.title: Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World Cup
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month.

The Guardian revealed last week that the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup is set to be awarded to the US, with transatlantic travel to cause additional problems for European sides, while the proposed dates of 5-30 January will clash directly with the WSL.

Fifa has yet to confirm the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup but the Guardian has learned Arsenal are guaranteed to be involved as 2025 Champions League winners with Chelsea likely to join them, although they would lose their place if Manchester City win this season’s Champions League. Based on this season’s schedule, an extended run in the Club World Cup would mean the two English clubs miss up to four WSL match weeks plus the fourth round of the FA Cup, playing havoc with the fixture list and causing major congestion at the end of the season.

Uefa will be granted places for six clubs – five to qualify automatically and one to take part in a six-team qualifier before the tournament, with the three highest-ranked clubs joining 13 automatic qualifiers to form a 16-team competition. While the process has still to be ratified by the Fifa council, it is understood Uefa’s spots will be given to the Champions League winners between 2023 and 2027 – currently double champions Barcelona and Arsenal, with this season’s title still up for grabs – topped up by the highest-ranked clubs in Uefa’s Champions League coefficient table.

Chelsea are currently third in Uefa’s coefficient table for the current four-year cycle, behind Barcelona and Lyon with a 17-point lead over fourth-placed Bayern Munich, and cannot be caught. Based on the current rankings, Bayern and Wolfsburg are next in line to qualify, although the latter have not qualified for this season’s Champions League and will not accumulate additional points, so are likely to be overhauled by Real Madrid or Paris Saint-Germain. Fifa plans to cap the number of participants from each country at two, so City winning the Champions League would cost Chelsea their place.

The WSL declined to comment on the issue as they have yet to be told of Fifa’s plans for the tournament, but sources conceded its impact is likely to prove challenging. The WSL has a winter break, which is scheduled for 21 December to 10 January this season, and although that could be pushed back slightly, aligning it with the Club World Cup is not viewed as practical due to the congested calendar.

As well as creating a lopsided season, moving the winter break would result in a backlog of WSL fixtures during the period when the Champions League knockout stage begins at the beginning of February. The issue of fixture congestion is a growing area of concern in the women’s game and 2028 will be particularly problematic due to the Olympic football tournament taking place in Los Angeles in August, just before the start of the European domestic season.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has expanded women’s football to 16 nations at the 2028 Games, and unlike the men’s version which is restricted to players under 23 with three overage exceptions, senior internationals are permitted to take part.

Fifa’s imposition of the Club World Cup in the middle of the European season has exacerbated the problem, and earlier this year European Leagues, a lobby group, extended their legal complaint to the European Commission about the world governing body’s alleged “abuse of power and dominant position” to include the women’s game.

Sports.title: AI predicts when Harry Kane will hit England century to end all debates
Sports.content:
AI predicts when Harry Kane will hit England century to end all debates

Harry Kane could become the first Englishman to reach 100 international goals as early as next year.

That is according to Google's AI assistant, Gemini, after he took his tally to 91 this week and found himself heralded as the greatest England player of all time.

4 AI has predicted when Kane could reach 100 goals for England Credit: Getty

Kane's brace in England's 3-0 home win over the Czech Republic on Tuesday extended his lead as the Three Lions' all-time top scorer.

Meanwhile, he also equalled Peter Shilton's record number of caps by making his 125th senior international appearance.

The 33-year-old will now be aiming to become only the fourth men's footballer ever to score a century of goals for his country.

Kane currently sits seventh on the all-time rankings, but nine more goals would see him only trail Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Iran legend Ali Daei.

When could Kane reach 100 England goals?

However, just how soon could he hope to reach 100 goals for England?

Gemini has crunched the numbers across both his entire international career and recent form for the Three Lions to predict an answer.

Since scoring on his debut against Lithuania in 2015, Kane has scored at a rate of 0.73 goals per game for England.

In recent years, though, his form in competitive matches has been even more impressive.

Across matches in the World Cup, Euros, Nations League and tournament qualifiers since 2024, he has scored around 0.80 to 0.85 goals per game.

As a result, Kane is predicted to need between 10 and 13 matches to score the nine goals needed to reach a century for England.

4 Kane reached 91 international goals with a brace against the Czech Republic Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Based on his career scoring rate, he is expected to do so in the summer of 2028, with 12 to 13 matches required.

This could see Kane bring up the tally at Euro 2028, which England will co-host with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

He could also do so in the lead up to the tournament, with Thomas Tuchel's side likely to play multiple warm-up matches.

However, Kane will make history even sooner if he can maintain his recent scoring form.

If he scores at a rate of 0.85 goals per game, the Bayern Munich striker will need just 10 to 11 matches to reach 100 goals.

This would see him do so in late 2027 during England's qualifying campaign for Euro 2028.

4 Kane has scored at a rate of 0.73 goals per game for England Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

It would require Kane to play every match until he achieves the feat, though.

Kane has featured in all but one of the Three Lions' last 14 matches, starting all 13 of those he has been a part of.

Meanwhile, he has scored six goals in four matches during the latest international break.

What's next for England?

England fans will be hoping that form can continue when England conclude their Nations League campaign in November.

Matches against Croatia and Spain look set to be followed by the knockout stages in March.

If England win their two-legged quarter-final tie, they would face a further two matches during June's Nations League Finals.

4 Kane's form since the start of 2024 for England could see him reach his century next year Credit: PA

Tuchel's men are then set to begin their Euro 2028 qualifying campaign in September 2027, with six matches between then and November next year.

Either the play-offs or a pair of friendly matches will then follow in March 2028 prior to the finals later in the summer.

Sports.title: When is Enzo Maresca’s Man City press conference? Follow guilty verdict fallout on talkSPORT
Sports.content:
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca will face the press this week for the first time since the club were found guilty on all 115 charges.

The news broke during the international break, as the Premier League released a 40-page statement that disclosed the Citizens won none of their charges.

3 There is now a cloud over Man City until the appeal process concludes Credit: Getty

One major finding from the report has declared that City inflated their financial position by over £900million between the period of 2009 to 2018.

The eight-time champions of the league continue to protest their innocence and have appealed the decision.

However, that won't stop the media wanting to ask the City boss questions about the brutal reality that lies ahead.

Ahead of Sunday's trip to Liverpool, Maresca will finally get the opportunity to speak to his players all together on Thursday after they have returned from international duty.

Many players will also want to speak to chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in order to provide security on their futures at the club.

When is Enzo Maresca's first press conference?

The press conference for Liverpool vs Man City will take place on Friday, October 9.

A time is yet to be confirmed but it is likely to take place in the morning.

This will mark the first time any member of the City hierarchy has answered questions and spoken publicly since the verdict was announced.

talkSPORT will be across the breaking news on talkSPORT.com with the live blog.

3 Guardiola''s Premier League legacy is being questioned by fans following City's guilty verdict Credit: AFP

We will be reacting live to any bombshell statements from the Man City boss.

If you want to watch along live, it will be on mancity.com and their official website.

Pep Guardiola was defensive after the charges dropped in February 2023, and has continued not to hold back regarding the subject throughout the years.

The Catalan originally revealed his frustration after news broke, and said: "My first thought is that we are already being condemned. What has happened this week after Monday is the same as what happened with [the] UEFA [case, in which Man City had a two-year ban from European football overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport].

"With UEFA we were condemned. We had already accusations, now we have just charges.Why should in that situation, when they told me before they defend the accusation from UEFA.

"The club proved we were completely innocent, why should we not think right now when we are being condemned from charges and suggestions?"

He also called out other Premier League clubs, saying: "You have to understand that between 19 teams of the Premier League is accusing us without the latest opportunity to defend and the words of my chairman, my CEO, my people explain everything during these three or four years, you know exactly on what side I am."

He added: "Another side I would say we are lucky we live in a marvellous country where we have a society where everyone is innocent until proven guilty. We didn't have this opportunity. We are already sentenced and tough. What is going to happen I don't know.

"Personally, I am happy we are here. Like UEFA, it happens, we have the chance to defend. I think we have good lawyers, but we can't say UEFA had bad, bad lawyers.

3 Man City owners and executives have continued to plea their innocence Credit: Getty

"I think the Premier League, supported by 19 teams to put it out for the Premier League, will have good lawyers too to defend their position like we're going to defend our position. I would have loved to wait and see and time will dictate what's going to happen.

"Just in case we are not innocent we will accept what the judge in the Premier League decides, but what happens if in the same situation that UEFA happened we are innocent, what happens to restore or pay back our damage?"

Many City fans will be looking at Maresca to see how they should react to the news.

Sports.title: Piers Morgan and Simon Jordan in heated clash over who is to blame for Cristiano Ronaldo saga
Sports.content:
Piers Morgan and Simon Jordan in heated clash over who is to blame for Cristiano Ronaldo saga

A debate over Cristiano Ronaldo's ongoing Portugal feud descended into a clash live on talkSPORT on Wednesday.

Piers Morgan joined White & Jordan to discuss the fallout from the veteran forward's latest saga.



3 Ronaldo's bombshell statement caused a heated debate in the talkSPORT studio Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

However, his appearance on the show included a heated back-and-forth with talkSPORT co-host Simon Jordan over where the blame lies in the ongoing debacle.

It comes after Ronaldo released a bombshell statement on Tuesday, having left the national team squad early.

The 41-year-old departed following last week's win over Norway in Oslo.



Ronaldo had been an unused substitute, but has now claimed he had been told pre-match that he would play 30 minutes off of the bench.

As a result, he has accused manager Jorge Jesus of breaking promises made to him regarding the fixture.



The five-time Ballon d'Or winner is Portugal's all-time leading scorer and appearance maker with 146 goals in 234 caps.

Who is to blame in Ronaldo saga?

However, Morgan and Jordan were unable to agree on whether Ronaldo is in part to blame for the saga.



Discussing whether he was right to release his statement, Jordan asked: "I know you work on the premise everything is a bleeding filibuster, but other people can have an opinion.

"In your objective, rounded mind, is there a possibility that the common denominator of fallouts might be some of Ronaldo's behaviour?

"Is there a possibility in your balanced, unsure, kissing Ronaldo's backside mentality?"

3 Morgan clashed with Jordan over whether Ronaldo is partly to blame for his Portugal exit Credit: TalkTV



As Morgan answered 'no', the talkSPORT co-host continued: "In your wide experiences of managing players and understanding the dynamics behind the scenes, you can't even see beyond the end of your nose that there might be a common denominator when problems occur. That might be Ronaldo's behaviour."

In response, Morgan quipped: "I’ve just tapped in while we’re talking, ‘Did Simon Jordan ever play football?"

Jordan hit back, though, with the former Crystal Palace chairman cheekily replying: "I owned a football club and dealt with players, you wally.

"What’s the matter with you? Do better. You’re a good journalist, at times."



The broadcaster was not finished, though, adding: "Simon Jordan was a junior footballer as a youth.

"He never played professional football because he wasn't good enough."

3 Morgan has defended his close friend Ronaldo amid his ongoing Portugal saga Credit: Getty Images - Getty

Morgan 'proud' of Ronaldo

Morgan, who regards Ronaldo as a close friend, had earlier in the show defended his stance on the matter.



The Football Uncensored host explained: "I'm proud of him because he stood up for himself.

"I think in life you have to stand up for yourself not only when you're disrespected, but when your boss lies to you.

"He's obviously reaching the end of his career, he's aware of his legacy and he wants to go out properly.

"The one thing in all the years I've known him is, you've got to be a straight dealer with him and you've got to respect him.



"It's never about money or fame or ego. But actually the key component to his make-up is respect and honesty.

"Even though it's a long statement, the reason I liked it was because he laid out in painstaking detail exactly what went on there."

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta lands huge pay rise as Arsenal contract extension is confirmed
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has penned a lucrative new long-term contract until 2030 to remain as Arsenal boss.

The Spaniard, who has been in charge since December 2019, had only been tied down until the end of the 2026/27 season.



3 Arteta has already guided Arsenal to silverware this season in the form of the Community Shield

talkSPORT revealed in May how talks to extend the 44-year-old's stay were set to take place in the summer after Arteta guided the club to a first Premier League title in 22 years.

And we then told you last month how terms on a new deal had been thrashed out, with an announcement expected during the international break.

That has now been confirmed by the Gunners, who are looking to scoop back-to-back Premier League titles for the first time in their history this season.



What has Mikel Arteta said about extending his stay?

Expressing his delight, Arteta told Arsenal's media team: "It's a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal.

"This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue.



“We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

“I'm extremely grateful to Stan and Josh for their trust and support, and feel honoured to be leading this club through such a special period in its 140-year history.



“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”

How much is Arteta's new contract worth?

Following Pep Guardiola's exit at Manchester City, Arteta was already the highest-paid manager in the division - earning around £10million-a-year.

And that is now believed to have been increased to £15m-a-year - a reward for ending 22 years of hurt.

3 Arteta's Arsenal side have won four of their opening five Premier League games, leaving them second in the table Credit: AFP



Mikel Arteta's Arsenal managerial stats Games - 361

Wins - 220

Draws - 67

Losses - 74

Premier League title - x1

FA Cup - x1

Community Shield - x3

Arteta's extension will take him to over ten years at the Emirates, bringing his association with the club to nearly 20 years.

He first joined as a player from Everton in 2011, before succeeding Thomas Vermaelen as captain in 2014, and then retiring at the club two years later.

What has been said about Arteta's new deal?

Bukayo Saka has already let slip that Arteta had agreed a new deal when speaking to talkSPORT’s England correspondent Faye Carruthers ahead of the Three Lions' Nations League defeat to Spain.

Lauding Arteta, the Hale End graduate said: “Yeah, a special manager and very important to the club.



“Hence why they gave him a new deal, because he deserves it.

“And yeah, he’s really transformed the club and got everyone dreaming again.

3 Saka has won the Premier League, FA Cup and three Community Shields under Arteta's tutelage Credit: Getty

“So, credit to him, he deserves it and I’m happy for him.”

Arsenal's club-record signing Declan Rice could soon follow Arteta's suit, with talkSPORT understanding that the midfielder is in talks to extend his stay until 2031.

He would become the latest Arsenal star to commit their future to the club.



Saka, William Saliba, Gabriel Magalhaes and Myles Lewis-Skelly all penned new long-term contracts at Arsenal in the last year.

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel not strong enough to play in the Premier League, says ex-Man United player
Sports.content:
JJ Gabriel not strong enough to play in the Premier League, says ex-Man United player

Phil Bardsley believes JJ Gabriel is not yet ready for the Premier League despite the player demanding first-team minutes.

The Manchester United wonderkid has asked to leave the club with European giants, including Bayern Munich, know to be interested.



3 Gabriel is yet to make a senior appearance for United, but is one of the most highly-regarded talents in the country Credit: Getty

The teenager turned 16 on Tuesday which allows him to depart Old Trafford and sign for clubs abroad following his demand to leave last month.

There has also been contact with Real Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain, and Barcelona.

Gabriel has not trained at Carrington since he walked out ahead of their Carabao Cup fixture with Brighton on September 16, when the youngster was due to receive his first team debut.



This was prior to his representatives demanding United should cancel his registration over a row about his playing time.

It has been reported that the youngster's representatives demanded that the teenager played at least 20 minutes in games against Sabah FK, Brighton and Bournemouth before beginning talks about signing a scholarship.



However, former Man United defender Bardsley believes the 16-year-old isn't ready for the physicality of the Premier League.

He told talkSPORT: "From the outside, physically I don't think he's ready to be thrown in at the level yet. I think from years gone by, you look at players who have physically developed...



"You have Rooney, for instance, who was ready to go and play at that age.

"Look at the boy at the minute, his abilities are obviously there, he's an outstanding talent and hopefully goes on to be a great player.

3 Wayne Rooney was just 16 years and 360 days old when he announced himself with a sensational goal for Everton against Arsenal Credit: Times Newspapers Ltd

"But I think the timing's a bit off, the way things are at the club and the way it came out.



"But I believe it's been orchestrated by agents, parents, and pushing for these things when you're at such a delicate age and you're in a transition into men's football. I think you need to be patient."

Wayne Rooney did it

Rooney himself admitted he was not shocked that Gabriel was wanting to leave Old Trafford.

Speaking to talkSPORT, the United legend said: "With the JJ situation, I've seen him growing up, he's been in [my son] Kai's team, and I think, if I'm being honest, everyone has seen it coming.

"There's been a desire to maybe play abroad, maybe in Spain. We have to remember he's 15, he's still a kid. That's a lot of pressure and you hope that the decisions are being made for the right reasons.



"I actually listened to Michael Carrick talk about it after the Brighton game and I thought he spoke really well.

3 Gabriel has been included in United's first-team squad photo Credit: Getty

"It's such a big story with everything that's going on at Man United that you forget there's a kid involved here."

Even the teenager has made it clear he doesn't want to stay in England, as talkSPORT understands he rejected Chelsea's interest.



Despite several attempts by the Red Devils to reconcile the situation, Gabriel’s family are seemingly intent on him leaving Carrington.

Sources close to the player believe Gabriel has an Irish passport, meaning he is eligible to join a club in the European Union.

Real Madrid and Barcelona are understood to be leading the race to sign the England Under-17 international, while Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich are also keen.
