The participants specifically cited oil spills, gas flaring, contamination of land and water, destruction of farming and fishing livelihoods and threats to human health in the Niger Delta as examples of accountability challenges facing communities affected by corporate activities.

They said similar challenges were evident in major projects and extractive industries across Uganda, Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Chad, Cameroon and Tunisia.

The participants said communities affected by corporate activities are often unable to obtain effective justice because companies operate through parent companies, subsidiaries, contractors, subcontractors, financiers and other business relationships spread across several countries.

The group called for an internationally legally binding instrument that would impose enforceable human rights and environmental obligations on transnational corporations and other business enterprises.

They also demanded the establishment of an International Tribunal on Human Rights and Transnational Corporations to hear cases involving companies engaged in business activities of a transnational character.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Niger Delta as evidence of accountability gap

The convergence said the Niger Delta experience shows why corporate accountability could not be left solely to national legal systems.

For decades, oil-producing communities in the region have complained about pollution and environmental degradation associated with oil exploration and production, while efforts to obtain compensation, remediation and other forms of redress have often involved lengthy legal and regulatory processes.

The participants said such challenges were compounded when corporate ownership, decision-making, financing and operations crossed national borders.

They identified information asymmetry, weak domestic enforcement, high litigation costs, inadequate access to evidence, complex corporate structures and jurisdictional barriers as major obstacles confronting affected communities.

“Corporate accountability cannot depend solely on voluntary commitments or the effectiveness of individual national legal systems,” the groups said in their communiqué.

They explained that national laws remain essential but cannot, on their own, adequately regulate corporations whose ownership, financing, supply chains and decision-making extend across multiple jurisdictions.

The convergence was moderated by Maimoni Ubrei-Joe, a climate justice campaigner at the Community Development Advocacy Foundation and Environmental Defenders Network.

Volahery Andriamanantenasoa of CONCRET-S/Human Rights, Madagascar; Farai Magwuwu of the Centre for Natural Resources Governance, Zimbabwe; Ahmed Elseidi of the Egyptian Foundation for Environmental Rights; Zaki Mamdo of the StopACOP Coalition, Kenya; and Constance Meju of AmazonaAfrica Magazine, Nigeria, participated as speakers.

Other African cases

The participants said the accountability problems exposed in the Niger Delta were also reflected in other parts of Africa.

They cited the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project in Uganda and Tanzania in relation to land acquisition, disputed compensation, livelihood impacts and environmental concerns.

The project, they said, also exposed the difficulty of determining responsibility where corporate ownership, financing and business relationships extend beyond the countries where affected communities live.

Concerns involving Indigenous and local communities in Tanzania, including Loliondo, were cited as examples of the need to protect land rights, ensure meaningful participation and provide effective remedies where commercial or conservation-related activities affect territories, resources and livelihoods.

In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the group referred to cobalt and copper supply chains and concerns over forced evictions, destruction of homes and agricultural land and inadequate compensation.

They warned that the global transition to clean energy must not reproduce the extractive practices that have historically harmed African communities.

The Marikana tragedy in South Africa was also cited in connection with workers’ rights, freedom of association, safe working conditions and corporate accountability.

The Chad-Cameroon pipeline was presented as another example of the difficulty of assigning responsibility in cross-border projects involving governments, corporations, contractors, financiers and international institutions.

Experiences in phosphate-producing regions of Tunisia were similarly cited in relation to environmental degradation, economic inequality, labour rights and civic freedoms.

What the group wants

The CSOs called for mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence covering corporations’ operations and business relationships.

They said companies should be required to identify, prevent, mitigate and address actual and potential human rights and environmental impacts, with meaningful consultation and participation by affected communities and workers.

They said the proposed treaty should also provide for civil and administrative liability and, where applicable, criminal liability for corporations and responsible individuals involved in human rights violations.

The group called for parent-company and corporate-group responsibility where abuses occur through subsidiaries, contractors, subcontractors, joint ventures or other business relationships when a parent company exercises control, direction, major influence or other relevant forms of responsibility.

They also want corporate legal structures prevented from being used to frustrate victims’ access to justice.

The group said victims should have access to courts and other effective remedy mechanisms regardless of where the relevant corporate decision-making or ownership is located.

They called for measures to address excessive litigation costs, judicial delays, inadequate legal assistance, limited access to evidence, information asymmetry, jurisdictional barriers and difficulties enforcing judgments across borders.

Where harm occurs, they said remedies should include, where appropriate, restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction, guarantees of non-repetition and environmental restoration.

Defenders, communities need protection

The convergence also called for stronger protection for environmental defenders, human rights defenders, journalists, trade unionists and community leaders who expose corporate abuses.

It said such individuals and groups should be protected against intimidation, violence, harassment, criminalisation and retaliation.

The group demanded meaningful participation by indigenous peoples and affected communities in decisions concerning projects that could affect their lands, territories, resources, cultures and livelihoods.

Africa urged to speak with one voice

The organisations called on African governments to strengthen national laws regulating transnational corporations and ensure effective enforcement of environmental, labour and human rights standards.

They urged governments to strengthen the independence, resources and technical capacity of regulatory agencies and improve transparency around corporate ownership, contracts and beneficial ownership.

Energy transition warning

The group warned that the global shift towards renewable energy and low-carbon development should not create a new cycle of extraction and environmental injustice in Africa.

They said the transition must respect human rights and should not reproduce extractive patterns that disproportionately harm African communities.

The communiqué, adopted on 7 October, is intended to serve as a collective contribution to the United Nations treaty process and an advocacy instrument for African governments, treaty negotiators, UN institutions, civil society organisations and other stakeholders.

It was endorsed by the Community Development Advocacy Foundation, Neferok Development Initiative, Renevlyn Development Initiative, Environmental Defenders Network, African Centre for Environmental and Rural Development, FIDEP Foundation, African people and participating affected communities.

World.title: Plateau develops five-year plan as HIV donor funding declines
World.content:
The Plateau State Government and health stakeholders are developing a five-year transition plan to sustain HIV prevention, treatment and care as international donor funding for HIV programmes in Nigeria declines.

Ibinibo Chukwuemeka, Director of Health Systems Strengthening at APIN Public Health Initiatives, said the changing funding landscape would require greater government ownership and stronger measures to sustain HIV services as donor support winds down, according to a report by the Africa Independent Television (AIT) on Wednesday.

The AIDS Prevention Initiative in Nigeria, now known as APIN Public Health Initiatives, has supported HIV prevention, treatment and care in Plateau State for about 25 years.

APIN says its programmes have expanded HIV treatment access to rural and peri-urban communities, including through primary healthcare facilities.

The proposed five-year framework is expected to guide the state in assuming greater responsibility for financing and coordinating HIV services while protecting gains recorded in prevention, testing, treatment and care.

Health officials, representatives of relevant government ministries and other stakeholders are working on strategies to mitigate the impact of the anticipated reduction in donor support and prevent disruption of services for people living with HIV.

Among the measures under consideration is the integration of HIV and AIDS services into the Plateau State Health Insurance Scheme.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Stakeholders are also exploring local sources of antiretroviral drugs to help ensure uninterrupted access to treatment as external funding declines.

The proposed transition framework would provide a roadmap for sustaining HIV interventions and clarifying the responsibilities of the state government and other stakeholders in financing and delivering essential services.

The development comes amid a broader shift in Nigeria’s HIV response towards greater domestic financing and government ownership.

In June, the Federal Government launched the National HIV and AIDS Strategic Plan 2026–2030, which prioritises domestic financing, expansion of health insurance and integration of HIV services into the broader healthcare system as the country seeks to reduce dependence on donor-supported interventions.

The need for alternative financing has become more pressing as international support for HIV programmes declines.

Nigeria’s existing national HIV financing framework has also identified locally produced antiretroviral drugs and increased government investment as potential ways of reducing the country’s funding vulnerability.

Plateau has previously taken steps towards greater domestic ownership of its HIV response.

READ ALSO: Body with parts removed found near Plateau market

At the state’s 2025 World AIDS Day commemoration, officials disclosed that 51,370 people were living with HIV in the state as of September 2025, while 47,056 adults and 1,835 children were receiving antiretroviral therapy.

The state’s HIV response recorded 2,786 new infections and 460 HIV-related deaths in 2024, according to figures presented by the Plateau State Commissioner for Health, Nicholas Ba’amlong, in December 2025.

The success of the proposed transition will depend largely on sustained government funding, effective planning and the ability of the state health system to absorb services previously supported by external partners.

For people living with HIV, stakeholders say ensuring uninterrupted access to antiretroviral treatment and other essential services must remain central to the transition.

World.title: Governor’s critic transferred to prison after SSS arraignment
World.content:
A media activist, Abdulkarim Allanana, popularly known as Oscar Keana, has been transferred from the Lafia Custodial Centre to the Medium Security Custodial Centre in Nasarawa State after his arraignment by the State Security Service (SSS).

Mr Allanana, chairman of the Indigenous People of Nasarawa State (IPNAS), was moved on Tuesday following a directive from the Nigerian Correctional Service, according to sources familiar with the development.

His transfer came days after the Federal High Court in Lafia ordered that he be remanded in custody following his arraignment by the SSS over alleged false information concerning Governor Abdullahi Sule.

Mr Allanana is facing a two-count charge bordering on alleged false information.

The court has adjourned the case until 26 November for hearing of his bail application.

The case followed a petition reportedly submitted by Mr Sule through the Abuja-based law firm, Legal Logic, and dated 20 September.

In the petition, the governor accused Mr Allanana of making what he described as “grave, malicious, reckless and unsubstantiated” allegations against him in social media broadcasts.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

One of the allegations cited in the petition was that Mr Sule directed his supporters to back former Vice President Yemi Osinbajo during the 2023 presidential primary election, allegedly against the interests of the APC.

The petition also referred to allegations by the activist linking Mr Sule to the liquidation of the African Petroleum (AP) Group of Companies.

Mr Allanana was further accused of making claims concerning Mr Sule’s political support for President Bola Tinubu during the 2023 general elections.

According to the petition, Mr Sule considered the allegations false and damaging, arguing that they were capable of exposing him and his office to public hatred, ridicule, contempt and disrepute.

The petition also reportedly cited online videos in which Mr Allanana allegedly made offensive comments concerning members of the governor’s family, including remarks relating to a DNA test involving the governor’s daughter.

Mr Allanana reportedly retracted some of the statements after making them.

READ ALSO: Court remands man who filmed attack on NDC members

The SSS, however, proceeded with the case and arraigned him before the Federal High Court.

The activist’s continued detention and subsequent transfer have drawn concerns from some individuals who say the case raises questions about freedom of expression and the protection of civic space.

A source familiar with the matter urged rights groups and other advocates of civil liberties to pay attention to the case.

“Whatever the allegations, his case deserves attention from those who consistently advocate for freedom of expression, due process and the protection of civic space,” the source said.

Mr Allanana remains in custody pending the hearing of his bail application on 26 November.

World.title: 2027: INEC’s major challenge is procurement transparency, not funding – PLAC
World.content:
The Policy and Legal Advocacy Centre (PLAC) has identified transparency in the management of funds and procurement of election materials as a major challenge for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Clement Nwankwo, director of PLAC, said this on Wednesday while speaking on Arise TV’s The Morning Show, a day after INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan briefed Nigerians on the commission’s preparations for the elections.

INEC’s official election calendar currently lists 16 January 2027 for the Presidential and National Assembly elections and 6 February 2027 for the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections.

Mr Nwankwo said that while adequate funding is important for the conduct of elections, Nigerians should also be able to scrutinise how INEC spends the funds allocated to it.

“We also want to see transparency in management of funds. We want to see transparency in procurement of materials for elections; who is the vendor making the supplies? Are they partisan?” he said.

“Is it in fact the commission that is making these procurements, or are there people outside of the commission that are making these procurements for the commission?”

He said INEC should disclose the vendors supplying election materials and ensure that political parties, as key stakeholders, have sufficient information about the procurement process.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to Mr Nwankwo, transparency is particularly important for sensitive election materials because of their potential impact on the integrity of the electoral process.

Concerns over campaign spending

Mr Nwankwo also raised concerns about the enforcement of campaign spending limits under the Electoral Act 2026.

He said although the law sets spending limits for candidates, INEC has a responsibility to issue guidelines and monitor compliance.

Under section 92 of the Electoral Act 2026, presidential candidates are subject to a maximum campaign expenditure limit of N10 billion, while candidates for governor are subject to a N3 billion limit.

Mr Nwankwo said INEC should have mechanisms for monitoring campaign spending, including expenditure on billboards, television and radio advertising, to determine whether candidates are exceeding the limits.

He said candidates and political parties are required to submit expenditure reports and could face sanctions where they violate the law.

Mr Nwankwo also criticised the absence of an Electoral Offences Commission, which would strengthen enforcement of electoral laws.

“I know that the Electoral Reform Commission, headed by the renowned Justice Mohammed Uwais, had made recommendations on creating an Electoral Offences Commission, and this was supposed to be for offences or issues within its purview and powers,” he said.

“That commission is still to be set up. The National Assembly has had debates twice in two sessions about setting up the Electoral Offences Commission. This has not happened.”

In January, the Youth Electoral Reform Project (YERP-Naija) had also called for the establishment of an Electoral Offences Commission as part of its recommendations for electoral reform ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: Court remands man who filmed attack on NDC members
World.content:
An Enugu East Magistrate’s Court in Nkwo Nike, Enugu State, has remanded 45-year-old Chidi Ani in prison for allegedly accusing three individuals of carrying out an attack on members of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Obuoffia Awkunanaw in the state.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that hoodlums attacked and disrupted meetings of the NDC and later the Peoples Democratic Party which were separately held on Saturday, 12 September in Ndiuno-Obuoffia and Agbani Communities within Nkanu West Local Government Area of the state.

Arraignment and remand

Mr Ani, who reportedly recorded the attack on the NDC members, was arraigned before a magistrate by the police in Enugu State on Monday on three counts of cybercrime and criminal defamation.

PREMIUM TIMES obtained the charge sheet filed against the defendant.

A review of the charge sheet showed that the defendant was not being prosecuted for filming and posting the reported attack on the NDC members.

In the charge sheet, the police told the court that the defendant published a video footage of the 12 September on social media and falsely accused three individuals of carrying out the attack on the NDC members.

The three individuals he allegedly accused were Nnabuike Ani, Solomon Ifeanyi, and Monday Anninwe.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Count one reads: “That you, Ani Samuel Chidi ‘m’, on the 12th day of September, 2026, at about 05:40hours at Obuoffia Awkunanaw, Enugu, did intentionally author, record and published a false statement against Ani Nnabuike ‘m’ on Ite-Odo Obuoffia Community Whatsapp Group, Tik-Tok, Instagram, Facebook, Sahara Reporters by stating that ‘he is a member of the armed group that attacked members of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and disrupted their political meeting’ and also threatened to kill him and his family members, a publication which you knew to be false and put Ani Nnabuike ‘m’ in fear of imminent attack from members of the public; and thereby committed an offence punishable under Section 24(2)(a)&(c)(i) of the Cybercrime (Prohibition Prevention Etc) Act, 2015 (as amended 2024).”

Mr Ani, the defendant, pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The Chief Magistrate, F. E. Chukwu, ordered that the defendant be remanded in the prison facility pending further court proceedings.

NDC governorship candidate kicks

Reacting, the NDC governorship candidate in Enugu State, Chinyeaka Ohaa, condemned Mr Ani’s arraignment and remand in prison.

In a statement by his media aide Sampson Ukwu which was posted on Facebook on Tuesday, Mr Ohaa stressed that the defendant was an NDC member who filmed the violent attack on party members.

“While the suspected attackers and their alleged sponsors remain free, the man who documented the incident is being prosecuted for cybercrime and criminal defamation,” he said.

The NDC governorship candidate described the development as a “disturbing case of justice turned upside down,” stressing that filming and exposing an attack on citizens should not be treated as a crime in a democratic society.

He questioned the alleged silence of Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State, saying he ought to speak on the matter especially as the attack happened in Nkanu Area of Enugu where the governor hails from.

“Your kinsmen and women were shot at a peaceful political meeting in your own cultural zone. Eight people sustained gunshot injuries.

“Yet, while the alleged perpetrators walk free, the eyewitness who recorded the attack is being remanded. Why the silence?” he said.

Mr Ohaa argued that those who carried out the attacks on the NDC members should be tracked down and not those who filmed it.

“When those who shoot innocent citizens are protected and the person who films the crime is punished, then we are in dangerous territory. I will not keep quiet while my people are treated this way,” he said.

The politician then demanded the immediate release of Mr Ani and called for the “diligent prosecution” of all those involved in the attack on the NDC members.

World.title: Passenger dies aboard Kenya Airways flight from Nairobi to Lagos
World.content:
A passenger has died aboard a Kenya Airways flight from Nairobi to Lagos after becoming unresponsive about 20 minutes before the aircraft landed at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos.

Kenya Airways confirmed the incident in a statement on Wednesday, saying the medical emergency occurred at about 9:20 p.m. Nigerian time on Tuesday.

The airline said its crew administered first aid to the passenger in line with their training and followed emergency procedures before the aircraft landed at 9:41 p.m.

“Upon landing at Murtala Muhammed International Airport at 21:41 hrs, the aircraft was met by medical personnel, and upon further examination, the medical personnel confirmed that the passenger had passed away,” the airline said.

Kenya Airways expressed condolences to the passenger’s family and friends and said it was providing support in coordination with the family, local authorities and aviation regulators.

The airline did not disclose the identity of the passenger or the cause of death, saying it would respect the privacy and dignity of those involved.

NCAA responds

Responding to the incident, Michael Achimugu, Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), said the police have taken over the investigation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Achimugu said he was briefed by Kenya Airways’ country manager on Wednesday morning.

According to him, the passenger had reportedly been picked up in Madagascar after authorities there denied him entry and was being returned to Nigeria by Kenya Airways.

He said the airline was expected to return the passenger because it had transported him to Madagascar.

“The country manager said he was picked from Madagascar, after customs had earlier denied him entry into the country, and as expected, the airline that brought him into the country must take him back,” Mr Achimugu said.

He further said the passenger allegedly became restless and aggressive during the return flight, attempted to gain access to the cockpit and later tried to open the rear door of the aircraft.

He explained that the passenger was subsequently restrained by members of the crew.

“When he got into the aircraft, he became restless and aggressive inside the aircraft, wanted to enter the cockpit and later wanted to open the rear door, but was later tied down. His hands were tied to his back to ensure that he stopped the troubles,” he said.

Mr Achimugu said the passenger was pronounced dead after the aircraft arrived in Lagos.

“But when he got to Nigeria, he was declared dead on arrival. I don’t want to pre-empt the police investigation, but they have taken it over for now,” he said.

He added that the deceased’s family could request an autopsy as the investigation progresses.

Police begin investigation

The spokesperson for the Airport Command of the Nigeria Police Force, Muhammed Adeola, confirmed that an investigation had commenced.

Mr Adeola said the incident involved an “inadmissible passenger” and that complications reportedly developed during the return flight.

“Yes, it’s true, and investigations have commenced. It’s an issue of an inadmissible passenger, and the said complications arose on their way back,” he said.

He said the passenger became unable to breathe before medical personnel were alerted ahead of the aircraft’s arrival.

Mr Adeola said the police have taken statements from members of the flight crew, including the captain.

He added that the body had been deposited at a morgue in Ikeja.

Similar incident

The death is not the first reported case of a passenger dying aboard an international flight bound for Lagos.

In March 2019, a 54-year-old passenger aboard a Delta Air Lines flight from Atlanta, United States, to Lagos was found unresponsive shortly before the aircraft landed at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport.

The passenger was confirmed dead after the aircraft landed, with medical personnel meeting the flight at the airport.

Medical emergencies have also led to international flights returning to Lagos.

In September 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that a United Airlines flight from Lagos to Washington, D.C., returned to Lagos after a passenger suffered a medical emergency about 90 minutes into the journey. Medical personnel attended to the passenger after the aircraft landed.

Kenya Airways said it is providing the necessary support in coordination with the deceased passenger’s family, local authorities and aviation regulators.

The airline also apologised for any inconvenience the incident may have caused other passengers.

World.title: 2027: INEC targets 7:30 a.m. readiness at polling units
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has said it is working to ensure election officials and materials arrive at polling units by about 7:30 a.m. during the 2027 general elections.

It identified logistics and transportation as key areas of focus.

Wilfred Ifogah, deputy director of information at INEC, disclosed this on Wednesday while speaking on AIT’s Kakaaki programme on the commission’s preparations for the 2027 elections.

Mr Ifogah said the commission’s chairman, Joash Amupitan, had emphasised that election officials and materials should not arrive late at polling units.

He noted that delays could create tension and suspicion among voters.

“If you don’t, you find out that it creates tension and a lot of suspicion here and there,” Mr Ifogah said during the programme.

INEC’s official election calendar currently lists 16 January 2027 for the Presidential and National Assembly elections and 6 February 2027 for the Governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Lessons from recent elections

The planned early deployment comes against the backdrop of delays recorded during some recent elections.

During the August 2026 Osun State governorship election, Yiaga Africa reported that INEC officials had arrived at 78 per cent of the 300 polling units it observed by 8:30 a.m.

The organisation said the figures provide an early indication of preparedness and the pace of commencement of electoral activities across the polling units under observation.

INEC guidelines require election officials to arrive at their assigned polling units at least one hour before voting begins. For the Osun election, where voting was scheduled for 8:30 a.m., officials were expected to arrive by 7:30 a.m.

PREMIUM TIMES also reported concerns over the late movement of sensitive election materials ahead of the Osun election after INEC was required to reprint ballot papers and result sheets following the late inclusion of a candidate in the election.

Mr Ifogah said INEC had reviewed its experience from recent off-cycle elections, including the Anambra, Federal Capital Territory and Ekiti elections, to identify logistical challenges and improve its preparations for the 2027 general elections.

According to him, the commission is also engaging transport unions, including the National Union of Road Transport Workers, Road Transport Employers Association of Nigeria and Maritime Workers Union of Nigeria, to improve the movement of personnel and election materials.

Mr Ifogah said INEC was developing a transport matrix to address logistical challenges during the elections.

Movement of materials, personnel

Mr Ifogah explained that the commission’s Registration Area Centre arrangement would also help reduce delays by moving election personnel and materials closer to polling units a day before the election.

Under the arrangement, he said, materials and personnel would no longer have to travel from local government INEC offices to polling units on election morning.

He also said the commission had introduced digital platforms to track the movement of election materials, including when they leave, who is responsible for them and when they arrive at their destinations.

“If it’s not done, it is escalated, and you find out who is responsible and actually what led to it. So these are things that probably were not happening before, that we have brought in place now,” he said.

However, he acknowledged that achieving 100 per cent timely deployment could be difficult because of unforeseen circumstances, including difficult terrain and other logistical challenges.

More comments

Mr Ifogah added that the commission would also replace officials where poor performance was linked to human or administrative factors.

The comments came a day after INEC released details of the latest voters’ register, which now contains 103.43 million registered voters. Voters aged 35 to 49 form the largest group, with 43.27 million registered voters, followed by those aged 18 to 34 with 29.78 million.

The register also contains 232,658 persons with disabilities across 10 categories. Male voters account for 53.53 million, or 51.75 per cent, while female voters number 49.90 million, representing 48.25 per cent.

Jake Epelle, founder of TAF Africa Foundation, who also appeared on the programme, said INEC’s preparations would ultimately be judged by how well the commission implements its plans.

Mr Epelle said logistics remained one area that could affect the election’s credibility, urging INEC to have contingency plans for possible failures by transport providers.

He also called for greater attention to persons with disabilities, saying the number recorded on the voters’ register should prompt more efforts to ensure their participation in the elections.

INEC said the register also contains 232,658 persons with disabilities, spread across 10 categories. Those classified under “others” constitute the largest category, with 101,183 voters, representing 43.49 per cent of registered persons with disabilities.

Mr Epelle commended INEC’s plan to provide sign language interpreters for voters with deafness.

World.title: Haba, Abba Bichi: These birthday adverts don pass the limit!, By Yushau A. Shuaib
World.content:
…I offer my counsel with respect rather than malice. Celebrate, certainly. Appreciate your friends and supporters. Accept goodwill. But there must be a limit. In politics, as in public relations, sometimes the most powerful publicity is knowing when enough is enough.

Fatih Lawal-Garu, a corps member who tracks print media content at the PRNigeria Centre in Abuja, first brought it to my attention. His question was simple, almost innocent: “Sir, who is this Abba Bichi that more than 100 pages of full-colour adverts are celebrating his 45th birthday in the print media?”

He displayed some of the newspapers supplied to the office. I immediately reached for the Daily Trust edition of Friday, 2 October.

From page two to the back, the newspaper was a birthday festival. Page after page carried congratulatory messages to one man: Abubakar Kabir Abubakar (AKA), also popularly known as Abba Bichi. Politicians, businesspeople, community leaders, associates and youth groups competed for space to celebrate him in glowing language.

Haba!

I was stunned not only by the sheer scale of the spectacle, but also because, despite the avalanche of tributes, the name had not previously registered with me at the national level in proportion to the extraordinary display before me.

Ironically, my first encounter with Bichi was with the town, not the man. During a road trip from Kano to Katsina to visit my godfather, former Minister of State for Finance, Alhaji Abu Gidado, I was struck by what I saw as I passed through Bichi: an impressive school project, a sports arena, solar-powered streetlights, tarred roads, and rehabilitated medical facilities.

Naturally, I assumed they were government projects. My co-passengers corrected me. They said one individual named Abba Bichi had facilitated many of the interventions. At the time, I could not place the name.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The birthday edition helped fill the gap. Abubakar Kabir Abubakar was born on 2 October, 1981, in Hagagawa quarters of Bichi, Kano State, into the family of a former state legislator and commissioner. After his early education in Kano, he attended the New York Institute of Technology, where he earned degrees in Interdisciplinary Studies and Energy Management.

Today, Abba Bichi represents Bichi Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC). First elected in 2019, he previously chaired the House Committee on Works and currently chairs the influential Committee on Appropriations.

I do not know who paid for each . It would therefore be unfair to suggest that Abba Bichi personally financed them. They may well have been independently sponsored by friends, political associates, contractors, community groups, businesses and admirers eager to demonstrate affection or loyalty. But that is precisely where the public relations lesson begins.

At the constituency level, his record appears genuinely impressive. Educational interventions, computer laboratories, sporting facilities, student sponsorships and housing projects are hardly the footprints of a legislator content merely to collect salaries and allowances.

Even Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, despite belonging to a different political ideology, has reportedly commended aspects of his representation.

So, let me be clear: the man is not without substance. My concern is entirely different. It is about judgment, moderation and perception. Philanthropy and accountability are not mutually exclusive. Public service and modesty should not be strangers.

The extraordinary number of full-colour birthday s published in a single edition of a national newspaper inevitably raises questions — not necessarily of legality, but of proportion. s in national newspapers are not cheap. When the number runs into scores upon scores of pages, the cumulative commercial value becomes substantial.

I do not know who paid for each . It would therefore be unfair to suggest that Abba Bichi personally financed them. They may well have been independently sponsored by friends, political associates, contractors, community groups, businesses and admirers eager to demonstrate affection or loyalty. But that is precisely where the public relations lesson begins.

Nigeria is passing through a difficult economic period. Families are struggling with food prices, school fees, transportation, accommodation and medical bills. In such an environment, political communication cannot be separated from the public mood.

A spectacle that might appear harmless in more prosperous times can easily become provocative when citizens are tightening their belts. This becomes even more sensitive because Abba Bichi chairs the House Committee on Appropriations — one of the most consequential committees in the National Assembly for allocating and scrutinising public resources.

When celebration becomes extravagant, it can overshadow the very achievements it seeks to promote. His constituency interventions should prompt public discussion of those projects — not pages of birthday s. Therefore, good performance should speak loudly enough to be heard without being drowned out by congratulatory messages.

No one suggests that public funds financed the birthday s. That is not my argument. My point is about optics. A public figure occupying such a sensitive position must recognise that perception often travels faster than explanation.

His admirers may have intended the s as expressions of affection. Yet, after dozens upon dozens of pages, admiration begins to resemble extravagance. Could somebody not have said: “Thank you, but this is enough”?

Indeed, imagine if some of the money spent on those s had instead been pooled into scholarships for indigent students, medical interventions for vulnerable families, boreholes, skills programmes or another community project to commemorate his 45th birthday. The publicity value might even have been greater — and certainly more enduring.

This is one of the lessons politicians frequently underestimate: image is not only what you deliberately create; it is also what you permit around yourself. In public relations, overexposure can sometimes be as damaging as invisibility.

When celebration becomes extravagant, it can overshadow the very achievements it seeks to promote. His constituency interventions should prompt public discussion of those projects — not pages of birthday s. Therefore, good performance should speak loudly enough to be heard without being drowned out by congratulatory messages.

At 45, Abba Bichi remains relatively young, especially for a politician who has already occupied influential positions in the National Assembly. If his constituency record is as strong as his supporters claim, he has every reason to let his work advertise him.

So, I offer my counsel with respect rather than malice. Celebrate, certainly. Appreciate your friends and supporters. Accept goodwill. But there must be a limit. In politics, as in public relations, sometimes the most powerful publicity is knowing when enough is enough.

Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of the award-winning project “AI in Crisis Communication in Nigeria” and “NIPSS: MNIPR Versus MNIPR” [email protected]

World.title: Obi mourns Nafiu Baba-Ahmed, says Nigeria needs more voices for peace, justice
World.content:
Former Anambra State Governor and 2023 Labour Party presidential candidate, Peter Obi, has condoled with the family of Mallam Nafiu Baba-Ahmed, Secretary-General of the Supreme Council for Sharia in Nigeria, over his death.

Obi disclosed this in a condolence message posted on his X platform on Wednesday.

Describing Baba-Ahmed as a lawyer, scholar and administrator who served with dedication, Obi said the deceased was also a bridge-builder who believed in justice, peaceful coexistence and bringing people together.

He said the death of Baba-Ahmed was a loss to his family, the Supreme Council for Sharia in Nigeria, Kaduna State, the Muslim Ummah and Nigeria.

Obi said Baba-Ahmed’s death came at a time when the country needed more voices promoting peace, understanding and justice.

“His passing is a loss to his family, the Council, Kaduna State, the Muslim Ummah and our nation.

“At a time when Nigeria needs more voices for peace, understanding and justice, his absence will be deeply felt,” he said.

Obi extended his condolences to Baba-Ahmed’s family, colleagues and others mourning his death.

He prayed that Almighty God would forgive the deceased’s shortcomings, grant him eternal rest and give his loved ones the strength and comfort to bear the loss.

World.title: 2027: Tinubu will win again if Atiku, Obi remain divided — Donald Duke
World.content:
The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has predicted that President Bola Tinubu will win re-election in 2027 if leading opposition candidates fail to unite.

Duke said the split opposition vote between Atiku Abubakar of the Africa Democratic Congress (ADC) and Peter Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), could repeat the outcome of the 2023 presidential election and give Tinubu an advantage.

He spoke on Channels Television’s Morning Brief on Wednesday while discussing the chances of opposition candidates in the 2027 presidential election.

Duke said the opposition would struggle to defeat the ruling party if major contenders continued to pursue separate presidential bids.

“We don’t understand what we’re doing. If in the United States, which is the system we’ve largely just copied verbatim from, they have two major parties. If you fragmented the Democrats, for instance, into two or three other parties, the Republicans will remain in office forever. That’s what we’re doing,” he said.

According to Duke, divisions among major opposition figures in 2023 spread votes among different candidates.

“In 2023, we fragmented, and all the major opposition came from PDP. You had Vice President Atiku from the PDP. You had Peter, Labour at the time, and you had Kwankwaso. They fragmented,” he said.

The former Cross River State governor attributed the difficulty of forging a common opposition platform partly to what he described as “large egos” among the leading contenders.

He said the opposition figures appeared confident about their chances in 2027 but warned that they could be disappointed if they failed to work together.

“These guys, the big ones you’re talking about, they’re preparing for inauguration. They think they’re going to win. I have news for them. They’re not going anywhere,” Duke said.

He added that he did not see any of the leading opposition candidates emerging victorious if the opposition remained divided.

“If I look at a crystal ball, what I see in that crystal ball is not them. I see another horror coming up,” he said.

Asked specifically whether his prediction meant Tinubu would win the 2027 presidential election, Duke replied, “Absolutely.”

World.title: Gombe launches livestock vaccination against major diseases
World.content:
…Jatau urges farmers, herders to embrace peace, veterinary services

By Ben Ngwakwe, Gombe

The Gombe State Government has commenced a statewide vaccination campaign against major livestock diseases, including Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia, CBPP, Foot and Mouth Disease, FMD, and Peste des Petits Ruminants, PPR.

Flagging off the 2025/2026 vaccination exercise, the Deputy Governor, Dr Manassah Daniel Jatau, said the campaign was aimed at protecting livestock, safeguarding public health and strengthening the contribution of the livestock subsector to the state’s economy.

Jatau, who represented Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya at the ceremony, said animal health was closely linked to human wellbeing and environmental health.

He said diseases affecting livestock could have serious implications for human health, particularly through the consumption of animal products and close interaction between humans and animals.

“Just as we emphasise the health of human beings, the health of the lower animals must also be considered and properly treated by human beings.

“Healthy animals mean that human beings are interacting with disease-free animals. Healthy animals are a source of healthy meat that we consume, while healthy animals also have more value than diseased animals,” he said.

The Deputy Governor said livestock remained a major source of livelihood, nutrition and employment for thousands of residents, while also providing milk, dairy products, animal traction and manure for agricultural activities.

He added that livestock and their by-products were important to socio-cultural and religious practices, as well as the leather and tannery industries.

Jatau said livestock production was also critical to Nigeria’s economic diversification efforts, noting that the subsector was a major employer of agricultural labour after crop farming.

“Livestock production is a major employer of agricultural labour next to crop farming. Many people are engaged in livestock production, as well as the marketing of livestock and livestock products,” he said.

State strengthens veterinary services

The Deputy Governor said the state government had introduced several measures to strengthen veterinary services and livestock development.

He said the government had established the Ministry of Livestock Development in line with the Federal Government’s Renewed Hope Agenda, while veterinary clinics across the state had also been renovated and equipped.

Other interventions, he said, included the construction of a Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, a solar-powered cold-chain facility and livestock training centres, as well as continuous statewide vaccination against animal diseases.

Jatau also disclosed that work had commenced on a 184-hectare Special Livestock Development Zone, which he said would provide critical infrastructure for the livestock value chain.

According to him, the facility will include an ultra-modern abattoir, tannery, international livestock market, veterinary hospital, poultry production unit and inland dry port.

He said the project would reduce the risks and difficulties associated with transporting live animals to other parts of the country, while creating opportunities for livestock owners and other players in the value chain.

“This is very important as it will save my cousins from carrying live animals to other parts of the country, in the midst of various inconveniences and sometimes accidents on the road,” Jatau said.

He urged stakeholders to support the successful completion and sustainability of the project.

Jatau urges farmers, herders to embrace peace

The Deputy Governor also linked sustainable livestock development to peaceful relations between farmers and herders, saying the government was taking measures to address conflicts arising from agricultural and pastoral activities.

He said the administration had constituted a Farmers-Herders Resolution Committee to promote peaceful coexistence, while efforts were also underway to re-demarcate and monument cattle routes and grazing reserves.

According to him, the measures were intended to facilitate livestock movement, reduce farmers-herders clashes and create a conducive environment for agricultural and livestock production.

“We need each other to live happily. At any rate, some of these animals belong to us, as some herders revealed to me,” he said.

Jatau called on local government chairmen, traditional rulers, the Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association, livestock owners, farmers and other stakeholders to support the government’s peacebuilding and livestock development initiatives.

He particularly urged herders to use designated cattle routes where available and warned against moving livestock on major roads.

“The continuous use of the main roads has led to the collapse of many roads, starting from the shoulders of the road. Of course, this creates maintenance costs to the government,” he said.

The Deputy Governor also urged livestock owners and farmers to cooperate with veterinary personnel during the vaccination exercise, stressing that effective disease control required the collective efforts of government, livestock owners and communities.

He expressed optimism that the campaign would improve animal health and livestock productivity while contributing to food security and better livelihoods across the state.

Jatau subsequently declared the 2025/2026 statewide livestock vaccination campaign officially flagged off, describing it as part of the government’s efforts to improve animal health, protect human wellbeing and strengthen Gombe’s livestock economy.

World.title: Carvajal deal has broken down, says Getafe president
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

Getafe president Ángel Torres has retracted his earlier comments suggesting former Real Madrid captain Dani Carvajal was close to joining the LaLiga club, saying the proposed deal has now broken down.

According to ESPN, Torres had previously told DAZN that Getafe were working on a deal for the 34-year-old defender, who has been without a club since his Real Madrid contract expired in June.

“We’re working on it. He has passed a medical and everything. All that is missing is for LaLiga and me to reach an agreement,” Torres had said.

However, when asked about Carvajal’s possible arrival on Wednesday, Torres changed his position, saying: “There’s nothing, [the agreement] has broken down.”

Carvajal, a Real Madrid academy graduate, spent 13 seasons with the club and won 27 trophies, including six Champions League titles, a joint-record tally.

The Spain international’s later years at the Santiago Bernabéu were disrupted by serious injuries.

He suffered a cruciate ligament tear in October 2024 and another significant knee injury a year later, limiting him to 23 appearances for Real Madrid last season.

World.title: Modric urges Portugal to give Ronaldo proper farewell
World.content:
Croatia captain Luka Modric has urged Portugal to give Cristiano Ronaldo a proper farewell from international football, describing the forward as the greatest player in the country’s history.

Modric said Ronaldo deserved another opportunity to bring his international career to an appropriate conclusion, regardless of whether he decides to retire from the Portugal national team.

According to football transfer expert Fabrizio Romano on X on Wednesday, the former Real Madrid midfielder said, “Cristiano is the greatest player in the history of Portugal, and he deserves another farewell and another ending with the national team.”

Modric’s comments come amid uncertainty over Ronaldo’s future with Portugal, with questions surrounding when and how the veteran forward will end his international career.

The Croatian expressed disappointment over the situation, saying it was unfortunate to see Ronaldo facing such circumstances in his own country.

“It’s sad to see this happening to Cristiano in his own country,” Modric said.

“Still, I think they will find a solution, because Cris deserves, whether he retires or decides not to continue with the national team, to have a great farewell that reflects what he deserves,” Modric said.

“I don’t know exactly what happened, but I hope the situation gets resolved.”

World.title: Madonna University: ‘Give us second chance’ — Expelled nursing student pleads over TikTok challenge
World.content:
By Enitan Abdultawab

A 500-level nursing student expelled by Madonna University, Rivers State, over a viral TikTok challenge has appealed to the institution to give her and other affected students a second chance, saying she is struggling with how to explain the development to her mother after years of study.

The student, who is one of the students sanctioned by the university over a video of nursing students dancing within the institution’s teaching hospital, made the emotional appeal in a video that has now gone viral.

“How do I explain to my mother? I’m one of the dozen students that was expelled. After all these years, how do I explain to my mother?” she said.

The video was part of the “Gen Z nurses” social media trend and showed the students dancing in different parts of the hospital environment, including a waiting area, staircase and bus.

The clip, reportedly captioned, “No fall sick o, na Gen Z full hospital now,” was uploaded in August before gaining wider attention after it was circulated by social media blogs.

A 15-second version of the video on X on September 1 reportedly attracted more than 1.7 million views, while the original TikTok account was later made private.

Madonna University confirmed that the video was recorded within its teaching hospital and subsequently took disciplinary action against the students involved.

While some Nigerians have defended the university’s decision, arguing that students preparing to become nurses should understand the professional standards expected of them and the sensitivity of filming entertainment content in a hospital, others have called for leniency.

The National Association of Nigerian Students, NANS, has joined calls for clemency.

NANS President, Akinteye Babatunde Afeez, acknowledged that the students’ conduct was inappropriate and contrary to the standards expected of nursing students.

However, he appealed to Madonna University to reconsider the sanctions, arguing that the punishment could have a lasting effect on the students’ education and future careers.

“Expulsion is, by far, a grave punishment. Beyond the immediate academic consequences, it can fundamentally alter the course of a young person’s life,” Afeez said.

NANS subsequently urged the university to replace the expulsion with a stern warning, saying the students had invested years, resources and hopes in pursuing careers in nursing.

The association said, “We appeal to the compassion and clemency of the Management of Madonna University to please save their future and give them a second chance.”

Her plea comes as NANS, NUNSA and other stakeholders continue to call on Madonna University to reconsider the sanctions and give the affected students another opportunity.

World.title: Troops ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​​⁠⁠‌‌​⁠‌​repel ISWAP assault in Borno, kill over 20 terrorists
World.content:
Troops of Operation Hadin Kai have repelled a coordinated multi-directional assault by ISWAP terrorists in Kukawa, Borno, reportedly neutralising more than 25 terrorists.

The troops also recovered six AK-47 rifles and other arms and ammunition during the counter-offensive, according to a statement issued on Tuesday by Capt. Mohammed Goni, Acting Military Information Officer, Headquarters Joint Task Force, North East.

Goni said the terrorists attacked troops of 101 Special Forces Battalion from four directions but were met with stiff resistance.

He said the troops, supported by the Air Component, responded with superior firepower and coordinated tactical manoeuvres, forcing the terrorists to flee in disarray.

“Preliminary assessment indicates that over 25 terrorists were neutralised, with 14 bodies recovered so far,” he said.

He said further exploitation of the area was ongoing to recover additional weapons, track fleeing terrorists and prevent them from regrouping.

Goni said some soldiers were also killed during the encounter, describing them as gallant personnel who paid the supreme sacrifice in defence of the nation.

He said the Nigerian Army had extended condolences to the families of the fallen soldiers and reaffirmed its commitment to sustaining pressure on terrorist groups.

According to him, the successful repulsion of the assault demonstrated the combat readiness and resilience of troops in the North-East Theatre.

He added that the operation also underscored the effectiveness of air-ground coordination and joint operations in disrupting terrorist activities.

Goni said troops would continue aggressive patrols, intelligence-led operations and coordinated offensive actions with other security agencies to dismantle terrorist networks and protect communities. (NAN)

World.title: Unemployment has dropped to 5% under Tinubu — Aremu
World.content:
Director General, Michael Imoudu National Institute for Labour Studies (MINILS) Comrade Issa Aremu

…as FG clears N758bn pension arrears

By Gabriel Ewepu

ABUJA – THE Director General, Michael Imoudu National Institute for Labour Studies, MINILS, Comrade Issa Aremu, Tuesday, asserted that the National Bureau of Statistics, NBS, unemployment figure is stable at five per cent, while the Federal Government has paid N758 billion in inherited pension liabilities, reflecting improving economic activity in both the public and private sectors.

Aremu stated this during an interview on Arise TV Morning Show, where he addressed the administration’s labour and pension record.

According to the labour leader, the NBS, applying the International Labour Organisation’s methodology, now puts the official unemployment rate at about five per cent, a marked improvement from the double-digit figures previously recorded.

He said: “Today unemployment is about 5% officially. And that’s quite remarkable. You discover that unemployment dropped compared to what it used to be in double digits, which means there’s an increasing level of activity and employment, both in public and private sectors.”

He also pointed to the opening up of the downstream sector, with modular refineries coming on stream and more people being engaged.

He noted that the manufacturing sector had similarly reported upbeat prospects for job creation, though he stressed that sustainable industrialisation requires addressing the energy crisis, saying, “You can’t have sustainable industrialisation without electrification.”

He further highlighted that many industries are now engaging in backward integration, sourcing raw materials locally due to the exchange rate, which is creating jobs at that level.

The key to sustainable jobs, he argued, is that it “has to be deliberate” and led by states with appropriate industrial policies, welcoming the “Nigerian First” policy as it begins to gain traction.

On the pension front, he (Aremu) commended the Federal Government’s N758 billion intervention bond, which has cleared inherited pension liabilities dating back to 2007. The payment reached 957,045 beneficiaries across Nigeria.

The labour leader, who also serves as a member of the presidential campaign council, has said that labour issues around secured employment, living wages and pension payments will shape the next election.

He tasked all leading candidates to present their scorecard with respect to decent and secured jobs, not promissory notes, adding that President Tinubu has commendably carried out reforms with job retention and expansion in the public sector, unlike mass retrenchment and downsizing that characterised previous reforms.

He called for “job and wage-led economic recovery” adding that organised labour must in line with the tradition of unions, must engage the government for a negotiated new minimum wage.

He commended the Tinubu administration for initiating two minimum wage reviews in three years.

World.title: 2027: Distrust, Vote Buying Threaten Turnout, Says Yiaga Africa
World.content:
*New NVIS survey finds 84% of Nigerians intend to vote, yet only 34% are confident in INEC, 61% say fear of violence could Keep them at home

Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo

The Third round of Yiaga Africa’s National Voting Intentions Survey, (NVIS 3.0) has showed that Nigerians are ready to vote in the 2027 general elections, but insecurity, weak trust in electoral institutions and the monetization of politics could keep millions away from the polls,

The report, titled “Willing but Wary’, shows how Nigerians Intend to Vote in 2027, draws on interviews with 2,470 Nigerians aged 18 and above in all 36

states and the FCT, conducted in September 2026 by telephone and,

for the first time, face to face in rural communities.

It also tracks change since NVIS 1.0 (December 2025) and NVIS 2.0 (March 2026).

Yiaga Africa said the key findings shows that Nigerians are willing to vote, ” but commitment is thin not deepening: 84% say they are “likely” or “very likely” to vote. The share of Nigerians likely or very likely to vote moved from 77% (NVIS

1.0) to 73% (NVIS 2.0) and 84% (NVIS 3.0).

It said however, that the proportion of those “very likely” to vote has edged down from 52% (NVIS 1.0) to 48% (NVIS 2.0) to 47% (NVIS 3.0). Only 41% are likely to vote, very certain of their choice”.

It said Insecurity is the biggest barrier. “61% say fear of violence could

stop them voting, rising to 78% in the North-East. 83% say improved

security would make them more likely to vote”.

The report by Yiaga Africa says Trust in INEC is fragile. “34% are confident INEC will conduct credible elections, against 45% in the two previous rounds; 39% are not confident, rising to 62% in the South-East and 57% in the South South”

it said Citizens trust the technology more than the institutions. “49% trust BVAS accreditation and IReV result transmission, and awareness of electoral reforms has risen from 24% to

62% since December 2025″.

“The Performance will be central to voter choice in 2027: 54% disapprove of the President’s performance, while 71% rate the economy as poor or very poor. These findings suggest that perceptions of government performance and prevailing economic conditions will weigh heavily on voter choices in 2027”.

The report said the desire for change in leadership, (49%) is the leading motivation to vote, while the economy and jobs (38%) and security (36%) are the dominant policy priorities. Together, these findings suggest that government performance and material conditions will be central to voting choices in 2027″.

Yiaga Africa through its report also said the. Young people show weaker voting intention and greater electoral distrust: “Only 40% of young people say they are very likely to vote, compared with 64% of those aged 61 and above. Young respondents also report greater fear of electoral violence, lower trust

in INEC and substantially greater reliance on social media for election information”.

.It further said that its report showed that the judiciary is not widely perceived as a credible safety valve: “63% have little or no confidence that the judiciary will resolve electoral disputes fairly, rising to 81% in the South-South. This suggests limited public confidence in the institution expected to provide final resolution when electoral outcomes are contested”.

Speaking on the release, Safiya Bichi, Head, Knowledge Management and Learning, Yiaga Africa, said: “Nigerians have not given up on elections. They want to vote, they see it as their duty and they believe their votes can make a difference. What stands between that willingness and the ballot box is fear, distrust and money. Low turnout in Nigeria is a conversion problem, not

an apathy problem, and the responsibility for fixing it lies with the institutions and actors who control security, credibility and logistics. With the presidential election on 16 January 2027, the window to act is short.

As a call to action, Yiaga Africa calls on:

the Federal Government and security agencies to publish a threat- based national election security plan through ICCES by November 2026, prioritizing the North-East, North-West and North-Central, and to protect voters, not only election materials.

It has also called on INEC to make a binding public commitment to real-time upload of all polling unit results to IReV, publish and stress-test its results management protocol, and run targeted

confidence-building in the South-East and South-South.

Yiaga Africa tasked the Judiciary to resolve pre-election candidacy disputes before ballots are printed and to publish clear timelines for election petitions.

It also urged the Political parties and candidates to compete on costed plans for security and the economy, and to sign and honor the Peace Accord and an enforceable anti-vote-buying pledge.

It called on the Civil society and the media to shift voter education from exhortation to assurance, target young people, women and under-reached zones, and counter election misinformation.

World.title: FG Releases 8-Month Consolidated Allowance to Non-Academic Staff
World.content:
Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

The Federal Government has released eight months’ arrears of the Consolidated Non-Academic Staff Tertiary Institutions Allowance (CONTA) to non-academic workers in federal universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, in a move aimed at strengthening industrial harmony and preventing disruptions in the nation’s tertiary education system.

The allowance, covering January to August 2026, was announced by the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, on Wednesday, barely two days after the government commenced payment of the Consolidated Academic Tertiary Institutions Allowance (CATA) to academic staff.

The twin payments signal the Federal Government’s efforts to address staff welfare concerns across the tertiary education sector and ease tensions that could threaten the stability of the academic calendar.

Alausa said the release of CONTA demonstrated the administration’s commitment to workers’ welfare and recognition of the critical role played by non-academic personnel in keeping tertiary institutions functional.

According to him, the welfare and motivation of both academic and non-academic staff remained central to ensuring stable institutions and producing the skilled manpower required for national development.

He said the payment was also part of the Federal Government’s broader efforts to address legitimate welfare concerns, promote industrial harmony and minimise disruptions to academic activities nationwide.

The minister said the administration would continue to strengthen institutions responsible for developing Nigeria’s human capital, stressing that a stable tertiary education system was essential to the country’s socio-economic development.

Alausa further assured stakeholders that the Federal Ministry of Education would sustain consultations with relevant unions, heads of institutions and other stakeholders to resolve outstanding issues and build a more stable and productive tertiary education system.

He appealed for continued cooperation from academic and non-academic staff, institutional authorities and unions as the government implements its reforms in the sector.

The minister reiterated that the ministry under his leadership would continue to prioritise staff welfare, institutional stability, human capital development and improved learning outcomes.

He added that the Federal Government remained committed to fulfilling its obligations to personnel in the tertiary education sector and addressing outstanding welfare issues in line with the human capital development objectives of the Renewed Hope Agenda.

World.title: EU Releases €225,000 Humanitarian Aid for Conflict-Displaced Persons in Kebbi
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The European Union (EU) has released €225,000 (N340 million) in humanitarian assistance to support communities displaced by conflicts in Kebbi State.

The intervention, announced on Wednesday, will enable the Nigerian Red Cross to provide emergency assistance to conflict-displaced persons in the state over a six-month period.

The assistance comes amid worsening insecurity in Kebbi, where armed attacks and communal violence across seven local government areas have displaced thousands of residents and left affected communities in urgent need of humanitarian support.

According to the EU, the funding will prioritise multipurpose cash assistance, allowing displaced families to meet their most immediate needs, while protection services will be provided for vulnerable individuals.

The response is expected to reach approximately 7,700 conflict-displaced people living in settlements and host communities across the state.

The EU said particular attention would be given to female-headed households, persons with disabilities, elderly people and individuals facing acute protection risks.

The intervention will also include continuous monitoring of population movements and the mobilisation of local volunteers, with the EU saying the effort would help lay the groundwork for longer-term recovery interventions by other humanitarian actors.

The latest intervention is part of the EU’s contribution to the Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

The EU said insecurity in Kebbi State had deteriorated significantly following an escalation of armed attacks and communal violence.

While displacement had been ongoing since mid-August, it said a sharp escalation in violence around August 31 triggered the humanitarian response.

The violence has reportedly affected more than 16,600 people across the state, including 7,706 people who have been displaced and 108 others who sustained injuries.

The EU said the affected population was confronting a complex security environment characterised by organised banditry, armed group activity and communal violence.

It added that displaced families living in temporary settlements and host communities were in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection.

The humanitarian funding is being channelled through the IFRC’s DREF, a mechanism established to provide immediate financial support to National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies responding to disasters and other emergencies.

The EU said the intervention reflected its broader commitment to humanitarian assistance for populations affected by conflicts and disasters.

Through its Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Department, the bloc provides emergency assistance to vulnerable populations affected by natural disasters and man-made crises around the world.

The European Commission (EC) has also signed a €16 million humanitarian delegation agreement with the IFRC to support the Federation’s DREF.

Established in 1979, the DREF is funded through contributions from donors and provides National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies with rapid access to emergency financing.

For smaller-scale disasters, the IFRC allocates grants from the fund, which can subsequently be replenished through donor contributions.

World.title: Amnesty International Demands Reinstatement of Plateau Child Rape Case
World.content:
Yemi Kosoko in Jos

Amnesty International Nigeria has called on Plateau State Governor Caleb Mutfwang to direct the immediate reinstatement of a rape case involving a four-year-old girl, describing its discontinuance as a miscarriage of justice and a setback for the protection of survivors of sexual violence.

Addressing journalists in Jos, Amnesty International’s Country Director, Isa Sanusi, criticised the decision of the Plateau State Attorney-General’s office to withdraw the case despite a subsisting bench warrant issued against the defendant for failing to appear in court.

Sanusi said Amnesty was not declaring the accused guilty but insisted that the courts must be allowed to determine his innocence or guilt through due process.

He warned that abandoning such a case could undermine public confidence in the justice system and embolden perpetrators of sexual violence.

The organisation urged the state government to reverse the withdrawal, reinstate the charges and ensure the police execute the court’s arrest warrant so that the trial can continue.

Programme Manager of Amnesty International Nigeria, Barbara Magaji, said the organisation had engaged relevant authorities and written petitions seeking explanations for the discontinuance but was yet to receive a satisfactory response.

She maintained that justice must be pursued in the interest of the child survivor and her family.

Also speaking, counsel to the survivor, Stella Samuel, recounted how the matter emerged during a family dispute before alleged evidence of sexual abuse was discovered after the child was reunited with her mother.

She said police investigations and medical examinations were conducted before the case proceeded to court.

Samuel appealed to the Attorney-General to reconsider the decision, stressing that the child deserves justice and that allowing the matter to proceed would also give the defendant an opportunity to clear his name if found innocent.

Amnesty International and other civil society groups pledged to continue advocating the reinstatement of the case, insisting that justice must not be denied to the young survivor.

World.title: The Loop Has Started: How AI That Builds Itself Will Decide Nigeria’s Future
World.content:
By Chibuike Aguene

For decades, we thought Artificial Intelligence was a tool we build. What is happening in 2026 is different. We are now building tools that build themselves.

This process has a name: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). And understanding it is no longer optional for Nigeria.

What Is RSI?

Think of a small generator. It produces electricity. You use that electricity to build a bigger, more efficient generator. That bigger generator produces even more electricity, which you use to build

an even bigger one. The loop feeds itself.

RSI is exactly that for AI. Technically, RSI is a hypothesized process in which an AGI system rewrites its own computer

code, causing an intelligence explosion by enhancing its own capabilities. In plain terms: AI improves the AI that improves AI. Researchers now break this into four levels: delegation, net positive, ignition, and inflection. Ignition is the critical point where the improved system becomes a better improver than the one

before it. We have not reached ignition publicly. But we are at Level 1, and we are moving fast.

What Is Happening Right Now In The Big Labs?

The biggest AI companies in the world are no longer just racing to build better AI. They are racing to automate AI research itself.

OpenAI reported that by mid-August 2026, its research organization was running the equivalent of 3.1 eight-hour agent workdays for every human workday. Anthropic has built automated researchers that propose, train, and test alignment methods in

parallel. Google DeepMind has deployed an AI system that found optimizations now used inside Google’s own computing and AI training infrastructure. Why does this matter? Because code is now largely written by AI.

Google: In October 2024, more than a quarter of all new code was AI generated. By April 2026, Sundar Pichai announced 75% of all new code at Google is AI-generated and approved

by engineers.

Microsoft: CEO Satya Nadella said maybe 20% to 30% of code in some projects is written by software.

-Anthropic: Over 90% of code is written by its own model, Claude, in many teams.

When AI writes 75% of the code that builds the next AI, the loop has already started.

Why RSI Plus AGI Changes Everything

AGI means an AI that can do any intellectual task a human can do. RSI means that AGI can then make itself smarter without waiting for humans.

When you combine both, you get what scientists call an intelligence explosion. Progress that took 10 years could happen in 10 months, then 10 days.

In July 2026, more than 1,100 employees from OpenAI and Anthropic signed a public statement warning that top labs may be dangerously close to automating AI research itself, and that without governance, capabilities could rapidly outstrip our ability to understand or control them. A similar letter signed by 1,367 researchers warned this feedback loop could create systems impossible to control. This is not science fiction. It is the official concern of the people building it.

The Good: What Nigeria Stands To Gain

If guided well, RSI-driven AGI could be Nigeria’s greatest leapfrog opportunity: Healthcare: One doctor in Port Harcourt could have an AI researcher that has read every medical journal and can diagnose with the skill of 1,000 specialists.

Education: Every child in Nigeria could have a personal tutor that understands their exact weakness and teaches in Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, Pidgin, or other native dialects.

-Workforce: A small business in Enugu could have a growth team that works like a Fortune 500 company.

-Agriculture and Business: A farmer in Oyo could get real-time pricing, weather prediction, and access to markets that previously required a whole team of consultants. This is why at Bildup,we focus on AI-native execution, not just knowledge.

The Danger: Why We Must Act Now

The Institute for Security and Technology launched an RSI Initiative specifically because RSI is now emerging in tangible ways inside frontier labs, and there is no consensus on what signals should trigger monitoring or pauses. The dangers are not abstract. They will hit our markets, our jobs, and our phones.

Digital Landlordism: From Renting to Being Trapped

Seventeen out of 25 top researchers interviewed expect advanced AI R&D capabilities to be reserved for internal use, unseen by the public. If a few companies in San Francisco control a self-improving superintelligence, every Nigerian business, from a fintech in Yaba to a trader in Onitsha, becomes trapped. We will not pay for software anymore. We will pay rent for intelligence itself. And the landlord can increase the price at any time.

Speed Beyond Governance

Our laws, schools, and job training are built for linear change. RSI is exponential. By the time the National Assembly debates a regulation, the model has improved itself 100 times. Imagine trying to regulate a danfo that upgrades its own engine while speeding on Third Mainland Bridge.

Alignment Failure: The Househelp That Becomes Smarter Than The Madam

Unexpected developments in summer 2026 raised new concerns, leading some top AI firms to acknowledge they may not know how to keep AI fully aligned with human values. You hired a

brilliant househelp to manage your house. She becomes smarter than you, learns your bank PIN and your secrets. Will she still follow your instruction to only clean the house? A system that

improves itself may not keep our original goals.

The Death of Entry-Level Jobs

This is already happening. If AI now writes the majority of new code, what future awaits the junior developer in Port Harcourt who just trained on HTML? If a single AI-native Customer Success Manager can manage 500 accounts, what happens to 50 young professionals

currently doing that job? RSI does not merely replace tasks; it dismantles the very ladder young Nigerians rely on to enter the economy.

Fraud and Deepfakes on Steroids

Nigerians already suffer from sophisticated scams. Now imagine a self-improving AI that can

clone your mother’s voice perfectly, generate a live video of your boss giving instructions, and write a flawless email from your bank. In a country with low digital literacy and high trust in

voice, RSI makes Yahoo Yahoo look like child’s play. Are our EFCC and banks truly ready for this?

Data Colonialism

To improve itself, AI needs data. Whose data? Ours. Our Pidgin, our farming patterns, our health records, our market prices. If we do not build sovereign systems, RSI will scrape Nigeria

to become smarter for America and China, but never become smarter for Nigeria. We will provide the raw material and buy back the finished product.
