Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.

The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination, except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.

Why does plague still happen today?

Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.

Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.

Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.

The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.

Evans, who wrote “Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”

Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”

Soldiers monitored a hospital in India, on September 27, 1994, during an outbreak of pneumonic plague. The soldiers were posted after more than 50 people escaped quarantine. John Moore/AP/File

Globally, how concerned do people need to be about getting sick?

WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.

People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.

“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.

There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.

“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”

For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.

Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.

In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

World.title: Facing Russian stonewalling, Trump admin ramps up pressure for info as it struggles to plan for potential plague fallout
World.content:
The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and has formally escalated its request for information from the country, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode.

The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

But Russia’s reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them.

The US escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday.

“We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.”

“It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Tuesday. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.”

US officials were in touch with the Russian government as early as last Friday, a State Department official said, including contact between the department’s health experts and the Russian Foreign Ministry. And that outreach has continued, an administration official said, as Rubio expressed hope Tuesday that the limited information sharing “will change in the next few hours and days.”

President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House Tuesday afternoon that he had “call scheduled” to speak with Russian leader Vladimir Putin about the issue “very soon.” He added US agencies would have more information to report “probably tomorrow.” However, the Kremlin on Wednesday said no call has been arranged between Putin and Trump to discuss the Russian plague scare.

The US has gotten limited cooperation so far. What little information has come out of Russia has faced deep skepticism, with officials unconvinced that the Kremlin is being fully forthcoming, according to people familiar with the situation.

Still, until the administration knows more through intelligence collection and diplomatic outreach, officials are not taking steps such as putting travel restrictions into place to prevent any potential spread, according to a US official. The US already advises against travel to Russia due to various factors, including the possibility of wrongful detention and the war with Ukraine.

Among the critical questions still outstanding: whether the 28-year-old lab worker who died last week contracted pneumonic plague — a severe but treatable infection — or another, unknown infectious disease. Staff at the Anti-Plague Institute study a range of other dangerous diseases, including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, according to the institute’s website.

US officials have also sought details on whether the disease was modified in any way, a process called gain of function that could dramatically alter the way the US and other countries might respond.

Rubio and other Trump officials have publicly downplayed the immediate threat to Americans, emphasizing that the administration is closely monitoring the situation and that pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics.

But behind the scenes, there is deep unease within the administration over the continued lack of insight, the people familiar with the situation said. Compounding those concerns is the Russian government’s outsized response, including quarantining the hospital where the lab worker was treated, according to the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district. Nearly 200 people are under observation, a regional news outlet reported.

The entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, Russia, on October 6, 2026. AFP/Getty Images

“We don’t know a lot right now about what actually happened,” said one US official. “But one thing most of us feel certain about: The Russians are going to act like the Chinese did with Covid. They won’t be forthcoming.”

Still, Trump on Monday characterized the situation as a “big problem” for Russia, suggesting that the US might need to provide some unspecified level of aid.

In a statement, a State Department spokesperson said that several federal agencies were “closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague,” but that many of the details surrounding it remained unconfirmed. They reiterated that Americans have long been advised not to travel to Russia for any reason.

“We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the spokesperson said.

In the days since the lab worker’s death, the National Security Council and State Department officials have led the administration’s push to gather information, piece together what happened and evaluate the potential risks, officials and others familiar with the situation said. Federal health agencies, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, have also been involved in the cross-government effort.

A source familiar with the outreach said Trump officials have also backchanneled with the World Health Organization — the international health body that Trump pulled funding from soon after taking office, but that the government has continued to communicate with in emergency situations.

WHO seeks greater clarity

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Tuesday that Russian health authorities reported that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk region, in response to a WHO request.

He said Russian health authorities told WHO that an epidemiological investigation was conducted, and contacts were identified, tested and put under medical observation. The Russian health authorities did not detect any high-threat pathogens among the contacts, Tedros said.

Tedros said the WHO is seeking clarification from Russian authorities regarding “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.” Asked on Wednesday about the WHO’s request, the Kremlin dismissed the media’s coverage of the situation and referred journalists to the public health watchdog.

Some Western media outlets have reported a second case linked to the episode, citing unspecified Russian media reports. CNN is not aware of any such reports and neither local media in Siberia nor local officials have confirmed a second infection.

“If they’re not transparent, if they’re not open to independent accountability, how is it possible to trust the Kremlin is telling us the full and accurate information?” said Lawrence Gostin, a global health law professor at Georgetown University who has worked closely with WHO. “Clearly, on its face, the lab was conducting extremely high-risk research and using shoddy biosafety measures.”

The Anti-Plague Institute’s relatively remote location in eastern Russia, combined with the pneumonic plague’s limited ability to quickly spread, has given health experts some comfort that any immediate threat can be contained.

Pneumonic plague is a bacterial infection, unlike the highly transmissible coronavirus strain that sparked the 2020 pandemic. And while the plague is fatal if untreated, there are now effective and widely available antibiotics to treat it.

While there is little indication that the incident will touch off another global health crisis, officials and outside experts said it has nevertheless reinforced how difficult it can be to monitor and prepare for potential biological threats.

The Health and Human Services Department may have the medical stockpile necessary to combat conventional pneumonic plague, those officials and experts said. But there’s little certainty whether it could do the same against a modified version — or how long it would take to develop a treatment if needed.

Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the episode also comes as health response capabilities both in the US and globally have been diminished by funding cuts and the strain of responding to other crises. WHO has proposed slashing its budget following a $600 million shortfall triggered by the US’ exit.

America’s ability to handle a new public health response, meanwhile, “is severely diminished” amid its efforts to combat measles outbreaks, she said.

“We are talking about a very depleted system. God forbid you layer another pathogen onto the already laborious and difficult work of going after measles,” said Nuzzo. “That would be a nightmare.”

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: Whistleblower says Trump demanded FBI probe into protesters over a TikTok he saw
World.content:
The FBI opened preliminary investigations targeting anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement protesters in Southern California, a former FBI intelligence official alleged in a whistleblower complaint, adding that she believed the move violated the law and agency policy.

The investigations were opened in early 2025 in the early weeks of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown following demands from President Donald Trump and other administration officials, according to the disclosure by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office.

CNN reviewed the complaint, which was filed by lawyers representing Fields to members of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN said the DOJ will continue to “vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law.”

“The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job.”

A statement from the White House also suggested the investigation was focused on violent acts, which it said are not protected by the First Amendment.

“These allegations are FALSE. The First Amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

CNN has also reached out to the FBI for comment.

In at least one instance, the FBI began preliminary investigations of protesters after the president demanded an investigation of people he saw in a TikTok video depicting demonstrators against ICE and Customs and Border Protection in Alhambra, California. The protesters were using bullhorns to warn neighbors about the presence of immigration-enforcement officers, Fields’ disclosure said.

Following the February 2025 protest in Alhambra, an analyst who worked under Fields “informed her that the squad had been ordered to run pre‑assessment checks on the two to four anti‑ICE and CBP protesters in the video accused of impeding an immigration arrest, even though FBI policy prohibits opening investigations based solely on First Amendment‑protected activity, and the squad did not yet have evidence of a crime,” lawyers representing Fields said in a letter to senators.

The investigations came after FBI Director Kash Patel told top FBI leaders that the president “was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested,” the letter said.

In a letter to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, citing the whistleblower complaint, Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla questioned the Justice Department on how many investigations into protestors were currently active and whether Trump had directed other, similar investigations.

Fields’ whistleblower complaint disclosed two separate incidents in which she said White House officials demanded the FBI investigate and arrest anti-ICE protesters.

A separate incident weeks earlier sparked a similar focus on free speech, according to Fields, when then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove demanded the FBI investigate a group of anti-ICE protestors outside a federal building in California.

In both cases, Fields noted that First Amendment protections prohibited such investigations and potential charges unless other action beyond speech had taken place.

When she raised the issue with one superior, Fields says she was told it had to happen.

The former analyst said she was stripped of her team and lost support from FBI leadership in her Los Angeles office, pushing her to ultimately resign from the bureau.

This story has been updated with additional information.

World.title: FM probes with EU security chief developments in Red Sea, Horn of Africa
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty received a phone call from Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Ambassador Nader Zaki said on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, that the call addressed bilateral relations between Egypt and the European Union and ways to develop and strengthen them. The two officials also discussed a number of regional and international issues of common interest.

The spokesman explained that the two officials discussed the rapidly unfolding developments in the Red Sea region and the Horn of Africa, as well as ways to de-escalate tensions and prevent their further expansion.

They reaffirmed the need to respect the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states, and to intensify regional and international efforts to contain crises and create the conditions conducive to restoring security and stability.

They also stressed the importance of continuing coordination with the European Union to support de-escalation efforts and reach sustainable settlements to regional crises.

The talks also addressed Egypt’s pivotal and constructive role in de-escalating tensions, promoting political and diplomatic solutions, and maintaining the ongoing and distinguished coordination between Egypt and the European Union to achieve this common objective.

World.title: Egypt’s foreign reserves rise to $57.35 bln in September: CBE
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly affirmed the State’s commitment to developing the non-banking financial sector in its various activities given its vital role in driving the national economy, attracting investment and expanding the participation of the domestic and foreign private sectors.

The prime minister also highlighted the sector’s role in providing citizens with safe investment avenues under the full supervision of the Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA), particularly through the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) and licensed investment funds.Madbouly made the remarks during a meeting he held on Tuesday evening October 6, 2026, in the New Capital with Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) Chairman Islam Azam to follow up on developments in the non-banking financial sector and activities under the authority’s supervision.

The meeting also reviewed the latest measures being taken by the FRA, within its supervisory and regulatory mandate, to enhance the efficiency of the capital market, insurance and non-banking finance sectors, increase their contribution to the national economy and protect the rights of market participants.The prime minister further said protecting the rights of participants in the sector is a top state priority, as reflected in the regulatory framework governing its activities and the successive decisions issued by the FRA, in line with market developments and the growing number of beneficiaries of the sector’s various activities, including insurance and non-banking finance.

During the meeting, Azam reviewed the latest developments in the regulatory frameworks governing these activities, including recent decisions aimed at improving service quality, meeting citizens’ needs, enhancing supervisory performance and strengthening the ability of the FRA and companies operating in the sector to detect, address and curb negative practices at an early stage.All measures, he said, would contribute to resolving customers’ complaints more quickly, raising their awareness of their rights and protecting their assets.

Azam also highlighted recent FRA decisions and their objectives, including strengthening safeguards for responsible financing, reducing defaults and fraud, combating impersonation and addressing various forms of money laundering.The measures include requiring financing entities to use one-time passwords (OTPs) to strengthen customer identity verification, ensure that customers are aware of the procedures and have agreed to the terms and conditions, and confirm their consent when financing is disbursed and used.

They also include requiring real-time connectivity with the credit information company and obliging consumer finance companies to obtain credit assessments based on customers’ behavioral analysis, while providing the necessary technological infrastructure in preparation for linking their databases with the FRA’s database.Azam explained that the full integration currently being organized and implemented between the FRA and all companies under its supervision would enable the FRA to access real-time and daily data from various markets and facilitate advanced analysis using artificial intelligence technologies.

Some of the resulting analysis will be made available to the market to help companies make more efficient decisions and improve the quality of insurance and financing products in line with customers’ actual needs, he added.In this regard, the FRA chairman said that providing customers with all information related to insurance and financing products and other investment vehicles, while informing them of their rights and obligations, constitutes a fundamental pillar of non-banking financial activities.

Other key pillars include data protection and effective mechanisms for complaints and grievances, he said, noting that these measures help assess the actual impact of financial services on customers’ lives and economic activities.

Azam also pointed to a number of recently issued decisions and instructions aimed at preventing misleading information and confusion between different savings and investment products and vehicles, as well as prohibiting the use of marketing statements or practices that could give customers inaccurate information.He added that the FRA’s implementation of financial inclusion targets under Egypt Vision 2030 is based on the need to protect and empower the most vulnerable groups.

Accordingly, the Authority is seeking to strike a careful balance between two complementary objectives: promoting the growth of financial activities by expanding access to financing and fostering innovation and competition, and protecting market participants to ensure that the desired growth is achieved in a responsible and sustainable manner without exposing customers to risks or burdens beyond their capacity.The meeting also addressed the FRA’s efforts to enhance the efficiency of companies and broaden the scope of risk management beyond credit risk to include market and operational risks.

Azam noted that Basel III standards are set to be applied to the non-banking finance sector starting next January. He also referred to a recently issued decision establishing controls for underwriting and pricing credit and guarantee insurance policies, including clear standards and stringent controls for developing reinsurance and risk-management policies.

The meeting further reviewed developments presenting promising investment opportunities, as well as the latest and upcoming offerings on the Egyptian Exchange, particularly those involving state-owned companies targeted for listing under the State Ownership Policy Document.It also highlighted the FRA’s role in building the capacities of employees of these companies and training them on the practical requirements for moving from temporary to permanent listing, including corporate governance, disclosure and transparency requirements.Azam also referred to ongoing preparations to launch short selling, stressing the importance of making the mechanism available alongside margin trading to improve price discovery, boost trading activity and attract new categories of investors, particularly foreign and young investors.

He noted that this development complements the launch of the financial derivatives market last March and the recent regulation of hedge fund activities, representing an integrated path toward modernizing the capital market under rules that ensure transparency and sound governance while protecting the rights of all parties.It is worth noting that the number of newly registered investors on the Egyptian Exchange exceeded 171,000 by the end of the second quarter of the current year, while trading values surpassed LE 6.4 trillion, an increase of approximately 78.3 percent compared with the second quarter of last year.

Meanwhile, investment funds recorded a 14.7-percent increase in net asset value by the end of the second quarter of the current year, reaching LE 471 billion across 224 funds.The number of fund units rose to 44 billion, with individuals accounting for 75 percent of the total, indicating growing confidence in investment funds as one of the key investment instruments in Egypt in recent months.

World.title: President al-Sisi heads to Korea at start of Asian Tour
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi will travel to the Republic of Korea on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, as the first leg of his Asian tour that will also include Malaysia and Indonesia.

The tour will begin with a state visit to the Republic of Korea, where President Sisi will hold talks with President of the Republic of Korea Lee Jae Myung, according to Presidential Spokesperson Mohamed al-Shennawy.

During the visit, the president will also participate in a roundtable with the heads and representatives of major Korean companies.

The tour will also include a state visit to Malaysia and a visit to Indonesia, the spokesman added.

World.title: PM reviews preparations for Egyptian energy journey session at Egypt Forum 2026
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly stated that the Egyptian Energy Journey session at Egypt Forum 2026 reviews the energy sector’s progress since 2014 through a comprehensive presentation of achievements, supported by figures, indicators, projects, and investments in electricity, renewable energy, and future expansion plans, alongside challenges and response methods.

Madbouly made the remarks during a meeting held to review the session’s axes, in the presence of Electricity Minister Mahmoud Esmat, Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk, Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi, and other senior officials, as part of preparations for Egypt Forum 2026 ordered by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to be held from October 19 to 24 at the St. Regis Hotel in the New Administrative Capital.

The Prime Minister pointed out that the session will also review the petroleum and mineral wealth sector’s progress during the same period, including developments in exploration, production, major discoveries, and efforts regarding foreign partners’ dues, stressing the need for the session to answer citizens’ questions and present future project plans.

World.title: Liberia: Jewel Howard-Taylor Indictment Uncertain as Lawyer Awaits Confirmation
World.content:
Judiciary sources expect a grand jury to indict the former vice president, but her defense says it has received no official word

By Willie N. Tokpah

MONROVIA – Uncertainty surrounded the case of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor on Wednesday. Judiciary sources said a Montserrado County grand jury was expected to indict her, but her lawyer said there was no confirmation that any indictment had been returned.



Sources within the Judiciary told FrontPageAfrica that the grand jury is expected to return an indictment against Howard-Taylor as early as today, October 7, 2026. The specific charges had not been made public as of press time.

Howard-Taylor’s lawyer, Attorney Gbawou Kowou, said the defense had heard similar reports but could not verify them. He said the defense was told that a first panel of special grand jurors failed to reach a conclusion and was disbanded on Monday. A second panel reportedly reached a decision early Wednesday.

“The second set reached a conclusion around 5 a.m. this morning,” Kowou said. “Again, we are hearing this from sources that we believe are credible. We do not have any confirmation to that effect at this point, but we are waiting.”

Neither the court nor the Ministry of Justice had publicly confirmed the grand jury’s decision as of press time.

What an indictment would mean

If returned, an indictment would move the case beyond the criminal complaint and the proceedings so far held before the Monrovia City Court and Criminal Court “C.”

The Ministry of Justice has charged Howard-Taylor with unlicensed importation of a controlled drug or substance. She is also charged with unlicensed sale, distribution, transit and transportation of a controlled substance, and illicit trafficking. Additional counts include criminal solicitation, criminal facilitation, criminal conspiracy and money laundering.

She was arrested on August 19 at Roberts International Airport, where security officers stopped her as she attempted to leave the country. She was then taken to Liberia National Police headquarters and held while investigators pursued the case.

4.2 tonnes of cocaine

The charges stem from a wider national security investigation into an alleged international cocaine network. Authorities have linked the investigation to the seizure of about 4.2 metric tonnes of cocaine, which they estimate to be worth hundreds of millions of U.S. dollars. Three foreign nationals have been charged in absentia in connection with the network.

Prosecutors allege that the network operated in Liberia and other countries. They also allege that Howard-Taylor had dealings with people accused of involvement in the trafficking operation.

Howard-Taylor denies the allegations. Her lawyers maintain that she is innocent and have challenged parts of the government’s case and the way the proceedings have been conducted. They have also stressed that a criminal complaint, an indictment and a conviction are distinct legal steps.

First female vice president

Howard-Taylor served as vice president from January 2018 to January 2024 under former President George Manneh Weah. She became Liberia’s first female vice president after the Coalition for Democratic Change won the 2017 presidential election.

If indicted, she would formally stand trial on the offenses set out in the indictment. An indictment is not a finding of guilt, and the prosecution would still have to prove its case before a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: He Pressed for Modad’s Exit. Now Witherspoon Says His Campaign Relied on False Information
World.content:
Spoon Network’s executive alleges that government insiders sought the former commerce minister’s removal, reopening questions about the controversy that preceded his resignation.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

MONROVIA — When public anger over a government vehicle engulfed Amin Modad, Stanton Witherspoon used his media platform to press for the commerce minister’s departure. Now, the Spoon Network executive is offering a different account of the campaign he helped advance: He says the information supplied to him was wrong.



According to an account of recent Spoon Talk appearances provided for this article, Mr. Witherspoon alleges that people within the Unity Party administration worked to force

Mr. Modad from office. He says he possesses recordings of discussions about the effort.

He is also calling for the former minister’s return to government, saying Mr. Modad brings “credibility and discipline.”

The reversal revives questions about a controversy that ended with Mr. Modad’s resignation in October 2024. It also raises a question about the public campaign against him: Was it driven by legitimate scrutiny, misleading information or, as Mr. Witherspoon now alleges, a deliberate effort by political insiders?

The material available for this article does not settle that question. The broadcasts and the recordings Mr. Witherspoon reportedly cited have not been independently reviewed. The alleged participants have not been identified, and the dates and precise contents of their discussions remain unknown.

For Mr. Modad, the reported remarks return attention to an argument he has maintained since leaving office: that accusations hardened into public judgment before the evidence received a fair hearing.

“I was condemned by the very public I was diligently serving and pushed to honorably resign,” he wrote in a Facebook statement supplied for this article.

The statement, titled “Accusations Are Not Evidence or Facts: A Lesson from My Experience,” describes his resignation as an effort to protect his family and reputation, remove a distraction for the administration and give investigative processes room to proceed.

At the center of the dispute was a vehicle purchased for his official use. Public criticism portrayed it as an extravagant personal benefit. Mr. Modad has disputed both that characterization and widely circulated descriptions of its price and specifications.

In his account, the Liberia Revenue Authority purchased the vehicle for the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and paid the vendor directly. He says the ownership documents named the ministry, and that the vehicle remained with the government after he resigned.

An LRA statement dated September 23, 2024, cited in the material supplied for this article, confirmed the authority’s role in the purchase and rejected accusations surrounding the transaction. Mr. Modad also pointed to documents and testimony presented during a Senate hearing as support for his account that the purchase followed legal requirements.

The difference between the vehicle as publicly described and the purchase documented before the Senate forms a central part of his defense.

Claims circulating during the controversy described a US$150,000 bulletproof vehicle comparable to one used by the United States president. According to the supplied account of documents presented at the hearing, the purchase price was approximately US$88,000 before taxes. Mr. Modad described it as an off-road vehicle intended to support work in rural communities.

“Our agenda was to make sure we take the Ministry to the people and supported the growth of Liberian business across the country,” he wrote.

His statement also challenged allegations involving a privately owned boat and a bank loan associated with Bella Casa Hotel. Those matters, alongside the vehicle purchase, formed part of his broader complaint that claims about his finances had been presented without sufficient regard for the underlying records.

The Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission examined his assets and financial records, according to the supplied material. Mr. Modad maintains that the examination and the Senate proceedings vindicated him. The underlying findings were not provided for independent assessment in this article.

Mr. Witherspoon’s reported acknowledgment shifts attention toward the origins of the information that drove the controversy, and the checks applied before it reached the public.

But an acknowledgment that information was inaccurate does not establish that it was deliberately fabricated. Nor does it, on its own, prove a coordinated effort within the government to remove a minister. Those allegations would require examination of the recordings, supporting communications and accounts from the people involved.

No response from the Unity Party leadership was included in the material supplied for this article.

Mr. Modad’s stated demand is for a standard of public scrutiny that gives evidence and a response their place before judgment is passed.

“We must demand evidence, hear both sides, allow due process to work, and give investigations the time and space necessary to establish the truth,” he wrote.

World.title: Liberia: LNP Seizes US$400,000 in Undeclared Cash at Cape Mount Checkpoint
World.content:
Grand Cape Mount County — The Liberia National Police has intercepted US$400,000 in cash during a routine security operation at the Tienii Checkpoint in Grand Cape Mount County, with authorities saying the money had not been declared at the Liberia-Sierra Leone border.

According to a release, the cash was discovered Tuesday, October 6, at about 1:52 p.m. during a search of a Liberian-registered vehicle, A53191, driven by Abu Toure, 58, of Brewerville, according to the police.

Preliminary police findings indicate that the money was not declared to authorities when it crossed the Liberia-Sierra Leone border.



Toure reportedly told investigators that the money represented proceeds from his cocoa business.

Following the discovery, police took Toure into custody and referred the matter to the Financial Crime Division of the Liberia National Police and the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) for further investigation.

The LNP stressed that the investigation remains ongoing and that no final determination has been made regarding whether any law was violated.

The police said the interception underscores the importance of security checks at border points as authorities seek to prevent financial crimes, money laundering and other activities that could threaten Liberia’s economic and national security.

The LNP commended officers assigned to the Tienii Checkpoint for what it described as vigilance and professionalism, reaffirming its commitment to working with relevant government institutions to combat financial crimes.

Authorities have not indicated whether the US$400,000 has been forfeited or what further action may be taken against Toure pending the outcome of the investigation.

World.title: Liberia: Partners Unite to Strengthen Accountability Under EU Funded Spotlight 2.0
World.content:
Monrovia – Partners implementing the EU-funded Liberia Spotlight Initiative 2.0 have taken a significant step toward strengthening accountability, learning, and evidence-based decision-making with the establishment of a multi-stakeholder Participatory Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting (PMER) Working Group.

The new working group was formally launched during a three-day meeting convened by the Programme Management and Coordination Unit (PMCU) from September 29 to October 1 at One UN House in Monrovia.

The gathering brought together representatives from government institutions, UNDP, UNFPA, UN Women, civil society organizations, the Civil Society National Reference Group (CS-NRG), the European Union Delegation to Liberia, and other key stakeholders.



The initiative marks an important milestone in efforts to ensure that programme results are not only tracked but also validated, understood, and used to improve the lives of women and girls across Liberia.

Jointly implemented by UNDP, UNFPA and UN Women under the leadership of the UN Resident Coordinator and funded by the European Union through the Spotlight Initiative 2.0 Fund, the programme aims to advance gender equality and eliminate violence against women and girls and other harmful practices.

Participants emphasized that achieving meaningful and lasting change requires more than reporting activities and outputs. It demands credible evidence that demonstrates whether interventions are making a tangible difference in the lives of women and girls, particularly those in rural, marginalized, and underserved communities.

To support this goal, the PMER Working Group will serve as the programme’s technical platform for strengthening coordination, accountability, learning, and results measurement. Through harmonized indicators, common methodologies, shared data sources, and standardized reporting practices, partners will be better positioned to measure progress and assess impact consistently across the programme.

Central to this effort is the Programme Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning and Knowledge Management (PMEL-KM) Plan, a comprehensive framework that integrates monitoring, evaluation, research, learning, reporting, accountability, and knowledge management. The framework operationalizes 45 programme indicators and provides a common system for tracking progress, assessing outcomes, and informing programme decisions.

Communities at the Center of Monitoring

A defining feature of the PMER framework is its commitment to participation and inclusion.

Rather than viewing women and girls solely as beneficiaries, the framework recognizes them as rights holders, leaders, and agents of change whose experiences are critical to understanding programme effectiveness.

Civil society organizations, community groups, and the Civil Society National Reference Group will play a key role in generating, interpreting, and validating evidence throughout implementation.

Participants highlighted several participatory approaches that will be used to strengthen accountability, including community scorecards, participatory monitoring visits, reflection and validation sessions, Most Significant Change methodologies, shadow reporting, and other social accountability tools.

These approaches are expected to complement routine monitoring by capturing changes in attitudes, social norms, relationships, service access, and lived experiences that may not be reflected through quantitative indicators alone.

Strengthening Data Quality and Trust

The PMER Working Group will also help improve the quality, consistency, and credibility of programme data.

Partners underscored the importance of maintaining high standards for accuracy, completeness, timeliness, reliability, validity, and traceability. Routine data verification, spot checks, source-document reviews, and quality assurance processes will be used to ensure that reported results are backed by credible evidence.

The programme will leverage existing platforms and national systems, including the Spotlight SMART Platform, EU OPSYS, GBV-IMS, and relevant government databases, while avoiding duplication and promoting stronger national ownership of data systems.

Given the sensitive nature of sexual and gender-based violence data, participants stressed that all monitoring and reporting processes must uphold survivor-centered, human rights-based, and do-no-harm principles that safeguard the dignity, privacy, confidentiality, and safety of survivors.

Tracking Progress Across Four Key Areas

The PMER system will support monitoring, learning, and accountability across the four strategic outcomes of Spotlight Initiative 2.0:

Strengthening laws, policies, and institutions to prevent and respond to violence against women and girls.

Promoting positive social norms and behaviors that prevent violence and harmful practices.

Expanding access to quality services and justice for survivors.

Strengthening the capacity and influence of women’s rights organizations and civil society groups to advance gender equality.

Together, these focus areas contribute to the programme’s broader vision of a Liberia where women and girls can live free from violence, fully exercise their rights, and participate equally in all aspects of society.

From Evidence to Action

While the PMER Working Group will provide technical leadership on monitoring, evaluation, learning, reporting, and data quality assurance, it will complement existing programme governance structures rather than

replace them. The PMCU will continue to oversee programme coordination and reporting.

Participants noted that the value of monitoring and evaluation lies not in producing reports, but in using evidence to improve decisions, identify challenges, adapt strategies, and capture lessons that can strengthen implementation.

Through structured learning and knowledge-sharing processes, Spotlight Initiative 2.0 aims to transform evidence and experience into practical solutions that benefit communities, government institutions, implementing partners, and the wider Spotlight Initiative network.

As implementation advances, partners reaffirmed their commitment to ensuring that accountability, evidence, learning, and action remain closely connected, helping deliver measurable and lasting progress toward safer, more equitable, and more empowered lives for women and girls across Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-President Sirleaf Admits Her Government Failed to Defeat Corruption, Says Menace Persists
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has made a candid admission that her administration failed to defeat corruption in Liberia, acknowledging that despite extensive institutional reforms during her 12-year presidency, the menace remains deeply entrenched and continues to confront the country today.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

“We did not succeed,” Sirleaf said Tuesday while delivering the keynote address at a Governance Commission symposium on good governance in Monrovia. The event marks the inaugural ceremony marking October as Liberia’s Month of Good Governance, an initiative declared by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.



The former president said she wished her administration had won the fight against corruption but conceded that its efforts fell short.

“I wish that I could, with all these efforts, have won the corruption fight. We did not. And we are facing the same thing today,” she said.

Sirleaf’s admission comes nearly two decades after she famously declared corruption “public enemy number one” during her inauguration in January 2006, shortly after becoming Liberia’s first post-war president and Africa’s first democratically elected female president.

She served two constitutional terms, leaving office in January 2018 after peacefully transferring power to then-President-elect George Manneh Weah.

‘Audits Were Published and Then Forgotten’

Reflecting on the shortcomings of her administration’s anti-corruption campaign, Sirleaf pointed to weak enforcement, inadequate funding for integrity institutions and the failure to prosecute individuals accused of wrongdoing.

“I have said so before, and I will say it again. Audits were published and then forgotten. Too few cases reached the courtroom, and fewer ended in conviction,” she said.

She also acknowledged that some institutions were given broad mandates without the budgetary resources required to effectively perform their functions.

Sirleaf said the experience taught her that establishing institutions and passing laws, while important, were insufficient to defeat corruption.

“Institutions are necessary, but they are not enough. Accountability without consequence will only be a report on the shelf,” she said.

According to Sirleaf, laws provide the framework for accountability, but their effectiveness depends on leaders, citizens and institutions working together to enforce them.

Reforms, But Corruption Fight Fell Short

Sirleaf defended the governance reforms undertaken during her administration, recalling that her government inherited a country emerging from years of civil war, institutional collapse and widespread public distrust.

“We inherited a nation that had been looted by the people who had lost faith in government,” she said.

She said her administration understood that sustaining peace would require rebuilding public confidence in state institutions.

Among the measures undertaken, she cited strengthening the General Auditing Commission and establishing the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission.

Her administration also established the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission and reviewed concession agreements signed during the civil war, canceling some contracts it determined were not in the national interest.

Sirleaf also pointed to the National Forestry Reform Act of 2006 and the 2009 Community Rights Law, which she said strengthened legal benefits for communities.

Through the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, she said Liberia became the first African country to meet the global standard for publishing information on what companies paid and what government received from the extractive sector.

Her government also passed the Freedom of Information Act in 2010, which she described as the first such law in West Africa.

The administration also secured relief of approximately US$5 billion in Liberia’s public debt, which Sirleaf said enabled the country to meet requirements for national reconstruction.

Yet, despite those achievements and the creation or strengthening of accountability institutions, she acknowledged that corruption remained unresolved.

‘It Starts From the Very Top’

Sirleaf said the responsibility for fighting corruption ultimately begins with political leadership.

“Accountability begins at the top, the very top, or it does not begin at all,” she said.

She argued that citizens are more likely to follow what leaders do than what they say.

“It’s not enough to make laws; enforcement is cardinal,” she said.

The former president stressed that public officials must lead by example and demonstrate integrity in the exercise of their responsibilities.

“It starts from the very top,” she emphasized.

She also called for Liberia’s integrity institutions to receive the full budgetary allocations required under the law, while challenging those institutions themselves to uphold the standards they are mandated to enforce.

Judiciary Must Enforce Its Decisions

Sirleaf also called for greater respect for the judiciary and implementation of court decisions, while warning against treating the courts as the sole solution to Liberia’s governance problems.

“The judiciary and our courts, yes, must be respected, and decisions rendered must be fully implemented,” she said.

But she added that the judiciary itself must be properly staffed with competent and highly principled officials capable of making decisions in accordance with the law.

“Waiting for the courts, waiting for the Supreme Court to take the lead to resolve the problem is not going to help us on this matter,” she said.

‘Exclusion Breeds Resentment’

Beyond corruption, Sirleaf used the symposium to place Liberia’s governance crisis within the broader context of the country’s history.

She recounted Liberia’s establishment by the American Colonization Society for the resettlement of freed Black people from the United States and the declaration of independence in 1847.

She noted that Liberia and Ethiopia were the only African countries to maintain their sovereignty during the period of European colonial expansion and the Scramble for Africa.

But Sirleaf said Liberia’s history was also marked by the exclusion of the indigenous majority from political and economic power.

She argued that the prolonged exclusion created resentment that eventually contributed to the 1980 military coup and the civil wars that followed.

“For more than a century, our Republic was governed and taught the school of loyalty, affirming the axiom that a government that answers only to a few will sooner or later serve only a few,” she said.

“This is what happened. Exclusion breeds resentment. Resentment bred the problems of 1980. And then 14 years of civil war that reportedly took 250,000 lives.”

She said the country’s years of militarism and civil war also destroyed infrastructure, weakened institutions and damaged Liberia’s democratic culture.

Accountability Is Not a Foreign Concept

Sirleaf rejected the notion that accountability and good governance are foreign concepts imposed on Liberia.

“Let us also be clear that accountability is not a foreign idea brought to us from outside,” she said.

She invoked the traditional Palava Hut system, where chiefs who abuse their authority can be challenged by elders and members of the community.

“Leadership is trust and can be withdrawn,” she said, stressing that public authority must be accompanied by responsibility and accountability.

For Liberia, she said, good governance should be viewed as a restoration of balance between government and citizens.

‘Freedom of Information Law Belongs to You’

Sirleaf urged Liberians to take greater responsibility for demanding accountability from their leaders and institutions.

She called on citizens to understand and use the country’s laws, particularly the Freedom of Information Act, as a tool for demanding transparency.

“To the citizens of Liberia, our Freedom of Information Law belongs to you as a democracy,” she said.

She also had a direct message for journalists.

“To our journalists, keep asking the hard questions,” Sirleaf said.

Analysts say her remarks at the Governance Commission symposium offered one of the clearest assessments of the limitations of her administration’s anti-corruption campaign, while placing responsibility for confronting the problem on Liberia’s current and future leaders, institutions and citizens.

Recognizing Sirleaf’s ‘Enduring’ Legacy

The event was convened by the Governance Commission in Monrovia and brought together government officials, diplomats, development partners, civil society leaders, media executives and governance stakeholders.

Alaric K. Tokpa, Acting Chairman of the Governance Commission, described Sirleaf’s participation as particularly significant because she was the first chairperson of the Governance Reform Commission, the institution from which the current Governance Commission evolved.

Tokpa praised Sirleaf’s political career and her role as Africa’s first democratically elected woman president, saying her journey from imprisonment to the Executive Mansion had helped challenge longstanding assumptions about women’s capacity to lead.

He also credited the establishment of the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Presidential Center for Women and Development with extending her influence beyond her presidency.

“Your leadership example and great legacy” should continue to inspire women and young people across Africa, Tokpa said in welcoming the former president.

He said the Governance Commission considered Sirleaf’s presence at the inaugural Good Governance Month event especially meaningful because of her historical connection to the commission and Liberia’s governance reform process.

Tokpa urged Liberians and Liberia’s international partners to embrace good governance as a requirement for national renewal, peace, stability and socioeconomic development.

He identified transparency and accountability, effective government, public participation and inclusion, the rule of law, justice, equity and decentralization of power as essential pillars of good governance.

World.title: Liberia: LSEZA Joins Africa’s Economic Zones Network, Eyes Investment, Jobs and Exports
World.content:
MONROVIA — For decades, Liberia’s economy has leaned on the same narrow pillars: iron ore, rubber, timber and, more recently, gold. Raw materials leave the country, and finished goods come back in.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Policymakers have long argued that breaking this cycle requires places where investors can set up quickly, operate under predictable rules and export at scale.



That argument has now gained a continental platform. The Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority (LSEZA) has secured membership in the Africa Economic Zones Organization (AEZO), the continent’s main network for the institutions that build and run economic zones. Authority officials say the move is designed to make Liberia West Africa’s leading destination for special economic zone (SEZ) investment.

A club of zone builders

AEZO is not a lender or a regulator. It is a peer network. The body was founded in November 2015 by Tanger Med, the Moroccan port and logistics complex that is itself one of Africa’s best-known economic zone success stories. It brings together the agencies and operators responsible for developing, managing and promoting economic zones across Africa, and it now counts roughly 80 members from more than 40 countries.

What members get is practical: a one-stop shop for information on partners and regulations, capacity-building, regional workshops and training.

Authorities that regulate and manage zones join as active members, with access to the full range of services and voting rights at AEZO’s annual General Assembly.

The scale of the network matters. AEZO has reported that Africa has about 203 active SEZs, with 73 more in development, spread across 47 of the continent’s 54 countries. Morocco, Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Kenya host the most. Liberia, a latecomer, now sits in the same room as the operators of those zones.

A long road to the starting line

Liberia’s zone ambitions are not new. The Liberia Free Zone Authority was created by an Act approved in July 1975, but it never transformed the economy. The modern framework came with the Special Economic Zones Act, adopted on October 9, 2017, which created LSEZA to oversee and regulate SEZs nationwide.

The law offers investors a defined package: special tax incentives, clear rights and obligations for licensees, developers and operators, the free transfer of funds from zone activities, and a one-stop shop in each zone for registrations, licences, permits and tax collection.

Yet for years, the Authority existed mostly on paper. Executive Chairman Prince Wreh has said that although LSEZA was established in 2017, it only became operational under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai. Wreh was appointed its first Executive Chairman in April 2024, followed by a Board of Directors. Since then, the Governance Commission has led a reform of the Authority’s internal structure aimed at efficiency, fiscal accountability and investor confidence.

Where the zones will rise

LSEZA says it is developing five potential zones, supported by land secured in six counties: Montserrado, Margibi, Grand Bassa, Grand Cape Mount, Bong and Nimba.

The most advanced concept is in Grand Bassa, where about 500 acres near the Port of Buchanan have been designated for export-oriented manufacturing, logistics and value-added industry. In Margibi, the Authority is pitching an “airport city” beside Roberts International Airport, combining residential, commercial, industrial, hospitality and recreational facilities.

The government frames the programme as part of Pillar 1, Economic Transformation, of its ARREST Agenda. The administration recently renewed its push to position the zones as platforms for investment, industrial expansion and employment, following a high-level engagement between LSEZA and the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs.

What membership could change for LSEZA

For a young authority with a limited track record, AEZO offers three things it cannot easily build alone.

The first is know-how. Morocco, Ethiopia, Rwanda and Ghana have each learned costly lessons about zone design, incentive structures and infrastructure sequencing. Peer exchange can help Liberia avoid repeating them.

The second is visibility. Investors scanning the continent for manufacturing sites tend to look first at countries already on the circuit. Membership places Liberia on that map.

The third is positioning under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). AEZO’s leadership has argued that African zones must connect quickly to global value chains as the AfCFTA takes hold. A Liberian zone that can export across the continent on preferential terms is a far more attractive proposition than one serving a domestic market of just over five million people.

What it could mean for Liberia

The promise is jobs. Liberia’s young, fast-growing workforce faces chronic underemployment, and SEZs are designed to concentrate the infrastructure, services and incentives that labour-intensive industries need. Spreading zones across six counties, rather than clustering them around Monrovia, could carry that opportunity to rural communities and ease pressure on the capital.

There is also the prospect of adding value at home: processing agricultural produce, timber and minerals before export rather than shipping them raw.

The caveats

Membership of a network is a beginning, not an outcome. Across Africa, many zones have underperformed, hampered by unreliable power, poor roads, weak port links and slow land titling. Liberia faces all of these constraints. Its zones will be judged not by declarations or affiliations, but by signed tenants, functioning one-stop shops, reliable electricity and the number of Liberians on factory payrolls.

Land is a particular sensitivity. Securing large tracts in six counties will require transparent engagement with host communities and respect for customary land rights if the zones are to avoid the disputes that have dogged earlier concessions.

For now, LSEZA has secured its seat at the continental table. The harder task, turning designated land into working industry, still lies ahead.

World.title: Cllr. Charlyne Brumskine Among Five Judges Sworn in at ECOWAS Court As Regional Bloc Chief Demands Impartial Justice
World.content:
ABUJA, Nigeria — Liberian lawyer, law professor and former vice-presidential candidate, Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, has been sworn in as a judge of the Community Court of Justice of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), giving Liberia a seat on the regional bench for the Court’s 2026-2030 term.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Brumskine was one of five judges inducted on Tuesday, October 6, at the ECOWAS Commission headquarters in Abuja. Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, Chairman of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, administered the oath of office.



Four other judges join her

The other newly inducted judges are Désiré Henri Aihou of Benin, Awa Bah of The Gambia, Henrietta Uzoamaka Didigu of Nigeria and Yaouza Ouro-Sama of Togo.

They succeed judges whose four-year mandates have ended: Ricardo Cláudio Monteiro Gonçalves of Cape Verde, Sengu Mohamed Koroma of Sierra Leone, Dupe Atoki of Nigeria, Gberi-Bè Ouattara of Côte d’Ivoire and Edward Amoako Asante of Ghana.

The new judges are expected to choose a president and vice-president from among themselves. Each will serve a two-year leadership term.

Chairman’s charge: impartiality and credibility

In his charge to the judges, President Faye urged them to uphold impartiality, independence and credibility as they take on the responsibility of administering justice in the West African bloc.

He said the judges must work to strengthen public confidence in the Court at a time when the region continues to face significant political, economic, security and environmental challenges.

About the Court

The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, headquartered in Abuja, is the judicial organ of the regional bloc. It is mandated to hear disputes over the interpretation and application of ECOWAS legal instruments and to provide judicial protection within the regional community.

Who is Charlyne Brumskine?

Brumskine was appointed to the Court in July 2026 for the 2026-2030 term. Her induction marks a shift from national legal practice and politics to regional judicial service.

Educational background

She is a graduate of Columbia University and the Howard University School of Law in Washington, D.C. That training laid the groundwork for a career built on constitutional law, gender rights and governance reform.

Career in law

Brumskine is the founder and managing attorney of CMB Law Group, LLC, a law firm based in Monrovia. She has practiced as an attorney and advocate on constitutional questions, the rights of women and girls, and reforms aimed at strengthening governance in Liberia.

She has also worked in legal education, teaching law at the University of Liberia’s Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law, the country’s leading institution for legal training.

In 2022, she finished first in Liberia’s Supreme Court Bar Examination, a feat that made her one of the country’s most notable young legal professionals.

Through her legal and philanthropic work, she has promoted education for girls, expanded access to justice and encouraged political participation among women and youth in Liberia.

Political background

Brumskine’s political profile rose in the 2023 Liberian general election, when she served as vice-presidential candidate of the Collaborating Political Parties (CPP), running alongside standard bearer Alexander B. Cummings.

Her political roots run through her family. She is the daughter of Charles Brumskine, founder of the Liberty Party and a former President pro tempore of the Liberian Senate. She later became involved in Liberty Party affairs, particularly during the party’s internal leadership dispute.

A new chapter

Her appointment places a Liberian jurist on a court that plays a central role in protecting rights and interpreting the legal framework of the West African community. It comes as Liberia continues to engage more closely with regional institutions on governance, human rights, rule of law and justice.

For Brumskine, the new assignment moves her from national legal practice and politics to a broader regional judicial role, alongside judges responsible for advancing the rule of law across West Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Expelled Montserrado District 10 Lawmaker Who Vowed Never to Beg Pres. Boakai Now Calls for Reconciliation
World.content:
Liberians who have watched him for years know better than to bet on the obvious. This is a man who has been an ally, a critic, an exile from his own seat and a mystery, sometimes within the same year. Whether Sunday brings a handshake, a new fight or a surprise nobody has predicted, the oath is the part the country will remember

MONROVIA — In Liberian public life, a man’s word is currency, and a man’s oath is something close to a mortgage on his name. Yekeh Kolubah took out a heavy one. Now, with a press conference set for October 11, the expelled lawmaker is being asked whether he is about to default.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

‘The Street General’



Long before he held a legislative seat, Kolubah was a man of the street. His brand was never polish. It was volume, defiance and the ability to put a crowd where he wanted it. Politicians courted him for that reason, and none more usefully than Joseph Boakai.

By Kolubah’s own telling, the call came from Boakai’s farm. Former President George Weah was about to announce a political movement, and Boakai wanted the street answered. “Yekeh, you need to get into the streets,” Kolubah recalls being told. He says he went, and in 2023 he helped carry Boakai and the Unity Party past Weah.

Then, he says, the favor was forgotten. “Today, they have turned around and made me their enemy,” he complained in remarks he made while still in the House. He claimed that people who had worked with him were told to “go and support Joseph Boakai,” and he asked a question that has hung over the feud ever since: “Does President Joseph Boakai even know my true value?”

A quick turn

The honeymoon was short. Within four months of the new government taking office, Kolubah had become one of its loudest critics, accusing it of failing to fight corruption and repeating the vices it had condemned under Weah. The ruling establishment came to see him as a nemesis. The opposition, especially members of Weah’s Congress for Democratic Change, embraced him.

He then did something few expected: he publicly apologized to Weah, saying he had not known Boakai was “more corrupt.” He promised to help ensure that Boakai and the Unity Party do not win in 2029. It was the language of a man not just leaving a political marriage but burning the house down behind him.

April 17

Almost three years into his second term, the House voted. On April 17, 2026, 49 lawmakers expelled Kolubah, following controversy over remarks attributed to him about the Liberia-Guinea border dispute. It remains one of the most debated decisions of the 55th Legislature.

For Kolubah, the explanation was never about a border. He blamed Boakai for using the Legislature to engineer his removal, and the opposition backed that reading, calling it punishment for criticizing the presidency. Government officials rejected it flatly, saying he was removed for wrongdoing. Kolubah took the fight to the Supreme Court, where the full bench has yet to rule and his District 10 seat remains vacant.

The word “delete”

Expulsion did not soften him. After appearing before the Supreme Court on April 29, he told reporters he would “delete” President Boakai. He never said what he meant or what he planned to do. He also called Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Koung “former leaders,” as though the offices had already changed hands.

Then he went on the road. He toured almost all of Liberia’s 15 counties, and along the way he was widely reported to have sworn the oath that now defines the story: that the day he reconciles with Boakai, it is he who killed his mother. The exact wording has circulated in different versions, but the weight of it is not in dispute. In Liberian culture, few vows go deeper.

The turn

Then, three weeks before his announced return, a Facebook post from his media consultant said the former lawmaker was set to reconcile with the President. It cited his frustration with the “disintegration and unseriousness” of the opposition. His PRO, Samson Moseray, reportedly confirmed that a meeting with Boakai was being planned, saying Kolubah had chosen to “mend fences and put Liberia first.”

Kolubah fed the speculation by promising to return to the country on October 10 and address the media. It was classic Kolubah: a date, a stage and a mystery.

Two interviews, two moods

His two interviews this week offered very different readings. On Sunday, the Spoon TV show asked him bluntly whether he was coming home to beg the President for forgiveness. Kolubah’s opening line was that he regrets his relationship with Boakai. Peacemakers rarely begin that way, and that there was little softening as the conversation went on. On the border dispute, Kolubah did not retreat, maintaining that the land Liberia occupies belongs to Guinea.

On Tuesday, before appearing on OK FM’s Morning Rush, he posted his message. “There is nothing wrong with reconciliation,” it began. It spoke of division as one of the reasons the country remains where it is, of healthcare, roads, infrastructure and education, and of choosing “peace, dialogue, and national development over division.” It did not name Boakai.

On the program, host Clarence Jackson asked whether he was ready to reconcile with the President. “Anything is possible in this world,” Kolubah said. Asked about the oath, he deflected: “Wait for the press conference on Sunday, October 11, and see the outcome.”

Nothing is settled. No agreement has been made public, and the President has not given his account of any talks. All that is known is that on October 11, Kolubah has promised to speak.

Liberians who have watched him for years know better than to bet on the obvious. This is a man who has been an ally, a critic, an exile from his own seat and a mystery, sometimes within the same year. Whether Sunday brings a handshake, a new fight or a surprise nobody has predicted, the oath is the part the country will remember.

World.title: Chinsali MP denies poll irregularities
World.content:
Chinsali Member of Parliament, Chanda Mwansa has denied all allegations of violence, vote buying and electoral malpractice during the August 13, 2026, General Election.

Mr Mwansa of the National Restoration Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and first respondent in the Chinsali Central Constituency election petition, has told the Chinsali High Court that he won the seat free and fair.

Mr Mwansa was making his presentation before Chipata Resident Judge Charles Kafunda who is sitting in Chinsali to preside over the petition case.

This is in a case in which losing United Party for National Development (UPND) candidate Christopher Chiponde Mulenga has petitioned Chanda Mwansa as Chinsali MP.

Mr Mwansa denied claims that he or his supporters distributed pens and money to voters in exchange for votes, saying there was no evidence linking him to the alleged electoral malpractice.

He also denied participating in or causing violence during the election period, adding that some of the violence alleged during the proceedings was directed at NRPUP members.

“The elections were free and fair, and I did not participate in or cause any violence during the elections,” Mr Mwansa said.

A witness Violet Mtonga, a NRPUP agent told the court that she had no evidence showing that Mr Mwansa personally distributed pens or money to voters she served as an election agent and covered Mwaba, Lubwa, Choshi and Chinsali Day polling stations.

Ms Mtonga also told the court that there were few incidents of violence during the campaign period where the UPND supporter was removing campaign posters belonging to NRPUP.

Another witness, Mr Innocent Mulenga a NRPUP party official, told the court that he was not aware that Mr Mwansa was distributing pens or money to voters.

He also said that he had no knowledge of a grey Toyota Spacio allegedly used to distribute the items.

He told the court that Mr Mwansa had told them to avoid violence before, during and after elections.

Meanwhile, Harrison Phiri, a businessman and executive officer at delight radio station told the court that his radio station issued disclaimers before hosting political discussions, stating that the views expressed during such discussions did not represent the position of the radio station.

He said radio stations were required to operate in accordance with IBA rules and ethical guidelines, adding that the station had never breached those requirements.

He said the station had not received any communication from the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) indicating that it had breached broadcasting regulations or relating to violence.

Mr Phiri further told the court that media houses which failed to comply with IBA regulations and ethical requirements have been suspended.

Meanwhile, Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) Presiding Officer Kingsley Kabengele told the court that the election results were recorded on the prescribed GEN 20 forms and that the results announced were correct.

Mr Kabengele said the ECZ had not received written reports confirming allegations of violence at polling stations.

He further told the court that some election diaries containing relevant information were sent to Lusaka and had not been produced before court.

“The results announced were the correct results, and the Commission did not receive any written report confirming that there was violence at the polling stations,” Mr Kabengele said.

The court also heard that failure by polling agents or stakeholders to sign GEN 20 forms does not, on its own, invalidate election results.

The court has since set October 16 and 29, 2026 for parties to file their written submissions before judgement is delivered.

World.title: Tonse Pamodzi Alliance To Contest All November By-Elections, Fields Jean Kapata In Mandevu
World.content:
The opposition Tonse Pamodzi Alliance will contest every by-election set for 5 November, and has chosen Ms Jean Kapata as its candidate for the Mandevu parliamentary seat. The alliance also pledged to stand together behind its presidential candidate, Mr Brian Mundubile, and his running mate, Mr Makebi Zulu, both of whom it says are unjustly detained.

The alliance announced the decisions in Lusaka after a meeting of its leaders, on the eve of nominations.

“We have resolved that we are participating in all of the by-elections,” the alliance said, presenting the meeting’s resolutions with leaders of its member parties seated alongside.

Beyond Mandevu, the alliance will field a candidate in Lumezi North, where it said a candidate had already been chosen. It will also contest the mayoral seat in Mbala and seven other ward by-elections that require fresh nominations. Full details of those candidates will be shared on Thursday, the alliance said, with every effort now going into filing nominations.

The meeting’s most important outcome, in the alliance’s own words, was a resolution to hold the coalition together. “We have made an absolute resolution that the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance will be alive and vibrant, and we are going to move into the future with unanimity,” it said.

That unity extends to its leaders in detention. “We are going to bind our hands together and support our presidential candidate, Honourable Brian Mundubile, and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, who have been unjustly incarcerated, as well as all our colleagues that are behind bars,” the alliance said.

“We are resolute that we must rise to the occasion and try to do everything possible to save our country within the ambit of the law.”

Leaders from across the coalition, including representatives of the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the Forum for Democracy and Development (FDD), endorsed the resolutions. Alliance figure Mr Mwenda offered a message of encouragement to supporters going through hard times.

“Times could be hard and challenging, but if we keep pushing, there is light at the end of the tunnel,” Mr Mwenda said. “God is watching us, and this pain that we are going through will be over. We keep praying for our leaders in prison, and all those across the country that are in detention and going through a difficult time. Don’t worry, it shall be well.”

Mrs Chalikosa turned to one of the opposition’s costliest mistakes at the August general election. She told members and structures that the alliance was dealing with the problem of double adoptions, which she said had cost the opposition a number of seats.

“Now that we have come together, you see a more united front and a properly structured alliance, with Pamodzi, Tonse and Woza working together, so that we give you what you want as the people of Zambia and what you deserve,” Mrs Chalikosa said. “So please hang in there. We are all working together to sort out all our differences.”

The FDD representative carried the same message to the grassroots, addressing members of Pamodzi, Tonse, Woza and their partners. “This thing is all about unity, and unity starts with you on the ground,” he said. “Once we are united, those that are bent on dividing us will have no way.”

The alliance’s entry sets up a crowded contest in Mandevu. The Leadership Movement (LM) has already adopted former University of Zambia lecturer Mr Ntazana Musukuma for the seat, and Mr Nebby Manda for Lumezi.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) will receive nominations on Thursday for the by-elections, which also include 11 wards across the country. Polling is on 5 November.
