World.title: Florida poll: Republicans lead in the races for governor and Senate
World.content:
Republican Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in the Florida governor’s race, according to a new NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group poll, while Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is up by 10 points in her matchup against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon.

Donalds, a congressman from the southwest corner of the state, is at 48% in the poll, compared with Jolly’s 41%, in a race in which Donalds has had a commanding financial advantage. (That advantage is just inside the poll’s margin of error, but Donalds has the edge in most of the range of possibilities.)

Moody is at 50% in the Senate race, compared with 40% for Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who got into the general election after a surprise primary victory over Democrat Alexander Vindman in August.

The results come amid broad Democratic optimism about the 2026 elections, with public polling showing the party making races in some typically red states into competitive contests this year. This poll suggests limits to that apparent momentum in other places.

The poll also took a snapshot of the state’s hugely influential bloc of Hispanic voters, largely congregated in South Florida. In 2024, Donald Trump won Hispanic-heavy Miami-Dade County by roughly 11 points, a significant reversal in a part of the state that had long been Democratic-leaning. Joe Biden won the county by 7 points in 2020.

But now, Florida Hispanic voters — including large Cuban, Nicaraguan, Honduran and Colombian populations — appear to be swinging back away from Trump, even as other high-profile Republican candidates hold comfortable leads among Hispanic voters.

Donalds holds a 48%-43% lead over Jolly among Hispanic voters, according to the survey, while Moody is up 47%-40% over Nixon. Trump’s job performance rating, however, is underwater, with 49% disapproving of his job performance, compared with 45% who approve.

Overall, 48% of all Florida likely voters approve of Trump’s job performance and 48% disapprove.

Before Trump’s gains among Florida’s Hispanic population in 2024, Democrats had generally won the demographic in the state by comfortable margins. Democrats argue that recent special election victories in Florida show the party has already started winning back the Hispanic vote, in part because of Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy. Unhappiness with prices and the cost of living has also affected Trump’s ratings among Hispanic voters.

“In legislative races in Florida, we have seen huge swings,” Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NBC News last week, speaking of the committee’s efforts in Florida House races. She said that on immigration, Trump and his party broke a promise “to go after the worst of the worst.”

By far the most important issue identified was inflation and the cost of living, with 30% saying it is likeliest to influence their votes. In both the overall sample and the sample of Hispanic voters, “direction of the state or country” (17%) was the second most important issue. The broader polling data put “immigration enforcement” as the third most important issue (16%), while the Hispanic sample put property taxes (13%) as the third most important issue. Immigration enforcement was the fourth most important issue among Hispanic voters (12%).

Questions about the Trump administration’s push to allow local and state policy to cooperate with federal immigration officials fell along party lines.

Among all voters, 85% of Republicans support the policy, compared with 18% of Democrats and 44% of those identified as independent voters who supported the harsher immigration enforcement tactics.

Property taxes have also been front and center in Florida during the midterms.

The state Republican Party and term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis support a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would increase property tax exemptions to the first $250,000 of a home’s value by 2028. The exemption cap is currently $50,000.

In the poll of all Florida voters, 55% back the amendment, 26% oppose it, and 19% are undecided. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of Republicans supported the idea, compared with 36% for Democrats and 43% for independents.

The overall survey questioned 625 registered voters, all of whom said they were likely to vote in the November elections. They were interviewed over the telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. from Sept. 28 to Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The same time frame and methods were used to survey 400 Hispanic registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.

World.title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson clash over Trump and seniority in Maine’s first Senate debate
World.content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.

Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV.

“It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.”

Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration.

She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.”

“I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said.

Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited.

In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader, Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events.

Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024.

Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority.

Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate.

Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade.

“In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said.

Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.”

Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature.

Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats.

Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts.

That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid.

“He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund.

Jackson doubled down.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate.

When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.”

Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration.

In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well.

“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.”

World.title: Republican John James seeks some distance from Trump in Michigan governor debate
World.content:
Republican Rep. John James on Tuesday sought to put some daylight between himself and President Donald Trump as he debated his opponent in the Michigan governor’s race.

Democratic nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, repeatedly tried to tie James to Trump during the hourlong showdown, saying he had failed to stand up to Trump and wouldn’t do so as governor, either.

James, who was boosted by Trump’s endorsement in his GOP primary campaign, pointed to the Iran war and tariff policy as issues over which he has disagreements with Trump.

“I’ve stood up to the president many times. I’ve said that I can agree with the president without worshipping him. I can disagree without attacking him, and I always put Michigan first,” James said.

James said he believed the conflict in Iran needed to end “quickly, as in yesterday,” echoing comments he made last month. James, who has voted against several resolutions in the House that sought to end the Iran war, also said he wants to “use whatever checks and balance power that we have to bring this war to a swift conclusion.”

His comments in his first debate with Benson in the key battleground state come as polls show voters nationally continuing to sour on Trump’s handling of the Iran war and the cost of living as the midterm elections draw closer.

Benson attacked James for voting against the Iran war powers resolutions while blaming high gas prices on the conflict.

“I struggle with that vote,” James said of the war powers resolutions votes. “I’m a combat veteran. I have been to war. She has not. I understand what war means, and so I voted to protect the troops and to fund them while they were in harm’s way.”

Benson pointed out that her husband served in the Army.

“Military spouses serve also, congressman,” she said.

Benson sought to link James to Trump’s tariff agenda, saying she dubs them the “John James tax,” while James said he had pushed back on the Trump administration’s tariffs against Canada.

“I’ve actually called out the administration specifically, talking with the trade ambassador and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children and negotiate a reciprocal, fair and mutually beneficial arrangement to make sure that we can bring our jobs back and protect our industry,” James said.

James, who promised in July to “back law enforcement, end sanctuary city policies” and “cooperate with federal immigration authorities to remove criminal illegal immigrants,” seemed to soften that stance Tuesday, saying he does not see a need for ICE presence in Michigan.

“We’re going to be cooperating with federal law enforcement as well as our communities. We’re going to make sure that we’re prioritizing violent offenders, and we’re going to make sure that we enforce the law,” he said. “Frankly, I don’t believe we’re going to need ICE presence in the state of Michigan, because we are going to be enforcing the law.”

James tried to tie Benson’s record to that of term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

Asked by moderator Rick Albin of NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids to point to a decision about which Whitmer did not listen to Michiganders, Benson did not cite a specific policy but said, “Where I think we need to listen to the people ... is a way to improve our Department of Health and Human Services.”

The candidates also clashed over data centers amid a growing public backlash to them, each accusing the other of profiting from them. Benson accused James of having voted for policies friendly to data centers while holding stocks in them, and James accused Benson’s family of profiting from one center’s construction. Benson denied that her family had profited from them, while James said any data center-related stocks he owns were held in broad mutual funds.

The nationally watched Michigan Senate race, in which the Democratic candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, is running against GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers, did not come up Tuesday. Republicans in particular have been eager to tie El-Sayed, a progressive, to other Democratic candidates in competitive races.

Neither candidate mentioned that race or tried to tie the other to either Senate nominee.

Democrats are looking to keep Michigan’s governorship in their party’s hands after Whitmer’s two terms in office. Trump carried the state by just over 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election. NBC News characterizes the race as leaning toward Democrats.

Benson and James are scheduled to debate again on Oct. 15.

World.title: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
World.content:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia, taking aim at each other on economic issues, data centers and President Donald Trump.

Public polls show Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden administration official, and Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, locked in a close race four weeks out from Election Day, with early voting kicking off next week.

The hourlong, town-hall-style debate was largely civil, featuring live and taped questions from voters. Jackson frequently ripped his opponent over her record as mayor, while Bottoms attacked his praise of Trump.

“My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on,” Bottoms said in response to a question about the Trump administration’s cuts to federal funding.

“I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” she continued.

Jackson responded, “I don’t owe anybody anything,” and said, “Nobody’s ever told me what to do.”

He then invoked Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular, term-limited governor — the first of multiple times he did so.

“I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said.

Trump endorsed Jackson’s rival, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the Republican gubernatorial primary. But Jackson still attempted to claim the MAGA mantle and leaned heavily into comparing himself to the president. Since winning the nomination in June, he’s backed off that approach and sought to link himself more to Kemp, who had also backed Jones.

Jackson took several shots at Bottoms over her tenure as mayor, accusing her of being responsible for regional inflation in the Atlanta area that he claimed exceeded national inflation rates and pointing to higher crime rates in the city during the Covid-19 pandemic.

“This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work,” Jackson said. “Bad mayors don’t make good governors.”

While the candidates were asked about housing and education, the event focused predominantly on economic issues and affordability, with both candidates repeatedly pressed about how they’d bring down costs. Both focused heavily on tax relief.

Bottoms emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state or local taxes on a raft of items, like auto insurance, groceries, hygiene products and diapers. Jackson reiterated his promise to cut state income taxes, property taxes and taxes on certain utilities.

Data centers and the controversial surveillance traffic cameras known as Flock cameras also took center stage.

On data centers, Bottoms repeated her desire to implement a pause on new construction. Jackson said he wouldn’t approve new construction as governor without first getting local community approval, establishing environmental standards and getting a commitment that local communities’ power bills would be reduced.

But the two sparred over the issue, as well, with Bottoms accusing Jackson of investing in data centers and Jackson accusing her of having approved building them as mayor.

Bottoms also said she wasn’t opposed to a moratorium on installing new Flock cameras, while Jackson said he was.

The issue of election security — which has hung over Georgia politics for six years — also came up.

Bottoms said she was “deeply concerned about Donald Trump’s rhetoric around our elections.”

Jackson, however, when he was asked whether he thought the U.S. Justice Department should be “overseeing and getting involved” in the state’s elections, deferred to Kemp again.

“I don’t think that’s necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it’s necessary,” he said.

Jackson has flooded the airwaves with ads, using tens of millions of dollars of his own money to outspend Bottoms 7-to-1 as of last week.

That disparity has worried many Democrats, who’ve seen this year as a prime opportunity to flip the governorship blue for the first time in 16 years.

Aiding Bottoms is the broader political environment in Georgia and nationally: Trump faces negative approval ratings and voter concerns about his administration’s handling of the economy.

World.title: Zach Lahn’s residency history and Rob Sand’s party come under fire in first Iowa governor debate
World.content:
Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand repeatedly returned to one topic in their first debate Tuesday night in the race to be Iowa’s next governor: questions about Lahn’s residency history in the state.

Sand, the state auditor, and Lahn, a businessman, met in Davenport as they run to succeed retiring Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds in an unusually competitive race for a state that has trended to the right in recent years.

Iowa has not had a Democrat in the governor’s mansion since Chet Culver was defeated in 2010, and Sand is the only Democrat currently elected statewide. While Sand has cast himself as an independent-minded candidate, Lahn labeled him a “radical liberal” and a “career politician” who supports liberal positions on taxes and immigration.

As the two men sparred over tax rates, economic growth, addressing the state’s cancer crisis and other issues on NBC affiliate KWQC, both repeatedly referred to the controversy over Lahn’s reported ties to Kansas, which include public records showing he voted there in 2018, 2020 and 2022 before he registered in Iowa in 2024.

Lahn responded Tuesday to reports that he still frequently flies to a second home in Kansas.

“I’m a sixth-generation Iowan. I live in Iowa today. I have lived in Iowa. Rob has been lying about this, and the issue is I have a blended family, and my kids split time,” he said.

The subject first arose in a conversation about education. Sand advocated for increasing teacher salaries and better oversight of the use of public funding, while Lahn called for stronger auditing of the school voucher system and limiting the program to lower-income families.

“I want to be the biggest advocate for public school kids in the state,” Lahn said.

Sand responded: “I don’t think you’re going to be the biggest advocate for public school students over a guy who sends his kids there. When you were running s saying that Marxists have hijacked the curriculum in Iowa, Zach, I’m pretty sure that that’s just more evidence that you don’t spend enough time in Iowa.”

Lahn called the attacks “the central lie of Rob Sand’s campaign.”

The controversy has been a drag on Lahn’s campaign, with Sand holding an advantage in public polling ahead of November’s election.

Throughout the debate, Lahn lambasted Sand as a “liberal billionaire” backed by his wife’s family’s money.

Sand’s wife, Christine, is the CEO of her family’s company, the Lauridsen Group, which owns several food and health product companies. Her family has donated more than $12 million to Sand’s campaigns over the years, having backed him since he first ran for state auditor.

Earlier in the night, the candidates were asked how they would address Iowa’s low economic growth rate and the question of affordability on Day 1 in office.

Lahn said he would prioritize homegrown businesses and make sure state government was “not prioritizing big out-of-state projects that are not employing people, like data centers.”

He did indicate he would support tax incentives for the White House-backed $15 billion steel mill project announced last week. He also praised President Donald Trump’s executive action loosening restrictions on tax-exempt “red dye diesel” fuel used for farm vehicles, which he said he proposed to Vice President JD Vance when he visited Iowa last month.

The rising cost of diesel, now $6.05 per gallon in Iowa, has been a major concern for farmers in the state, who have also felt the squeeze from rising fertilizer prices and tariffs, threatening the campaigns of GOP candidates in the heartland.

Sand called for a cap on utility fees, ending the privatization of Medicaid in Iowa, raising the minimum wage — which he has said should be set at $12 an hour — and importing prescription drugs from Canada.

Lahn wouldn’t commit to raise the minimum wage, which was last raised in Iowa in 2009 and is at $7.25 an hour. He said he would focus on industry deconsolidation and lowering taxes.

“We’ve had some great efforts to lower taxes for the people of Iowa, and Rob, you’ve opposed those efforts at every step,” Lahn shot at his opponent. “And so I think we have to be very honest here about where we’re standing. Rob is supporting the raising of taxes because that’s what liberals do: They want to raise taxes. I’m here to cut taxes.”

Asked to respond, Sand denied that he wants to raise taxes.

Both candidates made a point to address cancer rates in their opening statements. Iowa is one of three states where the incidence of cancer is increasing amid environmental risks associated with chemicals used by the agriculture industry, like glyphosate, PFAS and nitrates.

“Iowa is at a point where we are at the bottom for economic growth; we’re at the top for cancer growth,” Sand said.

Lahn cited “the fastest rate of new cancer in the country” as one of three issues that motivated him to run for office.

Lahn, who is backed by prominent members of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has made cancer rates a centerpiece of his campaign, frequently targeting the powerful agriculture industry. He called addressing cancer a “foundational question” and the “crisis of our generation.”

“For a very long time, we have seen the nitrate load in our water increase year after year,” he said. “We have to start to put in place real solutions.”

He voiced support for the state’s IWiLL program (Iowa’s Water and Land Legacy) to address water quality issues and high nitrate levels.

“I’m glad that Mr. Lahn brought up IWiLL and mentioned that he’s been supporting it and talking about it since he started the campaign. I’m glad that he’s been doing that,” Sand said. “I actually voted for it in 2010 because I lived here. You didn’t.”

World.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend
World.content:
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf and is expected to approach the U.S. northern Gulf Coast on Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Isaias would be the Atlantic Basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, which ends Nov. 30.

Maps show possible path

Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday before approaching the U.S. Gulf Coast the following day, according to forecasters. It is expected to rapidly strengthen.

"Hurricane watches will likely be required for a portion of the U.S. northern Gulf coast later today," the hurricane center said Wednesday. Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 45 miles from the storm's center.

The possible path of newly-formed Tropical Storm Isaias Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 6 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle.

Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.

Tropocal Storm Isaias is expected to impact the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News/Nikki Nolan

The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."

In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."

Beware the "I"-named storm

While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.

The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).

When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

World.title: Trump temporarily expands use of red-dyed diesel. Will it lower costs?
World.content:
President Trump's new executive order allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways is aimed at lowering costs for truckers and farmers grappling with diesel prices that remain near record highs. But experts say they are skeptical that the order could deliver sweeping savings.

"It might lead to savings for some, but there are a lot of details that will prevent this from having widespread relief," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News.

Mr. Trump announced the executive order on Tuesday during a midterm rally in Nebraska, saying the move will "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dye diesel for any reason."

Before the EO passed, farmers had to buy regular diesel for their trucks and on-road vehicles, which is subject to excise taxes, a White House official told CBS News in an email.

Now, they can use red-dyed diesel, which is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.

The EO comes as diesel prices remain high, although they've eased slightly after reaching a record high last month of $6.53 a gallon. High diesel prices are placing financial strains on the nation's transportation, construction and agricultural industries, which rely heavily on the fuel to move goods and power equipment.

On Tuesday, the national average for a gallon of diesel stood at $6.32, according to AAA, compared to $3.76 before the war in Iran started.

Read on to learn more about red-dyed diesel.

What is red-dyed diesel?

Red-dyed diesel is tax-free diesel intended for off-road vehicles, including farm and construction equipment.

The fuel is dyed red because it allows state law enforcement to easily spot it if drivers are using it on roads and highways in an effort to skirt taxes. Violators may face large fines or penalties, including tax evasion.

Mr. Trump's executive order temporarily removes the limits on red-dyed diesel, allowing all drivers to use it without incurring taxes or penalties. However, it doesn't entirely eliminate taxes on red-dyed diesel.

Instead, it defers the federal excise tax for the remainder of 2026 and directs the Treasury secretary to explore ways to eliminate the requirement to pay the taxes, according to the White House. That means drivers could potentially be on the hook for a payment down the road, experts said.

"Whether anyone who makes the switch to dyed diesel suddenly gets a tax bill is the most unanswered question I have," De Haan said in a post on X.

The White House official said drivers will be liable for the deferred tax only if the Internal Revenue Service, at the direction of the Secretary of the Treasury, takes action to enforce it.

Will the Trump administration's EO lead to cost savings?

According to a White House fact sheet on the executive order, drivers who rely on diesel could save more than $100 each time they fill up.

However, many states also have bans on using red-dyed diesel on roads and highways. The White House said it is working with states to encourage them to also waive the ban.

But if some states don't waive their bans, it could lead to a "convoluted patchwork" of enforcement, which may ultimately deter trucks that need to cross state lines from using red-dyed diesel, De Haan added.

"If one state is enforcing red-dyed diesel and a trucker crosses over with dyed diesel, that could spell trouble, and [lead to] enforcement issues," he said. "Most of the large end users that could stand to benefit from lower prices probably won't get much of the benefit behind this."

The impact on farmers will also be muted, given that they already get tax-free diesel in most states, De Haan noted.

"Most of them have thousands of liters that they've been buying at tax-free, at scheduled intervals, I should say, and so it's not really any huge advantage," he told CBS News.

The EO will allow farmers to use red-dyed diesel in personal vehicles, but it will yield only minimal savings, he added. "I don't think that any farmer is going to be jumping for joy at the prospect of saving, you know, 50 or 60 cents a gallon on their personal vehicle."

Fails to address the supply issue

Experts noted that the EO doesn't address the lack of diesel supply, the key issue keeping prices elevated.

"The U.S. has about 105 million barrels of diesel in inventory," Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News in an email. "This move doesn't increase or decrease that level."

In theory, the EO should still put downward pressure on diesel prices; however, swings in the diesel market could blunt progress toward lower prices, Kloza added.

Lowering prices without increasing supply could also stimulate demand, which could have the unintended consequence of driving up costs, De Haan pointed out.

"Part of the reason why we have these high prices is because economics is telling us that there are imbalances," he said. "So to ignore them and go ahead with this risks exacerbating the issue."

World.title: Space station crew returns home after eight-month mission
World.content:
The four people departing the International Space Station strapped into their Crew Dragon capsule and undocked early Wednesday, setting up re-entry and splashdown Thursday off the coast of Southern California to close out a 237-day stay in orbit.

With Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway at the controls, flanked on their left by European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and on the right by cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, the Crew Dragon "Freedom" backed away from the space-facing port on the forward Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time.

A camera inside the SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule looked over the shoulders of Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, left, and pilot Jack Hathaway, right, as the spacecraft departed the International Space Station Wednesday, on course for a Pacific Ocean splashdown Thursday to complete an eight-month mission. SpaceX/NASA

Sailing 260 miles above Cuba and the Bahamas, the capsule executed an automated loop over the top of the lab complex and slowly dropped away behind, exiting the safety zones around the station.

"We just wanted to give an enormous thank you to all of the team, our friends and colleagues on board the International Space Station, everybody in Houston, everybody at SpaceX, all around the world, with all of our international partners," Meir radioed as the Crew Dragon departed. "We have had the most incredible of expeditions ... and we will never forget it, and never forget all of your hard work."

After enjoying a final day in weightlessness, Meir and Hathaway will monitor a nine-minute and 20-second firing of the Crew Dragon's forward Draco thrusters starting at 10:46 a.m. ET on Thursday, setting up a fiery plunge back to Earth and splashdown off the coast of California at 11:34 a.m. ET.

Left behind aboard the space station were the Crew 13 fliers that replaced them — commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — who were launched to the station on Oct. 1.

Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 commander Pyotr Dubrov, cosmonaut Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They plan to remain aboard the station for eight months while Crew 13 is planning a six-month tour of duty.

In a brief ceremony Sunday, Meir turned command of the station over to Dubrov, saying Crew 12's departure would mark a "bittersweet" moment.

"We will be leaving our friends," she said. "But we know that we are going home to our friends, to our families, to all of our team members on the ground. So it's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us when one leaves a home like this up on the space station."

Prior to Crew 12's departure from the International Space Station Wednesday, the combined crews gathered for a change-of-command ceremoney so Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir could officially turn the lab over to veteran cosmonaut Pyotr Dubrov. In the process, they joined together in a group hug, or a "huggle," as Meir described it, with Meir and Dubrov visible upside down at bottom. NASA

She presented a symbolic "key to the space station" to Dubrov, who said "it's a great honor and a great responsibility to be the commander of such a magnificent place like International Space Station."

"It has a special meaning for me today, because 69 years ago on this day (Oct. 4) the first Sputnik was launched. Today is the dawn of the space era for humanity, and International Space Station is the greatest symbol of what we can do if we work together."

The combined crews then gathered in a group hug, or "huggle," as Meir described it, forming a circle with arms around each other's shoulders.

With splashdown Thursday, Meir, Hathaway, Adenot and Fedyaev will wrap up a 237-day and five-hour mission, flying around the planet 3,792 times and logging nearly 101 million miles from start to finish.

Meir, wrapping up her second flight to the space station, will have logged a total of 442 days in space, completing four spacewalks during the Crew 12 mission and three during an earlier stay. Adenot carried out three back-to-back spacewalks of her own, including one with Meir and two with Menon.

World.title: What younger women need to know about breast cancer
World.content:
"Survivorship starts at the day of diagnosis," says Dr. Eleonora Teplinsky — and for hundreds of thousands of American women each year, it's their new reality.

According to the American Cancer Society, 321,910 women in the U.S. will be newly diagnosed with invasive breast cancer in 2026. Rates of breast cancer are increasing across the board but the fastest rise is among younger women under the age of 50.

Breast cancer is also one of the most common cancers in adolescents and adults under 39.

While the mortality rate is decreasing over time thanks to earlier detection and innovation in cancer treatment, the increased rate of diagnosis is still a cause for concern.

This week on "Healthful," Dr. Teplinsky joined me to discuss why this is happening. She also shares the steps we can take to best protect ourselves and how to support loved ones through their fight.

Why are rates of breast cancer rising in younger women?

In Teplinsky's new book, "Beyond the Pink," she laments how some women are told "you're too young for cancer." But that's really not the case. Instances of breast cancer are rising 1.4% every year in women under 50. That's double the rate of increase (0.7%) in older women.

Teplinsky cites several possible factors as to why this might be happening. Diets high in ultra-processed foods and reduced physical activity are common in the United States and linked to higher breast cancer risk.

Environmental factors may have a role in increasing risk of breast cancer — but with little research to pull from, many doctors don't know how to advise patients on what to do to decrease their risk.

"There's a lot of interest in plastics and microplastics, things like parabens and phthalates," and how our exposure to them in the environment may impact women's risk for breast cancer, Teplinsky observed. "But these are all things that just don't have concrete data."

Then there are reproductive factors. Girls who start their periods at an earlier age are at higher risk for breast cancer in the future, as are women who have their first child later in life.

"Now, it's not to blame anyone for their choices," Teplinsky noted, but "it's what's happening in the breast during that extended time that the breast is exposed to hormones" that increase the risk, which needs to be paid attention to.

What we can do to lower our risk of breast cancer now

Teplinsky wants to make something very clear: "You can do all the right things and be diagnosed with breast cancer, and you can do none of the right things and not be diagnosed with breast cancer."

Cancer in general is multifactorial. A combination of lifestyle, environmental and genetic components come into play.

But while there is no sure way to prevent a breast cancer diagnosis, Teplinsky does have a few pieces of science-backed advice on what women can do right now to reduce the risk.

"Number one is eliminate alcohol," Teplinsky said, knowing "this is something no one wants to hear about." Alcohol is a carcinogen directly tied to causing cancer. "It can increase the risk, not just of breast cancer, but of multiple cancers."

Teplinsky also stresses the importance of incorporating some kind of exercise into your daily routine. She and I agree: "Movement is medicine."

Regular physical activity — ideally "about 150 minutes, on average, per week," as Teplinsky recommends — not only reduces risk of breast cancer, it also improves cardiovascular and bone health.

Limiting ultra-processed foods from your diet is another step anyone can take to reduce their risk of breast cancer. Teplinsky understands this can be a trickier risk factor to avoid completely. The American diet is rich in added sugars, processed meats and chemicals, and many ultra-processed foods are cheaper and more convenient.

"Can you make a small change? Can you swap out your soda for a seltzer? Can you add an extra vegetable to your plate?" Teplinsky suggested.

Menopausal hormone therapy and breast cancer

Millions of women with breast cancer are feeling left behind when it comes to menopause treatment. Hormone therapy has long been considered unsafe for breast cancer patients and survivors. Teplinsky encourages having a thorough conversation with a trusted healthcare provider.

There is a lot of nuance and it's an "evolving conversation," according to Teplinsky.

She says there are a number of factors to consider, like what type of breast cancer you have, what is your risk of recurrence, and when were you diagnosed?

There's also the personal preference. Teplinsky said some women "don't even want to think about hormones" while others feel like they have no other option and are "suffering" for symptom relief that could be found in taking hormones.

There is one type of hormone that Teplinsky says is safe for breast cancer survivors.

"Low-dose vaginal estrogen, which is local and does not get absorbed into the body, can be used in patients who have been diagnosed with breast cancer," Teplinsky said. "Vaginal estrogen can be used and should be used because it's life changing for so many of our patients."

Supporting breast cancer survivors

"Survivorship starts at Day One," Teplinsky said. She believes we should "zoom out" to care for the whole person rather than just the breast cancer diagnosis.

Supporting someone with a diagnosis takes a village. Healthcare providers, friends, family, and of course, the individual all play a role in fighting the disease.

"We find that social connection, being with people, finding your community really improves health outcomes" of women with breast cancer, Teplinsky said.

"Talking to people about your health, being proactive is so important," she added.

If the doctor finds something that deserves a second look, identifying the issue early can mean a world of difference in prognosis.

A large majority of Americans know someone who has breast cancer and there's an important role we can all play in our loved ones' lives.

October — Breast Cancer Awareness Month — "is a very hard month for survivors and thrivers. It can be really overwhelming," Teplinsky said. Reaching out, offering a listening ear or even just your presence can mean the world.

World.title: Oct. 7, 2023, Pearl Harbor and 9/11 echo the same failures
World.content:
Tel Aviv — With the first Israeli election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack just three weeks away, the country is grappling with conflicting accounts about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had warnings from regional allies that a massive attack was coming, even if there were no specifics on the timing or location.

Netanyahu has denied getting any warnings, and the fierce internal debate about it may be overshadowing a wider problem — with clear precedent — of overwhelming intelligence signals being misinterpreted or underestimated at the cost of thousands of lives.

Israel is not the only country to have failed to take action despite ample intelligence suggesting a catastrophic attack was imminent. The phenomenon has a name in intelligence circles: strategic intelligence failure. It happened 84 years ago at Pearl Harbor, and on Sept. 11, 2001.

Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu stands on Mount Hermon, on the Israel-Syria border, in a photo provided by his office, Sept. 9, 2026. Handout/Israeli government

Israel had in its possession Hamas' own secret plan for the attack a year before it occurred, according to Israeli officials. In the months and weeks before the invasion, Hamas both talked about it in public statements and shared videos showing them practicing for it.

In the hours leading up to the attack, Israeli intelligence agencies saw some Hamas leaders go underground and Hamas commandos gathering at different spots. Israel's domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, was alerted to the fact that Israeli SIM cards that had been distributed to Hamas fighters were activated — a sign of their imminent intention to cross into Israel.

A female Israeli soldier stationed at the Gaza border had warned her commander for months that she had seen Hamas operatives making apparent preparations for an attack.

Yet, on the evening of Oct. 6, 2023, Israeli military and intelligence officials likely never imagined what was about to happen early the next morning, when thousands of Hamas militants stormed across the border in pickup trucks, on motorcycles and even by motor-powered hang glider to rampage through communities and military bases.

"There was a lot of information. They just didn't understand it correctly," Shlomo Mofaz, a former senior Israeli military intelligence official who now heads the independent Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center, told CBS News.

America's intelligence failures

Before Japan launched its surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Pearl Harbor, as well as several other U.S. naval bases in the region, on Dec. 7, 1941, dragging the U.S. into World War II, there were signs of an impending strike.

U.S.-Japanese talks to avoid a clash had just broken down, and weeks earlier, the Japanese fleet had disappeared into the Pacific Ocean. Even as U.S. radar picked up over 180 Japanese aircraft on their way to Hawaii, American officers failed to understand what was happening.

In this photo provided by the U.S. Navy, the destroyer USS Shaw explodes after being hit by bombs during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, Dec. 7, 1941. U.S. Navy via AP, File

That's due in part to an overriding belief at the time among the top American brass that Japan was focused on battles closer to its borders, and wouldn't dare spark a war with the U.S.

Before the 9/11 attacks, U.S. intelligence agencies knew al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden was planning something. They had noted suspicious individuals from the Middle East were learning how to fly planes, but not land them. But they never connected the dots.

It was, in the words of the 9/11 Commission, a catastrophic failure "of imagination."

For decades, the U.S. had been concentrated on conventional threats posed by foes in a similar weight class, like the Soviet Union. Few had considered that small but determined terrorist groups like al Qaeda could cause such catastrophic damage, the commission said.

In all three cases, Pearl Harbor, 9/11 and Oct. 7, the stronger party failed to see that the weaker party wasn't deterred, but rather determined to keep fighting by any means necessary.

Israel thought it could contain Hamas while devoting most of its resources to much clearer and more potent threats, such as Iran and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, former senior Israeli security officials have said.

"Even when they understood that Hamas was going to do something, it was never in the dimension and in the force that they eventually did," Mofaz told CBS News.

World.title: Supreme Court wrestles with energy companies' bid to block major climate suit
World.content:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday grappled with a complex dispute involving an effort by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, to hold energy companies accountable for the effects of global climate change.

Eight of the court's nine justices heard nearly two hours of oral arguments in the case Suncor Energy v. Commissioners of Boulder County. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from the case, the Supreme Court said last week.

No reason was given for Alito's decision to sit out the case. His financial disclosure for 2025 shows that he had individual holdings in two energy companies, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Alito did not report holding individual stocks in either Exxon Mobil or Suncor Energy, the two companies that Boulder filed its lawsuit against in 2018.

Alito's recusal leaves open the possibility that the Supreme Court deadlocks 4-4 in the case. That outcome would mean the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court would stand, allowing Boulder's case to proceed.

Boulder's dispute against Exxon and Suncor remains in its early stages. At issue before the Supreme Court is whether the lawsuit can proceed or is barred by federal law. The high court also asked lawyers for both sides to address whether it has jurisdiction to review the Colorado Supreme Court's decision.

Demonstrators outside the Supreme Court building on Oct. 5, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Finn Gomez / Getty Images

In questions to both Kannon Shanmugam, who argued on behalf of Exxon and Suncor, and Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general, Justice Brett Kavanaugh repeatedly said that four of the Supreme Court's decisions dating back to 1972 make clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters of federal law.

"We don't have to reinvent the wheel, because we've said this multiple times and Congress, presumably when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this court's precedents establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal-law matter, unless Congress speaks otherwise," he said.

The Trump administration is backing Exxon, the nation's largest oil company, and Suncor, which operates two oil refineries in Colorado, in the case. Boulder's lawsuit, Harris said, "egregiously exceeds" constitutional limits of state authority.

"Interstate air pollution is an inherently federal area, and Congress hasn't authorized this suit in the Clean Air Act," she said.

But Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson stressed that the Supreme Court's review is "premature."

"It feels like we don't really know enough to be confident that the theories that you are proposing are actually applicable here," she told Harris.

Boulder's lawsuit against Suncor and Exxon

The lawsuit from the city and county of Boulder is one of dozens filed by states and local governments against energy companies in state courts that seek money damages for past and future harms that they allege are caused by the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which has led to global warming.

Boulder alleges in its suit that Exxon and Suncor's conduct has caused or contributed to climate change, which has in turn forced the city and county to confront extreme heat, larger and more frequent wildfires and damage to the ecosystem, among other issues.

The city and county raised several claims under state law and argued that the energy companies' production and allegedly deceptive marketing of fossil fuels has led to "unchecked" use of their products that has caused a rapid rise in the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

Exxon and Suncor attempted to move the case to federal court, but that effort was unsuccessful. The companies also asked the Boulder County District Court to dismiss the case on the grounds that federal law foreclosed the claims against them. When the state court denied that request, the companies asked the Colorado Supreme Court to step in.

The state's high court sided with the city and county of Boulder, and Suncor and Exxon appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

"It's taken a long time to get to this point, but it feels very positive that that effort that we started in this exact location eight years ago has gotten to the stage of going to the Supreme Court, and then hopefully the next step of having a full hearing in court," Boulder Mayor Aaron Brockett said after a rally in downtown Boulder on Monday.

"People care very much about climate change in Boulder. They recognize the existential threat that it provides to our society, and so people are very supportive of this lawsuit," Brockett added.

The Supreme Court's arguments

Shanmugam, who argued on behalf of Exxon and Suncor, told the justices during arguments that the Constitution and the Clean Air Act preclude claims that seek to address the harms caused by interstate greenhouse-gas emissions. He also warned that efforts like Boulder's to secure relief from the effects of air pollution undermine the government's control over foreign affairs.

Shanmugam called Boulder's lawsuit an "unprecedented effort" to use state law to regulate global conduct, which is not allowed under the nation's constitutional system.

"A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state," he said.

Shanmugam warned that if Boulder's lawsuit is allowed to go forward, 90,000 municipalities could file similar challenges and "have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers."

Chief Justice John Roberts, too, noted that if Boulder prevails before the Supreme Court, local governments in every state will file their own lawsuits similar to Boulder's.

"How would you think that will work out on the ground?" he asked Kevin Russell, who argued on behalf of Boulder.

Russell stressed that even if Boulder's case can move forward, more litigation over the specifics of the suit will follow.

But Roberts also said there are other instances where the Supreme Court has allowed state-court lawsuits involving issues with wide impacts to go ahead.

"There are a lot of familiar situations where conduct outside of a state has broad effects from other states and all that, and yet we allow state courts in a particular state to bring litigation that affects that, whether it's a mass tort sort of thing or maybe complaints about operations of the internet," the chief justice said. "I guess I'm not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we've allowed them to proceed in state court."

Justice Elena Kagan, meanwhile, said the case against the energy companies appears similar to lawsuits brought against tobacco companies in the 1990s and pharmaceutical companies in response to the opioid epidemic.

"This is chapter three," she said, noting that state claims against those companies could proceed.

But Kavanaugh said later that "this court has consistently said that air and water pollution are different in our federal enclaves."

Lawyers for Boulder city and county are urging the Supreme Court to dismiss the appeal on the grounds that it does not have jurisdiction. If the justices opt not to, they say the Colorado Supreme Court decision should be upheld.

"Since the founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders, even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere," Russell told the justices.

He also argued that Congress "stands at the ready" to intervene and enact federal law that preempts "unreasonable state laws."

"This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change; it merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct," Russell wrote in a filing.

He also told the justices that Boulder did not sue for emissions, which are regulated by the Clean Air Act, but over allegedly deceptive marketing and production, which that law does not regulate.

"It is not an effort to reduce emissions," Russell said. "Under our deception theory, they can continue to produce as much fossil fuels as they like and contribute to as much air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, as the market will bear when consumers are properly informed about the consequences of that decision."

A decision from the Supreme Court is expected by summer of 2027.

World.title: Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai
World.content:
Greetings from Lahore, Pakistan, whose high court offers an oasis for chatter and chai

Diaa Hadid/NPR

I'm always eager for an excuse to visit the Lahore High Court in the British-built quarters of Pakistan's second-largest city.

To me, the high court is a near-perfect specimen of British South Asian colonial architecture: Mughal in its curly arches that frame porticos, the Gothic detail that emerges through the red brick baked on the city's outskirts in pluming kilns.

Within, it's a sea of busy, flapping penguins: Pakistani lawyers in their uniforms of white shirts and black suits rushing between courtrooms.

They take a rest in the main square, all chatter and chai under the banyan trees that still shade the men and women of law.

Sponsor Message

It's a contrast to the wheezy, heavily polluted city. Lahore has far fewer trees outside its elite quarters — a signal of a broader crisis in Pakistan, where there's one standard for the masses and another for those who hold power.

For more Far-Flung Postcards, click here.

World.title: DIY fertilizer is a blessing as farmers face steep prices due to the Iran war
World.content:
DIY fertilizer is a blessing as farmers face steep prices due to the Iran war

toggle caption i Andy Higgins for NPR

On 12 acres outside of Lusaka, Kanangwa Newlove has built a paradise.

Shady fruit trees dot her fields. During the growing season, long tomato vines drape over trellises. There are tidy rows of corn, pumpkins and a local leafy green called blackjack. Eleven varieties of lettuce.

"I started taking vegetables to my workmates, and before I knew it I was supplying the supermarket," Newlove says. "It went on and on."

For many farmers, 2026 has been a challenging year. The Iran war choked off the Strait of Hormuz and dramatically halted international trade shipments — including fertilizers . Prices spiked globally. The effects were quickly felt in African countries, where smallholder farmers are often vulnerable to rapid changes in fertilizer costs.''

Sponsor Message

Newlove, however, didn't feel the pinch. For years, she's fertilized her plants with a homemade, fermented compost known as bokashi.

toggle caption i Andy Higgins for NPR

A solution from ancient Asia

With roots in ancient Korean farming traditions and popularized in Japan, bokashi is relatively easy to make. According to Newlove, it's also highly effective.

"We could now have a potent fertilizer —– organic —– which is ready in [weeks]. For us that was amazing," Newlove says. "It was a game changer, to be honest."

Bokashi has become so popular in Zambia, she says, that farmers now sell homemade bokashi compost at markets and swap tips on social media. The Kasisi Agricultural Training Centre offers bokashi training and often sends students to her farm to see it in action.

"[Zambian farmers] have been looking for alternatives — how to grow food but reduce costs," says Rabecca Mwila of the Knowledge Platform for Organic Agriculture and Agroecology in Africa . "Inputs such as bokashi have come in to provide a cushion for them."

Here's the recipe

For home composters, bokashi is a method of fermenting food scraps in an anaerobic environment — no oxygen allowed! But many farmers make a version of bokashi outdoors . Ingredients are often easy to find on a farm: leaves or crop residues, animal dung, charcoal and ash from a fireplace. Then, they add yeast and a source of sugar (molasses or bananas, in a pinch) to jump start the fermentation process. The mixture heats up as microbes break it down.

Sponsor Message

After a couple of weeks of fermentation, the concoction is buried underground near Newlove's crops, so it can break down completely.

toggle caption i Andy Higgins for NPR

"There's a lot of excitement from farmers because they've been able to testify that it's cheaper for them, and their soil is rebuilding," Mwila says. "They're able to see earthworms."

As climate change makes rainfall less predictable and dry seasons longer, Mwila says farmers are increasingly interested in inexpensive, sustainable options.

Many voice concerns about the longer-term impact of commercial fertilizers. "Because of the overuse of synthetic fertilizers and pesticides and herbicides, the soil is completely depleted," says Mwila.

Zambia once imported nearly all of its fertilizer. After global prices tripled following the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, finding alternatives became a matter of food security.

In addition to bokashi, the Zambian government has promoted the growth of its domestic fertilizer industry. Last week, a Chinese-Zambian conglomerate announced its intention to build a $1.5 billion fertilizer plant in the country.

Although global fertilizer prices largely dropped over the summer, including in Zambia, some fertilizers remain expensive in southern African countries, including Malawi, Tanzania and South Africa.

While the government subsidizes fertilizer, there isn't always enough to go around. Donald Zulu, a lecturer and researcher at Copperbelt University in northern Zambia, says that without subsidies — a farmer will pay about $400 USD to buy enough fertilizer to grow 2.5 acres of corn.

"It's quite expensive and out of reach for many smallholder farmers," Zulu says.

Do veggies like it?

Seeking an alternative, he started working with WeForest and local farmers to study how well bokashi worked on corn and cabbage in 2024.

"The results were very encouraging," Zulu says. "Bokashi echoed the yields of mineral fertilizer."

This suggested that small-scale farmers could use bokashi — which is cheaper — and grow a comparable amount of food. But to his surprise, the best-performing crops were planted with smaller amounts of both bokashi and mineral fertilizers.

toggle caption i Andy Higgins for NPR

"That's where bokashi becomes key in terms of helping farmers to be food secure," he said.

Sponsor Message

For farmers like Kanangwa Newlove, bokashi is less about the cost, and more about building a sustainable farming practice that preserves the land.

"Even when you're making it, you don't need to wear a mask because it's not toxic. There's no harmful chemicals," Newlove says. "So it's all just like a labor of love."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: U.S. moves long-range bombers from U.K. And, Israel allegedly warned before Oct. 7
World.content:
U.S. moves long-range bombers from U.K. And, Israel allegedly warned before Oct. 7

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

New information reveals that, over the weekend, the U.S. removed all long-range bombers from the British air base near where five men were arrested last week in a suspected terror plot. A U.S. official who is not authorized to speak publicly told NPR that the decision to abruptly send home a dozen B-1 bombers from Royal Air Force base Fairford was due to a "credible threat" from Iran, which potentially involved a drone attack.

toggle caption i Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

🎧 The war with Iran has shown that U.S. military bases, both at home and abroad, are now seen as more vulnerable, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. Iranian drones and missiles have targeted U.S. bases across the Middle East since the start of the conflict. For the past three decades, the U.S. has established these bases to protect its allies, but the rise of drone threats has changed this perspective. Now, the U.S. must defend a network of military bases — a task that is complicated and costly, Myre says.

Sponsor Message

High school students in France are blocking schools today, after hundreds of thousands of them marched across the country yesterday. They are joined by teachers, parents and labor union members. The movement, which began in a particularly run-down high school facing teacher absenteeism, aims to improve learning conditions and address inequalities in the French education system.



🎧 The French school system plays a crucial role in shaping the national identity, promoting the idea that anyone can achieve their goals if they apply themselves in l'école de la Republique, or the school of the republic, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. She adds that this concept is at the heart of France's democracy and vision of itself as a meritocracy and egalitarian society. Even elite public schools in Paris are joining the movement. French news reports show clashes between youth and police and cars, trash cans and schools burning. Initially, the far-right condemned delinquency, but many also saw police aggression. Critics argue that the government responded too late and then framed the issue as urban violence instead of addressing the students' demands.

A former head of Germany's foreign intelligence agency will appear before a federal judge today to face charges of espionage and attempted treason. Federal prosecutors accuse August Hanning of using classified information to brief a foreign intelligence agency. He served as the head of Germany's CIA equivalent for seven years from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors allege he shared sensitive political information for 12 years after leaving office. They have not yet disclosed who Hanning's alleged clients were.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Esme Nicholson says that categorizing Hanning's alleged actions as a major setback to Germany's security apparatus is putting it mildly. Prosecutors allege that a former aide to Hanning leaked documents intended for high-level briefings, raising concerns among Germany's western allies about the credibility of its intelligence agencies and whether their own agents have been compromised. This arrest coincides with a warning from Martin Jaeger, Germany's new foreign intelligence chief, that Russia is waging a "shadow war" in Germany through sabotage, cyber attacks, and disinformation campaigns. Nicholson says the consequences of this conflict are not only humiliating but also potentially dangerous.

As Israel marks three years since Hamas' surprise Oct. 7 attacks, new reports in Israeli and U.S. media say regional allies warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning to attack. Four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR that Netanyahu was personally informed about the potential attacks and his security agencies were notified multiple times in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023. Netanyahu has denied this, labeling the reports "fake news" and recently filing a defamation lawsuit against the news outlets that first published the information. He and his defense minister now warn that Hamas might attempt to attack again on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to Israel's national elections later this month.

Living better

Malte Mueller/Getty Images





Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Parental monitoring plays a key role in shielding kids from the dangers of social media and excessive screen time. Parents can empower their children to navigate the digital world confidently and safely by establishing clear boundaries early and having open conversations about online habits. Here are some ways guardians can help their kids use their devices more safely:

Sponsor Message

📱 Put the phone away during meals and bedtime. This will help protect sleep and reduce the risk of eating disorders.

📱 Apply rules around screen time to the whole family, including parents and guardians.

📱 Ask children open-minded questions about what they are doing online. Open communication helps kids feel comfortable sharing what they experience online.

📱 Establish early communication with children about cyberbullying, online scams, Instagram filters and privacy issues for their awareness.

On the ground

NPR

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

Morning Edition's Leila Fadel traveled to the battleground state of Maine to discover what issues are energizing voters. Maine residents could play a crucial role in deciding which political party controls the Senate. One of the most significant U.S. Senate races features Republican incumbent Susan Collins, who is seeking re-election against Democrat Troy Jackson. The race has been closely watched, especially after Jackson was nominated by the Maine Democratic Party after Graham Platner withdrew because of a sexual assault allegation. Listen to what has been happening in that contest.

Fadel was also on the ground with residents, figuring out what they cared about. Hear more about:

🎧 How the Trump administration's immigration enforcement has divided residents.

🎧 Whether Democratic policies and candidates are resonating, and why so many men voted for Trump in 2024.

🎧 How the economy and other key issues are influencing voters' decisions in the midterm elections.

Follow the reporting: Texas coverage airs Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, and Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in the Up First newsletter.

3 things to know before you go

NPR

The 2026 National Book Awards finalists are here, showcasing a diverse range of literary works, from nonfiction on the prison system to a novel about a patient navigator at a gender-affirming care center. Avengers: Endgame has reclaimed the number one position on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box office chart following its recent re-release in cinemas. It first became the highest-grossing film in history in 2019. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have earned the 2026 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine for their contributions to optogenetics, a field of neuroscience that examines the links between neuron activity and specific behaviors. Soon after learning of his win, Deisseroth spoke with Here & Now. (via WBUR)

World.title: Who will win the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics?
World.content:
Who will win the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics?

toggle caption i Kena Betancur/AFP via Getty Images

And the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics is … we don't know yet. That announcement is scheduled for Monday, and we'll be covering it here in the Planet Money newsletter and The Indicator podcast.

In the meantime, the week before the announcement is a great time to partake in a nerdy pastime: remembering all the amazing economics research that hasn't yet gotten a Swedish medal, and guessing who might get the world's most coveted wake-up call.

One quick note: The official name is the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. It's a mouthful, so we'll stick with "Nobel Prize in economics." Unlike the original Nobel Prizes, this one wasn't established by Alfred Nobel's will. Sweden's central bank created it in 1968 — a history we'll explore in a forthcoming episode of The Indicator.

Sponsor Message

Many factors go into choosing a Nobel laureate. Winners tend to be older, partly because the committee wants the passage of time to help them assess the candidates' impact on the field and/or broader world. Sometimes the committee picks research that speaks to the zeitgeist. Other times it's because of very technical work that has given economists stronger empirical tools to study the world.

So how might we make a guess? Well, there's one tool that economists love for making predictions: markets. Markets can aggregate the scattered information held by countless people, boiling down what they know about the world into a single number: a price — an idea famously articulated by economist Friedrich von Hayek, who, naturally, won a Nobel Prize back in 1974.

Those prices can sometimes offer clues about the future. For example, take the stock market. Many economists view it as a kind of giant information-processing machine. In this view, a company's stock price reflects the crowd's beliefs about that company's future profits. It can provide a kind of crystal ball. Although, of course, the crowd can be wrong.

[🎧 There is, of course, a classic Planet Money episode about this, and also about a cow.]

The same idea applies to prediction markets, which have really taken off in recent years. Instead of betting on a company's future profits, traders bet on whether a particular event will happen — say, who will win a Nobel Prize.

Sponsor Message

And, wouldn't you know it, there's a prediction market for who will win the 2026 Nobel in economics. There's just one problem: It's incredibly small, or as traders might call it, thin. Maybe economists are too rational — or too busy — to bet on something this unpredictable?

As of this writing Tuesday afternoon, Oct. 6, this prediction market for who will win the 2026 prize had recorded about $11,000 in trading volume. For comparison, Kalshi's main market for the 2024 presidential election recorded about $670 million — tens of thousands of times as much. That prediction market correctly favored Donald Trump to win the election.

With such little trading, however, this Nobel prediction market seems less like the wisdom of crowds, and more like the guesstimates of a small number of nerdy gamblers. As we sat down to write this on Tuesday, Oct. 6, we watched, somewhat frustratingly, as the market swung wildly over who was favored to win based on what seemed to be relatively small new bets.

But let's give this prediction market the benefit of the doubt and call it a starting point. It at least provides an excuse to explore some big economic ideas and methods and the people behind them.

By late Tuesday afternoon, we decided to stop hitting refresh. Ariel Pakes and Susan Athey were trading places at the top of Kalshi's rankings, with Robert Barro rounding out the top three.

Ariel Pakes: What happens when competitors merge?

Ariel Pakes is an economist at Harvard University who has made big contributions to an area of economics known as industrial organization. It studies how industries are organized and how that structure affects competition and the prices and choices of consumers. For example, how do prices and product offerings differ when a market is dominated by a single company versus many competing ones?

In 1995, Pakes, together with Steven Berry and James Levinsohn, published a landmark paper about the American automobile industry. The method they developed, known as BLP, helps economists figure out how consumers choose among competing products. Those estimates can help simulate whether a proposed merger or acquisition will raise prices, and by how much.

Sponsor Message

This isn't just an academic exercise. The BLP model has evolved over time, and antitrust regulators use these tools to estimate how a proposed merger could affect consumers — giving them evidence to weigh when deciding whether to challenge a deal.

Why has Pakes been leading the pack on Kalshi? Maybe it's because antitrust is hot right now, and his research speaks to the zeitgeist. Maybe it's because the empirical tools he's helped develop have had a considerable impact on policymaking. Or maybe it's because one high roller placed a bet with inside knowledge, or because they were like a Pakes superfan … We can't know. Anyways, moving on.

Susan Athey: Using machine learning to understand cause and effect

Susan Athey is the economics of technology professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business. As her title hints, she is a leading authority on the economics of digital technology, from the internet to cryptocurrencies to artificial intelligence.

Athey has been a prolific scholar. In 2007, she won the John Bates Clark Medal, a top prize for economists under 40 who make "the most significant contribution to economic thought and knowledge." The American Economic Association cited her contributions to "economic theory, empirical economics, and econometrics." She was the first woman to win the prize.

Since then, Athey has continued to tackle a wide range of topics. We previously cited her theoretical work aimed at designing a market that creates incentives to remove carbon from the atmosphere and slow or reverse climate change.

Athey also helped pioneer the use of machine learning — a branch of artificial intelligence — in economics. Machine learning is good at finding patterns in data and making predictions. Athey and her collaborators have helped adapt those tools to answer questions about cause and effect. For example, does a job-training program help workers make more money, and which workers see bigger benefits?

Sponsor Message

In addition to her theoretical and empirical contributions to the field, Athey has been an outspoken critic of her field's culture of bullying, discrimination, and sexual harassment. We spoke to her back in 2019, when the profession was reckoning with the underrepresentation and mistreatment of women amid the MeToo movement.

Robert Barro: Why expectations matter

Next up: Robert Barro. He's another economist at Harvard University. He, alongside Nobel laureates like Robert Lucas and Thomas Sargent, helped reshape modern macroeconomics around a simple idea: people and businesses look ahead, and policymakers have to account for that. Their expectations about future taxes, inflation, and government actions shape how they respond to efforts to stimulate the economy or control inflation.

Barro is particularly known for helping to develop a theory known as "Ricardian equivalence." The basic gist: if the government cuts people's taxes by borrowing, that may have a smaller stimulative effect than policymakers hope. That's because people anticipate that the resulting debt will eventually require higher taxes — and they may decide to save the extra money instead of spending it. Ricardian is a reference to the 19th century British economist David Ricardo. "Equivalence" refers to the idea that, under certain assumptions, taxing people now or borrowing and taxing them later has the same effect on consumer spending. That's because, according to this theory, people will save the extra money to cover higher taxes down the road.
