This idea has been hotly debated for decades. Critics stress that many households don't plan that far ahead, and those who are short on cash tend to spend the money instead of saving it.

Other potential winners

As we stated above, not many people seem to be betting at the Kalshi prediction market on the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics. And their rankings hardly exhaust the possibilities. Here are some other potential contenders:

Sponsor Message

Thomas Piketty and Emmanuel Saez: Tracking the rise of the very rich. Piketty is a professor of Economics at the Paris School of Economics. Saez is at UC Berkeley. The two did pathbreaking work on inequality that helped get us talking about "the one percent." (Check out our recent episode of Planet Money, "Middlegarchs are the new oligarchs," which touches on this research.)

Raj Chetty: Mapping the American Dream. If you read this newsletter, you probably know we're fanboys and fangirls of Raj. He's an economist at Harvard University, and he and his many collaborators have used massive government datasets and clever empirical methods to tackle some of the biggest questions in economics, including a bunch of work on how to revitalize the American Dream. (Raj Chetty has been a fixture in the Planet Money newsletter and podcast; check out: "Why the American Dream is more attainable in some cities than others"; "This housing program helped kids escape poverty — by changing who they befriended"; and "Affirmative action for rich kids: It's more than just legacy admissions.")

David Autor: How technology and trade reshape work. Autor, of MIT, is one of the most influential labor economists of our time. His research has helped transform our understanding of how technology changes work. He and his collaborators helped explain how the computer revolution contributed to growing income inequality. He also, of course, did very influential research on the "China Shock," which is still shaping heated conversations about the effects of free trade on the economy. (We've explored Autor's work many times in the Planet Money newsletter and podcasts. For a taste, check out "What if AI could rebuild the middle class?"; "Why economists got free trade with China so wrong"; "Are Cities Overrated?"; and "What the future of work means for cities.")

Janet Currie: Showing how childhood matters for the economy. Currie, an economist at Yale, has done a bunch of important work on how the conditions kids grow up in shape their economic outcomes as adults. Her research explores how disadvantages, from poverty to pollution, can have lasting consequences. And she's studied how various government programs can improve kids' health and ultimately their economic prospects.

Sponsor Message

Of course, some of these are our picks, and they're not listed on Kalshi. And newsletter writers, no matter how well-versed in the economics literature, don't have crystal balls. Nor do prediction markets. They merely aggregate information from a crowd of people willing to bet about the future. And, in the case of this prediction market, that crowd doesn't seem very big.

Stay tuned for next week's Planet Money newsletter for our analysis of who ended up actually winning the prize and why. If you're not already subscribed, you can subscribe here: npr.org/planetmoneynewsletter.

World.title: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry
World.content:
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize in chemistry

toggle caption i Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency via AP

STOCKHOLM — Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

Kagan, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai, 95 years old and born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science.

Sponsor Message

The so-called "Soai reaction" is named for the scientist's experiment.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.

This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.

The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

World.title: Over 1,000 children are buried at juvenile detention centers nationwide
World.content:
Over 1,000 children are buried at juvenile detention centers nationwide

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

When Veronica Spears read the letter, she began to shake.

"What's wrong?" her husband asked.

At the time, she said, she couldn't find the words to respond.

"The letter said they found out that my grandfather had a brother that was in a reformation institution," she later told NPR in an interview. "And he passed away at the age of 12. We never knew."

Spears' family is one of 16 that researchers with Georgetown University's Center for Youth Justice have linked to children who died at the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children in Cheltenham, Md. The center has been working since February to identify children who died at 40 reform schools and youth detention centers across the country, as well as any surviving family members, as part of its Forgotten Children Initiative .

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

To date, the researchers have identified the graves of over 1,000 children across 29 states. The largest burial site is located near the House of Reformation, now the Cheltenham Youth Detention Center. More than 230 Black boys were found buried in the woods across the street from the facility.

Sponsor Message

The small headstones are easy to miss, especially in the fall, when they seem to sink into the fallen leaves. A few pieces of trash from a nearby worksite mix with the leaves.

Chuck Copeland, Spears' cousin, hiked through tall trees and thorny brush one morning in late September. A pastor who lives about two hours away, he leaned in to read one of the headstones.

"He didn't count for nothing. He meant nothing to them," he said, grimacing. Then he read, "Thirteen years old from Baltimore, Mark Davis, 1885."

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

Established in 1870, the House of Reformation, where Mark Davis died, was the first juvenile detention facility for Black children in the American South, according to the Georgetown researchers. It was created to get Black youth out of adult prisons. Children as young as 5 years old were incarcerated for criminal offenses, as well as a number of non-criminal reasons, including being poor, homeless or orphaned, researchers found.

While there, the boys were forced to work without food and disciplined by white guards with a "brass-studded belt," according to a report from the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services. In the 1920s, the boys were leased to neighboring farms, with the institution taking most, if not all, of their pay. They were also forced to work in the reformatory's broom factory in conditions described by Baltimore City labor union investigators in 1926 as a "firetrap," according to the report.

Sponsor Message

The Georgetown researchers have not discovered why Spears' great-uncle, Arthur Hamilton, was incarcerated in the institution, and they have not found his remains at the burial ground. The family was told he died of tuberculosis in 1917.

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

Marc Schindler was a senior official at the Maryland Department of Juvenile Services when the state rediscovered the burial ground in 2024. When he went to work for Georgetown University, he continued researching similar sites across the country. His team has so far found graves tied to 40 institutions, from Salem, Ore., to Augusta, Maine.

Some of the graves are next to juvenile detention centers still in operation.

"I'm hopeful that in states around the country, people will step forward and we can see an appropriate response to what I think is unquestionably a national tragedy," Schindler said.

As states learn about these burial sites, some state lawmakers around the country have begun looking at options for restitution. In Florida, lawmakers established a $20 million fund for survivors who attended an infamous reform school that closed in 2011. In Arkansas, officials created a memorial to honor 21 Black boys who died in a fire at a correctional facility in 1959.

This year, Maryland lawmakers created a commission to research and identify all the children buried in Cheltenham. The commission, housed in the state attorney general's office, includes family members of the children, who will weigh in on the future of the site and how the state should make amends for how it treated the children at the reform institution.

"Understanding this history is tremendously important, but understanding how this history connects to our current practices is almost probably more important," state Senator Will Smith, who sponsored the bill creating the commission, told NPR.

Smith pointed to Maryland laws that result in hundreds of children being charged as adults every year. He said accounting for the state's past involves changing those kinds of laws. And this year, the state legislature took a step toward that goal. After more than a decade of pressure from advocacy groups, lawmakers passed Smith's bill removing some offenses, such as firearm possession, from the list of charges that automatically send young people to be tried in adult court. That change took effect this month.

Sponsor Message

Smith credits a trip the legislature's Black caucus took to the gravesite in Cheltenham with convincing lawmakers to support the change.

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

When Spears and Copeland visited the gravesite that day in September, they eventually reached a place where there were no more headstones. What's left are rows of gray cinder blocks — over 200, with no names or dates. Researchers believe Arthur Hamilton is buried somewhere in this part of the woods. Spears said she believes it, too.

"I don't have any proof, no," she said, placing her hand over her chest. "I felt it in my chest. I felt a heaviness. I knew then he was crying out to all of us — they all were — to let us know we're here and we were mistreated."

She pursed her lips and looked at the ground. After a while, Spears, Copeland and other family members gathered in a circle among the cinder blocks. They were all silent until Copeland, the pastor, began speaking. He lamented the history he was taught. The history he was not taught. The betrayal he feels.

"The first thing I learned in school to memorize was the Pledge of Allegiance," he said. Then he raised his hands, gesturing toward the graves around him. "Liberty and justice for all." He shook his head as his hands landed with a thud at his sides.

After another moment of silence, Copeland led the family in a prayer.

"Thank you for this opportunity to remember our uncle Arthur Hamilton," he said.

Copeland said he wants the children to know they aren't forgotten anymore.

World.title: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
World.content:
An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot

toggle caption i Rebecca Blackwell/AP

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu.

The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.

"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.

Sponsor Message

"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.

The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.

"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."

Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.

It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.

"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger, a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.

Sponsor Message

So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.

"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley, a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."

But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.

"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.

The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

World.title: 'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills
World.content:
'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills

toggle caption i Paul Sancya/AP

Christina Starks-Clay doesn't know how "Medicare for All" would work exactly, but she's willing to bet it'd be better than what she has now.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

While standing in line for a Sept. 11 town hall for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, she whipped out her phone and pulled up a screenshot.

It was of the $1,000 cashier's check she'd picked up at the bank that day to pay down a chunk of her son's dental bills.

Starks-Clay, an early childhood special education paraprofessional, still owed the dentist $389, even with good dental insurance. Her own cleaning a few weeks before had cost $600.

She tried to talk herself down at the bank, to focus on being grateful for what she could afford.

Sponsor Message

"I'm like, 'Tina, OK, you were in a position for this moment to do this,'" she said. "A lot of people couldn't do what I had to do today. I couldn't do it. But I did it. So I need to hear, how are you going to make this better for everyone?"

toggle caption i Kate Wells



/KFF Health News

Many who waited in the hot sun that afternoon in a line stretching blocks through downtown Lansing shared similar anxieties.

A man ahead of Starks-Clay talked about watching his brother rack up thousands of dollars in medical debt.

A professor emeritus at nearby Michigan State University worried aloud about his grandkids' medical care, because his adult kids were struggling to meet a $9,000 insurance deductible.

Healthcare workers who'd turned up for the event described patients choosing between affording medication or food, or how they themselves had been financially devastated by a medical crisis.

They all knew El-Sayed's rallying cry by heart, chanting it when the Michigan Democrat took the stage: "Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!"

Support for Medicare for All is at its highest in at least a decade, according to a new KFF poll. The survey found two-thirds of Americans now favor expanding the government health program that largely covers seniors (about half of whom are enrolled in private plans through Medicare Advantage).

Sponsor Message

But many people don't actually know how to define Medicare for All. Traditionally, the idea has been to establish a single health insurance program, run by the federal government, that would guarantee coverage for Americans and minimize or even eliminate private insurance. How much people like the idea depends on what they're told about it, pollsters have found.

Still, at a time when fewer than half of Americans say they can afford their healthcare, Medicare for All has become a progressive shorthand for radical, systemic change.

"Too many people don't have health insurance, too many people who do have insurance can't afford medical care, and many people are terrified about the costs of being sick," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who specializes in the politics of healthcare reform.

"And in an electorate that wants change, that is disenchanted with the status quo, Medicare for All is an important symbol," he said.

That's why Democrats running for Senate seats in the midterm elections in such states as Maine, Minnesota, and Florida tout their support for scrapping the current health insurance system in favor of broad Medicare coverage. But nowhere is the issue as central to a race as in Michigan, where Medicare for All has become synonymous with El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor and served as Detroit's top public health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All since his unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018. To Starks-Clay, that means he has a plan and will "stick to it," she said.

That's appealing to voters right now, said Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.

"When we ask people what do they want to hear from candidates in regards to healthcare, it's a plan to bring down healthcare costs," Kirzinger said.

Sponsor Message

American Dream or Pipe Dream?

Medicare for All has been the shiny object of progressive politics in previous campaigns, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential bid and the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Its popularity rises and falls in cycles, Oberlander said. And today, people are painfully aware their care is getting more expensive and harder to access.

In the first decade or so after the passage of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, the nation's uninsured rate was cut nearly in half. Insurance companies could no longer deny people coverage based on preexisting conditions. Since then, to cover more people, 40 states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, the government health program for those with low incomes or disabilities.

Now it feels as if we're moving backward, Oberlander said. "We are now, in the past two years, in an era where the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have reversed that progress."

Michigan, a battleground state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, saw some of the steepest ACA plan enrollment drops after the GOP-controlled Congress allowed enhanced tax subsidies, which helped people afford their premiums, to expire at the end of last year.

Insurance companies in Michigan hiked individual marketplace rates by an average of 20%.

And up to 355,000 Michiganders are expected to lose their Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of cuts included in Trump's signature law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to estimates from the Urban Institute, a left-leaning think tank.

At El-Sayed's town hall in Lansing, Darleana Ash said patients at the medical diagnostics lab where she works are increasingly skipping tests because they can't afford them.

toggle caption i Nic Antaya/Getty Images





Others drive hours from rural areas because their local labs have closed or are no longer in their insurance networks. She worries about the patients who must choose between their medications and groceries some months.

Sponsor Message

"If you got somebody that's 75, 80 years old, guess what? They're going to go without the medication, because they got to eat," she said.

Packed in near the front of the crowded town hall was Cindy Lou Coolich, a boisterous retiree wearing a campaign T-shirt and cowboy hat.

She spent years working for a company that helped uninsured people enroll in coverage, until she got sick herself. A bout of sepsis nearly killed her and left her disabled.

Suddenly, she was the one enrolling in Medicaid and living on $900 a month from Social Security. She lost the 15-acre horse farm she'd owned, and then everything else, she said. "Except my car."

The saving grace, oddly, was the death of her ex-husband. Because they'd been married for more than 10 years, she could benefit from his Social Security benefits. "So now I'm doing quite well!" she laughed.

But to her, it hardly seemed like the mark of a functioning healthcare system that someone had to die for things to get better.

A universal response

Democrats aren't the only ones responding to voters' healthcare discontent. Republican Mike Rogers, a former Michigan congressman and El-Sayed's opponent, recently released a brief healthcare plan.

"I just can't think of a more important issue to the people of Michigan than healthcare and costs, the rising costs," he said. At a press conference announcing his health platform, he broadly attacked El-Sayed and Medicare for All.

"[If] the government's going to give you something, they have to take it away from someone else," Rogers said.

Under Medicare for All, millions of Michiganders with private health insurance would lose that coverage, he said.

Pointing to estimates that Medicare for All would cost some $4 trillion per year, he said, "Guess what? People pay for that."

(A recent preprint study from Yale researchers found that the cost of implementing Medicare for All, estimated at $4.2 trillion, would save about $1 trillion in healthcare spending.)

Sponsor Message

Rogers' campaign declined an interview request from KFF Health News.

Concerns about increased taxation, disruption to the current system, and reduced access to services can make Medicare for All a political liability in a close election, Oberlander said.

"It doesn't matter if the fears that they're spreading are actually accurate," he said. "Politically, what matters is if they can scare people."

But even if El-Sayed wins in November, the chances of Medicare for All replacing the current system "remain very remote in the short to medium term," Oberlander said.

Given the staunch opposition from Republicans and many moderate Democrats, not to mention the lobbying power of the healthcare industry, massively overhauling the U.S. health system won't suddenly be achievable because of a single Senate candidate.

Thomas "Jermaine" Carey knows this. A self-described activist, he attended a recent El-Sayed town hall in Detroit feeling "kind of sold out" by what he calls the "straight-ticket" Democratic Party.

Medicare for All sounds good, he said. "Do I believe it?" He shrugged.

"It's still America," he said. "You still have super PACs, the lobbyists that control everything."

This story was produced as part of NPR's health reporting collaboration with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: What firefighters want you to know about lithium battery fires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Firefighters have raised alarms about hot, fast, hard-to-extinguish fires in lithium batteries from e-bikes in people's homes (including ones in Toronto and Peterborough, Ont., just this week) and huge storage batteries at a P.E.I. solar farm last month.

Concerns about lithium battery fires have led to bans of electric bikes and cars in some buildings , public transit and ferries , causing problems for people who rely on them. They've also made some people hesitant about trying electric vehicles .

This week is Fire Prevention Week , and lithium batteries are the official theme. Here's a closer look at why lithium battery fires are a challenge and what can be done to minimize the risks.

WATCH | Why lithium-ion batteries are so dangerous: Why lithium-ion batteries are so dangerous | Duration closed caption 2:08 Toronto has seen more than 200 per cent growth in lithium-ion battery fires since 2022, according to Toronto's Fire Chief. CBC's Lane Harrison explains what's behind the surge and why these fires are so difficult to fight.

How common are lithium battery fires?

Canadian fire departments don't track them in a consistent way, but a survey from the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs estimates there were 1,500 fires started by lithium batteries in 600 communities across the country last year. Their numbers are growing exponentially with the numbers of lithium battery-powered devices, says Paul Boissoneault, president of the association and chief of the Oakville Fire Department.

Lithium battery fires are most common for devices found in people's homes, especially e-bikes and e-scooters.

EV and energy storage batteries are far rarer, as they're rigorously tested and have built-in safety features like temperature sensors and systems that cool battery cells as needed. Canada-wide statistics on EV fires aren't available, although U.S. data suggests they're extremely uncommon compared to fires in gas-powered vehicles .

LISTEN | Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires: What On Earth 28:30 Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires EV fires can be scary and challenging to fight. But they’re not as common as they may seem. Online misinformation and a lack of reliable data can contribute to misconceptions about what happens when an electric vehicle battery fire erupts – and even firefighters aren’t immune.

Grid storage battery fires are even less common — a global database from the Electric Power Research Institute shows the one in P.E.I. was one of only six worldwide this year.

What causes lithium battery fires?

Batteries rely on the separation of their positive and negative terminals. That forces electrons to move through the device you're powering to get from one end of the battery to the other.

A barrier material keeps the terminals separated. When a hole (effectively a short circuit) forms in that barrier, fire happens, said Randy Narine, a professional firefighter in Brampton, Ont., who studies lithium battery safety through his company Clean Core Research, in an interview with CBC's What on Earth?

That hole can be caused by wear and tear over time or from damage, such as a collision or someone dropping a battery from a smaller device, such as an e-bike.

Lithium battery fires can also be started from overheating — due to overcharging or improper charging (such as with the wrong charger) or heat exposure from an external heat source, including a fire in a nearby battery cell in the same battery, since many batteries contain multiple cells.

WATCH | A reminder to check charging devices: Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices | Duration closed caption 2:11 Lithium-ion batteries are found in everything from phones and tablets to e-bikes and e-scooters. Regina Fire Chief Layne Jackson says you should keep an eye on your charging devices. It's one of many fire prevention precautions Regina Fire & Protective Services is highlighting this week.

What makes them dangerous compared to other fires?

They can burn "hotter and faster" than other fires, Boissoneault said. At a certain temperature, lithium batteries reach "thermal runaway," where heat triggers and speeds up chemical reactions in the battery that generate more heat.

This can lead to a "massive chain reaction" and a potentially explosive fire, Narine said.

They make their own oxygen. One of the battery's terminals is made of a metal oxide that breaks down into metal and oxygen gas during a fire , further sustaining the fire. That means normal techniques to smother fires don't work.

They generate toxic substances such as hydrogen fluoride as materials in the battery break down in the heat. They can also contaminate firefighters' clothing and equipment with toxic compounds such as formaldehyde and heavy metals that need to be removed afterward.

They can reignite hours, days or weeks later, thanks to thermal runaway and their oxygen self-generation. Boissoneault said that can have implications for how the burned batteries are transported and stored after a fire.

WATCH | Fire at P.E.I. solar farm could reignite, officials warn: The fire at this P.E.I. solar farm is finally out. Officials warn it could reignite | Duration closed caption 2:02 After two weeks of battling a fire at a P.E.I. solar and battery farm, firefighters have finally put it out, but officials warn it could reignite. Battery fires are notoriously toxic and difficult to extinguish.

Firefighters don't always feel prepared for them. Boissoneault said just 40 per cent of departments surveyed had formal training on dealing with lithium battery incidents, and even fewer said they had standard operating policies and the correct equipment to deal with such emergencies. Many also don't have a way to decontaminate their gear after a lithium fire.

How can they be handled and extinguished?

EV fires are typically sprayed with huge amounts of water. Narine estimated a gas car fire can be extinguished with less than 2,000 litres of water, whereas it can take tens of thousands of litres to put out a lithium battery fire .

While water can provide cooling and can sometimes be used to protect nearby materials from catching fire, it can't actually smother the battery fire.

WATCH | Why has a battery been burning for nearly 2 weeks at a Summerside solar farm?: Why has a battery been burning for nearly 2 weeks at Summerside's solar farm? | Duration closed caption 7:30 There have been a lot of questions around a fire that broke out in a battery bank at Summerside's Sunbank solar farm on Sept. 7. CBC News: Compass host Louise Martin reached out to lithium-ion battery fire consultant Paul Shoemaker, who's trained some firefighters on the Island, to get some of the answers.

In many cases, fire experts say, the fire just needs to burn out.

That's particularly the case for large energy storage batteries, said experts at a fire safety panel at the Energy Storage Canada conference in Toronto in September.

Adam Jakubowski, a firefighter and senior consultant with Energy Safety Response Group specializing in battery energy storage systems, said in many cases, putting water on a lithium battery fire simply prolongs a fire, which may reignite a week or month later. It can also lead to water runoff that could contaminate the environment.

WATCH | Toronto's fire chief calls e-bike batteries 'the greatest public fire risk': Toronto's fire chief calls e-bike batteries the 'greatest public fire safety risk' | Duration closed caption 3:02 Toronto's Fire Chief Jim Jessop is warning the public about the growing risk of lithium-ion battery fires after crews responded to two battery-related blazes within 24 hours this week.

What can you do to reduce the risk?

Buy batteries with certification labels such as CSA, cUL or CETL rather than cheaper ones that may not have safety features . Don't modify batteries to charge more quickly or hold more charge.

Charge devices properly, on hard surfaces, away from any combustible materials, and unplug as soon as they're fully charged, Boissoneault says. Charge with the right charger for that device. "Don't mix and match," says Jon McQuaid, vice-president of marketing communications and safety for Call2Recycle Canada, a non-profit focused on battery collection and recycling.

Recycle them only at battery-recycling dropoff sites , not trash or regular recycling bins, McQuaid said. He advises taping over the terminals (even for tiny button batteries) first to protect from debris or other batteries that could cause a spark, "which could then lead to a thermal runaway."

Damaged batteries need to be placed in special " damaged, defective or recalled " battery containers at select battery dropoff sites.

World.title: Immigration minister appears unaware of court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked that the federal immigration minister appeared to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely considered to be the cornerstone of the Canadian refugee protection system.

In an interview with Radio-Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab was repeatedly asked about the 1985 Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration case.

This Singh decision ruled that asylum seekers are guaranteed the Charter right to fundamental justice and led to the creation of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.

It is also a key argument in the legal challenge to the Carney government's immigration reforms that restrict who is eligible for Immigration and Refugee Board hearings.

"Honestly, I was extremely shocked," said Gauri Sreenivasan, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees. "It's very concerning that the minister in charge of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would not be fully aware of the Supreme Court's Singh decision."

Diab was interviewed in July by Radio-Canada's Les murs: le périple des migrants vers le Canada , a documentary podcast launched three weeks ago that examines Canada's asylum system.

She was asked a series of questions, including about the Safe Third Country Agreement and Bill C-12, the Carney government's immigration reforms passed last March .

One of the most controversial changes in C-12 was that asylum claims made more than a year after an individual's first entry into Canada are no longer referred to the Immigration and Refugee Board, but instead are given a pre-removal risk assessment.

The assessment is conducted by an Immigration Canada officer to ensure that a person is not at risk of being tortured or killed if returned to their country — and typically includes a written submission rather than an oral hearing.

WATCH | More about opposition to Bill C-12: Migrant rights rally calls on government to change immigration policy | Duration closed caption 1:23 Dozens gathered outside the Human Rights Monument in Ottawa on Sunday to call on the federal government to change directions with its immigration policy. Some in attendance say Bill C-12 has made it more difficult for migrants to live in Canada. Cameron Mahler has more.

Diab said in French that Bill C-12 "respects our Canadian Charter," adding that she herself is a lawyer and that the changes are meant to address the backlog in asylum cases.

When pressed about the argument that under the Singh decision asylum seekers have a constitutional right to an oral hearing, she replied that since the law is new, the government would continue to monitor the situation.

Radio-Canada then asked her point-blank if she was familiar with the Singh decision. After a pause, Diab asked that the name of the decision be repeated.

When told again that it was the Singh decision handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1985, she said she would have to check with her team.

"There are many Singhs and many decisions," said Diab .

WATCH | Diab asked about Singh decision: Immigration minister asked about court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees | Duration 1:33 In an interview with Radio-Canada's Les murs: le périple des migrants vers le Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Diab appeared unfamiliar with a Supreme Court decision that is widely considered the cornerstone of Canada's refugee protection system.

Radio-Canada then specified that it was the decision that led to the creation of the Immigration and Refugee Board, to which she responded: "Ah, OK."

With the Singh decision, the Supreme Court of Canada recognized, among other things, the right of asylum seekers to an oral hearing, according to several experts Radio-Canada spoke with.

"[The claimant] is entitled to a full hearing on their file so that they can explain their situation before a competent decision-maker," said François Crépeau, professor emeritus of public international law at McGill University and former United Nations special rapporteur on the human rights of migrants.

"That is why the Immigration and Refugee Board was created in 1989. It was to meet the requirements of the Singh decision."

Bill C-12 is being challenged in the courts. Lawyers allege it violates Canada's legal obligations under both domestic and international law.

Immigration Canada maintains that the Singh decision is respected by Bill C-12.

"The Supreme Court in Singh found that in order to meet the requirements of fundamental justice, an oral hearing is required when there is a credibility issue at stake. The Supreme Court did not find that in all cases an oral hearing is required," a department lawyer told a parliamentary committee studying Bill C-12 in February.

Crépeau disagrees: "Removing a full hearing … is a violation of the conditions set by the Singh decision."

Immediately after the interview, Diab's office insisted that the minister was well aware of the Singh decision, but that due to the language barrier she had not fully understood the questions.

The podcast interview was conducted in French, which is not Diab's first language.

However, during two appearances in English before two different Senate committees studying Bill C-12, the minister also did not answer questions regarding the Singh decision, deferring to department officials and lawyers.

'Issue of competence': advocate

"I believe there is certainly an issue of competence," said Louis-Philippe Jannard of TCRI, a Quebec umbrella association of more than 160 organizations working with refugees and immigrants.

"The issue of the Singh decision was raised during the legislative process for Bill C-12 before both the House of Commons and the Senate. So for it not to be on the minister's radar is surprising to say the least."

Radio-Canada asked the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) whether, given these criticisms, Diab still has the confidence of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

PMO spokesperson Renée LeBlanc Proctor said in an email to Radio-Canada that Diab plays an "essential" role in the implementation of the federal government's mandate to bring down immigration to "viable" levels while attracting the best talent in the world.

"She continues this work," Proctor said.

World.title: How the Canada-U.S. trade war might change your shopping habits
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canada-U.S. trade war has reshaped Canadians' view of their country, somewhat rekindled coast-to-coast-to-coast unity and dominated federal and provincial elections.

For more than a year it has been steeped in the national psyche, and just when we thought a deal was near with our friend-to-foe southern neighbour, we instead face a new — steeper — round of tariffs, bans and counter-tariffs.

Canada began imposing a new round of retaliatory levies on U.S. goods on Sept. 8, after the United States imposed new 50 per cent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods. The U.S. then responded late last month with a set of bans on Canadian imports on some alcoholic drinks, dairy byproducts, molasses and motorcycles, among others.

So, how could the latest in the dispute continue to reshape the Canadian economy? Could the scramble to adapt help us diversify trade partners more quickly? And, what products, if any, could become more difficult to access?

CBC News spoke to four experts in supply chains and retail to get a sense of what products could go up in price and how consumers may have to change their habits in the next few months.

They say the escalation between the two countries last month — which involved the U.S. raising tariffs after Canada and the U.S. failed to sign a new trade deal, then Canada imposing counter-tariffs, then the U.S. imposing full-scale bans — may be felt less in empty store shelves than in higher prices, fewer choices and longer waits for some products.

"Most goods should remain available, although some brands, models or specifications may disappear from the market," said Xiaodon Pan, an associate professor in supply chain and business technology management at Concordia University in Montreal.

The counter-tariffs are meant to focus on products where Canadian alternatives are available, and range from 15 to 25 to 50 per cent.

They cover areas such as steel and aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics — and include finished products as well as some components used to make other goods. Tariffs on U.S. automobiles are also still in place.

One analysis out of North Carolina found that toilet paper in the U.S. could become "more expensive, less soft" because of President Donald Trump's 50 per cent levy on northern bleached softwood kraft imported from Canada.

WATCH | Economists foresee stagnant growth: Canada's economy still resilient, but U.S. trade war taking its toll | Duration closed caption 2:00 Canada's economy has shown resilience in the face of punishing U.S. tariffs, but new import bans on a range of Canadian products are creating further drag. Accounting firm Deloitte has lowered its growth forecast for next year by 20 per cent.

'Prices are going up,' business prof says

Back at home though, Matt Poirier of the Retail Council of Canada says shop owners began stocking up as soon as they knew tariffs were coming after the trade deal fell through between Canada and the U.S. in August. The bulk of goods could prevent prices from significantly rising for at least couple months, he said.

"They've been working overtime to find either alternate sources of supply, domestic or global," Poirier said. "But it does take a while for those supply chains to reroute."

While the impacts of the tariffs could take a bit of time, they could still be significant once those inventory supplies dwindle by the end of the year.

Fraser Johnson, a professor at Ivey Business School at Western University in London, Ont., said retailers won't want to shock consumers and lose business in the short term, but, "in the medium to long term, prices are going up."

Johnson explained that while alternatives to U.S. products exist elsewhere, the increase of costs of U.S. goods will eventually lead businesses to boost prices on models from other countries as well.

Pan, of Concordia University, agrees. She said that while clothing and cosmetics, for example, may have more international alternatives, consumers are likely to start seeing "higher prices and fewer brands, styles, shades," in those areas.

Outdoor gear fanatics could see similar phenomena, the experts said. Watch out, gorpcore.

Appliances and electronics

Whether it's Maytag, GE, Frigidaire or high-end Wolf stoves, American companies take up a significant share the North American appliance market — but in Canada that could change very soon.

There's a new 25 per cent surtax on U.S. refrigerators, freezers, cooking ranges, washer and dryers and dishwasher parts.

While there are many South Korean and Chinese alternatives already readily available, prices for those products could go up as well as retailers try to recoup lost costs, as Johnson mentioned.

As for parts for people who already own appliances from American brands, that could get a little tricky.

"A specific control board, pump, sensor or repair component may have very few direct alternatives," said Pan of Concordia University.

She says the same goes for electronics and furniture.

What about shortages?

Construction materials are where things start to get more dicey.

Canada buys a lot of those from the U.S. — things like metal, plastic and foam building materials, paints, coats and adhesive, cement products and types of prefabricated wood. They're bulky goods that our shared border makes it easy to transport.

That's one industry facing possible shortages, says Saibal Ray, the James McGill Chair professor for supply chain management at McGill University in Montreal.

Car parts could be another, due to levies on steel and aluminum, Ray said, as "availability might be an issue."

Johnson agrees. "If you're thinking about making a major purchase; if you're going through a home renovation — buying and locking in your prices earlier rather than later makes a lot of sense," he said.

Aluminum cans are shown after being filled with craft beer during a production run at Black Plague Brewery in Oceanside, Calif., last year. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Again, it's not just finished products affected here. Source materials may cross the border several times before becoming, say, a car part or food container, Pan explained. She gave the example of aluminum cans for soda and beer.

Canada produces the aluminum for much of those, but the actual manufacturing is often completed in the U.S., she said.

"Because those capabilities take time to replace, tariffs can raise costs long before the underlying interdependence changes," Pan said. She said it's not just costs, but regulations are another hurdle to diversifying trading partners.

Elevators are another example Pan gave, of Canada-U.S. interdependence. There are North American "product standards, technical specifications, testing and certification," but if the European Union closer aligns with those standards, that would help producers in Europe more easily sell to Canada.

Similarly, Johnson says "business-to-business" costs will go up before they hit consumers, but all of that has a trickle-down effect and it's hard to predict the timing of when those extra costs could hit the bottom line because of how unpredictable these trade disputes have been.

"Eventually, all trade wars end," he said, noting the uncertainty is what's impacting small to medium-sized Canadians businesses right now.

"I don't know when, but I do know that at some point this is going to get resolved and we'll be able to … get on with our lives."

Is there a 'silver lining' in food prices?

What's more difficult to stock up on or lock in on prices is food, especially seasonal produce, the experts said. Plus, it's not just the trade war increasing costs, but skyrocketing oil prices due to the U.S.'s war on Iran, too.

But produce isn't really covered in the latest round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.

The U.S. has straight up banned Canadian alcohol, dairy and whey products, as well as molasses and sugar processing items, after Canada had retaliated against U.S. levies in August, with 50 per cent levies on each of those, but it made sure not to surtax items that aren't already available from Canadian producers.

Holstein cows at a dairy farm in Saint-Blaise-sur-Richelieu, Que. (Graham Hughes/Reuters)

Gary Sands, the senior vice president of policy and advocacy for the Canadian Federation of Independent Grocers, says he believes Canadian food providers won't have trouble replacing U.S. goods with Canadian ones.

"There's a silver lining to this," Sands said, explaining that he expects even more Canadian products and suppliers to get a boost as a result of the latest round of tariffs.

Already, CFIG members have seen a roughly 20 per cent rise in consumers purchasing Canadian products, he said.

"I've been here for 26 years. I've never seen anything like this. It's definitely a permanent shift," Sands said.

So, while consumers could see the retail landscape shift over the next few months, with changes in brands and specific models, maybe just maybe it could continue to lessen Canada's reliance on U.S. goods, Pan and Ray said.

"The broader lesson is that deep integration creates efficiency and mutual vulnerability at the same time," said Pan.

World.title: These 2 First Nations are pushing back against Sask. AI data centre
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two First Nations are challenging the construction of Bell Canada's AI data centre south of Regina, saying the project is moving ahead without consultation or adequate information about its environmental impacts.

Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation said a letter to Bell president and CEO Mirko Bibic issued Friday that the development in the rural municipality of Sherwood is being built on "unceded traditional Dakota territory" with neither consent nor consultation.

"Our Nation has responsibilities to its members, its territory and future generations, and will determine its own position on this development through its leadership and independent review," the letter states.

"As a sovereign nation and on treaty land, I believe we have the right to be consulted with," Chief Rodger Redman later told CBC News.

The First Nation has given Bell 10 business days to acknowledge its letter and 30 days to arrange a meeting involving provincial representatives.

Standing Buffalo is not a signatory to Treaty 4 but is protected under the Indian Act.

"We're asserting and operationalizing our sovereignty as Indian people, as Dakota people," Redman said, adding he is prepared to pursue litigation or judicial review if Bell does not respond.

Two First Nations are demanding consultation and information from Bell Canada and the government about an AI data centre being built south of Regina. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

The province, which has partnered on the project with Bell and George Gordon First Nation, says the artificial intelligence data centre is the largest private sector investment in Canadian history, bringing $52 billion in investment, up to 1,200 construction jobs and 600 permanent jobs to Saskatchewan.

Redman says partnership with George Gordon First Nation on the project does not resolve the duty to consult with other First Nations whose traditional territories could be affected by the development.

"They're trying to satisfy and check off the box of consultation. That's not consultation," he said, adding he believes Standing Buffalo, located just west of Fort Qu'Appelle, deserves the same level of disclosure about the project as the First Nations partner.

"There's 74 Nations in Saskatchewan. And none of those 74 that I know of have delegated George Gordon to speak on their behalf," Redman said.

Standing Buffalo is already involved in federal court litigation over its asserted right to consultation, Redman said.

"We have our own consultation framework. We sent the province a copy of that. Till this day, we're still waiting for them to fill out an application," he said.

Concerns over environmental impacts

Redman says the First Nation has not received the information necessary to assess the project's potential impacts on water, wildlife and crops.

"Were geographical, hydrological studies ever done? The environmental impacts... what it's creating within the air, the animals, the birds?"

He is also seeking information about how Bell will manage and dispose of retired computing, electrical and mechanical equipment, including potentially toxic electronic waste.

"What are we leaving for our next generation? A cesspool of toxic waste?"

Carry the Kettle calls for pause

Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation is separately calling on the provincial and federal governments, and Bell, to pause construction on the development until a proper environmental assessment is completed. The First Nation is also asking to be meaningfully consulted and accommodated under Treaty 4 rights.

In a letter sent Monday, Chief Cliff Thomson called the development "beyond irresponsible," citing already-limited water supplies in the area and his community's reliance on cattle.

Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation has called for an immediate pause on the data centre's construction. (Kirk Fraser/CBC News)

"We see drought conditions. We have an aquifer under our reserve to protect. We don't know where the water is coming from, and we don't understand the impacts," he wrote.

Thomson said Carry the Kettle will stand firm in protecting its land and treaty rights.

"All we hear are media reports of governments effectively asking our people to 'just trust us,'" he wrote. "That is not enough."

Bell, province respond

Bell Canada told CBC News it remains committed to engaging with local communities and First Nations on the project.

"Bell AI Fabric projects are developed in accordance with all applicable regulatory and environmental requirements," the company said, adding it will continue to provide relevant information through the appropriate processes.

A statement from Premier Scott Moe's office said the project, like any major development, "will be subject to applicable environmental assessment, regulatory and permitting requirements to help identify, assess, and mitigate potential environmental impacts and ensure compliance with relevant legislation.

"Our government is proud to support this investment and will continue working with Bell and our community partners as the project progresses," it read.

World.title: Nepal search for missing after flash floods officially ends, with nearly 5,300 people still unaccounted for
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The families of thousands of people who remain missing in Nepal weeks after catastrophic floods devastated the country have expressed mixed feelings after the government said this week that it is stopping the search for victims.

The office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah decided on Monday that search and rescue operations for victims of the Aug. 26 floods will cease. Instead, authorities will concentrate on rehabilitation and reconstruction, including restoring roads and bridges cut off by floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made aid deliveries difficult.

Rescuers have so far recovered the bodies of at least 1,455 people, but 5,285 others remain missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals.

Two weeks ago, Global Affairs Canada told CBC News that it was aware of 29 Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region whose whereabouts and well-being after the flash floods have not yet been confirmed, but cautioned that the number could fluctuate based on new information. CBC News has requested an update from the department, but did not immediately hear back.

Hopes for finding survivors were briefly revived after two Nepalese workers were rescued from an underground tunnel at the Trishuli hydropower project on Sept. 4, and again two days later when rescuers found a Chinese man at the same location.

WATCH | Rescuers found people alive several days later: 2 more people found alive 10 days after devastating Nepal floods | Duration closed caption 3:16 Two more people have been rescued alive in Nepal 10 days after devastating floods hit the country, including a worker trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a woman found inside a damaged home. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

Families of victims have held protests and vigils in Nepal, calling for search efforts to be improved.

"I am so angry at the government for giving up on search and rescue with thousands of people still missing. I just don't understand how they can do that when we still have hope left that our loved one can still be found," said Usha Khatri, who has spent days searching for her husband in multiple towns where the river flows and bodies have been recovered.

A general view on Sept. 28 shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of the Aug. 26 flash flood, at Betrawati Bazaar in Nepal's Rasuwa district. (Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images)

During her ongoing search, she has checked photos of bodies that were recovered but buried for preservation until identification is made.

"Either they have to give up the body or show some solid proof that my husband is gone, and only then can they declare him dead," Khatri said.

"They have abandoned us and they should not have stopped the search," said Mahesh Shrestha, whose brother was an engineer at a hydropower plant that was hit. "Our family demands they continue looking for him."

Death certificate, burial requirements

Others welcomed the decision and said they are seeking government-issued death certificates.

"After so many days and weeks, there is little or no hope of finding anyone alive. We are sure that none of our family members survived and we are just looking for a closure," said Nirajan Poudel, who lost five family members in the flood.

Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border | Duration closed caption 7:24 Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, says images obtained from satellites show that 'the lower part of a tongue of a glacier completely sheared off across a width of 1,300 metres' and dropped off a cliff onto a lake 2,000 metres below. Steiner said climate change played a role, and the area was known to be at a high risk for a collapse.

Several people whose relatives remain missing have performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in the Hindu tradition and performing the ceremony even without a body provides a sense of spiritual release for some families.

Poudel said the government has so far refused to issue death certificates, saying laws need to be amended first. Death certificates are necessary in Nepal for families to receive compensation, insurance and inherit properties.

Nepal's government did not immediately respond to a request by The Associated Press for more information about the death certificates.

The government estimates reconstruction and recovery will cost $4.77 billion US. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed.

World.title: Family of Hamilton-born hockey player Matthew Mayich says new university review into his collapse falls short
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Arizona State University, where Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich collapsed during a workout on a hot August day, says it commissioned an independent review to make recommendations on how to safely train athletes outdoors and how to respond to "adverse events or reactions."

A lawyer representing the family of 21-year-old Mayich says the review is "not what's needed right now," because it won't address who is responsible for what happened to the student hockey player.

In a separate review published in September, Arizona State University (ASU) official James Rund wrote Mayich collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined school hockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.

Mayich remains in hospital. His parents, Christina and John Mayich, previously told CBC News he's "a fighter" and they're not giving up on him. The family's lawyers at U..S. firm Hagens Berman have told CBC the 21-year-old suffered heatstroke and "needs a miracle."

Mayich's family and teammates raised questions and concerns

On Oct. 2, Jay Thorne, ASU's vice-president of media relations shared a communication from Rund — ASU senior vice-president — to university president Michael Crow.

In it, Rund said ASU retained former Supreme Court of Arizona Chief Justice Scott Bales to lead "an independent review of the facts that have been identified by the university, attorneys for the Mayich family, attorneys for members of the ASU hockey team, law enforcement agencies, and others as appropriate."

The Mayich family and their attorneys have questioned the circumstances of the Aug. 20 workout and how coaches and school officials responded to the player's collapse. Mayich's parents say their son — who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023 — was healthy prior to the workout. Lawyers have said the "military-style," session took place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

In a Sept. 28 anonymous letter to Crow, some of Mayich's ASU Sun Devils teammates alleged Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout and called for the university to place the trainers "responsible for approving, conducting and supervising the session" on leave pending an independent investigation.

Two days later, the school put ASU hockey coach Greg Powers on paid administrative leave.

WATCH | Mayich family demands answers: Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout | Duration closed caption 2:26 The parents of Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old NHL prospect from Stoney Creek, Ont., speak to CBC News after their son collapsed after 'military style' training at Arizona State University. Mayich is in critical condition and unlikely to recover, says his lawyer.

According to Rund's Oct. 2 letter, the new independent review by Bales will result in recommendations for:

Planning and approving outdoor athletic activities.

Staffing, policies and procedures for outdoor athletics, including "adjustments necessary to address changing conditions or adverse reactions."

Preparing for and responding to "adverse events or reactions" occurring during outdoor athletics.

Using outside consultants for planning and delivering "strength and conditioning and practice activities."

Student athletes at ASU will be invited to participate in the review with confidential and anonymous options, Rund said.

ASU requested Bales's review be completed by early December, Rund added.

"Justice Bales is a respected choice, and he will do an excellent job," lawyer Rob Carey said in an Oct. 2 statement to reporters on behalf of the Mayich family. "But ASU hired him to review policies that may help prevent a tragedy like this in the future."

Investigation not set up to answer key questions: lawyer

"What is necessary, and what the Mayich family has asked for and deserves, is an investigation of what went wrong on that field and who is responsible," Carey said. "Justice Bales has not been asked to answer those fundamental questions."

Carey said ASU needs to answer how the workout happened, why it didn't stop when players were in "visible distress" and which ASU and athletics association rules were broken.

The university, Carey said, should "expand Justice Bales's mandate to cover the questions that matter and let him bring in the expertise he needs," or, it should have a second independent investigation into the actions of ASU employees.

He added Bales's findings should be made public and until "the work is done," ASU should keep coaches who were involved away from players.

ASU said Sept. 30 that it appointed assistant coach Mike Corbett to lead the hockey team after it put Powers on leave.

CBC Hamilton asked ASU to respond to the family's concerns. The university did not respond prior to publication.

In an Oct. 5 news release, Arizona State Legislature House and Senate education chairs Matt Gress and Hildy Angius said they welcome Bales's review, noting they had called for an independent investigation.

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

World.title: Israelis mourn anniversary of Oct. 7 attacks as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its two million people living in dire conditions.

In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters and the site of a music festival that Hamas-led militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel. It is the first anniversary that all the hostages are home, marking a new stage of grief.

For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of misery and difficulties after an Israeli retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people. Most of the population of about two million people live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip's cities reduced to rubble.

More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military, and despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.

For the broader region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years. Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with Hezbollah, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas.

Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Arab Gulf countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for, even if they weren't directly connected.

Commuters in Tel Aviv conduct a moment of silence on the highway as part of a memorial ceremony on Wednesday. (Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images)

Families mourn at music festival site

In Reim, the town where the music festival was underway on the day of the attacks, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. They hugged at 6:29 a.m. local time — the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago — as booms from explosions in nearby Gaza were heard.

Anya Davitashili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she comes to the site every Saturday because it's where she feels closest to him.

"I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning; it's in front of my eyes all the time," she said. "Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing."

Hundreds of people came to pay their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site.

In Kfar Aza, where Hamas militants killed dozens of Israelis before taking 19 hostages back into Gaza, residents held a vigil for those killed, standing in silence as a trumpet played a solemn bugle call. A resident read out a roll call of the dead.

Zion Regev, a community leader in the kibbutz, said most residents remain displaced and have yet to return, the trauma of Oct. 7 continuing to shape their lives.

"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," Regev said of the vigil. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after October 7th."

Released hostage marks 1st anniversary of freedom

Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time, after being released from 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 metres underground in a dark, damp tunnel.

People attend a memorial service in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, southern Israel, where many community members were killed and abducted on Oct. 7, 2023. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

Bohbot, who was abducted from the Nova music festival, was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.

In the 11 months since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation, written a book, begun a speaking career, travelled with his family and celebrated all the holidays and birthdays he missed.

WATCH | Netanyahu accused of ignoring warnings before Oct. 7: What Netanyahu knew before the Oct. 7 attacks | Duration closed caption 6:03 New allegations are emerging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ignored warnings about the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attacks, and as CBC senior international correspondent Margaret Evans explains, they come just weeks before a pivotal election.

In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a fierce promise that Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his five-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.

The newborn, Michele, is "not a symbol for my people, she is more of a symbol for the enemy," Bohbot told The Associated Press. "So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever."

Palestinians struggle to recover in Gaza

No events are expected on Wednesday in Gaza, but Hamas in a statement praised the Oct. 7 attacks as an example of "heroism, resilience and national solidarity" and said it had returned the Palestinian cause to the world's attention.

"The conflict with the enemy did not begin on that day, as its final chapters are not written yet," it said.

Palestinians walk along a street in Gaza City on Tuesday, surrounded by buildings destroyed by Israeli military strikes in the Israel-Hamas war. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Palestinians in the territory said the extent to which their lives had deteriorated over the past three years was previously unimaginable.

"We witnessed death, destruction and bombardment that we had never known before," said Walid Akram, a Gaza City resident who, like most in Gaza, has been displaced by the war.

Raed Khozeiq's coastal neighbourhood in Tel al-Hawa was largely flattened. Nothing about his life now is the same, he said.

"No country in the world has gone through what we have experienced here," he said. "A war of extermination, starvation, the absence of schools and universities — nothing remains."

Israel's offensive has devastated the narrow strip and displaced around 90 per cent of its population, often multiple times. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a severe hunger crisis.

WATCH | Israel cleared rubble from Gaza. Here's why that matters: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures, but says around half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by UN agencies and independent experts.

While a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period.

Hamas portrayed the Oct. 7 attacks as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians' dream of an independent state appears even more distant.

Middle East altered

A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government's official memorial services took place on Oct. 5, closer to the Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the attack. The separate commemorations are indicative of the deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.

The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced.

The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran's military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and upending global markets far from the battlefield.

Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel's far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.

World.title: Immigration, high-speed rail and Bill 21: Where new PQ government could test Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Before he even attempts to trigger a promised referendum on independence, Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has a more immediate agenda — and much of it relates to the federal government.

The Parti Québécois leader said Tuesday he would collaborate with Prime Minister Mark Carney when it serves Quebec's interests. He said his first discussion with him was cordial and involved a shared commitment to reduce homelessness in the province.

But veteran political observers say extensive collaboration is unlikely. In fact, it benefits the PQ to show that remaining in Canada doesn't help Quebec.

"When you have a partner who wants to show that you don't work with him, it's difficult to work well together," said former federal Liberal leader Stéphane Dion.

André Lecours, a political science professor at the University of Ottawa, says there's "really no incentive" for the PQ to work with Ottawa.

"On the contrary, you want some friction, you want some tension," Lecours said in an interview.

Here is a look at those friction points.

WATCH | How this minority government could test Ottawa: What will a new PQ government mean for Canada? | Duration closed caption 2:28 How will the election of a Parti Québécois minority government affect Quebec's relationship with Ottawa? CBC Radio’s The House host Catherine Cullen explains how the PQ could shake things up at the federal level.

Slashing immigration levels

The PQ wants to drastically reduce the number of newcomers in the province. The party wants to cut the number of permanent immigrants to 35,000 — a substantial reduction from the 60,000 expected this year.

The party also wants to reduce non-permanent immigration quotas by half, setting a target between 200,000 and 250,000 people, while protecting sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing and health care.

To achieve this, the PQ needs help from Ottawa.

The federal government controls final approvals for permanent residency and issues the visas for temporary foreign workers and international students. St-Pierre Plamondon wants full power over these levers transferred to Quebec — which is something the federal government has rejected in the past.

"There's nothing that Ottawa can do that would make the PQ happy on immigration," Lecours said.

WATCH | Carney says he wants to work with PQ government: Carney says it's 'time to act,' work together with incoming Quebec premier | Duration closed caption 4:02 Prime Minister Mark Carney said he spoke with Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the morning after his election win and 'discussed the ways that we would work together.' On the question of a future referendum on separation, Carney said it's 'not a time to wait for something a few years down the road; it's a time to act.'

The future of high-speed rail

The PQ is opposed to the federal government's proposed high-speed rail line that would connect Toronto to Montreal and on to Quebec City.

Federal Transport Minister Steve MacKinnon has described the project as a way to "build a strong economy and create new opportunities for Canadians."

The federal government is planning to present this fall the first segment of the route, running from Ottawa to Montreal.

St-Pierre Plamondon, however, has argued the project does not address the needs of Quebecers.

Lecours said the high-speed rail line is unlikely to go forward with the PQ in power, saying there's "no way the federal government is going to do the project if the Quebec government is opposed to it."

Legal battles: Bill 21 and the Crown

The Supreme Court of Canada is expected to issue a ruling by the end of the year on whether to strike down Bill 21, the controversial provincial legislation that forces some public servants to uncover their heads and bans the wearing of religious symbols on the job.

Lecours said the ruling on the use of the notwithstanding clause has the "potential to be explosive."

If the country's highest court strikes down the law, the PQ is likely to use the defeat as potent political ammunition, arguing it proves Quebec's values can only be protected through independence.
