Mexico City’s 2026 Parades and Public Events

Mexico City’s government publishes the programme on its official tourism portal. It lists the Great Day of the Dead Parade for Saturday, 31 October, at 2 p.m. local time, or 4 p.m. ET.

The route runs along Paseo de la Reforma from the Diana Cazadora fountain to the Zócalo, the main square. Two Mexican outlets, ADN40 and UnoTV, reported the same date and time in late September and early October.

Planned floats honour Juan Gabriel, the singer-songwriter who died in 2016. Others honour film director Emilio “El Indio” Fernández and the Red Queen of Palenque, an ancient Maya noblewoman.

The rest of the city’s 2026 calendar, as published in its guide, is busy:

Saturday, 17 October: the 18th Monumental Alebrije Parade of giant papier-mâché fantasy creatures, run by the Museum of Popular Art, from the Zócalo to Reforma.

the 18th Monumental Alebrije Parade of giant papier-mâché fantasy creatures, run by the Museum of Popular Art, from the Zócalo to Reforma. 18 October to 1 November: a marigold festival on Reforma with 140 flower growers and farmers from Tláhuac, Milpa Alta and Xochimilco.

a marigold festival on Reforma with 140 flower growers and farmers from Tláhuac, Milpa Alta and Xochimilco. 23 October to 8 November: “The Path”, a light installation on Reforma.

“The Path”, a light installation on Reforma. Saturday, 24 October, 7 to 11 p.m.: a 19-kilometre night bike ride along Reforma and Avenida Juárez.

a 19-kilometre night bike ride along Reforma and Avenida Juárez. Sunday, 25 October: the Mega Procession of the Catrinas, a citizen-organised march in skeleton costume.

the Mega Procession of the Catrinas, a citizen-organised march in skeleton costume. 29 October to 2 November: the Monumental Ofrenda in the Zócalo, plus community altars at 12 sites.

the Monumental Ofrenda in the Zócalo, plus community altars at 12 sites. 29 October to 4 November: a Day of the Dead festival in Chapultepec Park’s second section.

a Day of the Dead festival in Chapultepec Park’s second section. 31 October to 2 November: the cemetery celebrations in Mixquic.

This year the Zócalo altar honours La Catrina, the elegant skeleton created by the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada. Its centrepiece is a 32-metre papier-mâché sculpture, the guide says.

The parades are free to watch from the street. A separate guide covers the 31 October parade and where to stand.

Music runs alongside. Oaxaca-born singer Lila Downs plays the Auditorio Nacional on Sunday, 1 November, UnoTV reported, as covered in this concert preview.

Mixquic and the Cemetery Vigils

For a quieter, older version, the city guide points to Mixquic, on the south-eastern edge of the capital. It calls the village’s festival the most traditional in Mexico City.

Families there begin on 29 September with the Call to the Souls, when they clean the tombs. The guide highlights local dishes such as mixmole, romeritos and calabaza en tacha, a candied pumpkin.

The guide’s advice for visitors: arrive hours early because of traffic and ask before taking photographs. Keep a respectful silence during La Alumbrada, and never sit or step on the tombs.

Outside the capital, check the US government’s rating before booking a rural celebration. The State Department’s advisory, reissued in late May 2026, says “do not travel” to Michoacán, its highest level.

It rates Oaxaca at Level 2, with no restrictions for Oaxaca City, Monte Albán, Puerto Escondido or Huatulco. Yucatán, home to Mérida, sits at Level 1, the lowest.

Etiquette for US Visitors at Altars and Graves

Most rules follow from one fact: cemeteries are family spaces, not stage sets. The city guide calls the tombs sacred family spaces.

Ask first. Request permission before photographing people, graves or a family’s altar.

Request permission before photographing people, graves or a family’s altar. Keep off the graves. Do not sit, stand or step on tombs, even when paths are crowded.

Do not sit, stand or step on tombs, even when paths are crowded. Lower your voice. Stay quiet during candle vigils such as La Alumbrada.

Stay quiet during candle vigils such as La Alumbrada. Look, do not touch. Food and objects on an ofrenda are offerings to the dead, not snacks or souvenirs.

Food and objects on an ofrenda are offerings to the dead, not snacks or souvenirs. Save the costume for the street. Face paint suits parades and the Catrina procession; at a vigil, dress as for a memorial.

Face paint suits parades and the Catrina procession; at a vigil, dress as for a memorial. Mind the words. Calling it “Mexican Halloween” misreads a religious and family occasion.

Calling it “Mexican Halloween” misreads a religious and family occasion. Travel smart. The State Department tells US officials to use regulated taxi stands or apps such as Uber or Cabify, not street-hailed cabs.

The advisory also bars US government staff from travelling between cities after dark and urges US citizens to follow the same rules. Plan any late cemetery visit around a ride back you have booked in advance.

Is the Day of the Dead a Public Holiday in Mexico?

Not in labour law. Article 74 of Mexico’s Federal Labour Law lists the mandatory rest days, and neither 1 nor 2 November is among them.

The next statutory holiday is Monday, 16 November, the third Monday of the month, which marks the 1910 Revolution. Banks follow their own calendar, set by the CNBV, the national banking and securities regulator.

Its rules, published in the Official Gazette on 10 December 2025, close banks and other supervised firms on Monday, 2 November 2026. Currency exchange houses may open on every day of the year.

Detail on shops, offices and services is in the guide to Mexico holiday closures on 2 and 16 November.

Street food stays cheap through the season. ANPEC, a small-shopkeepers’ alliance, put the average tamal at 25 pesos (about US$1.39) in January 2026, Publimetro reported.

A stew taco averaged 16 pesos (about US$0.89) in the same figures. Conversions use Banco de México’s FIX rate of 6 October 2026, 17.97 pesos per US dollar.

What It Means for US Readers

The calendar is friendly for a long weekend. The big parade falls on Saturday, 31 October, and the two main days on Sunday and Monday.

Mexico City keeps standard time all year. It is two hours behind New York until US clocks go back on 1 November, then one hour behind.

Bring cash before the weekend, because banks shut on Monday, 2 November. Exchange houses may stay open, but rates and hours vary by branch.

Overall, the State Department rates Mexico at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, citing terrorism, crime and kidnapping. Mexico City carries the same Level 2 rating.

For broader timing, see the region-by-region guide to the best time to visit Mexico. An expat guide to 1 and 2 November in Mexico City adds neighbourhood tips.

More practical coverage sits on the Rio Times Mexico page.

What Is Not Known

Road closures, transit changes and viewing areas for the 31 October parade were not in the city’s guide on 7 October. Float line-ups and timings can still change.

No official 2026 price survey for pan de muerto or marigold bunches could be confirmed for this guide. Whether federal and state offices give staff 2 November off was also not confirmed.

The Lila Downs concert date rests on UnoTV’s report. The venue’s own listing could not be checked.

Local customs differ widely. The dates above describe the common pattern, and individual villages may honour children and adults on different days.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Day of the Dead in 2026?

The main days are Sunday, 1 November, for children and Monday, 2 November, for adults. Some families begin remembrances in late October.

What day is the Mexico City Day of the Dead parade in 2026?

The city’s official guide lists the Great Day of the Dead Parade for 2 p.m. on Saturday, 31 October. It runs along Paseo de la Reforma to the Zócalo.

Is the Day of the Dead the same as Halloween?

No. UNESCO describes a fusion of Indigenous rites and Catholic feasts in which families welcome the souls of their dead relatives home.

Is the Day of the Dead a public holiday in Mexico?

It is not a mandatory rest day under the Federal Labour Law. Banks must close on Monday, 2 November 2026, under rules from the banking regulator.

Why is 1 November for children and 2 November for adults?

The days follow the Catholic feasts of All Saints and All Souls. UNESCO notes that Indigenous practice assigns each dead person a day by age and cause of death.

Can tourists visit cemeteries during the Day of the Dead?

Yes, in places such as Mixquic, but behave as a guest at a memorial. Ask before taking photos, keep quiet during vigils and never sit or step on graves.

Is it safe to travel to Mexico for the Day of the Dead?

The US State Department rates Mexico and Mexico City at Level 2, exercise increased caution. It says do not travel to Michoacán.

Sources: Primary: Mexico City government tourism portal, Day of the Dead 2026 in Mexico City; UNESCO, Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead (2008); Diario Oficial de la Federación, CNBV closing days for 2026, 10 December 2025; Federal Labour Law, Article 74; Law on Time Zones in Mexico; US Department of State, Mexico Travel Advisory (May 2026); Banco de México, FIX exchange rate, 6 October 2026. Regional: ADN40, 26 September 2026; UnoTV, 2 October 2026; Expansión, October 2025; ADN40, 27 October 2025; Publimetro, 18 January 2026 (ANPEC prices) (all accessed 7 October 2026).

World.title: Gorditas Mexico Guide To Fillings And Prices
World.content:
MEXICO · FOOD

Key Facts — The country Mexico, whose traditional cuisine UNESCO listed as cultural heritage in 2010.

— The dish A thick corn cake, griddled or fried, then split and stuffed.

— The classic Chicharrón prensado, pressed pork crackling; beans and requesón cheese are common too.

— What happened Average price rose 8.7% to 25 pesos (about US$1.39) by January 2026.

— Where to eat Sonora Market, La Vikina and Mixcoac Market in Mexico City.

— What it means for you Carry small peso notes; most adults pay cash for small purchases.

What a gordita is, what goes inside, what it costs in 2026 and how US visitors can order one in Mexico City.

Gorditas are thick corn cakes that Mexican cooks griddle or fry, slit open and stuff with fillings such as pressed pork crackling. In January 2026 a gordita cost 25 pesos (about US$1.39) on average, according to Mexico’s small-shopkeeper alliance.

For a US visitor, two gorditas make a full street breakfast for under US$3. The dish shares only its name with the fast-food item sold in the United States.

This guide covers the dough, fillings, regional styles, 2026 prices, where to look in Mexico City and how to order. For the wider menu, see this guide to 25 Mexican dishes and where to eat them.

What Gorditas Are and How They Are Made

The word means “little fat one”, a nod to the thickness of the dough. Spain’s Royal Spanish Academy defines the Mexican “gorda” as a corn tortilla “thicker than the common one”.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. We never share your email.

The dough is masa, made from corn cooked with lime, a process called nixtamalisation. UNESCO, which listed traditional Mexican cuisine as cultural heritage in 2010, names that technique among its foundations.

Cooks pat the masa into a thick disc and cook it on a comal, a flat griddle. Many then fry it in oil or lard for a crisp shell.

Once cooked, the cake is slit along one edge to make a pocket. The filling goes inside, followed by salsa, onion, coriander or cheese.

That pocket is what sets a gordita apart from its masa cousins on the same street-stall menu:

Gordita: a thick round cake, split after cooking and stuffed like a pocket.

a thick round cake, split after cooking and stuffed like a pocket. Sope: a thick disc with a pinched rim, topped rather than filled.

a thick disc with a pinched rim, topped rather than filled. Tlacoyo: an oblong or triangular cake with the filling sealed inside before cooking.

an oblong or triangular cake with the filling sealed inside before cooking. Pupusa and arepa: stuffed corn cakes from El Salvador and from Venezuela and Colombia, familiar to many US diners.

Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat to do, where to go in Mexico › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American culture, food and life. × This week Tonight Where to eat Before you go Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Fillings to Know, From Pork Crackling to Beans

Chicharrón prensado is the filling that appears at nearly every stall in local guides to Mexico City gorditas. It is pork crackling and trimmings pressed into a dense block, then reheated with chilli until soft and spicy.

The other fillings named most often by Chilango, a Mexico City listings magazine, and the business daily El Financiero are these:

Frijoles: refried beans, the standard meat-free choice.

refried beans, the standard meat-free choice. Requesón: a soft, ricotta-like fresh cheese, often mixed with chicharrón.

a soft, ricotta-like fresh cheese, often mixed with chicharrón. Papa and haba: mashed potato or fava-bean paste, both cheap and filling.

mashed potato or fava-bean paste, both cheap and filling. Tinga de pollo: shredded chicken stewed with tomato and chipotle chilli.

shredded chicken stewed with tomato and chipotle chilli. Carnitas, suadero and pastor: taquería meats, offered by stalls that also sell tacos.

taquería meats, offered by stalls that also sell tacos. Combinations: Gorditas Mixcoac’s “La Ricota” pairs chicharrón with requesón, El Financiero reported in 2022.

Toppings follow. Mexico City’s tourism portal notes that nearly everything off a comal can come with dry white cheese, crema (soured cream) or both.

Ask for “con todo” to get every topping, or “sin queso” and “sin crema” to skip the dairy. The same portal suggests the second option for delicate stomachs.

Regional Styles and the Sweet Gorditas of La Villa

Gorditas change flour and shape as you travel. The Comarca Lagunera, the Torreón area spanning Coahuila and Durango, is known for gorditas made with wheat flour rather than corn.

Chilango reported that style in 2022, with northern fillings such as asado, a red-chilli pork stew, and picadillo, minced meat. Mexico News Daily, an English-language outlet in Mexico, also describes flour versions in Coahuila and Durango.

Not every gordita is savoury. Around the Basilica of Guadalupe, the Catholic shrine in northern Mexico City, vendors sell Gorditas de La Villa.

Mexico City’s tourism portal describes them as small, slightly sweetened corn discs cooked on comales and wrapped in brightly coloured tissue paper. It calls them the obligatory sweet reward for pilgrims to the Virgin of Tepeyac.

Pilgrim numbers peak around 12 December, the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe. A separate guide covers Virgin of Guadalupe Day in Mexico City and what to expect there.

What a Gordita Costs in 2026, in Pesos and US Dollars

The most recent national figure comes from ANPEC, the National Alliance of Small Shopkeepers, a lobby group for Mexico’s corner stores. Its January 2026 figures, reported by the newspaper Publimetro, put the average gordita at 25 pesos (about US$1.39).

That was two pesos (about US$0.11), or 8.7%, more than in January 2025. Conversions here use the central bank Banco de México’s FIX rate of 6 October 2026, 17.97 pesos per US dollar.

The same ANPEC list gives a sense of scale for other street staples, at January 2026 average prices:

Taco de guisado (stew taco): 16 pesos (about US$0.89)

Tamal: 25 pesos (about US$1.39)

Gordita: 25 pesos (about US$1.39)

Quesadilla: 27 pesos (about US$1.50)

Sope: 30 pesos (about US$1.67)

Huarache, a long sandal-shaped masa base: 40 pesos (about US$2.23)

Comida corrida, a set lunch: 90 pesos (about US$5.01)

Averages hide a wide range. In November 2022 Chilango found Mexico City stalls charging from 15 pesos (about US$0.83) to 35 pesos (about US$1.95) per gordita.

Its examples, converted at the October 2026 rate, show how style and filling move the price:

La Vikina , Calzada del Hueso at Calzada de Tlalpan: fried chicharrón, requesón or bean gorditas from 15 pesos (about US$0.83) in 2022.

, Calzada del Hueso at Calzada de Tlalpan: fried chicharrón, requesón or bean gorditas from 15 pesos (about US$0.83) in 2022. Gorditas Mixcoac , Mixcoac Market: from 15 pesos (about US$0.83), with loaded “atascadas” up to 42 pesos (about US$2.34) in April 2022, per El Financiero.

, Mixcoac Market: from 15 pesos (about US$0.83), with loaded “atascadas” up to 42 pesos (about US$2.34) in April 2022, per El Financiero. El Güero , San Juan de Aragón Market: “ahogadas”, double-cooked and bathed in salsa, from 20 pesos (about US$1.11) in 2022.

, San Juan de Aragón Market: “ahogadas”, double-cooked and bathed in salsa, from 20 pesos (about US$1.11) in 2022. Gorditas 100% Laguneras , Colonia Ajusco in Coyoacán: wheat-flour Laguna style from 35 pesos (about US$1.95) in 2022.

, Colonia Ajusco in Coyoacán: wheat-flour Laguna style from 35 pesos (about US$1.95) in 2022. Raíces Centro Cultural, Colonia Banjidal: a plate of three cracked-corn gorditas for 65 pesos (about US$3.62) in 2022.

Expect more today. ANPEC’s figures show the street staples it tracks rose between 6.6% and 21.4% in the year to January 2026.

On those figures, budget roughly 25 to 45 pesos (about US$1.39 to US$2.50) per gordita at stalls in 2026. Loaded versions and sit-down antojerías, cafés that specialise in masa snacks, cost more.

Where to Find Good Gorditas in Mexico City

The safest bet is a busy public market. Mexico City’s government tourism portal names several gordita spots in its borough-by-borough food guide.

Sonora Market (Venustiano Carranza): known for its herbal and folk-magic stalls, it also sells pork-rind gorditas, pambazos and pozole, the portal says.

(Venustiano Carranza): known for its herbal and folk-magic stalls, it also sells pork-rind gorditas, pambazos and pozole, the portal says. La Vikina (Calzada de Tlalpan at Calzada del Hueso, in the south): its crunchy gorditas with single, double or triple fillings “gather crowds”, according to the portal.

(Calzada de Tlalpan at Calzada del Hueso, in the south): its crunchy gorditas with single, double or triple fillings “gather crowds”, according to the portal. Comal Oculto (San Miguel Chapultepec): a tiny restaurant the portal credits with lifting gorditas and suadero to “an excellent flavor level”.

(San Miguel Chapultepec): a tiny restaurant the portal credits with lifting gorditas and suadero to “an excellent flavor level”. Mixcoac Market (Benito Juárez): El Financiero called Mixcoac the neighbourhood of legendary gorditas in 2022; Gorditas Mixcoac had then traded for over 40 years.

(Benito Juárez): El Financiero called Mixcoac the neighbourhood of legendary gorditas in 2022; Gorditas Mixcoac had then traded for over 40 years. Basilica of Guadalupe (Gustavo A. Madero): the place for sweet Gorditas de La Villa.

Hours skew to breakfast and lunch. Several stalls in Chilango’s 2020 guide opened around 8 a.m. and closed by mid-afternoon or early evening.

Stalls move and prices change, so check a recent listing or map review before crossing the city for one.

If your trip continues south, masa takes other forms, from Oaxaca’s giant tlayudas to the market snacks in this Puebla restaurant guide.

How to Order, Pay and Eat Safely

A few phrases cover most stalls, and even basic Spanish speeds things up:

“Una gordita de chicharrón, por favor” : one pork-crackling gordita, please.

: one pork-crackling gordita, please. “¿De qué tiene?” : what fillings do you have?

: what fillings do you have? “Con todo” or “sin queso, sin crema” : with everything, or no cheese and no cream.

or : with everything, or no cheese and no cream. “¿Pica?” : is it spicy?

: is it spicy? “¿Cuánto es?” : how much is it?

: how much is it? “Para llevar”: to take away.

Pay in pesos and carry coins and small notes. INEGI, Mexico’s statistics office, found that 85.2% of adults mostly paid cash for purchases up to 500 pesos (about US$28) in 2024.

That share was down from 90.1% in 2021, as cards and transfers grew. Break large notes first: a 500-peso note (about US$28) is a lot of change for a 25-peso (about US$1.39) snack.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises travellers to avoid street food. Those who eat it should choose food cooked and served steaming hot and skip raw vegetables.

The agency also lists fresh salsas made from raw fruit or vegetables among foods to avoid. It recommends a hepatitis A vaccine for unvaccinated travellers to Mexico aged one or older.

Locals apply a simpler test, echoed by Mexico City’s tourism portal. Eat where the queue is long and the food turns over fast.

What It Means for US Readers

Many Americans know the name from Taco Bell’s Cheesy Gordita Crunch, a soft flatbread wrapped around a crunchy taco shell. A Mexican gordita has no shell: it is corn masa, with the filling inside the dough.

At 25 pesos (about US$1.39), a gordita is cheap by US standards. A card-only traveller is still likely to struggle at stalls, so plan cash for every street-food stop.

Health planning is simple but worth doing before the flight. The CDC’s Mexico page, last reviewed on 3 September 2026, recommends hepatitis A vaccination for unvaccinated travellers.

Gorditas fit any itinerary, from a Mexico City layover to a long food trip. For timing, see the region-by-region guide to the best time to visit Mexico.

More on Mexico as a food destination in 2026 and wider practical coverage sit on the Rio Times Mexico page.

What Is Not Known

No government body publishes a price index for gorditas. ANPEC’s averages, as reported by Publimetro, do not state which cities or how many stalls were sampled.

The individual stall prices above date from 2022 and were not re-checked at each stall in October 2026. Opening hours and even locations can change without notice.

US dollar values move with the exchange rate. A stronger or weaker peso will change what a gordita costs a US visitor, even if the peso price stays the same.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a gordita in Mexico?

A gordita is a thick cake of corn masa, griddled or fried, then split and stuffed like a pocket. The name means “little fat one”.

How much does a gordita cost in Mexico in 2026?

The average was 25 pesos, about US$1.39, in January 2026, according to the small-shopkeeper alliance ANPEC. Loaded versions and sit-down restaurants charge more.

What is the most popular gordita filling?

Chicharrón prensado, pressed pork crackling stewed with chilli, appears at nearly every stall in Mexico City guides. Beans, requesón cheese, potato and stews are common alternatives.

How is a gordita different from a sope or a tlacoyo?

A gordita is split and stuffed after cooking. A sope is topped like an open tart, and a tlacoyo is an oblong cake with the filling sealed inside.

Is it safe for US visitors to eat gorditas from street stalls?

The CDC advises avoiding street food and says those who try it should eat food served steaming hot. It also recommends skipping raw salsas and getting a hepatitis A vaccine.

Is a Mexican gordita the same as a Taco Bell gordita?

No. Taco Bell’s Cheesy Gordita Crunch wraps flatbread around a hard taco shell, while a Mexican gordita is a stuffed corn cake.

Are there sweet gorditas?

Yes. Gorditas de La Villa, small sweetened corn discs wrapped in coloured tissue paper, are sold around Mexico City’s Basilica of Guadalupe.

Sources: Primary: Banco de México, FIX exchange rate, 6 October 2026; INEGI, National Financial Inclusion Survey (ENIF) 2024, 13 March 2025; UNESCO, Traditional Mexican cuisine (2010); Real Academia Española, Diccionario, “gordo, gorda”; CDC, Health Information for Travelers to Mexico; CDC, Food and Water Safety; Mexico City government tourism portal, Street Food, Gustavo A. Madero, Coyoacán, Venustiano Carranza and Miguel Hidalgo food pages; Taco Bell, Cheesy Gordita Crunch. Regional: Publimetro, 18 January 2026 (ANPEC prices); Chilango, 16 November 2022; Chilango, 16 November 2020; El Financiero, 21 April 2022; El Financiero, 25 April 2023; Mexico News Daily, 7 June 2025 (all accessed 7 October 2026).

World.title: Who Runs Chile’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026
World.content:
CHILE · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country 18.5 million people (2024 census); a leading copper and lithium supplier.

— Who governs President José Antonio Kast since 11 March 2026; Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz.

— What happened Codelco said on 6 October it is auditing possibly double-counted output.

— The numbers Copper exports reached US$43.3 billion in January–August 2026, up 19.3%.

— The families The Luksic, Angelini and Paulmann families control big listed groups.

— For US investors Seven Chilean companies, including SQM, list on the New York Stock Exchange.

A new conservative government, a state copper giant under audit and a handful of family groups decide where Chile’s money goes.

The Chile economy is run by a short list: a conservative government, an autonomous central bank, state miner Codelco and family groups. They matter to Americans because Chile is a leading supplier of copper and lithium, and seven Chilean companies trade on Wall Street.

This guide sets out who controls the money, the mines and the brands, as of October 2026. Figures carry their dates, and claims made by companies are attributed to them.

The Referees: Kast, Quiroz and the Central Bank

José Antonio Kast, a conservative, was sworn in as president before Congress on Wednesday, 11 March 2026, according to the Senate. He received the presidential sash from the president of the Senate.

His background is set out in the Rio Times profile of who José Antonio Kast is. The wider balance of power is covered in the guide to Chile politics and who holds power.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Mexico sells record US$60.6bn to the US in August” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Economic policy runs through Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz. On Tuesday, 6 October, he presented the government’s annual report on the state of public finances to Congress.

Quiroz says the programme rests on three pillars: lighter regulation, tax competitiveness and fiscal consolidation. A new reconstruction and development law cuts the corporate income tax from 27% to 23% by 2029, the Finance Ministry says.

The ministry also says about half of 1,000 stalled sector permits were cleared in seven months. That, it says, released more than 40 investment projects worth US$10.4 billion.

On Wednesday, 30 September, Quiroz sent the 2027 budget bill to Congress. He called it a moderate expansion of spending, with emphasis on jobs, public works, housing and security.

Interest rates are set by the Banco Central de Chile, which is autonomous under the constitution. Its president, Rosanna Costa, has led the board since February 2022 and joined it in 2017, the bank says.

The bank kept its policy rate at 4.5% at its September 2026 meeting. Annual inflation was 4.1% in August and unemployment 9.6%, its statistical bulletin shows.

The Comisión para el Mercado Financiero (CMF), the financial regulator, supervises banks, insurers and listed companies. Its chair is Catherine Tornel.
