World.title: US, Greece to jointly combat security threats, Rubio says
World.content:
Marco Rubio speaks at the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue in Athens on Oct. 7, 2026. | Aris Messinis/AFP via Getty Images

Rubio called Greece a “strong and model NATO ally” and a “source of stability in an unstable world.”

ATHENS — The U.S. and Greece are launching a new counterterrorism information-sharing program, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday during an official visit to the Greek capital.

In a press conference alongside his Greek counterpart Giorgos Gerapetritis, Rubio said Greece was particularly exposed to threats posed by mass migration, human trafficking and different forms of terror.

“What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by inaction, and by failure to address challenges,” he said, calling Greece a “strong and model NATO ally” and a “source of stability in an unstable world.”

World.title: Reform probe clears Farage aides caught in donations sting
World.content:
A party official, granted anonymity to discuss internal matters, told POLITICO the pair’s futures will only be decided after the conclusion of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

Scotland Yard is investigating multiple “potential offences” arising from the broadcast of footage showing discussions about how the party could receive donations from an overseas donor and also asking a bogus company to pay for polls commissioned by officials.

On Wednesday, a Reform spokesperson said: “Having concluded the review, the investigation found no evidence that any laws were broken.

“We consider that the production company — Verbatim — acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course.”

While the internal investigation cleared Orr and Jukes of breaking the law, the report said it “does not excuse” the “foolish” way they spoke to the undercover reporter.

In a statement, Jukes welcomed the finding he did not break the law, and said: “I am also considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me.”

Reform published its report just before Kemi Badenoch — leader of their right-wing Conservative rivals — delivered her party conference speech in Birmingham.

In her speech, Badenoch referenced the police investigation into Reform, and rejected calls for her to do a deal with Farage. “To those who say ‘unite the right,’ we are not uniting with that,” she said.

World.title: UK hopeful of deal with EU on Made in Europe
World.content:
Brussels is in the process of updating its trade rules to favor EU producers over those outside the bloc — and London fears some of its businesses will be locked out.

The U.K. has urged the EU to guarantee that British producers won’t be affected. Brussels says it can’t give those guarantees now as the rules are still working their way through the bloc’s cumbersome legislative process.

Yet in the event a deal isn’t reached, London believes its Brexit trade deal, the Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), could force Brussels to think again.

“Our arrangements in terms of how we trade are underpinned by the TCA. That’s a strong arrangement between us which is independently overseen,” Falconer said.

“It provides lots of protections to both sides. Our basic position to our friends is, look, I don't think European competitiveness is enhanced by putting further impediments in the way of our industrial base.”

There are those in Brussels who agree. In-house lawyers at the EU Council have advised member countries that the bloc’s plans for the Industrial Accelerator Act could violate the union’s international trade deals, according to documents seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Berlin und Paris: Diesel-Versprechen an Trump erfordert keine neue Freigabe
World.content:
In einem Treffen hinter verschlossenen Türen räumten die Länder am Mittwoch ein, dass die Freigabe keine neuen Barrel Diesel umfassen würde, so die beiden Diplomaten. Stattdessen handele es sich um Barrel, die bereits im Rahmen einer umfassenderen europäischen Verpflichtung zugesagt worden waren, zwei Drittel davon Raffinerieprodukte. Diese Vereinbarung wurde im März, wenige Wochen nach Ausbruch des Krieges im Iran, von der Internationalen Energieagentur (IEA) vermittelt.

Die genauen Mengen, die die beiden Länder freigeben werden, sind noch unklar. Sie werden jedoch einen Teil der verbleibenden Bestände ausmachen, für deren Freigabe im März eine Zusage gemacht wurde, wie die Diplomaten und ein Sprecher der deutschen Regierung bestätigten.

Von den zugesagten 2,65 Millionen Tonnen Öl, Diesel und Jet-Fuel hat Deutschland bislang nur 600.000 Tonnen auf den Markt gebracht. Inwieweit Frankreich seine Zusage, 14,6 Millionen Barrel freizugeben, bereits erfüllt hat, bleibt unklar. Doch das Land hat erklärt, dass es von dieser Zusage noch mindestens 8 Millionen Barrel übrig habe, die es im Rahmen der jüngsten Bemühungen freigeben könne, wie zwei weitere Diplomaten gegenüber POLITICO sagten.

Die Länder, die über einige der größten Vorräte an raffinierten Erdölprodukten in Europa verfügen, wurden von der Trump-Regierung dafür kritisiert, dass sie ihren im März zugesagten Anteil noch nicht vollständig bereitgestellt haben. Deutschland führt dies laut einem Dokument, das POLITICO vorliegt, auf die schwache Nachfrage nach den Barrel zurück.

Es ist unklar, ob sich die Länder letztendlich dazu entschließen werden, zusätzliche Barrel bereitzustellen. Ein europäischer Beamter erklärte am Montag gegenüber POLITICO, dass die neue Zusage „zwangsläufig“ eine erneute Freigabe impliziere. Wie zwei weitere mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Personen sagten, wird heute eine außerordentliche Sitzung der IEA stattfinden.

Dieser Schritt erfolgt vor dem Hintergrund der Verunsicherung in anderen Mitgliedsländern darüber, wer wann wie viel bereitstellen würde. Einige osteuropäische Länder wie Bulgarien äußerten zudem Bedenken, dass der Abbau der Reserven zur Bekämpfung der Preise sie im Falle einer Versorgungskrise verwundbar machen würde, so die Informanten.

World.title: WHO seeks clarity on second pneumonia case in Russia amid plague fears
World.content:
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros said in his social media post.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he had a "call scheduled" with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" to discuss the situation.

The WHO is looking into the death of the laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, suggested this could be a case of pneumonic plague, as did several initial media reports.

Pneumonic plague is fatal unless patients receive treatment with antibiotics.

Russian authorities have said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast.” Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample.

The WHO said Tuesday that "no cause of death had officially been confirmed."

World.title: France and Germany say diesel promise to Trump won’t require new stock release
World.content:
But in a closed-door meeting of EU energy officials Wednesday, the countries acknowledged that the release wouldn't include new barrels of diesel but rather barrels already pledged under a wider European commitment to release 100 million barrels, two-thirds of which were refined products, the diplomats said. That deal was brokered by the International Energy Agency in March weeks after the outbreak of the war in Iran.

The exact quantities Germany and France will release remains unclear, but they will represent a portion of the remainder of the stocks committed in March, the diplomats and a German government spokesperson said.

Of the 2.65 million tons of oil, diesel and jet fuel promised, Germany has so far released only 600,000 tons onto the market. It remains unclear how much France has contributed of its own commitment to release 14.6 million barrels of oil products. However, Paris has indicated privately that it still has 8 million barrels left under the March commitment, which it will contribute under the latest push, two other diplomats told POLITICO.

The countries, which boast some of the largest reserves of refined oil products in Europe, have been criticized by the Trump administration for not contributing the full share committed in March. Germany attributes that to weak demand for the barrels, according to a document seen by POLITICO.

It's not clear whether countries will ultimately decide to commit additional barrels, with one European official telling POLITICO Monday that the fresh commitment "necessarily implied" a fresh release. France on Wednesday signaled it could release 2 million barrels of diesel on top of the quantities agreed in March — as part of the G7 vow to prioritize releases of the motor fuel over the next 20 days — but stopped short of offering a clear commitment, two diplomats said. An extraordinary meeting of the IEA will take place today, two other people familiar with the matter said.

The move came amid confusion from other member countries over who was committing how much and when, with some Eastern European countries like Bulgaria also expressing concern that blowing through reserves to combat prices would leave them exposed in the event of a supply crisis, the people said.

World.title: EU-Parlament verschärft vor Šefčovič-Reise Haltung zur China-Politik
World.content:
„Ich möchte, dass er mit einem möglichst starken Mandat dieses Hauses dorthin reist“, sagte Hilde Vautmans, die Verfasserin des Berichts, am Dienstagabend in einer Debatte. „Europa verfügt über wirtschaftliche Macht. Es ist an der Zeit, diese einzusetzen.“

Die Äußerung deckt sich mit Positionen, die Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron Anfang der Woche in einem gemeinsamen Papier vereinbart haben. Sie sprechen sich dafür aus, der EU-Kommission mehr Befugnisse zu geben, um Importe aus Ländern, die „schwerwiegende und systematische Verzerrungen“ in der EU verursachen, zu beschränken oder sogar zu unterbinden.

Mehrere Europaabgeordnete lobten die gemeinsame Haltung der beiden größten Volkswirtschaften der EU. Der polnische Europaabgeordnete Mariusz Kamiński von den Europäischen Konservativen und Reformisten ging weiter. Er nannte „pragmatische wirtschaftliche Beziehungen“ zu China unverantwortlich oder schlichtweg dumm. China sei eine „kommunistische Diktatur, die eine Bedrohung für die freie Welt darstellt“, sagte er.

Damit steht er nicht allein. Vielen Abgeordneten genügt es nicht, lediglich gegen Chinas aggressive Exporte aus subventionierten Überkapazitäten vorzugehen. Die EU-Kommission müsse sich auch mit Menschenrechtsverletzungen in China, der Aggression gegen Taiwan und Chinas Rolle bei Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine befassen.

„Wir müssen anerkennen, dass China sich in einer Weise verhält, die unsere Interessen gefährdet. Nicht nur im Handel, sondern auch in den Bereichen Sicherheit und Verteidigung“, sagte der spanische Europaabgeordnete Nicolás Pascual de la Parte von der Europäischen Volkspartei. „Die Menschenrechtslage hat sich nicht verbessert, ist aber in den letzten Jahren von unserer Agenda verschwunden.“

Vautmans wertete die Debatte als Beleg dafür, dass die EU dabei sei, eine einheitliche Haltung gegenüber China einzunehmen. „Das ist nicht mehr nur die Position des Europäischen Parlaments oder einer einzelnen Fraktion“, sagte Vautmans nach der Debatte. „Es setzt sich zunehmend die Erkenntnis durch, dass Europa eine kohärentere China-Politik braucht: offen für Dialog und Zusammenarbeit, aber viel entschlossener, seine Interessen zu verteidigen, wenn es nötig ist.“

Der Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

World.title: Menopause drug Lenzetto returns to Spanish pharmacies in November
World.content:
Lenzetto, one of the hormone therapies most widely used to relieve menopausal symptoms, will once again be available in Spanish pharmacies from the second half of November, its manufacturer Gedeon Richter has confirmed to Euronews.

 

"We anticipate the product will be available in pharmacies from the second half of November," the pharmaceutical company said in response to questions from Euronews. Gedeon Richter says it will do "everything possible" to guarantee a stable level of production for the rest of the year and in 2027, although it acknowledges that global supply restrictions could prevent it from fully meeting existing demand.

The company traces the origin of the current shortage of the medicine in Spain to the sharp increase in demand for hormone treatments for menopause in Europe. In an email, the company explained that growth has been far higher than expected and that both manufacturing capacity and the supply of the device used to administer Lenzetto, the applicator, have been unable to keep pace with rising demand.

Gedeon Richter stresses that "the situation is temporary" and that it "is not related to any quality or safety issue with the medicine". The problem, according to the company, is simply that high demand has outstripped its manufacturing capacity.

To increase the availability of its medicine, the laboratory says it is maximising its current production capacity and working to expand both the number of suppliers and the manufacturing options. It is also seeking to improve the supply of applicators and to increase its production capacity, among other measures.

These plans include a new plant and a new production line. In Romania, Gedeon Richter has also launched a specific investment project to strengthen its manufacturing capacity. The company warns, however, that expanding pharmaceutical production takes time because of quality controls.

The company also acknowledges that the measures taken will not resolve the situation overnight. It says it is therefore working to ensure the changes allow it to improve supply as quickly as possible.

A problem affecting other markets

The shortage of Lenzetto does not only affect Spain. Gedeon Richter confirms that there is currently a global shortage of the medicine, although the severity of the problems varies between markets depending on local demand, forecasting capacity and logistical possibilities.

The situation has for months made it difficult to obtain some hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms. The lack of Lenzetto forced patients and health professionals to resort to other estradiol products, which eventually created a domino effect for some of the alternative treatments.

The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has also identified the shortage of Lenzetto and is analysing possible coordinated measures at European level. In Spain, the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (Aemps) has also reported supply problems affecting other medicines, such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva.

"The supply problem began in April with Lenzetto and has subsequently affected other transdermal hormone therapies such as patches and gels," Aemps said in a statement (source in Spanish) released in early October. "The Ministry of Health has been in contact with the holders of other hormone treatment options that are currently not reimbursed, in order to explore their possible inclusion in the pharmaceutical services provided by the National Health System."

Related Spanish Nutrition Agency issues menopause guidelines based on male studies

Richter responds to Aemps criticism

Aemps has said that some of the supply forecasts previously communicated by Gedeon Richter "have not always been accurate" and that it was not informed in sufficient time about interruptions that could affect the continuous supply of the medicine.

Asked by Euronews about these remarks, the company does not respond directly to the accusations, but says it maintains "close contact" with Aemps and works "in a collaborative way" with the agency to address the situation.

Gedeon Richter also says it has improved its forecasting systems in response to demand it describes as "unprecedented" and that it continues to provide information to the authorities as new data become available.

The laboratory does not, however, guarantee a full recovery of supply in the short term. The company says its aim is to be able consistently to meet patient demand from the second half of 2027.

World.title: Espionage scandal involving ex-BND chief: second arrest over suspected treason
World.content:
One of the biggest espionage scandals in Germany's history has seen a second arrest. Following the detention of former BND chief August Hanning, 80, his long-standing confidant Manfred D., 64, has now also been taken into custody. Federal prosecutors accuse both men of having used state secrets over many years to support private consulting activities and foreign interests, specifically Azerbaijan. Manfred D. is already being held in pre-trial detention, while Hanning is being brought before an investigating judge.

 

What has happened?

Police have arrested a second man in connection with the espionage case. According to reports, he is called Manfred D. and previously served as office manager to former intelligence chief August Hanning. The two men have known each other since the late 1990s and worked closely together for many years at the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and later at the Interior Ministry.

What exactly are the allegations? Prosecutors say Manfred D. obtained classified documents from the intelligence service and passed them on to his former boss Hanning, allegedly in return for payment. The arrangement is believed to have been in place since 2010. The aim: former BND head Hanning is said to have used the confidential information to prepare, among other things, an analysis for Azerbaijan and to earn private income as a consultant.

Months of monitoring by investigators

Senior public prosecutor Dr Ines Peterson said: "Presumably in spring 2010, the defendants agreed that Manfred D. would continuously obtain valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service for the accused Hanning in return for payment." Hanning is alleged to have used the material for private consulting work. To track the men, investigators bugged Manfred D.'s rooms and monitored him for months.

Hanning is under investigation for serious offences including treason and espionage. His alleged accomplice, Manfred D., has been charged with aiding and abetting and is already in custody on remand.

World.title: Italians and Czechs push Brussels to ease green rules as energy crisis hits industry
World.content:
Italy and the Czech Republic have warned Brussels that the European Union's industrial base risks lasting damage unless the bloc eases the burden of its green rules, according to a letter seen by Euronews.

 

The joint warning, issued amid an unprecedented energy shock, reflects mounting pressure from EU capitals to protect domestic manufacturing as high energy and carbon costs collide with the bloc's decarbonisation targets.

"While security of supply remains the immediate priority, the combination of some of the world's highest energy prices, high carbon costs and exceptional fuel prices risks further weakening European manufacturing and accelerating the relocation of production and investment," reads the letter.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni visited her Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš in Prague last week to coordinate the plan of action between Rome and Prague ahead of next week's summit of EU leaders in Brussels.

Rome and Prague are targeting the bloc's carbon market, currently under political scrutiny, as well as its recently weakened methane rules, as they seek a broader coalition within the European Council.

The joint proposal outlines several targeted interventions designed to provide immediate economic oxygen to struggling European factories. Chief among them are the extension of free carbon allowances for heavy industry under the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and freezing the phasing out of free carbon allocations for sectors affected by the bloc's carbon border tax.

The push comes amid growing concern over European competitiveness, which is set to feature prominently on the agenda when EU leaders meet on October 15.

Italy and Czechia framed these measures as "temporary" interventions that "preserve long-term climate objectives". But several of their demands would amount to significant changes to the way the EU applies its climate rules to industry.

"A temporary suspension of the EU ETS would provide immediate relief to European industry from carbon costs. However, in the absence of sufficient support for such an option, it is worth considering a number of targeted and immediately actionable alternatives that the European Council could promote to alleviate the impact of the current shock and complement measures already announced at European level," reads the letter.

Related European leaders meet industry heavyweights in power shift for business

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto recently went further, arguing that the ETS should be suspended until economic conditions improve.

"There would be better times" to reintroduce the carbon market in order to protect the environment, he said.

"A tax like the ETS today is unjust, absurd, unsustainable in international competition, and creates inequalities because it falls indiscriminately and equally on all European end consumers," Crosetto wrote on X.

The Meloni-Babiš initiative is the latest sign of a broader push among EU capitals to give greater weight to industrial competitiveness when implementing the bloc's climate policies.

Austria's Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer made a similar case on the sidelines of a competitiveness ministers' meeting in Brussels on 24 September.

Hattmannsdorfer called for "economic patriotism" to keep industries and jobs in Europe, arguing that maintaining European production is crucial for regional wealth, welfare and environmental standards.

World.title: Iran threatens pre-emptive strikes as US questions who runs Tehran
World.content:
Iran's army spokesman said on Wednesday that the armed forces were prepared to carry out pre-emptive strikes in the war against the US, as senior IRGC figures claimed tighter control over the Strait of Hormuz and Washington questioned how much authority Iran's civilian leadership actually holds.

 

"Should circumstances require it, we will conduct pre-emptive operations down the line in order to prevent the enemy from committing any act of aggression or intrusion," spokesman for Iran's regular army Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia told the state-run IRNA news agency.

IRGC officials separately said Hormuz was firmly in Tehran's hands, despite a parallel US naval blockade of the vital waterway.

"The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces have full control over it, and this situation will continue until Iran's legitimate demands are met," Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior IRGC adviser, said in a media interview.

He claimed that some vessels were using small boats to smuggle oil through the strait to larger tankers.

"Soon, a small number of the routes that violators have created by blasting and destroying some of the existing rocky passages in the Strait of Hormuz will be blocked," Naqdi said.

A second IRGC adviser, Brigadier General Amirahmadi, said international bodies had recorded an average of around 10 ships per day transiting the strait, against nearly 125 before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February.

"These ships are mainly those that pass through the waterway and designated route with the permission of the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.

Washington questions Iranian authorities

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a speech on Wednesday that the government was engaged in negotiations while simultaneously facing what he called "an all-out war on every front."

"We speak from a position of dignity and power, and at the same time we are vigorously pursuing a programme of resistance and resilience," Pezeshkian said.

On the country's severe electricity shortages, he said the government would close sports and cultural centres if necessary to reduce consumption.

Vance, confirming that Washington had held talks with Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, said it was unclear how much authority the two men wielded within Iran's power structure.

"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance told Reuters after a campaign event in Alaska.

He said the main US objective was to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear arms and suggested Tehran should take a concrete step on enrichment to demonstrate it was not seeking one.

"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity," Vance said.

Speaking in Maryland on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said Iran was "no longer such a bully" and claimed full US control over the strait.

"They were the bully of the Middle East. They're not so much the bully anymore, but we have to finish up. And it's only a question of which way do we want to do it, the nice way or the not-so-nice way. And pretty soon you'll find out," he said.

Trump has repeatedly questioned its decision-makers, calling for "new leadership in Iran," and said the new Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — who still has not made a single public appearance since he was appointed supreme leader in March — was "a sick man".

However, in a June podcast, Trump suggested the younger Khamenei is in charge. "They say he is giving approval, because that's the way it has been for a long, long time," the US president said.

World.title: Longevity: why do Poles live shorter than Western Europeans?
World.content:
"We are lagging behind not only in terms of average life expectancy, but also in the number of years we spend in good health. And that is a metric that really needs to be improved," Mordaka told Euronews during the Economic Forum in Karpacz.

 

He pointed out that around 60% of deaths are caused by two major groups of illnesses: cardiovascular diseases and cancers. In both cases, prevention and earlier intervention in response to risk factors can play a key role.

Prevention in Poland is still underfunded

According to the doctor, the problem does not come down solely to individual choices made by Poles. The way the healthcare system operates is also crucial. Poland is among the EU countries that devote the smallest share of health spending to preventive care.

"The EU average is around 6% of health budgets, while in Poland it is just under 2%. And without funding it is impossible to reverse this trend," Mordaka said.

At the same time, many of the factors that affect the length and quality of life remain in patients' own hands. Mordaka draws attention to the so-called Life's Essential 8 – eight areas that are critical to cardiovascular health.

These include keeping blood pressure, blood glucose and cholesterol under control, maintaining a healthy body weight, getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and not smoking. Regular physical activity is also vital.

"These are the small, everyday choices. Do we go to the shop and buy a sugary drink, or do we buy water instead?" the expert asked.

Dr Robert Mordaka in the Euronews studio in Karpacz Paweł Głogowski, Euronews

Obesity and smoking can cut life expectancy by many years

One of the biggest current threats to health is obesity. According to Mordaka, studies indicate that it can shorten life by as much as 15 years. Another major factor is smoking, which can take several years off life expectancy, depending on how many cigarettes are smoked per day and how long the habit continues.

A lack of physical activity also has a negative impact on how long we live. That is why one of the simplest ways to improve health is to increase the amount of movement in everyday life. The expert advises starting with two basic elements: reviewing your diet and increasing your physical activity.

"Let’s take a close look at how we eat. Let’s plan a healthy plate and adapt it to our age and state of health. And the second thing: let’s start moving," Mordaka urged. "Exercise is the best medicine," the expert concluded.

According to World Health Organization guidelines, adults should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week. This does not have to mean intensive workouts; it can be brisk walking, cycling or other forms of moderate exercise.

World.title: Europe’s travel and tourism industry to grow 3.1% in 2026, new figures reveal
World.content:
Travel and tourism is set to grow by 3.1% in Europe in 2026 – outpacing the wider economy – despite global uncertainty, the latest World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) research has revealed.

 

The continent should outperform global tourism, which is expected to grow by 2.5% across the year despite tensions in the Middle East and the wider cost of living crisis.

International visitor spending in Europe will increase by 5.8%, while leisure spending is up 3.1%, with business travel up 4.2%.

The new figures were released during the opening press conference of the WTTC's 26th Global Summit in Malta, which Euronews Travel is attending.

Nicknamed the “Davos of travel”, the annual summit is bringing together more than 200 CEOs and government officials alongside 1,000 delegates.

“This is a sector that is ready to invest and innovate, but governments must create the right conditions – enabling seamless travel, strengthening connectivity, developing talent and supporting sustainable growth,” Gloria Guevara, WTTC’s President and CEO, said.

“The choices made today will determine how much of this opportunity Europe captures.”

What’s happening at the WTTC summit?

Panels at WTTC's FUTU[RE]SET Global Summit will focus on the key issues that the travel industry is facing today, such as encouraging tourism growth without harming local communities, while sustainability, accessibility and more will be on the agenda.

Speakers include Justin Trudeau, the former Prime Minister of Canada; Apostolos Tzitzikostas, European Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism; and Nick Adams, the first U.S. Presidential Envoy for Tourism.

“The WTTC Global Summit brings together the leaders shaping the future of Travel & Tourism,” WTTC chairman Manfredi Lefebvre, said.

“Malta’s Government has shown strong leadership and commitment to our sector, making it an ideal host for these important discussions.

“Over the coming days, we will strengthen partnerships, advance new initiatives and help ensure Travel & Tourism continues to drive growth, investment and opportunity around the world.”

World.title: Madrid versus Latin America: Where is housing more affordable?
World.content:
For the price of one square metre of housing in Madrid, you can buy almost two in central Mexico City and nearly three in Buenos Aires, Bogotá or São Paulo. But higher property prices do not necessarily mean a heavier burden on local wages.

 

The key question is how much of their income locals need to spend to afford a home.

If you compare rents with wages, the gap shrinks and in some cases even flips.

In the Madrid region, renting an 80-square-metre flat at December 2025 asking prices would have absorbed 71% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs that year, according to a study by Fotocasa and InfoJobs.

In Buenos Aires, a two-room apartment comes to almost 80% of an average worker's income.

And in parts of the Santiago metropolitan area, anyone on the minimum wage can end up spending between 78% and 96% of their take-home pay on the rent for a small flat.

These measures illustrate the pressure on incomes, although differences in flat sizes, geographical coverage and wage definitions mean they are not directly comparable.

A commonly used affordability benchmark is to spend no more than 30% of income on rent. Taking Spain's modal salary (the most frequently recorded salary, rather than the average), which was €16,520 in 2024, and dividing it by 12 gives approximately €1,377 a month before tax. Applying that benchmark leaves about €413 a month for rent.

At that price, searches on housing portals found nothing available in Madrid. The closest option was €500 for a flat of barely 30 square metres.

The exercise produces virtually the same result in Barcelona. For €500, you can find somewhere noticeably larger than in the national capital, but the search returned just three homes.

How much housing costs in Madrid

Existing homes in Madrid were advertised at an average of €6,471 per square metre in August, according to property website Idealista. This is 2.2% more than a year earlier and below the April peak of €6,619. The slowdown has not reached the cheapest districts: in Villaverde, the borough with the most affordable homes per square metre, prices have jumped 25% in a year.

Rents, meanwhile, show no sign of hitting a ceiling. In September, they set a record of €23.4 per square metre a month, 4.8% more than a year ago. A study by InfoJobs and Fotocasa, comparing advertised salaries with asking rents for an 80-square-metre home, put the cost at 71% of gross pay in the Madrid region in 2025, compared with a national average of 50%.

The Madrid regional government has not designated any “stressed” housing areas under Spain's Housing Act, which allows rent limits in those areas. Other regions, including Catalonia, the Basque Country and Navarre, have used the mechanism.

A woman, holding a set of keys in her hand, protests during a housing demonstration. AP Photo

The national government has also sought to intervene. After parliament rejected two housing decrees on 2 October, the cabinet approved replacement measures on 6 October, including rental contract extensions, limits on annual rent increases and protection against evictions for vulnerable households. The new decrees still require parliamentary ratification.

Madrid versus other Spanish cities

Madrid is not the most expensive provincial capital for buying a home, although it is for renting. According to Idealista, in August San Sebastián was more expensive: €6,680 per square metre versus Madrid's €6,471. Behind them came Palma (€5,835) and Barcelona (€5,440).

For rentals, Madrid led the way with €23.4 per square metre in September, ahead of Barcelona (€20.1) and Palma (€19.6), while the national average was €15.1.

At the same time, Madrid’s asking house prices rose 2.2% in the year to August, the smallest increase among the cities compared here. Seville (11.5%) and Bilbao (10.6%) recorded the largest increases.

Barcelona, a cap Madrid does not have

Barcelona has been officially designated a stressed housing area since 2024.

According to the Catalan Land Institute (Incasòl), the average rent on new contracts was €1,137 a month in the first quarter of 2026, 4.7% less than two years earlier.

The latest asking-rent figures also show a contrast: rents in Barcelona fell 0.8% in the year to September, while in Madrid they rose 4.8%.

Supply remains contested. In the first quarter, 8,156 contracts were signed in Barcelona, 17% fewer than in the same period of 2024.

The regional government counters that the number of active contracts for regular residential rentals across municipalities with rent caps has increased by 20,994 since the measure was introduced. Idealista's spokesperson argues that advertised supply is falling most sharply in the most heavily regulated markets.

Housing costs still stretch wages across Spain

San Sebastián, the priciest provincial capital for buying, has seen advertised rents fall by 2.5% in a year. In Bilbao, advertised rents are down 0.3%, although sale prices are up 10.6%. The city has been declared a stressed area until October 2028.

In Valencia, which, like Madrid, has no declared stressed areas, rents are just 0.5% below their all-time high. Meanwhile, Seville's sale prices, despite a rise of 11.5%, remain 12% below the 2007 peak, when prices reached €3,322 per square metre.

Palma has seen the sharpest rent increase among the cities compared here, with prices up 7.3% to €19.6 per square metre. The Balearic Islands are the most expensive region in which to buy (€5,595 per square metre).

Despite these differences, renting remains expensive relative to wages. According to InfoJobs and Fotocasa, renting an 80-square-metre home at the end of 2025 would have absorbed 76% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs in Barcelona province, 72% in Madrid province and 64% in the Balearics.

Latin America compared: Lower prices, but homes still out of reach

Mexico City is the most expensive Latin American city surveyed in Deutsche Bank’s Mapping the World's Prices 2026 report, which compares 69 cities worldwide. City-centre homes cost €3,441 per square metre, followed by Rio de Janeiro (€3,264), Santiago (€2,507), São Paulo (€2,397), Bogotá (€2,329) and Buenos Aires (€2,328).

These figures are below Madrid’s August asking price of €6,471 per square metre, although the comparison mixes Latin American city centres with Madrid’s city-wide market.

The picture changes when you set rents alongside minimum wages. In Madrid, an 80-square-metre flat at Idealista's average asking rent costs about €1,872 a month, roughly 1.3 times the minimum wage, equivalent to €1,424.50 gross a month when spread over 12 payments. In Mexico City, the average rent for a two-bedroom flat of 65 square metres is about 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage.

In Buenos Aires, the rent on a two-room, 50-square-metre flat also exceeds twice the minimum wage, and in Bogotá the average asking rent is about 2.1 times the monthly minimum wage.

The flat sizes differ, but the figures illustrate how lower prices can still leave housing beyond a low-paid worker’s reach.

Five cities, five housing crises

Behind these affordability pressures lie different policies and housing conditions. Mexico City and Colombia limit annual rent increases, while Argentina has relaxed rental rules. The following examples show how these approaches sit alongside the pressures on local incomes.

Mexico City: Rising rents despite limits on increases

Asking rents rose 9.6% in the year to June, more than double inflation, according to the Inmuebles24 index.

A two-bedroom flat costs an average of 21,921 pesos (€1,069) a month. Nearly two million people, one in four inhabitants, live in rented housing, according to the city government.

A Mexican man holds a sign reading AP Photo

Buying is even further out of reach. A calculation by the financial publication 'Expansión' estimates that a monthly income of around 85,800 pesos (€4,187) is needed to buy a 60-square-metre home, almost nine times the 2026 minimum wage.

To improve affordability, the city already has a rent cap. The Supreme Court has upheld a rule limiting annual increases in agreed rents to the previous year's inflation. For 2026, that cap is 3.69%.

But it only applies to existing contracts. Meanwhile, the indices compiled by property portals track flats coming onto the market.

Buenos Aires: Rents after deregulation

Argentina took the opposite path. Javier Milei's decree scrapping the Rent Act came into force at the end of 2023, allowing rental terms to be negotiated freely.

Following deregulation, the supply of rental flats in the capital surged. Advertised supply in Buenos Aires is now 3.4 times greater than at the low point in February 2023.

Graffiti on the outskirts of the Hotel Montreal AP Photo

Asking rents rose 19.2% in the first eight months of 2026, below estimated inflation of around 21.5%.

A two-room flat costs 886,527 pesos (€516) a month, close to 80% of what the average employed worker in Argentina earns, 1,104,227 pesos (€643), according to Indec, the national statistics office.

Buying is another story. A two-room flat on the market costs around €116,000 on average. According to a calculator by the Argentine daily La Nación, buying a 50-square-metre flat, depending on the neighbourhood, requires between six and 35 years of a person's entire income.

São Paulo: Rent weighs on low-income households

São Paulo has the highest asking rents of any Brazilian state capital, at 65.36 reais (€11.2) per square metre in August, according to the FipeZAP index. Asking rents rose 5.74% in 12 months, outpacing inflation at 4.22%.

Asking prices for houses in July were above 12,000 reais (€2,042) per square metre.

High rents are also the largest component of Brazil’s housing deficit. An estimated 5.77 million households in Brazil, representing 7.4% of the total, needed better or more affordable housing in 2024, with high rents the biggest reason.

In South America's biggest economy, 3.59 million low-income households spent more than 30% of their income on rent in 2024, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the country’s estimated housing deficit.

The state of São Paulo accounts for 26.9% of those households.

A protest in São Paulo calling for the extension of the eviction moratorium AP Photo

Bogotá: Rent limits in a tight market

In Colombia, a 2003 law limits annual rent increases to the previous year's inflation, setting the 2026 cap at 5.10%. Monthly rent cannot exceed 1% of the property's value either. Even so, the market is highly strained.

Bogotá’s rental vacancy rate is just 1.9%, and an average apartment was advertised in the first quarter at 3.76 million pesos (about €1,035) a month. That is more than double the 2026 minimum wage of 1,750,905 pesos (about €482), following a 23% increase.

The minimum-wage rise also pushed up the maximum permitted price of social housing. That ceiling is tied to the minimum wage and has risen 76% in four years. At the start of the year, the government published a draft decree to stop minimum-wage increases from automatically raising that price ceiling.

Santiago de Chile: 11 years' income to buy a home

A Chilean family on an average income would have to spend everything it earns for 11.4 years to buy a home at the average price, according to a late-2024 estimate from the Chilean Chamber of Construction. Beyond five years, the indicator classifies housing as unaffordable.

Renting also puts pressure on low-paid workers. In metropolitan municipalities such as Independencia or La Florida, a two-bedroom flat of under 50 square metres costs between 345,000 and 421,000 pesos a month, according to Fundación SOL. That absorbs roughly 78% to 96% of the take-home minimum wage used in its study.

Informal housing adds another layer to the crisis

In Latin America, between a fifth and a quarter of the urban population lives in informal settlements, according to CAF, citing UN-Habitat and ECLAC. More than 30% of the urban population lives in inadequate conditions, according to the housing yearbook produced by CAF and the Lincoln Institute.

The crisis also affects people who have built their own homes in neighbourhoods without basic services.

In Madrid, aside from exceptions such as the Cañada Real settlement, the problem is mainly one of affordability: there are homes available, but often at prices wages cannot support.

Across the cities examined, the common challenge is the gap between housing costs and what people earn. Lower prices alone do not make a home affordable if rent still consumes most of a worker’s income, leaving little for other essentials.

World.title: Iran parliament votes to criminalise interviews with 'hostile' foreign media
World.content:
Iran's parliament voted 174 to six on Tuesday to pass an article banning Iranian nationals from giving interviews to or participating in discussions with media outlets designated as "hostile" by the Intelligence Ministry, or with outlets owned, managed or funded by operatives connected to countries classified as adversaries of the Islamic Republic.

 

Violations of Article 22 of the bill on "countering the penetration of intelligence services and foreign governments or entities" carry sixth-degree penalties under the Islamic Penal Code, including imprisonment of more than six months up to two years, fines, 31 to 74 lashes, deprivation of social rights and other restrictions.

The bill classifies foreign governments into two tiers: a "level 1 government" is a state formally designated as hostile under Iranian law or by decision of the Supreme National Security Council.

"Level 2" is defined as a state that has planned or carried out actions aimed at damaging Tehran's political, defence, security, economic, social or cultural interests.

The list of level two governments is to be drawn up by the Intelligence Ministry and the IRGC intelligence organisation, then approved by the Supreme National Security Council.

A proposal by Tehran MP Alireza Salimi to exempt government officials from the scope of Article 22 was also approved at the same sitting.

President Masoud Pezeshkian's cabinet had formally opposed the bill. At its 22 August meeting, the cabinet said the legislation had "serious flaws," including restrictions on scientific activity, the acceleration of elite emigration and negative consequences at national and international level.

First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref had warned of consequences for science and technology. Presidential legal deputy Majid Ansari said "criminalising broad and general categories in this bill could harm citizens' rights."

Pezeshkian AP Photo

Parliament also passed Article 20 of the same bill, under which anyone who accesses unpublished official information by virtue of their job may not share it with a foreign agent without prior authorisation. The penalty is four to 10 years in prison and a permanent bar from the post through which the information was accessed.

The legislation follows months of hardline rhetoric from Iranian officials against Persian-language broadcasters outside Iran.

On 26 August, armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi accused BBC Persian, Iran International and Radio Farda of links to US and Israeli intelligence organisations and said their staff could be placed in the Islamic Republic's "military targets bank".

Abolfazl Shekarchi, senior spokesperson for the armed forces of the Islamic Republic ایرنا

Following the parliamentary vote, the bill still needs further approval to become law. The Majlis must complete its examination of remaining articles before sending the text to the Guardian Council, which reviews legislation for compatibility with Sharia and the constitution.

If the Guardian Council raises objections and the Majlis insists on its position, the Expediency Council makes a final ruling.

The parliament that passed the article emerged from elections in which turnout was reportedly at around 41%, the lowest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Turnout in Tehran was around 24%. The leading candidate in the capital won some 598,000 votes, compared with more than 1.6 million for the leading Tehran candidate in the 2016 elections.

World.title: South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
World.content:
South Sudan's first general election is set for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts over whether the poll can be held credibly.

South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22. It will be the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

But political tensions are high as preparations lag. Debate over the election intensified after President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.

Some voters are skeptical that the election will take place

Many are worried not only about the electoral logistics and insecurity in the country known for violent power struggles and political instability, according to Denis Logonyi, a Juba-based journalist.

Will elections happen in South Sudan? To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"People are having different views on these elections," Logonyi told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about elections," Logonyi told DW.

"There has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain," one voter said.

Another voter told DW that while South Sudanese are eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.

Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, the voter said.

Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline

Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.

On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue. Thirty-nine parties took part in discussions on the critical issues ahead of the election.

The meeting was initiated by Kiir, with some civil society groups left out, according to Logonyi. Minister of Cabinet Affairs Dr. Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges.

"Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted," Lomuro said.

"A credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."

According to Albino Akol Atak, the Deputy Rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline.

"The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear. We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles," Atak said.

Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, Secretary General of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said the success of the election would depend entirely on urgent, comprehensive collaboration.

"The South Sudan Opposition Alliance strongly believes that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders," Reath said.

"Given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."

Sudan has a history of planning then postponing elections

South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.

Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals — including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off since.

South Sudan's President Salva Kiir is set to contest in the December election Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.

"The absence of Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."

The 2018 power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country. However, tensions between the two persisted.

In March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest and later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.

South Sudan's former Vice President Riek Machar pictured in court in Juba in September 2025 Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP

Key conditions envisioned for elections under peace deal not fulfilled yet

"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."

The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."

Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal are unfinished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.

Analysts have long been warning that the legitimacy of any election without these key issues being addressed would be undermined.

"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."

According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.

How instability persists in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote

South Sudan is facing severe flooding, displacement and food insecurity. These conditions could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.

For communities displaced by conflicts in particular, there's uncertainty over how they would register and cast their ballots.

Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict.

Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process.

Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.

For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability.

This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

World.title: China's Golden Week reveals cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
World.content:
Chinese visitors are returning from trips after the 13-day Golden Week holiday. Their subdued spending has raised fresh questions about domestic demand in the world's second-largest economy.

Ya Xi just returned to Shanghai on a red-eye flight after her Golden Week trip to Southeast Asia. "I can stay up all night for a cheaper ticket," she told DW.

She was among the 31.19 million passengers who traveled during the 13-day holiday period that followed the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 25 and China's National Day on October 1.

Many of them spent their budgets more cautiously this year.

"I earn less this year, so I'm lowering my budget for this year's Golden Week," said Xi, who is in her mid-20s. "I spent 5,000 yuan (about €660) on my flight, which was the largest expense of my trip."

Golden Week is viewed as a barometer of the Chinese economy with Beijing using it as an opportunity to showcase the world's second-largest economy's spending power. State media, for instance, reported a record-breaking 25.204 million passenger trips on China's railway network on October 1.

State media reported record-breaking train passenger numbers over Golden Week Image: CFOTO/picture alliance

However, early data indicated more moderate spending per traveler and broadly flat passenger traffic, according to Citigroup analysts. Traffic volume during the first four days of the holiday rose just 0.1% year over year, far below the 3.5% increase seen during this year's Labor Day vacation.

Selective spending among younger consumers

Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese Economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told DW that Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly selective.

"My read is that people are willing to get out and spend. They're just being much more careful about how much and what they spend on," Lee said.

But being cautious doesn't mean staying frozen, she added. "They'll spend on travel, concerts, restaurants, experiences, and tech… if they think it's worth it, they'll economize pretty aggressively elsewhere."

Xi's Golden Week trip followed this pattern, paying more for significant experiences and economizing elsewhere: "Eat, drink, and be merry," said Xi, indicating she was willing to spend more on food. For example, she set a 200-yuan (about €26) budget for each meal.

Many Chinese are opting for budget travel options instead of luxury trips Image: CFOTO/picture alliance

Guo-Chen Wang, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told DW that the budget-travel trend among Chinese visitors was ongoing.

"The number of trips is increasing, butconsumption remains strained, as I saw in past years," Wang said.

The Chinese government attempted to boost Golden Week spending by providing coupons worth more than 310 million yuan (€41.2 million). Wang remained unconvinced about the effectiveness of such a measure: "That's an old solution to an old problem."

A sign of China's weak domestic demand

It isn't the first Golden Week to see weak consumer demand. During last year's holiday season, the average spending per trip was 911.04 yuan (around €121), the lowest in three years, according to Reuters.

"Beijing still believes the low spending was due to consumers' reluctance [to spend]," Wang said. "In fact, we think Chinese consumers are unable to spend."

While savings kept increasing in Chinese banks, Wang said the vast majority of the savings are held by a small proportion of the population. "In other words, the majority of Chinese people don't have savings."

"The fundamental issue is the wealth gap in Chinese society," he said. "I don't know whether Beijing really neglected this problem or was simply unwilling to face it."

China’s tourism surge: expansion, regulation and challenges To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A recent International Monetary Fund publication, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, once again noted that China's domestic demand has been weak since the pandemic, when the property market correction began.

Lee, however, saw weak spending during this Golden Week as a confidence problem.

"Theproperty downturnhas hit household wealth, income and job expectations are still pretty soft, and several years of weak prices have trained people to wait for discounts and hunt for value," she told DW.

Tightened cross-border rules played a limited role

Weeks before the Golden Week, China's tightened travel restrictions took effect on September 15. The new restrictions ban citizens from leaving the country if they are deemed to pose a risk to national as well as industrial or technological security.

Wang expected Chinese tourists to turn to domestic travel under the new rules, but the outcome did not match his expectations. "The volume of travel abroad is in fact growing, though not by much," he said.

Lee said she saw little evidence of a broad chilling effect on ordinary outbound tourism, with the Golden Week numbers serving as a "useful reality check."

"The September rules give authorities more room to verify travel purposes and ask for additional information in some cases," Lee said. "They still leave plenty of room for ordinary overseas tourism."

Mi Tang in Taipei contributed to this article.

Edited by: Kate Martyr

World.title: German spy scandal threatens national security
World.content:
The arrest of Germany's former intelligence chief August Hanning could undermine national security, experts warn, as allies may reconsider their intelligence relationships.

The arrests of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, are threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Manfred D. is accused of selling around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005 following seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year.

On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."

DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to Florian Flade, a reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings the BND delivered to the German government, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries.

"This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast . "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war."

Broken trust, broken credibility

Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the Central Intelligence Agency in the US is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country.

If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China — though there is no suggestion of that as yet.

"There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries."

That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital.

"There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added. Ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told.

Security loopholes in Germany's parliament spark concern To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war" and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" — though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia.

Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D. and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place.

The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners.

For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022.

Florian Flade is an espionage expert and guest in DW's Berlin Briefing podcast this week Image: DW

New rules for old officials?

The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. After leaving the BND, Hanning founded his own security consultancy business, where he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be.

Timo Lange of the NGO LobbyControl said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives.

"It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union."

But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant."

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

World.title: France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters
World.content:
France is suspending the use of stun grenades against protesters as allegations of student brutality draw more anger. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is scheduled to address protesters later today.

France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks.

"I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday.

He emphasized that the suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened."

Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports of serious injuries to teenage protesters drew public anger.

French regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported this Monday that a 15-year-old had his hand and a part of his lower arm blown off after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated during protests.

Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests, with the officer having been charged on Tuesday.

France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French prime minister to deliver speech

Wednesday's order comes before an address by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to protesters later Wednesday evening.

The demonstrations are also taking place at a difficult time for the French government as it tries to rein in its debts while facing demands to spend more on public services.

How long have students been protesting in France?

Protests first began mid-September in the Paris region after students began mobilizing against perceived inequalities in the education system.

From the outset, pupils said teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement weren't as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto of "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."

Demonstrations then spread to all parts of the country, including smaller towns with high schools.

On Tuesday, trade unions joined student protests. The Interior Ministry said nearly 256,000 people took part in protests nationwide on Tuesday.

Protests turned violent in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square toward the end.

More than 6,500 people have been arrested over the course of the last two weeks, most of them minors.

Student protests in France: Schools shut as unrest grows To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
World.content:
August Hanning has been remanded into pretrial detention after his arrest. The case has prompted calls for transparency when spies leave the government.

Former German foreign intelligence agency boss August Hanning appeared before a federal judge in the western city of Karlsruhe on Wednesday following his arrest on espionage and treason charges Tuesday.

He has been ordered to remain in detention ahead of his trial, according to federal prosecutors.

Manfred D., Hanning's former chief of staff at the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), was also detained.

What are the charges against Hanning?

Manfred D. is accused of having stolen secret documents and turned these over to Hanning, who, as a private-sector security adviser, in turn reportedly sold the secret documents to an as yet unnamed foreign spy agency or agencies.

Nouripour: Hanning arrest a 'huge success' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.

Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.

The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.

Who was Hanning selling data to?

Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. The Azerbaijan Media and Broadcasting Council vehemently denied the accusation, calling it "unfounded" and adding, "The malicious intent of the ‌forces behind this disinformation operation is ‌to ​damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations."

DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?
World.content:
Lawmakers of the center-right CDU may have voted for the far-right AfD candidate for parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's Social Democrats warn of a "unique breach of taboos."

Following events in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, speculation is rife that lawmakers from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) helped elect a far-right extremist as parliamentary speaker.

This would not only violate prior internal agreements, but also come despite the insistence of CDU Chairman, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, that his party would not cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) anywhere.

In the first session of the parliament in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, following the AfD's election victory on September 6, Tobias Rausch was elected parliamentary speaker — the first time a representative of a far-right party had held such a position since the end of World War II.

Rausch was backed by his own party and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Rationality (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, as had been expected. However, he also received four additional votes by secret ballot. Most observers believe these votes could only have come from right-wing CDU lawmakers.

Far-right AfD wins first state parliament speaker post To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Leading members of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) were quick to take to the streets in protest in Berlin on Tuesday, marching from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to nearby Bebelplatz — the very spot where, in 1933, the Nazis burned books by authors they deemed unacceptable. The march concluded with SPD Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius leading the crowd in the German national anthem. Many participants displayed copies of the German Basic Law, a symbol of democracy to stand up for the rule of law and the constitution.

Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) summarized the situation, "Electing far-right extremists to such an office represents a taboo brake. Not only the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could have happened." Klingbeil's SPD is, after all, the junior coalition partner in the federal government.

The events in Magdeburg thus also cast a shadow over the governing coalition.

Did the AfD receive votes from the CDU?

It didn't help much that the leader of the CDU parliamentary group, Thorsten Frei, was careful in his wording.

"It's a secret ballot, so of course, in principle, anybody is suspect." he said. He also added, "The fact that this happened is, in my view, extremely troubling and cause for concern."

The result of the first election in the new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt thus offers only a glimpse of the fierce debates to come on how to deal with the AfD. The far-right party won 44% of the vote after having campaigned on extremely tough immigration policies, climate change denial and calls for the near-total abolition of public broadcasting.

Despite its election victory, the AfD does not have a parliamentary majority on its own. In the small eastern state, the regional branch of the party has been classified by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

Will CDU politicians help elect an AfD state premier into office?

So once again, the debate about the "firewall" returns. The term refers to the stance taken by democratic parties of ruling out any form of cooperation with the AfD.

At the city and municipal levels, this approach has long since stopped working. Many political analysts have pointed out that the "firewall" has not benefited the CDU, but cooperating with the AfD is also seen as a slippery slope.

Georg Maier, the SPD Interior Minister of the state of Thuringia, agrees. "If the CDU continues down this path, it will contribute to its own downfall. The firewall does serve a purpose."

Germany's great divide: Is Friedrich Merz losing the center? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

BSW co-leader Fabio De Masi told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper, "We have to pull the AfD out from behind the firewall. Until now, it hasn't had to prove anything and has been able to conceal its internal contradictions. I don't want the AfD to continue growing behind the firewall."

The BSW, a party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that has retained some left-wing positions while also aligning itself with the AfD on social issues, paved the way for Rausch's election as parliamentary speaker when it announced that it would vote for him.

The BSW barely managed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. How closely its five MPs want to work with the AfD in the future remains to be seen.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD caucus leader Oliver Kirchner recently expressed criticism of BSW co-leaders De Masi and Mohamed Ali, who both have an immigrant background.

"Am I now supposed to spend five years in politics with people who are under the leadership of Mohamed Ali and this half-Italian guy who says, 'They're all Nazis'?" Kirchner told the right-wing magazine Compact earlier this month.

Up until now, support from the BSW has been seen as the AfD's only real chance of coming to power in Saxony-Anhalt. The other parties — the CDU, the SPD, the Greens and the Left Party — continue to categorically rule out any cooperation with the AfD. Whether that will remain the case in the coming weeks is now the big question.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai
World.content:
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

Nobel chemistry prize goes to scientists who answered questions about homochirality

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
