World.title: Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte addresses an event in Pagadian City, Zamboanga del Sur, in late May 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – House prosecutors on Wednesday, October 7, presented P96 million in manager’s checks as they sought to establish a “pattern of concealment” involving the year-end balances of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

On Day 35 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) division head for central Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed the father and daughter had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million.

The account, opened at the BPI-Julia Vargas branch, was renewed 12 times and reached P41.72 million after its final rollover in February 2011.

When the time deposit matured in March 2011, a settlement account was opened and the funds were converted on the same day into a manager’s check for P41.72 million.

Defense lawyer Michael Poa initially objected to the presentation of the bank records, questioning their relevance to the case.

Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson then asked the House prosecutors whether they were trying to establish through their direct examination a “pattern aimed at proving concealment.”

Private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih answered in the affirmative.

“We wanted to establish a pattern,” Alih said. “Our point is that the manager’s checks being circulated did not reflect on the year-end balance because they were considered ‘floating.’”

In the interjections of Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, Galvez explained that when a manager’s check is issued, the amount is deducted from the client’s account and transferred to the bank’s settlement account — an account separate from the customer’s account.

The funds will then remain in the settlement account to back the manager’s check while it is unitized. If the manager’s check remains unused for six months, the amount may be returned to the client’s account, Galvez said.

“A similar time deposit that became a manager’s check in the amount of P55 million was also running during the same years, simultaneously with this P41 million. It’s a total of P96 million,” Alih said.

The prosecution presented three more manager’s checks dated April 19, 2012 and October 17, 2012; and October 7, 2013 purchased by the Duterte patriarch. It has a total value of P41.72 million.

‘Tinikling’

Senator-judge Bam Aquino said it was the first time he had heard of such transactions and asked Galvez whether deliberately purchasing manager’s checks and leaving them unutilized was a known practice in banking circles “to keep money.”

Galvez said it was usual for some manager’s checks to be unutilized and requested to be returned. However, he could not determine whether some clients were deliberately purchasing manager’s checks for the purpose of having the funds returned after six months.

“I cannot answer… if some clients are purposely buying manager’s check to return it after six months,” said Galvez.

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III later said the practice is allegedly called “tinikling” in banking circles. Tinikling is a traditional Philippine folk dance wherein a dancer or dancers step, hop, and jump between two moving bamboo poles.

P96 million not reflected in SALNs

Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said he reviewed Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) for 2010 and 2011 but did not find the P96-million time deposit accounts in the documents.

Poa came to the defense of Duterte, saying she may have been unaware of the accounts.

“The operative word is if she’s aware… And as we demonstrated during cross, all these time deposits and transactions wala pong prima ng bise presidente (there’s no signature of the Vice President) and all off them were done by the former president,” Poa added.

The Vice President declared zero cash in hand and bank deposits in her SALNs from 2019 to 2024. – Rappler.com

World.title: Anyare? Villars’ AllHome, AllDay confirm store closures
World.content:
From a peak of 72 stores two years ago, AllHome is down to 34 stores, while the store count of AllDay drops from 40 to 13, as of September 2026

MANILA, Philippines – From fast-growing just a few years ago to fast-declining.

Villar-owned retail companies AllHome and AllDay confirmed on Wednesday, October 7, the decline in their number of outlets in light of recent financial troubles and stiff competition, in separate disclosures to the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE).

The Villars’ home improvement brand AllHome said its total store count stood at 34 as of September 29, 2026, down 26% from 47 as of December 31, 2025.

Based on AllHome’s annual reports, it had 15 stores in 2016, 18 in 2017, 23 in 2018, 45 in 2019, 50 in 2020, 57 in 2021, 60 in 2022, 72 in 2023, and still 72 in 2024.

From its peak in 2023 and 2024, the number of AllHome stores has dropped by 81%.

Rappler graphic based on AllHome annual reports and Philippine Stock Exchange disclosures

“The company confirms that it has closed certain stores as part of its store network optimization program. These measures are intended to improve operating efficiency and support long-term profitability within its existing retail business,” AllHome said.

The company, which started in 2013 with four stores and debuted in the PSE in 2019, said it “remains engaged in its core retail business.”

AllHome has three categories for AllHome stores: large mall-based, large free-standing, and small specialty.

“The company continues to operate its remaining store network. The company’s store closures and resizing of underperforming locations are intended to optimize productivity and maintain a more efficient cost structure,” it added.

“Store operations have been realigned based on sales throughput, customer traffic, and operational requirements, allowing the company to right-size manpower and reduce excess costs while maintaining service quality and operational effectiveness.”

AllHome had a net loss of P36.4 million from January to September 2025, and a net profit of P384 million in the same period in 2024, based on unaudited annual reports.

The PSE had asked AllHome and AllDay to respond to news reports that the Gokongwei Group’s Shopwise would soon take over the space of AllHome at Vista Mall in Santa Rosa City, Laguna.

STILL OPEN. The AllHome store at the Villar family’s Vista Mall, Santa Rosa City, Laguna, on October 4, 2026. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler

PRICE DROP. Shoppers visit the AllHome store offering a ‘Price Drop’ at Vista Mall in Santa Rosa City, Laguna, on October 4, 2026. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler

Rappler’s photo editor Leanne Jazul was in the area on Sunday, October 4, and was able to take photos of the retail outlet. One of his photos shows AllHome having a “Price Drop” sale.

Supermarket business

With respect to its grocery brand AllDay Marts, the separate Villar company said its total store count was 13 as of September 29, 2026, down 50% from 26 as of December 31, 2025.

CLOSED. A shuttered AllDay Convenience Store in Antipolo City, Rizal, in November 2025. Photo by Isagani de Castro Jr./Rappler

AllDay, which was incorporated in December 2016, said the company “remains engaged in its core grocery retail business,” and that it would “continue to operate its remaining store network.”

“The closure of certain stores…is aimed at improving the company’s long-term profitability, overall operational efficiency, and aligning store network with market conditions,” it added.

Based on AllDay annual reports, it had a peak of 40 stores in 2023 and 2024. Thus, its number of stores has fallen by 67%.

Rappler graphic based on AllDay Marts annual reports, corporate disclosures, and press release

AllDay disclosed a net profit of P369 million as of December 2023, which fell 27% to P268 million as of December 2024. Sales also fell 9.2% from P10.1 billion in December 2023 to P9.25 billion in December 2024. It said this was “brought about by low-performing stores where there is intense market competition.”

On Wednesday, AllDay said that in order “improve profitability,” it would “optimize its supermarket operations by selectively adopting smaller mini-mart formats to enhance operational efficiency and better serve its target market.”

“The company will also focus on cost discipline, and active liquidity management, including working capital optimization and prudent cash prioritization — while maximizing the value of its existing footprint to restore sustainable profitability,” it said.

HAKOT. Shoppers take advantage of AllDay Supermarket’s ‘Hakot Sale’ in select stores in Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Pampanga, based on photos posted online by the retail chain. Photo from AllDay Supermarket’s Facebook page

Last July 2, AllDay Supermarket’s official Facebook account posted an “AllDay Payday Hakot Sale” with steep discounts ranging from 50% to 75% on selected items at its stores in Mandaluyong City; Taguig City; Santa Rosa City, Laguna; General Trias City, Cavite; and in Pampanga. The posts also showed consumers taking advantage of the sale, filling up grocery carts with various discounted items.

The president and chief operating officer of AllHome and also of all AllDay resigned last year amid a drop in corporate earnings, as disclosed in September 2025.

AllHome and AllDay chairman Manny Villar had reported record sales for AllDay in 2021 or five years ago, describing it as “stellar” and “consistent performance.” (READ: Tracking the fallout of Manny Villar’s spot in Forbes’ list of richest individuals)

In the same release five years ago, then-AllValue president and now-senator Camille Villar said AllDay’s growth since it started operations was “a product of our propensity to innovate and remain on the cutting edge of retail consumer trends.”

She added, “AllDay has and will always continue to innovate to stay a step ahead of the local supermarket landscape.”

Retail was seen as complementary to the Villars’ housing projects, having built over 500,000 homes that made it the “largest homebuilder” in the country. This “synergy,” AllHome said in its 2022 annual report, gave “AllHome easy access to a captive market and ideal locations in growing residential communities nationwide, enabling its rapid store network growth.”

In 2025, Rappler published this exclusive report on some suppliers of the Villars’ coffee retail brand Coffee Project not getting paid on time. – Rappler.com

World.title: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of ‘mirror image’ molecules
World.content:
NOBEL PRIZE. Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry during a press conference at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden, October 7, 2026.

This year's prize was awarded for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favor a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals

STOCKHOLM, Sweden – Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a long-standing riddle of asymmetric “mirror image” molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing, the award-giving body said on Wednesday, October 7.

Soai, 76, is Japanese, and Kagan, 95, is French, and their work built on a discovery by the 19th century French chemist Louis Pasteur.

“This is the most exciting day in my life, I am very glad to share this prize with professor Henri Kagan,” Soai said, speaking by phone to the Nobel Prize press conference, adding he had been out shopping when receiving the news.

The Nobel committee was still trying to contact Kagan to inform him of the award.

The chemistry Nobel, always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, followed those for medicine and physics announced on Monday and Tuesday.

‘Right-handed’ and ‘left-handed’ molecules

Many of the molecules essential to life exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands. Yet living organisms almost exclusively use only one version, a phenomenon known as “homochirality” — from the Greek word for hand — that has puzzled chemists for more than a century.

This year’s prize was awarded for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favor a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.

“The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need methods for selectively preparing them,” Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said.

“In developing such methods the findings of this year’s laureates are important. They provided powerful tools for that,” he said.

Building on work by Louis Pasteur

The first link in the chain in solving the problem was work by Pasteur, who died before the Nobel Prizes were first awarded.

He was looking at tartaric acid, important in the production of wine, and noticed that bacteria only ferment one of the two forms of tartaric acid — that which is naturally found in grapes. With the other there is no fermentation.

That proved that some substances occur in two forms and that they have different properties, sometimes very damaging to health.

How to create the right form of a chiral substance was a problem not solved until Kagan and Soai were able to produce asymmetric reactions, creating an excess of one form.

The importance of the work is illustrated by the case of the thalidomide scandal in the early 1960s, when thousands of children were affected by birth defects caused by a sedative, thalidomide.

When researchers analysed what had happened, they realized that it was the active substance’s mirror image that caused the harm.

Prizes established in will of Swedish inventor

Established in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars.

Nobel, a chemist by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank.

Sometimes overshadowed by more famous laureates in the fields of physics, literature and peace, the chemistry awards have still recognized many influential discoveries such as nuclear fission and genetic sequencing techniques.

Last year’s chemistry award went to scientists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for the development of so-called metal–organic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of fresh water.

The laureates will receive their medals from Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. The awards are followed by a lavish banquet at Stockholm City Hall.

They also share 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), as well as the fame of winning arguably the world’s most prestigious science award.

The peace prize, the only Nobel not presented in Sweden, is awarded separately in Oslo. – Rappler.com

($1 = 10.0309 Swedish crowns)

World.title: PSC steps in as Asian Tour’s 108th Philippine Open dangles $1 million
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Some of the biggest names on the Asian Tour — and the brightest talents the Philippines can offer — set out to win Asia’s oldest national golf championship when Manila Southwoods, which is being spruced up to perfect championship shape, hosts the 108th playing of the Philippine Open in just over a month.

The Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) has stepped in to make sure that the event will be one to remember, putting up a $1 million (around P63 million) kitty for the 72-hole championship beginning November 12 at the world-class Masters course of the SW complex in Carmona, Cavite.

“It is a tradition that the PSC certainly wants to continue with,” PSC Chairman Patrick Gregorio said after making the pledge to make the tournament a big Asian Tour leg. “We wouldn’t want such a big event be put on the shelf.

“It’s the Philippine Open, it’s the pride of the country.”

The Open first came to being in 1913 and has been held yearly save for seven times, the first being in 2003 because of a name dispute, the next two in 2013 and 2016 because of super typhoons that battered the country, and then four years from 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Frenchman Julien Sale won the revival last year also at the Masters, and he is expected to banner the foreign challenge that will try to prevent a Filipino from again winning since Miguel Tabuena triumphed in the 100th staging at Luisita.

Tabuena, who played in the final season of the now-defunct LIV 1.0 Golf League, and fellow Philippine Asian Games team members Justin delos Santos and Carl Corpus will be on the starting roster, with Tabuena having innate knowledge of one of the local courses he calls home.

That win was the second Open title for Tabuena, who, at 32, has become the face of local pro golf, even as another past champion in Angelo Que is also given an equal chance at 47 years old since he is enjoying one of the finest two-year stretches of his career.

Meanwhile, the management of Manila Southwoods has not stopped in conditioning the Jack Nicklaus-designed Masters since being awarded the rights to host the event for the second straight year.

It will be one of the narrowest versions of the Masters the field will see come the second week of November as the roughs are now being allowed to grow and the fairways reduced in width to punish errant tee shots.

The Asian Tour also did its part in making sure the event goes on as scheduled even after the withdrawal of BingoPlus as the title sponsor.

The online betting app decided to not back the event just over a month ago, threatening to shut down everything before the Asian Tour and the governing National Golf Association of the Philippines pushed all the right buttons to get it going again. – Rappler.com

World.title: [DECODED] What a fake Duterte tells us about our bigger AI problem
World.content:
Disinformation spreads rapidly because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks

Have you ever heard of a “Lance Duterte”? He’s a Facebook persona claiming to be a grandson of former president Rodrigo Duterte and the son of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Like his supposed family members, Lance has attracted a huge following on social media. He has over 382,000 followers on Facebook, and his posts rack up thousands of engagements each — many of which come from fans and supporters who gush over his conventionally attractive features. Some even tout him as a future celebrity or politician.

But as our researcher Alex Culla found out, Lance is not real. He’s a synthetic online persona made from AI.

READ: [DECODED] No, this ‘handsome’ Duterte grandson is not real

When Alex pitched the story, I thought the name sounded familiar. Then I remembered: six years ago, I wrote a fact-check article about a Facebook account with the name “Lance Kurt Dong Duterte.” He falsely claimed that Tricia, daughter of former vice president Leni Robredo, sent a hate message to him via private message.

But this happened back in 2020, before consumer AI chatbots like ChatGPT became publicly accessible. And as Alex pointed out in her Decoded piece, the profile picture of the 2020 version of this persona looked different from the one currently active today.

So the persona has been around for years, but its posts today now include videos to make the lie appear more believable, thanks to the accessibility of AI.

Lance isn’t the first AI piece built around the Duterte name. Back in 2025, we also reported on how AI-generated images of Duterte statues were being shared by Facebook pages known for glorifying the Dutertes. These fakes were created a few months after the former president was arrested over a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.

READ: [DECODED] What makes AI-generated Duterte statues so popular online?

These things happen because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks.

Over the past week alone, news reports have quoted different AI researchers, employees, and former staff on the lack of safety culture in AI companies.

From OpenAI to Google DeepMind, current and former employees have expressed concerns about the risks of self-improving AI systems and warned that companies are doing too little to protect the world against AI’s potential dangers.

Another former OpenAI safety employee said that “the time for trial and error is over,” because AI capabilities have far outpaced the systems’ ability to act in ways that match human goals and values. He even argued that advanced AI systems should have safeguards in place comparable to those used in the nuclear power and aviation industries.

Even Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned its potential IPO investors that AI could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors.” The company said in its IPO prospectus: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”

These warning bells echo concerns that advocates have long raised about social media. Cambridge Analytica whistleblower Chris Wylie once said that digital products should have moral standards and safety testing like those imposed on consumer goods. “We do not allow any other consumer product to just be released without any kind of safety standards,” Wylie said in a Rappler+ briefing back in 2023.

Three years later, we’re still grappling with the same concerns, now made worse by the unchecked development of AI.

READ: We need an alternative to big tech platforms: Introducing MUNI

Which is why Rappler built MUNI, a platform where facts and trusted voices can thrive. It’s a community space for verified information, where you can read news, chat with reporters, and talk with like-minded individuals who share your interests.

MUNI is not limited to Rappler. You can also find other newsgroups there, including Daily Guardian in Iloilo and SunStar in Cebu, so you can also join their chat rooms and take part in their discussions.

You can explore MUNI by downloading the Rappler app for free from the App Store or Play Store. MUNI is a tab on the Rappler app where you can join as many chat rooms as you want.

I encourage you to join the #EverydayTech channel on MUNI, where Rappler’s tech reporters host casual discussions about tech issues that matter every weekday at 10 am and 4 pm. We’d love for you to join the conversations! – Rappler.com

World.title: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music
World.content:
'I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing,' Marcos says in an interview with Gary Valenciano

MANILA, Philippines – Back in September 2024, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had caused an uproar for hiring a band to play at his private birthday party.

While the Philippines is known as a music-loving country, it wasn’t just any band, that Marcos hired — it was acclaimed British pop-rock outfit Duran Duran, which was flown in just for his 67th birthday celebration.

But the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) had attested that the party, held at a Pasay City hotel, was thrown by “old friends,” and that the Duran Duran performance had merely come as a surprise to Marcos. Then-communications secretary Cesar Chavez had even told reporters in a message that the band’s appearance came “at no cost to the government.”

This wasn’t the President’s first music-related controversy, however.

Just a few months before that, in January 2024, the son of the former dictator had also found himself in hot water when the public caught wind of him using the presidential chopper to get to British band Coldplay’s concert at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan.

It was “unmissable,” he had told reporters in a chance interview several days after the show.

“It was, by the way, fantastic. Ask anybody who attended the concert. The show they performed was spectacular. I haven’t seen anything like it,” he said.

It seems, then, that the country’s biggest music fan happens to hold the state’s highest position. And Marcos was always one to make his affinity for music known.

Around the time of the 2022 presidential elections, an old clip of him playing the saxophone had gone viral. He had revealed in an interview with Gary Valenciano that premiered on October 5 that this, along with the flute, were instruments he had picked up in his youth. He had even gone on to join several orchestras.

Play Video

Marcos had first studied music while he was pursuing his secondary education in England in the ’70s. He was a self-confessed troublemaker then, and was sent to his housemaster to receive his punishment.

“He said, ‘You’re here all the time. You’re always in trouble. Go find yourself a hobby so that you can occupy your time by doing something constructive,’” he recalled.

Play Video

Back then, he had been listening to a lot of music anyway, so it only seemed like the natural choice. What had served as his musical awakening, he shared, was Lou Reed’s “Walk on the Wild Side,” which he had heard another student play out loud while he was making his rounds before class. Aside from playing the flute and the saxophone, he would later also study music theory.

“It’s a fascinating thing because unlike any other art form, music doesn’t exist anywhere else except in your brain. Think about it. A sculpture you can touch, a painting, you can look at and you can see the brushstrokes. All the other forms. This is just sound and it only becomes music because your brain interprets it as music. But the universality of it, everyone understands,” Marcos told Valenciano in the interview.

The President views music as an integral part of his life — as something he cannot live without. If anyone were to take it away from him, he tells Valenciano, he wouldn’t know how to manage.

“I just don’t know how I would get through the day,” he explained. “It’s the only thing that can change my mood. There are two things that can change my mood. Music’s one of them. The other one’s my children.”

Even Marcos’ big life events have specific songs associated with them. He and this art form have long been intertwined. “I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing.”

But even as a big music fan, the President can’t seem to figure out why Filipinos excel so much at holding a note. He said that whenever his foreign friends would ask him why his countrymen were such good singers, he had never been able to give a proper answer.

Apparently, what he does know, though, is that Filipinos make the best concert audiences.

“I’ve heard it from Elton John, I’ve heard it from Sting. I’ve heard it from The Corrs. I’ve heard it from many of these artists that come. And they said, ‘The audience does all the work for me. I don’t have to sing. I don’t have to perform because the audience is singing for us,’” Marcos explained.

Most Filipinos are lauded for always enthusiastically singing the lyrics back to the performing artist as loud as they can. It’s become a big indication of who the Filipino people are as enjoyers of music.

In Marcos’ case, perhaps much of his repertoire as a music fan reflects in his willingness to do anything to catch his favorite bands perform live — even if it means flying a high-profile music act in for a private show or riding the presidential chopper to the Philippine Arena to beat the evening traffic, much to the ire of taxpayers. – Rappler.com

World.title: [In This Economy] Cesar Virata, technocrat who helped finance a dictatorship
World.content:
How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

Cesar Virata, who died on October 2 at age 95, was a familiar presence at big events of the UP School of Economics, attending in his wheelchair.

That is the extent of my personal acquaintance with him. I did not know him closely, and I leave the intimate recollections to his family, friends, and colleagues.

He may well have been as wise and kind as those who knew him remember. On Facebook, I saw an outpouring of condolences from my friends for whom Virata was a tito (uncle/respectful title for an older person), ninong (godfather), mentor, friend. Those qualities deserve their place in the tributes and obituaries.

But Virata’s long service to the Marcos dictatorship deserves equally serious attention.

The fact is that Virata headed the finance department/ministry from 1970 to 1986 and served as prime minister from 1981 until the dictatorship fell. These were positions at the very heart of a government that, in the end, impoverished Filipinos and left the country with debts that outlived the regime.

How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

Lending Marcos credibility

In my 2023 book False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, I discussed how Marcos’ technocrats helped make the regime’s massive foreign borrowing possible. Virata was a central figure in that group.

To the uninitiated, technocrats are officials whose authority rests on specialized expertise. Under Marcos, they included economic managers with advanced degrees and international connections, people who could speak the language of bankers and development institutions.

This mattered enormously for the Marcos dictatorship. Borrowing requires lenders willing to believe that you can repay. Officials like Virata helped present the Philippines as a country whose economy was being managed competently—even as political power became increasingly concentrated in the hands of the dictator and his cronies.

The technocrats’ credibility helped the regime obtain money from foreign banks and institutions such as the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF). The backdrop is that the economic managers were confronted with the task of maintaining a fixed exchange rate and maintaining an ample supply of dollars. The borrowings, totaling more than $25 billion over the Marcos years, helped finance the government and prolonged its ability to operate.

In the book, I described this as effectively “deodorizing” the Martial Law regime. Technical competence gave international creditors reasons to keep dealing with a dictatorship.

Of course, the technocrats and Marcos’ cronies were often at odds. They were characterized once as separate if opposing spokes in a wheel, connected by the hub that was Marcos. Political scientist Teresa Encarnacion Tadem’s research documents how crony interests undermined Virata’s group, even as its relationships with international financial institutions strengthened its position within the government.

Those conflicts show the limits of the arrangement. Marcos retained the power to accommodate his cronies and disregard technical advice, while continuing to benefit from the credibility lent by his economic managers. Both groups could serve the same regime while disagreeing bitterly about its policies.

Eventually, some technocrats left one by one. Gerardo Sicat, for instance, left his position as director-general of the National Economic and Development Authority in 1981, just as the economy was tumbling into decline and crisis. Virata remained to hold the fort.

Many years later, Sicat would write a tome of a biography for Virata, titled: Cesar Virata: Life and Times Through Four Decades of Philippine Economic History. Published in 2014, it offers a sympathetic account of Virata’s predicament as the chief technocrat during the crisis years. As Hal Hill’s review explains, it portrays a reformer battling Imelda Marcos and the cronies, attempting to restrain spending, and eventually offering a resignation that Marcos refused.

But this defense leaves important questions unanswered. The disappearance of congressional opposition after Martial Law may have made economic reforms easier to implement. It also removed democratic checks on the borrowing and spending that helped bring the country to ruin. Economists should count those costs to our institutions as well.

As well, the unsuccessful offer to resign doesn’t erase the consequences of remaining in office. Virata’s credibility continued to help Marcos obtain foreign financing even as the regime’s abuses and economic failures became increasingly evident.

Behest loans

Truthful reminiscences of Virata’s life and times must acknowledge the fact that technocrats like him were crucial in propping up the dictatorship and the crony capitalism that flourished at that time.

Consider an admission by Virata himself that I quoted in False Nostalgia, drawing on economist James Boyce’s account. In 1984 Virata admitted, “We were quite liberal in guaranteeing loans,” referring to “behest loans” or loans that were granted by president Marcos to select friends and family members, obtained from government financial institutions.

Virata explained that some companies had been interested in making money from equipment purchases rather than operating the businesses those purchases were supposed to support. He called this “one of the major faults in our system.”

A loan guarantee is a promise to pay if the borrower cannot. It can help a worthwhile project obtain financing, but it also exposes the guarantor to losses. When public institutions extend guarantees too freely, as Virata admitted to doing, private business failures can become public financial obligations.

That is why Virata’s admission matters. It points to a gross failure in how the Marcos regime assessed and assumed financial risks. The public was left exposed to projects whose supposed developmental benefits might never materialize.

Indeed, state-owned banks like the Development Bank of the Philippines, and even the old Central Bank, were left with deteriorating balance sheets as it became impossible to collect the behest loans that they gave out to cronies. Rescuing crony businesses in the 1980s weakened the institutions financing them, which themselves needed rescuing. The costs, in short, spread far beyond the favored borrowers.

Debt moratorium

Then there’s the 1983 debt moratorium. In October that year, not long after senator Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. was killed on the tarmac, Virata and then-Central Bank governor Jaime Laya had gone to New York to seek a 90-day moratorium on principal payments to private creditors. By that time, the country could no longer meet its debt obligations as scheduled.

The same government that had borrowed so heavily was now asking for more time to pay.

Sure, the Philippines faced a hostile international environment: higher global interest rates and the international debt crisis also battered other developing countries. Virata alone did not cause the Philippine crisis, and negotiating relief was necessary once the country was in trouble.

But decades of bad domestic decisions had made us weak and vulnerable. Foreign borrowing came with repayment obligations, and politically favored projects could fail to generate the income needed to meet them. In hindsight, therefore, economic managers must be assessed on the risks accumulated during their tenure alongside their efforts to manage the eventual collapse.

It didn’t help that Virata was tone-deaf about people’s increasing economic hardships. In a controversial interview in the June 1, 1984 issue of Mr & Ms Special Edition, Virata was quoted as saying, “Well, I do not know what they mean by crisis… They never had it so good.”

They never had it so good.

He argued that basic needs were being supplied and that people should not mistake the absence of luxuries for a crisis. Recall that this was months after the debt moratorium, amid an economic crisis aggravated by crony capitalism and reckless borrowing. In effect, Filipinos were paying for the failures of a government whose prime minister was assuring them that life had never been better.

Whatever his disagreements with Marcos behind closed doors, Virata was on record publicly defending the regime’s economic record. His own words complicate the picture of a technocrat merely trying to contain the damage.

Sanitized legacy?

There is a familiar defense of officials who stay under an abusive leader: they are supposed to have restrained the damage from within.

Sure, sometimes they do. But that defense still leaves a difficult question: How much did their continued service help the government survive and carry on with the very practices they opposed?

For economists like me, this is an uncomfortable question worth asking. Expertise gives us influence, but things get complicated when we lend that influence to institutions and political leaders with dodgy reputations. Technocratic competence can make a government more credible even when its use of power deserves public resistance. Recently, we’ve seen that play out as well in the dictatorial regime of Rodrigo Duterte—the subject of my second book, Twin Plagues.

In Virata’s case, complicity lies in his sustained role in financing and administering the dictatorship. He didn’t necessarily steal public money or order an abuse, but nobody can deny the responsibilities he held and the regime his work helped to sustain.

People can remember his kindness and generosity, and we sympathize with the family and friends. But the country as a whole must also never forget what happened under the government Virata willingly served for so long.

There have been stringent efforts to memorialize Virata in past years, like a biography written by Sicat as well as the 2013 renaming of the UP Diliman College of Business Administration (CBA) into the Cesar E.A. Virata School of Business or VSB (a highly contested move until now; many students and faculty still insist on calling their college the CBA rather than the VSB).

At any rate, Virata’s passing should at least prompt a fuller reckoning with his record as a public servant. His personal virtues belong in his obituary—but so does his complicity in the Marcos dictatorship. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

World.title: Religious Leaders Explore Faith’s Role in Tackling Global Challenges
World.content:
ASTANA – Religious leaders and international experts gathered in Astana on Oct. 7 to discuss how faith communities can contribute to addressing pressing challenges, with artificial intelligence, climate change and the rights of children with incurable diseases among the key issues on the agenda.

The discussions took place at the 24th Meeting of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions, which brought together representatives of Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Shinto and the Baha’i Faith, as well as government officials, international organizations and experts from 20 countries.

Participants considered two draft international documents: the Code of Ethics for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Religious Sphere and the Role of Religions in Combating Climate Change. The meeting also presented the Charter on the Rights of Children with Incurable Diseases as a separate agenda item.

Vice President of Kazakhstan and Head of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions Erlan Karin said the documents reflect the need to strengthen the practical role of spiritual diplomacy amid growing global instability.

“Armed conflicts and humanitarian crises have weakened respect for international law. Radical ideas and hate speech are growing. This is also happening online. Climate and technology risks are deepening existing social inequalities, and the crisis of trust is becoming a systemic challenge,” Karin said.

“In this situation, spiritual diplomacy can play a special role. It does not replace political talks, but complements them and keeps communication channels open where diplomatic dialogue is difficult. It helps rebuild trust and reminds us of the value of every human life,” he added.

Karin noted that the Astana Peace Declaration, adopted at the eighth congress, provides a common framework for advancing peace, security and efforts to counter extremism.

“One of the first results of implementing the Astana Peace Declaration is the launch of the International Online Center for Spiritual Knowledge. It brings together the congress materials, expert research and studies, as well as educational resources about world religions and cultures,” he said.

Climate change as a moral responsibility

Speaking about the document on the role of religions in combating climate change, Karin described climate change as not only an environmental or economic issue but also a moral challenge.

“The document enshrines universal principles of environmental responsibility and encourages religious communities to promote education, solidarity and support for the most vulnerable groups and regions,” he said.

Karin noted that the document is aligned with Kazakhstan’s international initiatives on environmental and water security, including President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

“Human beings and nature are part of one whole. That is why the initiative seeks to foster an environmental culture, change daily habits and affirm personal responsibility for preserving nature,” Karin said.

Fatih Mehmet Karaca, deputy president of the Presidency of Religious Affairs of Türkiye, emphasized the concept of stewardship and humanity’s responsibility toward nature.

“Waste is not merely an individual economic behavior. We see food and energy waste, a culture of fast consumption, and single-use products. Fighting waste means respecting nature’s rights. The values Islam calls us to are clear: gratitude, contentment, moderation, sharing and responsibility,” Karaca said.

Karaca also highlighted the issue of climate justice, noting that vulnerable communities often bear a disproportionate share of climate change consequences.

“It is not enough to see this as a matter of protecting nature. It is also a matter of justice and of the right of future generations to clean air, clean water and safe food,” he said.

Ethics of AI

The proposed code on AI seeks to establish ethical principles for the use of emerging technologies in religious contexts, including protecting spiritual heritage and preventing the distortion of religious texts.

Karin said Kazakhstan views AI as an important tool for development but highlighted that technological progress must be accompanied by greater ethical responsibility.

“Our country considers AI a powerful tool for progress. At the same time, technological development cannot outpace our moral responsibility. The broader the capabilities of algorithms, the greater the human responsibility,” he said.

Karin noted that AI could help preserve spiritual heritage and expand access to religious knowledge, while also creating new risks.

“It is really important to counter the distortion of religious texts and the creation of digital fakes on behalf of spiritual leaders. We have to avoid algorithmic discrimination and manipulation of people’s convictions,” he said.

Director of the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, Nihal Saad, said AI presents both opportunities and challenges for societies. Its responsible use requires keeping human dignity and ethical considerations at the center.

“Used wisely, AI could help transform education, improve health care, strengthen food security and support sustainable development. The challenge is ensuring that it advances in ways that uphold human dignity and ethics. We have to ensure that ethics are built into the design of AI systems rather than added as an afterthought,” Saad said.

She noted that although the two draft documents address different issues, they share an emphasis on responsibility, dialogue, cooperation and common values.

A call for unity

Jo Bailey Wells, deputy secretary general of the Anglican Communion and bishop for Episcopal Ministry in the Anglican Communion, said the three issues on the agenda, climate change, AI and the rights of children with incurable diseases, are not traditionally viewed as specifically religious matters. However, they are closely connected to values shared across faiths.

“Each expresses the values we have been talking about for many years. For example, human dignity, protecting family life, raising the role of women, combating radicalism, reducing poverty, valuing integrity in public life, countering corruption and defending human rights. They are all reflected here. We have come a long way with these shared declarations,” Wells said.

She highlighted that the challenges cannot be addressed by individual governments, professions or religious communities alone.

“The opportunity is to walk together and not just talk together. To put our convictions into action as we serve causes beyond our individual interests,” Wells said.

“The crises described cannot be resolved by the specialists and technicians, whether in climate and the environment, in artificial and superhuman intelligence, or in medicine and palliative care. Nor can they be resolved by any single group, government, or nation. They require a level of cooperation that transcends our differences,” she added.

Karin outlined several priorities for the congress, including promoting the agreed documents and initiatives, establishing mechanisms for expert support and consolidating the results of discussions.

The upcoming 25th anniversary session of the Secretariat in 2027 and the ninth Congress in 2028 are expected to serve as important milestones in the organization’s development.

“We need to enter a new stage in the development of the congress with concrete results and a clear understanding of the steps required to address future challenges,” Karin said.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Green Climate Fund Launch Climate Investment Platform
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) have signed an agreement to establish the Qazaqstan Climate Investment Platform (QCIP), a national mechanism designed to prepare climate projects for financing from international and domestic financial institutions.

The agreement was signed under the GCF Readiness 3 program during the fund’s Regional Dialogue with countries of Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The project is valued at more than $1 million.

The signing brought together Chairman of the International Green Technologies and Investment Projects Center Saken Kalkamanov and GCF Regional Director for Eastern Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East Thomas Eriksson.

Platform to build pipeline of investment-ready climate projects

QCIP will serve as a national mechanism to coordinate climate investments and prepare projects for potential financing from the Green Climate Fund and the Development Bank of Kazakhstan, among other financial partners.

Its key objective is to move from individual technological initiatives and project proposals toward structured investment projects that are ready to attract climate financing. The platform will also help integrate climate priorities better into Kazakhstan’s public administration system.

A steering committee chaired by the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources will oversee the platform’s environmental and climate integrity and coordinate cooperation with government bodies responsible for tariffs, finance, planning and economic regulation.

Platform to support Kazakhstan’s climate priorities

The QCIP secretariat will be based at the International Green Technologies and Investment Projects Center. It will provide operational support and coordinate cooperation among government agencies, project developers, financial institutions and international partners.

The platform is expected to connect Kazakhstan’s national climate priorities and technological solutions with potential sources of financing, helping build a pipeline of investment-ready climate projects. QCIP will also serve as a practical mechanism for implementing Kazakhstan’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution and its implementation plan.

The agreement and creation of QCIP are expected to support a more systematic approach to preparing and attracting climate finance in Kazakhstan, while strengthening cooperation with international financial institutions and developing a sustainable portfolio of projects aligned with the country’s climate objectives.

World.title: OTS Advances Space Cooperation With Joint Satellite Launch Planned for 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan, Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan have signed a framework agreement to expand cooperation in the space industry, with Kazakhstan completing the assembly of the engineering model of the OTS-SAT satellite and planning its launch in 2027.

The agreement was signed in Antalya on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress, which runs from Oct. 5 to 9, and establishes a framework for cooperation in space technologies, satellite development, scientific research, industrial cooperation and specialist training within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS).

The agreement gives the four countries a basis for developing joint space initiatives and expanding technological and industrial cooperation.

OTS-SAT to become first practical space project

The OTS-SAT project is a 12U satellite being developed by Kazakhstan’s Ghalam company in Astana as part of cooperation among OTS member states. The engineering model of the satellite has now been assembled in Astana, while the launch is planned for 2027.

The project is designed to demonstrate technologies in orbit and test new technical solutions for satellite subsystems in the space environment. It also combines spacecraft development, operational management and regional cooperation among participating countries.

OTS Secretary General Kubanychbek Omuraliev welcomed the signing of the framework agreement, saying it demonstrates the organization’s commitment to scientific, technological and industrial cooperation across the Turkic world.

According to Omuraliev, the agreement creates an institutional foundation for new joint space initiatives and allows the experience gained through OTS-SAT to be used for broader cooperation.

Earlier, Kazakh Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev expressed confidence that the successful implementation of OTS-SAT would become the first practical space project of the OTS, strengthen technological partnerships among Turkic states and create new opportunities for joint space initiatives.

Space cooperation expands beyond satellite development

The new framework covers a broader range of cooperation, including space technologies, scientific research, industrial collaboration and training of specialists. For Kazakhstan, the agreement provides an opportunity to expand cooperation with OTS partners while developing domestic scientific, technological and manufacturing capabilities in the space sector.

The Aerospace Committee described the agreement as an important step toward strengthening international space cooperation and developing the shared scientific, technological and industrial potential of OTS member states.

World.title: Tokayev Meets Newly Elected FIDE President Timur Turlov
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with newly elected International Chess Federation (FIDE) President Timur Turlov on Oct. 7, congratulating him on his election and highlighting the growing international profile of Kazakhstan’s chess community.

Turlov was elected FIDE president on Sept. 26 in Samarkand during the organization’s General Assembly, held alongside the 46th World Chess Olympiad, receiving 110 of 196 votes.

During the meeting, Tokayev said Turlov’s election reflects the growing standing of Kazakhstan and its chess school internationally, reported the presidential press office.

President Tokayev also emphasized the importance of chess for Kazakhstan, describing it not only as a sport but also as an important tool for developing the intellectual potential of younger generations.

More than 278,000 people in Kazakhstan now regularly play chess, according to the presidential statement.

Tokayev outlines priorities for chess development

Tokayev highlighted the recent progress of Kazakhstan’s chess community, particularly the national women’s team, which won silver at the World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand.

He also outlined several priorities for the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, including strengthening national team training, developing an effective system for identifying and preparing young talents, promoting chess in the education system and expanding chess infrastructure across the regions.

Tokayev also called for stronger cooperation between the national federation and FIDE, including professional development programs for Kazakh coaches and arbiters, joint educational initiatives and the organisation of major international chess competitions in Kazakhstan.

Turlov thanked Tokayev for his support for chess development and briefed him on plans to promote chess globally, expand international cooperation and implement new projects involving national chess federations.

Turlov has headed the Kazakhstan Chess Federation since 2023. During his tenure, Kazakhstan hosted the World Chess Championship match and the World Team Rapid and Blitz Championships.

His election as FIDE president gives Kazakhstan a new role in the governance of the international chess community, while his work with the national federation has included efforts to expand the country’s role as a host of major international chess events.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Send 150 Athletes to Asian Para Games in Japan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will send 150 athletes to the fifth Asian Para Games, which will take place on Oct. 18-24 in Japan’s Aichi Prefecture and the city of Nagoya, with the national team set to compete in 12 sports.

The Kazakh team will compete in one team sport and 11 individual disciplines. The largest groups will represent para judo with 26 athletes, para swimming with 21 and para cycling with 13, reported the Kazakh Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

The delegation will also include athletes in sitting volleyball, para taekwondo, para table tennis, para shooting, para athletics, para archery, wheelchair tennis, para powerlifting and boccia.

The first competitions involving Kazakh athletes are scheduled to begin on Oct. 16 with the individual events in para table tennis. The official opening ceremony will take place on Oct. 18 at Mizuho Athletic Stadium in Nagoya.

Around 4,000 athletes from 45 countries are expected to compete at the games, with 502 sets of medals to be awarded across 18 sports.

Kazakhstan to make wheelchair tennis debut

The games will mark Kazakhstan’s first participation in wheelchair tennis at the Asian Para Games. The country will also debut in para athletics for athletes with intellectual impairments. Kazakh athletes will compete in the T20 athletics class and in Class 11 in para table tennis.

The team completed 23 training camps and took part in 22 international competitions as part of its preparations, winning 63 medals.

“We are confident that our athletes will be able to demonstrate their preparation to the fullest at the upcoming competition and compete for strong results,” said Kairatbek Seitbekov, head of the Sports Department at the Center for Sports Training of Persons with Disabilities.

Kazakhstan’s Asian Para Games record

Kazakhstan has participated in the Asian Para Games since 2010 and has won 105 medals, including 20 gold, 35 silver and 50 bronze.

At the inaugural games in 2010, Kazakhstan sent 63 athletes across six sports and won seven medals – two silver and five bronze.

Four years later in Incheon, 78 Kazakh athletes competed in nine sports and won 24 medals, including seven gold, six silver and 11 bronze. At the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, Kazakhstan fielded 90 athletes in nine sports and collected 33 medals – five gold, 15 silver and 13 bronze.

The country recorded its strongest performance at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, where 131 Kazakh athletes won a record 41 medals, including eight gold, 12 silver and 21 bronze.

Earlier, Kazakhstan finished the 20th Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with 84 medals, 12 gold, 24 silver and 48 bronze, placing eighth in the overall medal standings, as the continental competition concluded Oct. 4.

World.title: Kazakhstan Shifts Investment Strategy From Capital Inflows to Economic Value Creation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is shifting its investment strategy from attracting foreign capital in terms of volume to directing investments toward projects that create production capacity, deepen processing, expand exports and develop local supply chains, according to Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Ardak Zebeshev.

Kazakhstan has accumulated $156.4 billion in foreign investment, making it the largest recipient of foreign direct investment in Central Asia. The next challenge, according to Zebeshev, is to turn that capital into broader economic value.

“Several years ago, the main indicator was the volume of foreign direct investment received during the year. This indicator is still important for the macroeconomy, but it says little about the quality of the investment process,” he told the Kazinform news agency.

The shift comes as global competition for investment becomes increasingly focused on specific parts of production chains, including processing, components, engineering, digital infrastructure and export-oriented manufacturing.

From attracting investors to targeting economic needs

According to Zebeshev, Kazakhstan is entering a new stage in which investment policy will focus on projects capable of creating new production capacity and higher-value products.

“The new stage for Kazakhstan is about directing capital toward industries capable of creating new production capacities, increasing the depth of processing, forming supply chains and expanding exports of products with high added value,” he said.

This approach reflects broader changes in global investment flows. Citing UNCTAD data, Zebeshev said global foreign direct investment increased 6% in 2025 to $1.6 trillion, but growth was uneven. Investment in developed economies rose 11%, compared with 2% in developing economies, while the number of cross-border transactions declined 7%.

Capital is increasingly concentrated in areas such as data centres, semiconductors and digital infrastructure, he said. For Kazakhstan, the restructuring of global supply chains creates opportunities in areas where the country can combine natural resources, energy, transit infrastructure and access to several major markets.

“Companies are reconsidering where to locate new capacities. Demand is growing for energy-intensive digital infrastructure, critical materials, new logistics routes and raw-material processing. Countries that can simultaneously offer resources, energy, transit and access to several markets stand to benefit,” Zebeshev said.

Investment flows show changing priorities

Kazakhstan remains the largest recipient of foreign direct investment in Central Asia, accounting for about 70% of the region’s accumulated investment, according to Zebeshev.

At the end of 2025, accumulated foreign investment in Kazakhstan reached $156.4 billion, equivalent to around 51% of GDP. In the first half of 2026, the country attracted another $9.4 billion.

The structure of new investment is also changing. Trade accounted for the largest share in the first half of the year, attracting $2.2 billion, followed by financial and insurance activities with $1.9 billion, manufacturing with $1.8 billion, construction with $1.1 billion and mining with $816 million.

The figures underline the scale of Kazakhstan’s existing investment base, but the government is also looking at what those investments produce inside the economy.

“Earlier, we promoted Kazakhstan as a country with a resource base and a favourable geographical position. Now a more targeted approach is being formed, based on investment proposals for specific niches,” Zebeshev said.

An investment proposal, he explained, is intended to assess the full economic potential of a particular industry or product, including its competitive advantages and the reasons why production should be located in Kazakhstan.

“We are essentially moving from the ‘investor–project’ model to the ‘economic need–project–investor’ model,” he said.

Under the first model, the country responds to an investor’s existing interest. Under the second, investment becomes an instrument for addressing a specific economic development need.

From capital volume to economic impact

For Kazakhstan, the next stage of investment policy does not mean abandoning traditional measures of foreign investment.

“The volume of direct foreign investment remains important as an indicator of the scale of international capital’s participation in the economy. However, assessing the structural result requires a broader set of parameters,” Zebeshev said.

These include the number of production facilities launched, the depth of localization, participation of domestic suppliers, production of higher-value goods, exports, productivity and the retention of technological competencies within Kazakhstan.

The country already has many of the basic advantages needed to compete for such investments, including natural resources, energy potential, transport connectivity and access to major markets across Eurasia and China.

“The next stage does not imply abandoning quantitative targets, but requires a more comprehensive assessment of results. The scale of attracted capital should be considered together with the production capacities, supply chains, export opportunities and technological competencies that are formed inside the country,” Zebeshev said.

World.title: EBRD Projects Central Asia’s Strong Growth Despite Energy and Water Risks
World.content:
ASTANA – Central Asia is expected to remain one of the fastest-growing regions in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development’s (EBRD) economies in 2026 and 2027, although rising energy costs, water scarcity and tighter financing conditions could weigh on the outlook, according to the bank’s latest Regional Economic Prospects report.

The EBRD forecasts economic growth in Central Asia at 5.8% in 2026 and 5.3% in 2027. Forecasts were revised upward for Uzbekistan, supported by strong domestic demand, and Mongolia, driven by record mining output. At the same time, disruptions to fuel supplies from Russia remain a downside risk for the region.

“Inflationary pressures increased across the region amid higher food and energy prices, reflecting elevated global energy costs linked to the conflict in the Middle East and fuel-market disruptions in Russia,” reads the report.

In Kazakhstan, economic growth narrowed to 4.1% year on year in the first half of 2026, according to the EBRD.

“At the same time, non-oil sectors remained robust. Manufacturing output increased by 9% year on year over the same period, supported by strong performance in machine building, particularly the production of motor vehicles, trailers and semitrailers, as well as equipment repair and installation, food processing and chemicals,” it added.

The report, titled “Running Dry,” also identifies growing constraints in three key areas – oil exports, water and global savings. The EBRD said these pressures reveal vulnerabilities in energy systems, food supply chains and financing conditions across its regions.

The broader economies where the EBRD invests are projected to grow by 2.5% in 2026, before accelerating to 4% in 2027. The 2026 forecast was revised down by 0.6 percentage points compared with the bank’s previous forecast in June.

Energy pressures

The EBRD report highlights the impact of higher energy prices on economies across its regions. Oil prices rose from around $65 per barrel before the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East to more than $100 per barrel in April 2026. Prices remain 30% to 60% above their pre-conflict level, while refined products, particularly diesel and jet fuel, have experienced even larger increases.

Gas markets have also tightened. According to the EBRD, gas prices have risen by more than 70% since February, while global seaborne liquefied natural gas exports have fallen by 40% as Middle Eastern cargoes have largely stopped.

The developments are particularly relevant for energy-producing economies such as Kazakhstan. Higher energy prices can support export revenues, but volatility in global energy markets also creates risks for economies dependent on commodity exports.

“Disruptions along the Caspian Pipeline Consortium export route, together with fire- and powerrelated incidents at the Tengiz field in early 2026, resulted in an 8.9% contraction in oil and gas output in January-July 2026,” reads the report.

“Consequently, the authorities revised the country’s annual oil production target from 98 million to 96 million tons, with output likely to fall short of the previous year’s level,” it added.

Kazakhstan is seeking to reduce its reliance on hydrocarbons, with construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture increasingly contributing to economic growth.

The EBRD also noted that oil and gas account for around two-thirds of primary energy use across its regions. Reducing dependence on fossil fuels will require greater investment in renewable energy, energy storage and nuclear power.

Water scarcity becomes an economic concern

Water availability is another major issue highlighted by the EBRD. The report notes that drought is increasingly affecting agriculture, transportation and energy generation, making water availability an important economic consideration alongside energy security.

In Central Europe and the Baltic states, 38% of land faced medium or high agricultural drought risk in 2026, compared with an average of 12% since 2010. Low water levels on the Danube and Rhine have also disrupted industrial shipments and reduced output from hydropower and nuclear plants by around one-third.

The issue has particular significance for Central Asia, where agriculture and energy production depend heavily on shared water resources.

Kazakhstan faces similar challenges. More than 44% of the river flow feeding the country’s waterways originates outside its borders, making cooperation with neighboring states increasingly important for water security.

The country’s dependence on transboundary water resources is particularly important for agriculture. Inefficient irrigation systems and growing demand for water are adding pressure to already limited supplies.

“Water scarcity, extreme weather and higher financing costs are compounding the effects of high energy costs, putting further pressure on growth,” said EBRD Chief Economist Beata Javorcik. She stressed the need for investment in resilience to help economies withstand future shocks.

Inflation and financing remain challenges

Inflation across the EBRD regions has stabilized at around 6%, after reaching 6.7% in April. The bank said inflation remains around two percentage points above its pre-pandemic average.

“Energy accounted for about a quarter of headline inflation, with limited pass-through to other components,” said the report.

At the same time, financing conditions have tightened. The EBRD linked higher long-term interest rates to falling national saving rates in advanced economies, persistent inflation, government deficits and increased corporate borrowing for investment in artificial intelligence.

Higher borrowing costs could make infrastructure, energy and water projects more expensive, increasing pressure on governments and businesses to prioritize investment and improve efficiency.

For Kazakhstan, these challenges come as the country seeks to maintain economic growth while diversifying its economy. Kazakhstan accounts for more than half of Central Asia’s combined GDP, giving its economic performance significant weight in the region.

Despite the external risks, the EBRD expects Central Asia to maintain strong economic momentum, with projected growth of 5.8% in 2026 and 5.3% in 2027. The outlook will depend partly on energy supply stability, domestic demand and the region’s ability to manage growing pressure on water and other critical resources.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Wheat Export Record as Grain Rail Shipments Rise
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan exported a record 8.87 million tons of wheat from September 2025 to August 2026, as strong demand from Central Asian markets and Afghanistan helped drive shipments to the highest level on record, according to the Grain Union of Kazakhstan.

The figure represents a 16.2% increase from the same period last year, said Yevgeniy Karabanov, head of the union’s Analytics Committee.

The export surge coincided with growing railway shipments of grain. According to the Ministry of Transport, 10.8 million tons of grain were transported across Kazakhstan’s railway network in January–September, up 12% from the same period last year. Export-bound grain shipments reached 8.4 million tons, an increase of 14%.

Central Asia remains the main destination

Central Asian markets accounted for the majority of Kazakhstan’s wheat exports in the 2025/26 marketing year. Kazakhstan shipped nearly seven million tons of wheat to Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Turkmenistan, representing 78.7% of total wheat exports. Uzbekistan alone accounted for 60.8% of all shipments.

Railway data for January–September shows a similar concentration of grain flows toward the region. Kazakhstan transported 5.5 million tons of grain by rail to Central Asian countries, 33% more than a year earlier.

Uzbekistan received 4.11 million tons, up 44%, while shipments to Tajikistan rose 16% to 1.18 million tonnes. Smaller volumes were sent to the Kyrgyz Republic and Turkmenistan. Demand from Afghanistan also remained strong. Wheat exports to the country increased 2.6 times over the marketing year, according to the Grain Union.

The ministry reported that 762,000 tons of grain were transported by rail to Afghanistan in January–September, 4.3 times more than during the same period of 2025.

Kazakhstan expands its export geography

Kazakhstan also recorded sharp increases in wheat shipments to several markets outside its traditional destinations. Exports to Iran increased 617 times, while shipments to Türkiye rose 27 times and those to Russia 12 times. Exports to Uzbekistan increased 42%, Tajikistan 5.7% and the United Kingdom threefold.

Kazakh wheat also entered markets that had not received shipments during the previous marketing year. Around 6,000 tons were exported to France and 23,600 tons to Tunisia.

At the same time, exports to several destinations declined. Shipments to Turkmenistan fell to 28,000 tons, while exports to Azerbaijan decreased to 220,000 tons, Italy to 242,200 tons and Georgia to 39,400 tons.

Exports to China fell more than fourfold to 43,200 tons. Karabanov said the decline was offset by a 1.43 million-ton increase in shipments of feed meal to China, up 65%. Railway data, meanwhile, points to continued growth in grain flows to China, with 750,000 tons transported there in January–September, 54% more than a year earlier.

New harvest drives railway loading

The increase in grain transportation has continued into the new harvesting season. In September, grain loading reached 1.45 million tons, a record monthly figure and 7% above the level recorded in September 2025, according to the ministry.

The ministry attributed the continued growth in grain transportation to preparations for the new harvest and said a special grain headquarters had been established to coordinate railway shipments. The headquarters coordinates participants in the transportation process, monitors the readiness of railway infrastructure and rolling stock, and addresses operational issues that may arise during the harvest season.

According to the ministry, Kazakhstan has 16,900 grain wagons, 17,800 covered freight wagons and more than 2,000 locomotives available for grain transportation. The ministry said the existing rolling stock is sufficient to handle the expected volumes, with additional capacity available if needed.

Strong demand supports export growth

According to Karabanov, the acceleration in wheat exports in August was linked to early harvesting and low wheat stocks in importing countries. Strong demand from Central Asia and Afghanistan persisted throughout the marketing year, helping Kazakhstan expand wheat exports despite weaker shipments to several individual markets.

The record export result also highlights the importance of railway capacity for moving the new harvest to Kazakhstan’s main export destinations, particularly Central Asia, China and Afghanistan.

World.title: EU prepares to expand without Georgia: what ‘candidate status on paper’ means
World.content:
The European Union is preparing for a new round of enlargement and drawing up concrete roadmaps for four leading candidates — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

Georgia is no longer part of this process. The European Commission does not mention it at all in its main communication. An accompanying 149-page document explicitly says that Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold.

Against this backdrop, the political conflict between Tbilisi and Brussels has become increasingly clear. So has their different understanding of European integration itself. The European Commission says democratic reforms and alignment with EU foreign policy form part of the conditions for membership. Leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, meanwhile, have increasingly openly portrayed some of Brussels’ demands as pressure that harms the country’s interests.

“A candidate only on paper”

On 6 October, the European Commission published a communication titled “Communication on Pre-Enlargement Policy Reviews – Preparing for a Wider Union” (“Pre-Enlargement Policy Review — Preparing for a Wider Union”).

The document outlines how the EU itself should prepare for future enlargement. One of the main areas involves gradually integrating candidate countries before they achieve full membership.

At the same time, the European Commission is considering stronger safeguards in case a new member violates the EU’s fundamental principles after joining. In the most serious cases, such a mechanism could even suspend the member state’s voting rights in the Council of the EU.

The European Commission will prepare roadmaps for four countries — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

The main 25-page communication does not even mention Georgia.

On 6 October 2026 in Brussels, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos described Georgia’s position in response to a question from a Georgian journalist:

*“As you know, Georgia is a candidate country only on paper. I regret that. I would like Georgia, with the huge support of the Georgian people, to be at the same level as Moldova and Ukraine today.

How we continue working with the country will depend to a large extent on how the member states assess its future. But much of what is happening in the country [in Georgia] will appear in the enlargement reports at the end of October. You can imagine which direction things will take.”*

The working document accompanying the communication does mention Georgia among the enlargement countries, but it adds an important caveat:

“Georgia’s accession process has been de facto halted in line with the conclusions of the European Council.”

This is an important point: the EU has not revoked Georgia’s candidate status, and it did not take any new decision to do so on 6 October.

However, despite retaining its formal status, Georgia does not rank among the candidates for which the European Commission is now planning the next stage of accession.

A common starting point, different trajectories

Georgia applied to join the European Union in March 2022, at the same time as Ukraine and Moldova.

It received candidate status in December 2023, subject to fulfilling nine steps set out by the European Commission.

The three countries then took sharply different paths.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova in 2024. In Georgia’s case, however, EU documents state that steps taken by the authorities since 2024 have harmed the country’s European path and effectively halted the accession process.

[On 28 November 2024, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028 and would reject all EU budget grants — JAMnews]

The new 2026 package makes the difference even clearer: Moldova and Ukraine now rank among the four leading candidates, while Georgia does not.

“Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t”

Statements by Georgian Dream show that relations between Tbilisi and Brussels have become increasingly confrontational.

Georgian authorities respond to criticism from the EU not only by defending their policies, but also by openly rejecting and criticising Brussels’ demands themselves.

Government representatives also frame compliance with some EU demands as a question of protecting Georgia’s national interests.

Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili contrasted Marta Kos’s statement about Moldova’s progress with economic indicators. He said Georgia’s economic growth was higher.

Papuashvili linked this difference to Georgia’s approach to Brussels’ recommendations:

“[Moldova] deserves more and more praise, but our experience tells us that the more Brussels praises you, the more its decisions and imposed directives harm you.”
