Papuashvili also compared poverty rates in the two countries and linked the differences to their respective approaches to Brussels’ policies.

*“What is the difference? Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t. […] The conclusion is clear: those who listen to Brussels suffer; those who do not listen to Brussels but listen to their own people come out ahead economically. The only thing Moldova is really ahead of us in is Brussels’ beautiful words.

We certainly do not need such beautiful words if those words only mean that we suffer from policies imposed by Brussels,”* Papuashvili said.

Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirchkhalia gave a similar response.

He said the Georgian authorities were ready to carry out the reforms needed for European integration, but that Georgia had “red lines” and national interests that it could not sacrifice to join the EU.

He compared compliance with Brussels’ political demands to “blind obedience” and said Georgia wanted EU membership “not at any cost”.

“If Brussels now considers a country’s ‘progress’ to depend on how blindly it follows specific political demands, then this is no longer merit-based European integration, but an assessment of blind obedience. […] So when we are told that Georgia is ‘lagging behind’ Ukraine and Moldova, our answer is simple: Georgia chooses dignity and peace!” Kirchkhalia said.

What the European Commission says

The European Commission’s 2026 document sets out very different criteria. Alongside economic development, the central issues in the accession process include the rule of law, democratic standards and alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP).

According to the document, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and North Macedonia fully align with the CFSP, while Moldova and Ukraine demonstrate a high level of alignment. Georgia and Serbia need to make significant progress in this area, while Georgia and Turkey have low levels of alignment.

The European Commission sees this as an indication of a candidate country’s strategic choice and says these issues must be resolved before accession.

The document also gives Russia a separate focus. According to the European Commission, enlargement directly counters Russian influence because the accession process requires countries such as Georgia and Serbia to fully align with EU foreign policy and legislation. This includes sanctions, energy, trade, foreign investment and visa policy.

The document also states:

“At present, the Georgian authorities are not actively pursuing EU and NATO membership, while Ukraine is making changes to achieve full compatibility with NATO.”

This ranks among the strongest formulations in the new document because the assessment concerns not just the implementation of a specific reform, but the authorities’ overall political course.

The opposition on Moldova’s example

Salome Samadashvili, one of the leaders of the opposition Lelo — Strong Georgia alliance, contrasts Moldova’s example with Georgian Dream’s narrative about a so-called “second front”.

She says Moldova did not open a “second front” against Russia. Instead, the EU is helping Moldova strengthen its security and defence capabilities in response to threats from Russia.

Samadashvili also links Moldova’s European progress to its efforts to tackle oligarchic influence, arguing that Georgia has gone in the opposite direction.

“Unfortunately, Georgia has gone in the opposite direction: an oligarch has taken complete control of the government, destroyed all state institutions, and as a result, our EU accession agenda has been cancelled,” Samadashvili says.

Ban on opposition parties

The political context of Georgia’s relations with the EU is also visible in the European Parliament’s current agenda.

On 7 October, the European Parliament is due to hold a debate officially titled “Attempts by the ruling Georgian Dream party to ban opposition parties in Georgia”. A vote on the corresponding resolution will take place on 8 October.

This is a separate procedure from the European Commission’s enlargement package, and it would be incorrect to directly link the two.

However, the two processes also illustrate the different political contexts between Georgia and the other leading candidates. The EU is working on the next stages of integration with four countries, while the European Parliament is discussing the possible banning of opposition parties in Georgia.

The next important assessment of Georgia will come at the end of October, when the European Commission publishes its enlargement reports.

EU enlargement without Georgia

World.title: Ex-German intelligence chief arrested as investigators probe links to Azerbaijani intelligence
World.content:
German intelligence passed information to Azerbaijan

Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has not specified which foreign country is involved. However, according to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer and whether he prepared analytical materials for the officer using classified information.

Hanning has also served for many years on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.

Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was detained on 6 October. His former chief of staff, Manfred D., was also arrested as part of the same investigation.

According to the Federal Prosecutor’s Office, Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage involving treason, obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service. Manfred D. is suspected of attempted treason and aiding and abetting espionage.

The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations have yet to be considered by a court on their merits. No final judicial decision has been made in Hanning’s case.

Around 2,000 BND documents

According to investigators, several years after leaving the BND, Hanning reached an agreement with his former employee to provide him with classified information.

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office believes that around spring 2010, Hanning and Manfred D. struck an agreement under which D. would regularly provide his former boss with important information obtained from the BND in exchange for payment.

Manfred D. worked with Hanning at the BND before following him to Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior. In 2012, he returned to the BND, where he held a senior position in the offices of subsequent heads of the intelligence service until March 2026. In this role, he had access to classified information.

According to preliminary findings by investigators, between 2010 and 2022, Manfred D. provided Hanning with around 2,000 documents. A significant proportion contained classified information and were intended exclusively for internal use within the BND.

Some of the materials contained information intended for the BND leadership, as well as for regular meetings of intelligence service representatives at the German Federal Chancellery. According to an investigation by WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the documents included material on Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military, as well as information obtained from Germany’s partner intelligence services.

Prosecutors say Hanning intended to use the information for commercial purposes as part of his private consultancy work.

How did Azerbaijan connection emerge?

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office does not mention Azerbaijan or any other country in its official statement.

According to the official account, Hanning once used classified information obtained from Manfred D. to prepare an analysis for “an employee of a foreign intelligence service”. Investigators have so far been unable to establish whether the analysis was actually passed to its intended recipient.

The possible Azerbaijan connection emerged in reports by German media citing sources familiar with the investigation.

According to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer. The magazine also reports that the analysis Hanning prepared using classified BND information was intended for this individual. The same information has also been reported by WELT, t-online and other German media.

Hanning sits on board of German-Azerbaijani Forum

Another factor drawing attention to the possible Azerbaijan connection is Hanning’s longstanding public ties with the country.

He has for many years served on the board of the Deutsch-Aserbaidschanisches Forum (German-Azerbaijani Forum).

In an announcement about the election of the forum’s new leadership in August 2025, Hanning was again listed as a board member. The same list also included Elmar Mammadov, a representative of Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR in Germany.

The forum describes itself as an independent platform promoting political, economic, academic and cultural ties between Germany and Azerbaijan. LobbyControl, a German organisation that monitors lobbying in Germany, has previously described the forum as one of the lobbying organisations with close ties to the Azerbaijani authorities.

Hanning has served on the forum’s board for many years. As early as 2017, Tagesspiegel reported that the former BND chief was a member of the organisation’s board. It said that even then, the forum’s structures included former ministers, MPs and senior government officials.

Previous ‘Azerbaijan case’ in Germany

The current espionage investigation is not the first major scandal in Germany involving Azerbaijan.

In recent years, German authorities have investigated a number of criminal cases involving the alleged bribery of politicians in Azerbaijan’s interests.

In July 2025, a Munich court gave former CSU MP Eduard Lintner a nine-month suspended prison sentence for his role in transferring funds originating from Azerbaijan in an effort to influence decisions by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). The court explicitly described this as vote-buying.

In January 2026, former CDU MP Axel Fischer was given a 14-month suspended prison sentence. According to the court, while serving in PACE, Fischer received tens of thousands of euros from Azerbaijan and, in return, made positive statements about the country and passed on confidential documents.

Legally, these cases are unrelated to the current investigation into Hanning. The Lintner and Fischer cases concerned political corruption and lobbying on behalf of the Azerbaijani government’s interests. The Hanning case concerns state secrets and suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Classified documents discovered during unrelated investigation

Suspicions of espionage involving Hanning emerged under unusual circumstances.

In September 2025, German law enforcement officers searched Hanning’s home and offices as part of a separate criminal investigation into the kidnapping of the children of businesswoman Christina Block. Hanning also denied the allegations in that case.

During the searches, investigators reportedly discovered classified BND material. The documents were subsequently handed over to federal authorities, and in May 2026 a covert investigation into Hanning and Manfred D. was launched.

The findings of the investigation could have serious implications for Germany’s intelligence service. BND chief Martin Jäger said an internal review was also under way and that the initial suspicions had been further substantiated. German lawmakers responsible for overseeing the intelligence services have called for a comprehensive investigation into what happened.

If reports of Hanning’s links to Azerbaijani intelligence are confirmed, the case would go beyond previous scandals involving Azerbaijani lobbying in Germany: this time, the issue is not political influence but the possible transfer of classified German intelligence to a foreign intelligence service.

World.title: Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev’s statement about ‘Ukrainisation’ of Armenia
World.content:
Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

“Armenia turning into a new Ukraine represents another sign of Russia’s geopolitical anxiety and the deepening crisis in Armenian-Russian relations,” political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan said in response to Dmitry Medvedev’s sensational statement.

“Armenia’s current leadership decided that changing the country’s course would serve its interests. I am sure that this will not lead to anything good either. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” said Russia’s deputy Security Council chairman.

By a change in course, he meant Armenia’s drive towards European integration. Yerevan has not officially responded to his remarks.

Only parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan told journalists: “Armenia cannot be anything else. Armenia is Armenia, and it will always be Armenia.”

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan believes that Russia “is irritated and unbalanced because the situation in the war is not just bad, but very bad”. At the same time, the analyst says Armenia should take the statement from Moscow seriously and try to assess how real the threat is:

“We should not treat this threat as either an absolutely inevitable scenario or empty bravado. It involves real risks stemming from Armenia’s energy and economic vulnerabilities. It also contains elements of psychological pressure.”

Comment

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan says Russia fears losing its influence in the South Caucasus:

“Against the backdrop of setbacks on the Ukrainian front, Moscow’s resources remain limited, while its influence across the post-Soviet space has weakened. But the most unwelcome development for Russia is that all of this now shows a clear trend towards further deterioration.”

In his view, Russia can still wage a war of attrition in Ukraine, but casualties, economic sanctions and international isolation are creating significant tensions inside the country.

The analyst says that under these conditions, Russia sees the departure of any ally as a “stab in the back”. This leads to an unbalanced response, as Medvedev’s statement demonstrates:

“The aim of the threat is to instil fear in Armenian society and stop the process of rapprochement with the West, which stems from our security and development interests.”

Mehrabyan believes the threats from Moscow carry some real risks:

“The possibility of a direct military invasion is currently close to zero for one simple reason. No matter how many threats Medvedev spews, Russia has no way to invade a country with which it has no border. But Russia has powerful hybrid tools, and it can and does use them.”

Among the existing risks, the political analyst highlights Armenia’s economic and energy dependence on Russia.

He points to the Upper Lars checkpoint, the only land route linking Armenia with Russia. Whenever the route closes, it creates problems for Armenian exporters and importers. Mehrabyan also notes that Armenia receives gas from Russia, as well as fuel for its nuclear power plant:

“Cutting off gas supplies or suspending deliveries under the pretext of repairs, or closing the border on sanitary grounds, could trigger internal upheaval in Armenia and force the country to operate under a state of emergency.”

According to Mehrabyan, Yerevan has so far managed the potential risks without shocks or conflicts, but he is not confident that it will continue to do so.

He stresses that the current situation also creates potential security risks. In particular, he suggests that “Baku could sell its pressure on Armenia to Moscow”, and that Russia would have no objection to such a deal.

The political analyst says Russia is behaving like a wounded beast. He urges the Armenian authorities to summon the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry and hand him a formal protest note instead of making public demarches.

At the same time, he says Armenia needs to emphasise once again that its closer ties with the European Union and the United States serve Armenia’s interests and do not target Russia.

Mehrabyan identifies energy and economic diversification among Yerevan’s priorities. He says Armenia urgently needs to secure gas supplies from Iran, which could cover 85% of the country’s needs. He also expects the authorities to:

continue army reforms and work to strengthen the country’s borders;

deepen military and technical cooperation with various countries, including France, India and Greece;

ensure domestic stability and resilience;

strengthen strategic communications and combat disinformation.

Ruben Mehrabyan believes Armenia needs to prepare for modern warfare, including hybrid attacks:

“Armenia must not give Azerbaijan or Russia any reason to be tempted to commit aggression against us.”

Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

World.title: Giorgi Davitadze case: how it drew attention to what is happening in Georgia’s prisons
World.content:
36-year-old prisoner Giorgi Davitadze says that about 10 prison staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi, Georgia, sexually assaulted him.

Authorities have not yet investigated Davitadze’s case. The Penitentiary Service, however, calls his allegations “a complete lie” and has released silent video footage as evidence. Davitadze’s family says the footage is incomplete and that authorities have not released the actual footage showing the alleged abuse.

Georgia’s Public Defender says the video provided to the office does not show the abuse Davitadze described.

Davitadze’s case has unfolded in a particularly sensitive context for Georgia. The allegations concern sexual abuse inside the very system that Georgian Dream made one of the main targets of its promised reforms when it came to power.

What Giorgi Davitadze says

The public learned about the alleged sexual abuse of Giorgi Davitadze on 2 October, during a hearing at the Court of Appeals.

Davitadze told the court that on 21 December 2025, about 10 prison staff sexually assaulted him and subjected him to degrading treatment in a de-escalation room, a special facility for temporarily isolating prisoners experiencing severe emotional or psychological distress.

“They took me down to the de-escalation room and raped me — with a finger, with a hand. […] Ten people, the guards, raped me. You can see everything on the camera,” Davitadze told the court.

He said he later attempted suicide.

Davitadze demanded that the authorities punish the prison staff he named, threatening to go on hunger strike if they failed to do so.

Davitadze’s allegations sparked widespread attention in the media and society.

The severity of the allegations drew particular attention, as did Davitadze’s claim that surveillance cameras should have captured the incident he described.

Davitadze’s family demanded the full release of the footage, while civil society organisations said the prisoner’s allegations required an effective and comprehensive investigation. The Penitentiary Service, in turn, categorically denied the allegations of sexual abuse.

It later emerged that government agencies had known about the alleged abuse since December 2025.

The Public Defender’s Office was also aware of the case. On 26 December, Davitadze’s lawyer told the office that his client had suffered ill-treatment.

That same day, a representative of the Public Defender’s Office went to the Rustavi prison and spoke with Davitadze. He repeated his account, saying prison staff had subjected him to abuse, including sexual abuse.

The Public Defender’s Office passed the information to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which opened an investigation. The office also demanded that video footage from the period identified by Davitadze be preserved in the archive.

More than nine months have passed since then. The investigation remains incomplete, and Davitadze is still being held in the same prison whose staff he accuses of abuse.

What the video released by the Penitentiary Service shows

On 2 October, the Penitentiary Service released footage that, according to the agency, shows Davitadze being taken to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and the events that followed.

The video has no sound.

The footage shows Davitadze and about 10 prison staff members. One of them wears disposable medical gloves.

The staff search Davitadze, including with a metal detector. Several people hold the prisoner’s arms behind his back. The staff then forcibly search Davitadze after pinning him down on a bed.

The Penitentiary Service says prison staff must search prisoners when moving them to a de-escalation room. According to its account, Davitadze refused to undergo the search and insulted the staff, so they carried out the search by force.

The service calls the allegations of sexual abuse “a complete lie” and says “there was not only no sexual violence against Davitadze, there was no violence of any kind.”

The Penitentiary Service says it had not previously released the footage because the case remains under investigation. The agency also says it has continuously archived video footage related to Davitadze since 3 March 2026.

Family says the released video is incomplete

Davitadze’s family says the video released by the Penitentiary Service is incomplete.

His mother, Irma Davitadze, says she saw five video files covering about 20 minutes in total and believes the footage had been edited.

On 3 October, family members and Davitadze’s supporters held a protest outside the prison. They demanded the release of the full footage, an impartial investigation and the resignation of prison director Shota Trapaidze.

Another demand from the family is to transfer Davitadze to another prison, away from the staff members he accuses of abuse.

The prisoner’s father, Avtandil Davitadze, says:

“[These staff members] come to his cell, shout something, say something that insults his dignity, provoke him, and then what should never happen begins.”

However, Justice Minister Paata Salia says transferring a prisoner to another facility requires the authorities to follow certain procedures and meet specific conditions. The minister says officials are considering the request and will transfer Davitadze if he meets those conditions.

What the ombudsman says

The Public Defender’s position has become one of the most contentious aspects of the case.

According to an official statement from the Public Defender’s Office, its representatives requested and reviewed the relevant video footage but found no details showing the severe abuse Davitadze described.

However, the office stresses that authorities must investigate the allegations regardless and verify the prisoner’s complaint by collecting and comparing all available evidence.

The Public Defender also calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make the findings of the investigation public as soon as possible.

On 5 October, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani repeated on TV Pirveli that the footage released so far does not show sexual abuse itself. When asked whether inserting a finger into a prisoner’s body could form part of a search procedure, Ioseliani initially said he needed to check the relevant regulation:

Journalist: [Davitadze says] he felt a finger penetrate his body. Is that part of the search procedure?

Public Defender: We need to see what the regulation says — whether it allows such a thorough search. However, the regulation does require searches, including with a detector and scanner.

When the presenter asked whether he therefore ruled out the possibility of something that does not appear in the footage, Ioseliani replied: “The Prosecutor’s Office must investigate what we cannot see.”

Questions that remain unanswered

Public organisations say the footage and explanations released by the Penitentiary Service cannot provide an adequate response to such a serious allegation. More than ten organisations have called for an effective and comprehensive investigation. They include the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the Social Justice Center, Transparency International — Georgia, the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED), the Institute for Development of Freedom of Information (IDFI), the Civil Society Foundation, Safari and others.

In their statement, they raise eight main questions:

Why did authorities need to move Davitadze to the de-escalation room?

What exactly did he do before the authorities took this step?

Was the measure necessary and proportionate?

Why were about ten staff members in the room?

Who were they and what did each of them do?

Does the published video show the full sequence of events without interruption?

Does the original video still exist, and can an independent expert examine it?

Do recordings from other cameras exist?

“The video released by the Penitentiary Service cannot replace an independent and effective investigation,” the organisations say.

Why the video has no sound

Another question concerns the fact that the released footage has no sound.

On 5 October, journalists asked Justice Minister Paata Salia whether the original recording had sound. The minister did not answer. When they asked whether cameras installed in de-escalation rooms can record sound at all, Salia said he could not comment. Later, speaking on Imedi TV, the minister said Georgian law does not provide for audio recording.

Salia also could not explain why authorities moved Davitadze to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and referred journalists to the Penitentiary Service for an answer.

The minister says authorities are investigating Giorgi Davitadze’s original allegation and that they need to complete the investigation before giving a final answer.

“If anyone attempts to destabilise or disrupt the operation of penitentiary institutions, whether from inside or outside, the authorities will respond strictly, as provided by law,” Salia said.

He also mentioned that some public statements may contain signs of a criminal offence, but he did not name any specific individuals or give examples.

Prisons — one of the most painful issues in modern Georgia

The issue of violence in Georgian prisons goes beyond human rights.

It holds a special place in the country’s recent political history. In 2012, conditions in the penitentiary system became one of the key factors behind the change of government.

On 18 September 2012, less than two weeks before the parliamentary elections, Georgian television channels broadcast footage recorded at Prison No. 8 in Tbilisi.

The footage showed guards beating, humiliating and sexually abusing prisoners. The broadcasts triggered mass protests in Tbilisi and other cities.

The footage exposed a problem that human rights groups had already raised. A 2013 Human Rights Watch report said the images highlighted a longstanding problem of torture and ill-treatment of prisoners.

The government at the time acknowledged the systemic nature of violence in prisons. The ministers responsible for prisons and internal affairs resigned, and authorities arrested several penitentiary staff members. Within days, the prison system became one of the central issues of the election campaign.

In the parliamentary elections on 1 October 2012, Mikheil Saakashvili’s United National Movement lost power, and Bidzina Ivanishvili’s Georgian Dream coalition took control of the government.

One of the new government’s main political promises was to reform the penitentiary system that had developed under the previous government and protect prisoners’ rights.

But data from recent years and reports by human rights organisations show that violence and ill-treatment by security, law enforcement and penitentiary authorities remain serious concerns. The problem extends beyond prisons to police stations, the detention process and protests.

In June 2026, Georgian human rights organisations said in a joint statement that, in their assessment, torture and ill-treatment in Georgia had become a “systemic and widespread practice”. Amnesty International describes a similar situation.

At the same time, the penitentiary system continues to grow in scale. According to official statistics, Georgia’s penitentiary system received a total of 22,767 convicted people in 2025 — 25.5% more than the previous year. This marks the highest figure since the authorities began keeping the relevant statistics.

In 2024, Georgia ranked second among 46 Council of Europe countries in terms of the number of prisoners per 100,000 people.

What is happening in Georgia’s prisons

After the allegations by Giorgi Davitadze became public, several incidents occurred at Rustavi Prison No. 6. According to the Public Defender, its representatives met three prisoners on 3 and 4 October who had protested against the treatment of Davitadze. They told the representatives why they were protesting and described their conditions in prison.

The Penitentiary Service denies that the authorities moved these prisoners to de-escalation rooms because they had expressed solidarity with Davitadze. According to the agency, the authorities moved them to protect the safety of the prisoners and prison staff.

For example, the service says that on 2 October one prisoner kicked the prison’s deputy director in the stomach. On 4 October, two other prisoners allegedly “physically insulted” staff members — that is, attacked them — while returning from a walk. The agency also released video footage showing these incidents.

Later that same evening, on 4 October, an incident also involved Davitadze himself. According to the Penitentiary Service, he called over a prison employee and, in front of him, swallowed “several small objects of unknown origin”. Staff offered to transfer Davitadze to Vivamedi Clinic, but he refused.

The following day, the Public Defender’s Office said its representative had met with Davitadze. According to the prisoner, he felt well and had refused the transfer to the clinic as part of his protest. Davitadze said he would not go to the clinic until the authorities returned the three prisoners who had protested in his support from the de-escalation rooms to their cells.

Amid these events, reports also emerged of possible violence against another prisoner. According to lawyer Anna Akopova, her client Lasha Chachanidze suffered a beating at the same Prison No. 6 after he shouted from his cell to express solidarity with Davitadze. The lawyer says authorities transferred Chachanidze and two other prisoners to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

Akopova says the prisoner has multiple injuries on different parts of his body. According to her, about ten people took part in the alleged assault. The lawyer is demanding a medical examination and the preservation of the relevant video footage, which could establish Chachanidze’s condition when staff took him out of his cell and when they returned him.

The Penitentiary Service categorically denies the allegation and says nothing of the sort happened. The Public Defender’s Office said it had received information about the case and would visit the prisoner.

Saba Skhvitaridze, who authorities detained during pro-European protests, also wrote about the tense situation at Prison No. 6. According to a statement published on his Facebook page, authorities transferred some prisoners to other facilities, placed others in de-escalation rooms and several prisoners went on hunger strike. Skhvitaridze also reported that authorities beat a prisoner and that some prisoners injured themselves.

Giorgi Davitadze remains in the same prison, whose staff he accuses of sexual abuse.

The Prosecutor’s Office investigation, which it launched in December 2025 after the Public Defender’s Office filed a complaint, remains incomplete. The Public Defender’s Office says it continues to monitor the investigation and calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make its findings public as soon as possible.

The Penitentiary Service denies all the allegations, including reports of a hunger strike among prisoners, and insists that “complete calm” prevails at Rustavi Prison No. 6.

The Giorgi Davitadze case

World.title: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately
World.content:
Following the killing of Dmitry Pushkaryov, who Georgia extradited to Russia, the Georgian Social Justice Center (SJC) said that Georgia should immediately halt the extradition of prisoners to Russia.

The organisation said resuming the practice of extraditing prisoners to Russia was incompatible with human rights.

After Georgia extradited Dmitry Pushkaryov, he was killed in an attack on Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) officers. According to Russian authorities, Pushkaryov killed one officer and wounded three others while attempting to escape.

“The mere fact that Dmitry Pushkaryov was killed does not directly establish that Georgia violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by extraditing him. However, his death raises even more serious questions about how thoroughly the Georgian authorities assessed the risks he faced in Russia, what guarantees they obtained from Russia, whether an independent mechanism existed to monitor compliance with those guarantees, and whether the Georgian side subsequently monitored the person’s situation,” the SJC said.

According to the organisation, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) indicates that information that emerges after a person’s transfer can also matter when assessing how well-founded the state’s initial risk assessment was.

The SJC believes that continuing extraditions to Russia — particularly without proper public justification, a rigorous individual risk assessment and effective independent monitoring mechanisms — could put Georgia in breach of its international human rights obligations.

The organisation calls on the Georgian government, the Ministry of Justice and the Prosecutor General’s Office to immediately suspend extraditions to Russia. The SJC believes the practice should remain suspended until the situation in Russia changes significantly and the international community reaches a consensus on the issue.

The Centre also calls on the Prosecutor General’s Office to publish statistical data on extradition requests received from Russia since 16 March 2022, the decisions made on those requests and the extraditions carried out.

The organisation is also demanding that the Ministry of Justice explain the legal grounds for changing the moratorium recorded before the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Sumbaev v. Georgia.

The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.

“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

World.title: Georgia without an opposition? How ruling party moved to ban its opponents through constitutional lawsuit
World.content:
The ruling party Georgian Dream has asked Georgia’s Constitutional Court to ban five opposition parties. Four of them crossed the five per cent threshold in the 2024 parliamentary elections. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, election stability risks, a total of 784,820 voters — 37.79% of those who took part in the election — voted for the four parties.

What legal grounds does the government cite for seeking to ban the five parties? What does the term “collective United National Movement” mean? How has the list of parties facing a ban changed, and under what conditions does European law allow such a ban? JAMnews examined the Georgian Dream lawsuit, relevant legislation and European practice to answer these questions.

Georgian Dream registered its latest lawsuit with the Constitutional Court on 24 September 2026, under case No. 1979.

The list of parties facing a ban includes Unity — National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia — Lelo, Gakharia for Georgia and Federalists.

As of 5 October 2026, the court has not yet published a decision on whether it will accept the lawsuit for consideration on the merits, and it has not yet set a hearing date.

The First Chamber is hearing the case, with Vasil Roinishvili serving as the reporting judge. Under the law, the court must issue its final decision within nine months of the filing — no later than 24 June 2027.

If the court upholds the lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections could disappear from the country’s political system.

Under current legislation, the authorities can also ask the court to ban another political organisation that acts as a “successor” to an already banned party.

An election campaign promise

Bidzina Ivanishvili at a Georgian Dream rally, April 2024.

The idea of banning opposition parties did not emerge spontaneously within Georgian Dream. Its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili, publicly stated even before the 2024 parliamentary elections that, after the vote, the government would deliver a “strict political and legal verdict” to the “collective National Movement”.

In other words, the idea of banning the opposition did not emerge after the election. It formed part of the election campaign itself.

“After the election, we will have the opportunity to deliver a strict political and legal verdict to the collective National Movement.”

Ivanishvili also explained why, in his view, this did not happen in 2012. He said the government did not yet have sufficient resources at the time:

“Over these years, we have accumulated enough resources to begin fully strengthening our sovereignty…”

A statement made almost six months before the election gradually turned into a concrete political plan. In August 2024, Georgian Dream openly announced that it needed a constitutional majority in the election to declare the “collective National Movement” illegal. The European Commission included the plan in its report that year.

Then EU High Representative Josep Borrell, speaking in the European Parliament, described the promise to ban opposition parties as one of the worrying developments during Georgia’s election campaign.

Two years later, that campaign promise has turned into a concrete lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

Three lawsuits, three lists — how the number of parties facing a ban grew

The lawsuit changed three times over the course of one year.

The Constitutional Court registered the first lawsuit on 31 October 2025, under case No. 1912. Eighty-eight members of parliament signed it. They sought to ban three political forces:

Unity — National Movement

Coalition for Change

Strong Georgia — Lelo

Later, on 21 April 2026, 89 MPs filed a second lawsuit, No. 1958. They added a fourth party, Federalists, to the list.

The list of parties facing a ban grew again in September 2026.

On 24 September, the Constitutional Court registered lawsuit No. 1979, signed by 88 MPs. This time, the authorities are seeking to ban five parties, including former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s party, For Georgia.

The law gives the Constitutional Court a maximum of nine months to rule on such a case. Each new lawsuit has therefore sparked debate over whether that period starts again from the beginning.

The authors of the lawsuit hope the Constitutional Court will complete the process by January 2027, by which time all five parties would have been banned.

Opposition representatives, meanwhile, argue that Georgian Dream is actually prolonging the process by adding new parties.

On what grounds can a party be banned?

Georgia’s Constitution sets out specific grounds for banning a political party.

It prohibits parties whose goals include overthrowing or forcibly changing the constitutional order, undermining the country’s independence or violating its territorial integrity. The authorities can also ban parties that promote war or violence or incite national, ethnic, regional, religious or social hatred.

Only the Constitutional Court can ban a political party.

The Georgian Dream lawsuit relies on these constitutional grounds and argues that the listed parties’ activities target the state.

A significant part of the argument draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission, known as the Tsulukiani Commission.

One of the lawsuit’s key arguments concerns the opposition parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the 2024 election, parliament and the government.

The plaintiffs also link the opposition parties’ actions to “sabotage”, calls for Western sanctions against the Georgian authorities and attempts to “punish” the country.

The lawsuit, for example, treats the opposition’s refusal to recognise the election results and its view that Georgian Dream is an illegitimate government as “sabotage”.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also cited the legitimacy of the government when explaining why the authorities added Gakharia’s party to the list.

He said that although the party, unlike its “fellow opposition parties”, agreed to take part in parliamentary work, it still does not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government:

“It is true that they entered parliament, but to this day they do not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government. Under these circumstances, the spirit of this political party’s activities is no different from that of the other relevant political parties,” he said.

Why these parties?

The lawsuit explicitly cites the parties’ political influence as a reason for seeking their ban. It also mentions other opposition parties, such as the Republican Party, which does not appear on the list, and says:

“At present, they do not have significant influence on politics or a realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold. Accordingly, at this stage, there is no apparent need to ban them.”

A brief overview of the five parties facing a ban: Политические силы, объединенные “Грузинской мечтой” в единый “черный список”, имеют разное происхождение, историю и идеологию. Некоторые из них действительно произошли из политической семьи «Единого национального движения». Некоторые пытались занять независимое пространство именно между ЕНД и «Грузинской мечтой». Политическое же ядро партии Гиорги Гахария и вовсе вышло из самой «Грузинской мечты». «Единство — Национальное движение» «Единое национальное движение» экс-президента Михеила Саакашвили — самая старая партия в этой пятерке и единственная, имеющая опыт пребывания у власти: в течение 9 лет она являлась правящей партией Грузии. На выборах 2024 года ЕНД официально получила 211 216 голосов — 10,17%. Уже долгие годы партия переживает кризис лидерства и на данный момент находится в режиме переходного управления. В августе 2026 года был создан временный управляющий совет, руководителем которого стал Иракли Павленишвили. Избрание постоянного председателя партии должно состояться позже. Главным лицом, принимающим решения в партии, по-прежнему остается Михеил Саакашвили, который уже пять лет находится в тюрьме. ЕНД позиционирует себя как резко проевропейская и евроатлантическая политическая сила. Её историческое ядро — это политическое наследие правительства Саакашвили. Именно правление ЕНД в 2004-2012 годах является главной мишенью большей части иска «Грузинской мечты» и обвинений комиссии Цулукиани. Coalition for Change Coalition for Change was created ahead of the 2024 elections and brought together several different political forces. The coalition included Nika Melia and Nika Gvaramia’s Akhali party, Zurab Japaridze’s Girchi — More Freedom and Elene Khoshtaria’s Droa. Akhali is a pro-European centre-right liberal party. Girchi — More Freedom has a more distinctly right-libertarian economic platform, while Droa has a liberal and activist profile. In the 2024 election, the coalition received the largest number of official votes among the opposition forces — 229,161, or 11.03%. Most of its leaders had previously been associated with the UNM. The coalition brings together parties that broke away from the UNM or emerged independently at different times. Strong Georgia — Lelo The core of Strong Georgia is the Lelo party, which Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze founded in 2019. Both entered politics after careers in business. A broader coalition formed around Lelo in 2024. It included Ana Dolidze’s For People, Aleko Elisashvili’s Citizens and Levan Tsutskiridze’s Freedom Square. The coalition sought to present itself as an independent alternative to both Georgian Dream and the former ruling UNM. The party has a pro-European, centrist-liberal profile. Economic development, institutional reform and Western integration have remained central themes in Lelo’s programmes. In 2024, Strong Georgia officially received 182,922 votes, or 8.81%. Gakharia for Georgia Giorgi Gakharia’s party stands out from the other four parties in the group because of its origins. Gakharia was not a member of the government under Mikheil Saakashvili. Instead, he served as economy minister, interior minister and eventually prime minister under Georgian Dream. He resigned as prime minister in February 2021 and founded his own For Georgia party in May. The party initially sought to present itself as an alternative to both Georgian Dream and the UNM. It received 7.79% in the 2021 municipal elections and 161,521 votes, or 7.78%, in the 2024 parliamentary election. Gakharia’s case shows how broadly Georgian Dream applies the concept of the “collective National Movement”: today, the category also includes a political force led by one of Georgian Dream’s former leaders. Federalists Federalists are the newest party among the five. Giga Bokeria, Tamar Chergoleishvili and their allies founded the party in August 2024 after leaving European Georgia. Giga Bokeria chairs the party, while Tamar Chergoleishvili heads its Tbilisi organisation. The party identifies individual freedom, human rights, European development, free competition, decentralisation and strong democratic institutions as its core principles. Politically, it is a pro-European and liberal force with a more right-wing economic platform. Federalists did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Bokeria and Chergoleishvili’s group has a long-standing political conflict with Mikheil Saakashvili and today’s UNM.

At the same time, the lawsuit notes that the question of whether these parties are unconstitutional could arise in the future if they gain significant influence over the political process.

Initially, the “Federalists” also fell into the category of parties with “no realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold”. However, in March 2026, they joined the “Opposition Alliance”, a nine-party coalition. In April, Georgian Dream also called for the Federalists to be banned.

Thus, according to the lawsuit, a party’s political influence is one of the factors that the plaintiffs themselves take into account when seeking to ban it.

Представители оппозиционного альянса, март 2026 года

How all opponents of the government became the “collective National Movement”

The “collective National Movement” is neither a party nor a legally recognised political organisation. It is a political term coined by Georgian Dream that it has used for years to group various opposition forces into a single political camp, thereby portraying its opponents as a common “enemy”.

Over the years, the boundaries of this category have gradually expanded. It has come to include not only the National Movement itself (UNM, the former ruling party) and parties that broke away from it, but also forces that positioned themselves as alternatives to both the UNM and Georgian Dream. These include Mamuka Khazaradze’s Lelo and Giorgi Gakharia’s party, even though Gakharia himself previously served as prime minister for Georgian Dream.

The term then expanded further. Irakli Kobakhidze included not only opposition parties but also non-governmental organisations and media outlets as part of the “collective National Movement”:

“They are all in the same pot… All the radical opposition parties, all these radical NGOs, their radical media,” Kobakhidze said.

According to Georgian Dream’s current narrative, the political differences between these forces are not significant. The ruling party portrays them as different parts of a single network controlled from abroad. This logic brings together parties with different histories, leaders and political platforms under the “collective National Movement”.

The rhetoric has gradually acquired a specific political goal. In 2024, Kobakhidze compared removing the “collective National Movement” from the political system with banning the National Socialists in post-war Germany.

A year later, he said: “This crisis within the collective ‘National Movement’ must deepen, and it will deepen, ultimately leading to the complete destruction of the collective ‘National Movement’. Only then will Georgia develop a healthy democratic system.”

What does the attempt to ban the parties mean? Views

Representatives of the opposition parties themselves see the Georgian Dream lawsuit not as a separate legal dispute but as part of a broader process of restricting political competition.

Their main argument is that the government is using the courts to remove from the political arena forces that remain its electoral competitors.

Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of the Strong Georgia — Lelo alliance, points to the fact that the list of parties facing a ban has changed several times. He says that each new lawsuit restarts the nine-month period for considering the case.

He believes this allows the government both to retain the option of banning the parties and to delay a final decision.

Giga Lemondzhava, a representative of Coalition for Change, sees the party ban as a new stage in what he describes as authoritarian politics. However, he says political struggle cannot be ended simply by cancelling a party’s legal registration.

The National Movement takes a similar position. One of its leaders, Levan Khabeishvili, called on the opposition in a letter sent from prison not to focus entirely on the parties’ legal status: “Don’t get hung up on the issue of banning parties! They have banned the country!”

His message is that accepting the legal framework created by Georgian Dream would make the opposition dependent on an agenda set by the government. Political resistance, he argues, should not depend on a party’s registration.

The case of Giorgi Gakharia’s party is particularly notable. For Georgia took part in the 2024 election, later entered parliament and does not support violent struggle against the government. Given all this, the party’s MP Giorgi Sharashidze questions how the main constitutional grounds cited in the lawsuit apply to them:

“Unconstitutionality, calls for violence, calls to overthrow the government… What does any of that have to do with us? … We even entered parliament.”

Giorgi Gakharia, meanwhile, sees his party’s addition to the “blacklist” as part of a broader process. In his view, the authorities are trying to leave no functioning critical opposition within institutional politics:

“Regardless of whether they ban us or not, we will not back down in the struggle to restore Georgia’s democracy and protect its European and Euro-Atlantic path.”

The Federalists’ case exposes another contradiction. The party did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Its leaders previously belonged to former President Mikheil Saakashvili’s political team, but they have been in sharp conflict with both Saakashvili himself and the UNM, the party he founded, for many years. Despite this, the authorities also regard them as part of the “collective National Movement”.

Party leader Tamar Chergoleishvili says banning a political competitor is unacceptable to her regardless of her attitude towards that competitor:

“Of course, we see all the other parties as competitors, but we want to defeat our competitors on a level playing field, through fair competition, not as a result of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s bans.”

Georgian Dream explains the process very differently.

According to the authorities, the issue is not about eliminating political competitors but protecting the democratic system. Georgian Dream MP Levan Machavariani argues that opposition parties that appear different on the surface are actually parts of the same political network. He says dividing them into “radical”, “semi-radical” and relatively “constructive” forces is artificial and serves as a way for a common political centre to assign them different tasks.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze follows the same logic. He says the government promised voters to “neutralise foreign agents” and is now fulfilling that promise:

“We made a promise to voters that we would neutralise foreign agents in our country, and we are genuinely fulfilling that promise.”

Kobakhidze also uses this argument to explain the ban:

“It is very important that the state make a decision on this issue — a decision that serves the national interest.”

When can democracy ban a political party?

Europe has precedents for banning political parties, but authorities treat such bans as an extreme measure, usually in very different circumstances from those in Georgia. Banning five parties at once would be unprecedented.

Under the standards of the Venice Commission, authorities may justify dissolving a party if it uses violence or advocates overthrowing the democratic constitutional order. A peaceful call to change the political system or constitution does not, in itself, justify a ban.

European practice focuses not on how radical a party’s position is, but on whether its goals and actions pose a real threat to the democratic order and whether sufficient evidence supports that conclusion.

European case law also sets a high threshold. Spain banned Batasuna after authorities established its links to the ETA terrorist organisation. In Turkey, in the Refah Partisi case, the court considered evidence that the party sought to establish a theocratic system and had made statements linked to the use of force.

In Germany, meanwhile, authorities ultimately did not ban the NPD in 2017, even though the Constitutional Court found that the party’s goals were incompatible with the democratic order. However, the court concluded that the party lacked the real ability to achieve those goals.

What Europe says about Georgia’s case

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has taken a particularly strong position on Georgia.

Even before the 2024 election, a PACE monitoring delegation said Georgian Dream’s calls to ban the opposition threatened political pluralism.

In 2025, PACE described the planned ban as targeting “virtually the entire functioning democratic opposition” and said such a move would effectively create a one-party system in Georgia.

In June 2026, the Assembly made its position even clearer.

Resolution No. 2664 says the initiative to ban “virtually all democratic opposition parties” is unacceptable. It says implementing the initiative would effectively create a one-party dictatorship in Georgia, which would be incompatible with membership in the Council of Europe. The Assembly called on the authorities to withdraw the lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

The European Commission’s 2025 report also describes “serious democratic backsliding” in Georgia and says legislative and institutional changes threaten political pluralism. The report also notes that the ruling party has effectively consolidated control over the legislative and executive branches of government.

What happens if the parties are banned?

Banning the five parties could have consequences far beyond cancelling their names and legal registrations. The issue is what kind of political competition will remain in Georgia ahead of the next parliamentary election in 2028.

If the Constitutional Court upholds Georgian Dream’s lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the five per cent threshold in 2024 could disappear from the political arena. According to official Central Election Commission figures, nearly 800,000 people voted for them in total — about a quarter of all voters.

The current legislation also allows the authorities to extend restrictions to people linked to the banned parties. The court can prohibit them from establishing or joining other parties, standing as candidates in elections or holding political office. Authorities may also terminate the mandates of sitting elected MPs.

A new party name would not automatically provide a way around the ban. The law already includes the concept of a “successor party”. If a new political force substantially repeats the goals, activities or membership of a banned party, the court can ban it as well.

Under the Georgian Dream scenario, all of this could effectively leave the country without political parties or politicians representing the current opposition.

The process is not taking place in isolation. In recent years, the government has also adopted several laws that have sharply tightened the legal environment for foreign funding, grants and the activities of NGOs and media outlets.

Meanwhile, anti-government protests continue in Georgia, and the political confrontation between the authorities and their opponents remains highly tense.

The 2028 election is key to understanding the political significance of these developments. If the court upholds the lawsuit and the current restrictions remain in force, Georgia could enter the next parliamentary election with all four opposition forces that crossed the threshold in 2024 legally dissolved. The mechanism for quickly banning possible successor parties would already be in place.

Ban on opposition parties in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice
World.content:
Azerbaijan drafts anti-corruption bill

Azerbaijan has drafted a separate bill aimed at encouraging and protecting people who report corruption. The bill was submitted to the Milli Majlis on 5 October and is due to be discussed by a parliamentary committee on 6 October.

The initiative comes amid continuing complaints that police officers demand money from citizens, while journalists investigating corruption are sentenced to lengthy prison terms. Existing legislation already provides protections for people who report corruption. The key question, therefore, is from whom – and how – the state intends to protect citizens after they report such cases.

Protection provided by law

Article 11-2 of the Law on Combating Corruption prohibits disclosing the identity of a person who reports corruption without their consent, as well as threatening them or their relatives. It also prohibits dismissing an employee because they have filed a complaint, transferring them to another position, making unlawful deductions from their salary or obstructing their career progression.

If an employee provides evidence that retaliatory measures have been taken against them, the burden of disproving the allegation falls on the employer. The law also prohibits assigning a complaint for review to the person against whom it was made or to anyone with an interest in the outcome of the investigation.

Information registered through an internal reporting procedure must be examined within 20 working days, after which the person who submitted it must be informed of the outcome. If a complaint concerns the head of an organisation, the person may approach a higher-ranking official or a specialised anti-corruption body. The obligation to investigate reports and inform complainants of the outcome therefore existed before the new bill was introduced.

However, a 2025 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) points to significant gaps in the implementation of these safeguards. Azerbaijan has no specialised body, unit or official dedicated exclusively to protecting people who report corruption. The authorities were also unable to provide examples of the provision placing the burden on employers to disprove evidence of retaliation being applied in 2023-2024.

The report also notes that public disclosure through the media and social networks is not recognised as a protected channel for reporting corruption. This gap is particularly significant for people who report wrongdoing to journalists rather than to state bodies.

Alleged $300 bribe demand and claim of violence

On 28 August, Gündəlik Naxçıvan reported that a young driver had been detained. According to the outlet, police officers said the driver was under the influence of alcohol. He denied this and said he was willing to undergo a medical examination at a hospital.

Instead of being given a medical examination, he was allegedly asked to pay 500 manats (about $300):

“They told me: either you pay the money now, or they will take both you and the car away.”

According to the outlet, after the driver refused to pay, additional traffic police officers arrived at the scene. Five or six officers allegedly used force against him. Witnesses said the driver suffered a broken arm and ribs as a result.

The complaint therefore concerns not only an alleged demand for a bribe, but also claims that force was used instead of allowing the driver to undergo a medical examination and challenge the allegation against him.

Threats of drug possession and other criminal charges

On 10 September, Gündəlik Naxçıvan published another complaint from residents of Ordubad. People who had returned from Russia said they were taken from their homes and brought to a police station, where they were tested for drugs in a toilet without a doctor present.

One complainant, who asked to remain anonymous, said his test was negative but that he was nevertheless asked to pay 10,000 manats (about $5,882). He said that after being threatened with arrest and torture, he paid 5,000 manats (about $2,941).

Similar allegations have been made in the past. In a Toplum TV report published on 17 December 2025, Shiraz Guliyev, who had returned from Turkey, said he was asked to pay 300 manats (about $176.50) near the Sadarak customs checkpoint on the grounds that he had allegedly dropped a cigarette butt. Guliyev said he told officers that he did not smoke, but was threatened with arrest on charges of resisting police if he refused to pay.

In June 2025, blogger Mehman Huseynov alleged that officers from Baku’s Khatai district police station No 37 beat five teenagers and released them after receiving money from their parents.

Lawyer Khalid Bagirov told Meydan TV that the problem was not the absence of mechanisms for holding officers accountable, but that those mechanisms were not being effectively applied.

What do the official figures show?

The Main Anti-Corruption Directorate under the Prosecutor General’s Office said it reviewed 5,655 complaints in the first half of 2026. A total of 54 criminal cases involving 102 people were sent to court. Of the calls received through the “161” hotline, 4,062 were registered as reports of corruption-related offences.

The figures show that investigations are being carried out. However, the number of cases sent to court does not indicate how effectively people who report corruption are subsequently protected from pressure or retaliation.

This distinction is particularly important in cases involving complaints against the police. A person who complains about an officer with the power to detain them, take them to a police station and formally record offences is seeking more than the return of money. They also need guarantees that those powers will not be used against them in retaliation. Receiving a complaint and protecting the complainant are two separate tasks.

According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Opinion from Yerevan: Baku steps up pressure on Armenia with new tools
World.content:
Opinion on Baku’s tougher rhetoric

Statements by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev should be seen as a “public expression of dissatisfaction with Nikol Pashinyan’s government”, according to political analyst Suren Surenyants.

Speaking at the eighth congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party, Aliyev said, among other things, that the blame should not be placed solely on Armenia’s former leadership.

“It is true that Armenia’s former leaders are war criminals and must be punished, but it was Armenia’s current government that made territorial claims against us and insulted the dignity of the Azerbaijani people with inappropriate and uncivilised statements. We must never forget this,” the president stressed.

Political analyst Suren Surenyants analysed what prompted the recent statements by Aliyev and his aide Hikmet Hajiyev, as well as Azerbaijan’s tougher rhetoric more broadly.

“Baku is effectively signalling that it is dissatisfied with the way Pashinyan is fulfilling his commitments and, if necessary, could use his previous positions and statements as an additional means of exerting pressure,” he said.

‘We would like to make peace not only with the Armenian government, but with the Armenian people’

Against the backdrop of Aliyev’s tough statements, the head of the foreign policy department of the Azerbaijani presidential administration also addressed the peace agenda with Armenia. Speaking at the CAMCA Regional Forum in Baku, he said Azerbaijan intended to build a long-term architecture for peace:

“That is why we always say that we want to make this peace not only with the Armenian government and the country’s prime minister. We want to make peace with the Armenian people. And that is why we continue to expect changes to Armenia’s Constitution. Of course, this is an internal matter, and we fully refrain from interfering in this process.

“We are waiting for just one final step – amendments to Armenia’s Constitution concerning territorial claims against Azerbaijan. After that, I think the final peace agreement will become a reality.”

Baku is demanding amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace treaty. Azerbaijan argues that the document contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no wording that could give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. A draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is currently under discussion. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that it should not contain a reference to the Declaration of Independence. At the same time, he insists that constitutional change is something Armenia itself needs.

Expert commentary

Political analyst Suren Surenyants notes that Armenia is building its entire policy around the peace agenda with Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan, far from softening its rhetoric, has been toughening it in recent months:

“One possible explanation is that Azerbaijan is seeking to consolidate as quickly as possible the political gains resulting from the military advantage it achieved through the war, recognising that the current balance of power will not last forever.”

In his view, this interpretation is also supported by statements from the Azerbaijani president’s aide. In particular, he points to Hikmet Hajiyev’s remarks that a peace treaty will only be signed after Armenia changes its Constitution, despite peace having already been established:

“This is not a contradiction, but a division of labour. One formulation is intended for an international audience, while the other is addressed to Yerevan, reminding it of the need to fulfil its commitments.”

Surenyants also considers the statement about seeking peace not only with the Armenian government but also with the Armenian people noteworthy.

According to him, this means Azerbaijan wants changes in Armenia to acquire “legitimacy enshrined through a referendum and to be made as irreversible as possible”.

The political analyst suggests Baku is in a hurry because the regional balance of power could change, primarily due to the growing Iranian factor:

“If Iran is able to capitalise on its regional influence, a shift in the balance of power in the South Caucasus could limit Baku’s ability to exert pressure on Armenia.”

Surenyants notes that:

Tehran has repeatedly said that any violation of Armenia’s territorial integrity, changes to international borders or alteration of the geopolitical status quo in the region constitute “red lines” for Iran;

Iran is particularly sensitive to the development of transport links through Armenia, viewing them through the prism of its own security and regional influence.

Surenyants argues that the demand for changes to Armenia’s Constitution is taking on additional significance and cannot be seen simply as a “mechanical precondition” for signing a peace treaty.

“Azerbaijan is seeking to achieve its desired outcome within Armenia at both the legal and political levels. And that outcome will not be limited to removing the reference to the Declaration of Independence,” he argues.

The analyst notes that discussions have intensified again in Baku, in particular about the return of Azerbaijanis to “Western Azerbaijan”, by which they mean virtually the entire territory of Armenia. He believes these developments will not end with changes to Armenia’s Constitution and is convinced that Azerbaijan will then present Armenia with a new list of demands:

“Does all this mean that Azerbaijan is preparing for a new military escalation? At present, there is not enough publicly available evidence to draw such a definitive conclusion.”

The political analyst believes Baku has not yet obtained everything it wants from Armenia and is therefore stepping up political pressure. In his assessment, this is driven by concerns that it may become more difficult to secure all its demands in the future:

“And Baku is rushing to get everything it wants while there is a government in Yerevan that regards Baku’s demand for constitutional amendments as part of its own agenda, and before regional developments close the ‘window of opportunity’ for exerting unilateral pressure on Armenia.”

World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts mine resolution co-authored by Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. The UN Human Rights Council has adopted a resolution titled “Impact of anti-personnel mines on the full enjoyment of human rights: Strengthening victim assistance,” which Azerbaijan co-authored and actively promoted, the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry said.

The resolution was adopted without a vote, with 70 states joining as co-sponsors.

During the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Azerbaijan organized a public dialogue to promote and keep the joint initiative on the agenda and co-hosted a side event dedicated to the issue.

Azerbaijan, one of the countries most heavily contaminated by mines in the world, faces a severe challenge posed by anti-personnel mines, the ministry said.

“Anti-personnel mines and unexploded ordnance have a long-term and severe impact on the full enjoyment of human rights, with serious consequences for the lives of victims and their family members. In this regard, we welcome the particular attention given to victim assistance in the resolution,” the ministry said.

The ministry emphasized that mine action is a fundamental element of sustainable peace and plays an important role in post-conflict recovery.

“Mine clearance not only enables the safe and dignified return of former internally displaced persons to their homes, but also makes an important contribution to the recovery of conflict-affected areas and communities, as well as ensuring socio-economic development,” it said.

The ministry also welcomed the resolution's focus on the interlinkages between mine action, peace and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

“Mine clearance is also important for ensuring more effective adaptation to climate-related risks. In this regard, we consider it important that the resolution contributes to developing and deepening understanding of the link between mine action and adaptation to climate risks in the context of human rights,” the ministry said.

The scale of casualties caused by mines once again demonstrates the need to mobilize stronger international support, partnerships and sustainable financing for mine action and victim assistance, according to the ministry.

It welcomed the Human Rights Council's call on member states to increase financing for mine clearance and victim assistance, including through alternative sources of financing and public-private partnerships.

“Azerbaijan once again emphasizes the importance of strengthening international cooperation, solidarity and sustained support in addressing the mine threat and highly values the contribution of mine action to the protection of human rights and the promotion of sustainable peace and development,” the ministry said.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Afghanistan discuss agricultural trade, investment
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Today, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan discussed expanding agricultural trade, investment and technology cooperation during a meeting between Azizbek Urunov, Uzbekistan’s presidential representative to the World Trade Organization and chairman of the Committee for Food Safety, and Afghan Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock Minister Attaullah Omari in Tashkent.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Agriculture of Uzbekistan, following a meeting held on the sidelines of an international conference marking World Cotton Day and a global technical forum on food security and the Sustainable Development Goals in landlocked developing countries.

The sides discussed expanding bilateral foreign trade and agricultural cooperation, increasing trade in agricultural products, strengthening investment ties and promoting the exchange of advanced agricultural practices and modern technologies.

Moreover, the officials exchanged views on cooperation in livestock farming, as well as the production and processing of meat and dairy products, according to the Uzbek side.

Expanding agricultural exports and imports, introducing modern technologies in the livestock sector, sharing expertise and implementing mutually beneficial projects were identified as promising areas of bilateral cooperation.

"The expansion of agricultural ties between Uzbekistan and Afghanistan will contribute to strengthening food security in the two countries, developing trade and economic relations and enhancing sustainable agricultural cooperation in the region," the Uzbek side said.

The sides also agreed to continue dialogue on priority agricultural projects and identify practical opportunities for cooperation between businesses and sector institutions.
