World.title: Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Russia's First Deputy PM review joint economic projects
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov discussed implementing agreements reached at the highest level and expanding trade and investment cooperation during a meeting in Tashkent on Oct. 7.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.

Manturov arrived in Uzbekistan to attend meetings of the Uzbekistan-Russia Intergovernmental Commission and the Council of Regions between the two countries. At the start of the meeting, he conveyed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s greetings and best wishes to Mirziyoyev.

The Uzbek president welcomed the results of the Intergovernmental Commission and the third Council of Regions meetings held the previous day, according to the presidential press service.

"The steady growth of mutual trade and the promotion of cooperation projects in industry, energy, metallurgy, peaceful atom and other sectors were noted with satisfaction," the press service said.

The sides emphasized the need for coordinated measures to further increase trade, accelerate joint projects within industrial zones and maintain active contacts between regions and businesses.

In addition, the meeting focused on the practical implementation of agreements reached during recent high-level Uzbek-Russian talks, with both sides reaffirming the importance of expanding economic and industrial cooperation.

The sides also emphasized the importance of strengthening interregional cooperation and expanding direct business contacts to support the implementation of joint projects.

World.title: Uzbekistan puts forward proposals at CIS foreign ministers' meeting
World.content:
Photo: the telegram channel of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Today, Uzbek Foreign Minister Baxtiyor Saidov participated in a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) in Turkmenistan’s Avaza national tourist zone, where participants discussed regional and international issues and prospects for expanding multilateral cooperation.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan's Foreign Minister, Baxtiyor Saidov, on his Telegram channel.

The meeting was held in restricted and expanded formats, according to Saidov’s post on social media.

The participants exchanged views on pressing issues on the international and regional agenda and discussed preparations for the upcoming meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State.

Saidov said Uzbekistan put forward proposals and initiatives aimed at expanding trade and economic ties, developing efficient transport and logistics chains, strengthening humanitarian and youth exchanges, advancing digital cooperation and jointly addressing contemporary security challenges and threats.

"We put forward several proposals and initiatives aimed at expanding trade and economic ties, developing efficient transport and logistics chains, enhancing humanitarian and youth exchanges, advancing digital cooperation, and jointly addressing contemporary security challenges and threats," Saidov said in his post.

The CIS Council of Foreign Ministers is one of the CIS’s key coordinating bodies, bringing together the foreign ministers of member states to discuss foreign policy coordination and cooperation on issues of common interest. Its meetings also provide a platform for preparing matters to be considered by the CIS Council of Heads of State.

World.title: France suspends stun grenade use at student protests
World.content:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades by police at student-led demonstrations, as allegations of police brutality mount after days of sometimes violent demonstrations across the country.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across France on Tuesday, local time, demanding better conditions in high schools.

That same evening, President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis.

A student in Paris holds a board reading 'GenZ will win'. (AP: Teresa Suarez)

Mr Lecornu will speak later Wednesday on the school protests as well as the national finances, his office said, against the backdrop of heated debates over the country's 2027 budget.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said he had suspended the police use of stun grenades at the protests.

A 15-year-old lost a hand in the northern city of Lens on Monday after police fired a stun grenade.

"I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Mr Nunez said.

He stressed that this suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened".

Thousands gather in France for high school protests Police have fired tear gas at protesters blockading French high schools as students, teachers and parents take to the streets over school conditions.

Last week, a 14-year-old student in north-west Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth.

A policeman was charged on Tuesday over that incident.

Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Mr Nunez said.

"It took several children being maimed for life for Nunez to give up using grenades against high school students," said Manuel Bompard, national coordinator of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI).

The government has blamed the LFI for stoking tensions around the protests.

'Need something more'

The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.

While most schools reopened on Wednesday, more than 500 remained at least partially closed with students blocking doors with mounds of rubbish bins.

Parents, teachers and union workers joined the demonstrations in Paris and other cities for a national day of mobilisation on Tuesday.

At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces wounded in the protests on Tuesday, which saw a quarter of a million people mass across France, the interior ministry said.

Most of the day's demonstrations were peaceful but there were sporadic clashes across the country with protesters throwing projectiles and security forces using tear gas.

Mr Lecornu announced a half-day of class time would be set aside in schools on Wednesday to allow for "internal democratic" dialogue, intended to give students and staff the opportunity to voice their issues.

However, student union leader Ryad Rani told local press that the effort was "yet another attempt to muzzle the debate" and to gain time.

Riot police use a water cannon in Rennes. (AP: Jeremias Gonzalez)

And the union representative for school principals, Nicolas Bonnet, told broadcaster franceinfo that "to get out of this crisis, we will need something more than simple consultation periods".

Mr Lecornu condemned the violence and told lawmakers the violence would not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered "police repression" against protesters.

More than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested.

The government has reported that at least 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.

The prime minister's office said 85 teaching staff have also been injured.

AFP

World.title: NASA's Curiosity rover captures dawn on Mars
World.content:
NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing jagged crags formed billions of years ago.

Curiosity, which is about the size of a Mini Cooper, landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a 5 kilometre-tall mountain rising from the crater floor.

Panoramic Martian views The Mars Perseverance rover provides a panoramic look at the Jezero Crater site on the Red Planet.

The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved cliffs in the distance, in August.

"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

"We think it once was wind-blown sediment, maybe sand or maybe even ash that blew into the crater from nearby volcanic activity.

"After the sediment hardened into rock, eons of wind carved up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," the Curiosity project scientist said.

The yardang layer most likely formed about 3 billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Mr Vasavada.

This layer spans about 16 kilometres across the north-western reaches of Mount Sharp.

"However, the yardang layer doesn't appear to be part of the continuous stack of layers that make up the layer-cake of Mount Sharp. It was added on a little later. It's above what geologists call an unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top," Mr Vasavada said.

'You can almost feel the silence'

The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of 1km in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.

Curiosity's five years NASA's Curiosity rover has already taught us a lot in the past five years, but NASA scientists think there is still much more to come.

Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.

Mr Vasavada said NASA hopes Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to scrutinise the geology there.

Curiosity has been studying the geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harbouring microbial life.

It is one of two NASA rovers operating on Mars.

The Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.

Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.

"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona," Mr Vasavada said.

" You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky. But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It's like Earth, but it's definitely Mars. "

Reuters

World.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to duo for 'spectacular' chemical reaction
World.content:
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a press release.

" The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular. "

Dr Kagan, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Dr Soai, born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science.

The duo's research into molecules' mirror images has "been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals", the press release said.

Many molecules of life come in versions that look alike but are not exactly identical, like right and left hands. One mirror-image of the chemical carvone smells like mint, for example, while the other has a whiff of caraway.



When designing drugs to treat diseases, scientists want to be selective about which mirror-image they are getting. They want the version of a molecule that will treat a cold, not the kind that will make the sniffles worse.



Dr Kagan and Dr Soai found ways to make chemistry pick a side, designing and manipulating reactions to produce the desired mirror-image.

The so-called "Soai reaction" is named for the experiment.

There are six Nobel prize categories: medicine, physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics. (AP Photo: Jacquelyn Martin, File)

Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.

This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded on Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.

The physics award on Tuesday recognised a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.

The literature prize is set to be awarded on Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.71 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organisation.

AP

World.title: 'Hard to describe': Melbourne Jewish community marks October 7
World.content:
Melbourne's Jewish community has honoured those murdered in a deadly assault on Israel on October 7, 2023, with some saying their pain remains hard to describe.

Three years ago, several thousand Hamas militants infiltrated southern Israel on a Jewish holiday and killed more than 1,200 civilians and took more than 250 people hostage.

At a commemoration service at the Beth Weizmann Jewish Community Centre in the Melbourne suburb of Caulfield today, attendee Atida Lipshatz said the impact of the horrifying events had been immense.

"It's so hard to describe that pain. There's the before and there's the after," she told the ABC.

"Our lives all changed to know how much hatred there is against us."

President of the Jewish Museum of Australia, Gideon Klein, said the world changed on October 7, 2023 "in a very profound way for lots of people".

"There's been a lot of casualties, not only for Israelis but also on the Palestinian side, and a lot of trauma," he said.

"We've certainly seen an incredible amount of fraying of social cohesion here in Victoria, as well as around the country."

He said the terrorist attack in December last year at Bondi Beach was impossible to separate from what happened in Israel.

Similar events have been held nationally today, including in Sydney.

Ilan Rimer says pro-Palestinian demonstrations on the October 7 anniversary do not help social cohesion. (ABC News: James Oaten)

Organiser of the Caulfield event and chief executive of Zionism Victoria, Ilan Rimer, said people were still grieving, tired and anxious.

"There is some hope still that things can be turned around in Australia after we've seen an explosion of antisemitism and anti-Zionism, but it's a real mixture of all those feelings put together."

He said October 7 should be a date focused on the atrocities against Israel.

"For those wishing to memorialise others, there are hundreds of other days to pick from," Mr Rimer said.

October 7 also a key date for Palestinians, activists say

Also today, a small number of demonstrators gathered in support of Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered retaliatory attacks by Israel in response to the Hamas attacks, and to continue ongoing calls for a ceasefire.

The Gaza Health Ministry, a body under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered by the United Nations as reliable, has said more than 74,000 Palestinians have died in the conflict.

Tasnim Sammak has friends and family in Gaza. (ABC News: James Oaten )

Activist Tasnim Sammak from Free Palestine Coalition Naarm said she had lost more than a dozen family members in Gaza.

"We're continuing to see the mass murder and destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza," she said.

She said many Jewish people were sympathetic to the Palestinian perspective.

"The survivors [in Gaza] are living in tents, trapped and without access to basic aid for their basic needs," she said.

World.title: Schoolgirl cold case inquest seeks to solve five-decade-old mystery
World.content:
An inquest into the disappearance of Mackay schoolgirl Marilyn Joy Wallman has heard of a supposed deathbed confession about a family member's involvement.

Marilyn disappeared soon after 7:42am on March 21, 1972, after cycling a kilometre down a dirt road to catch a school bus.

Noel Morris, who was related to the Wallman family by marriage, has been named as a person of interest in her disappearance and will appear as a witness at the inquest.

Noel Morris has been named as a person of interest in the inquest. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

Counsel assisting Coroner David O'Connell, John Aberdeen, said Mr Morris was implicated in the teen's death in two similar stories told by other members of the Morris family.

"It's an odd thing to raise, Your Honour, and that's the reason it's taken very seriously," Mr Aberdeen said.

He said the inquest would also hear that Mr Morris drove a car of a "similar description" to one police sought after Marilyn's disappearance.

Alleged drinking confession

Witness Errol James Morris, 77, made a statement to police in 2016, saying he recalled a conversation with his brother Lionel, known as Joe.

"He came up to me about 20 years ago when he was drinking and said words to the effect of 'someone in our family was involved in the disappearance of Marilyn Wallman,'" Errol Morris said.

Marilyn Wallman's family have been notified of the development in the case. (Supplied)

"I said he was stupid for saying that, and he reaffirmed it was someone in our family."

Errol Morris said the conversation occurred when he was driving Joe home and they were possibly in the area of Wallmans Rd.

"I just thought he was being foolish; he was a regular large drinker, and at that time I didn't think very much about it."

Statement contradicted

Witness Denis Riddel denied he told his neighbour he believed his cousin, Noel Morris, was involved after seeing him interviewed on television in 2018.

Mr Aberdeen said Mr Riddel's neighbour said she heard him sobbing in the back yard.

"She said she asked you if you were all right, and you said that after watching the current affairs show last night you knew that Noel Morris did it," Mr Aberdeen said.

"You said after hearing what Joe Morris said on his deathbed to his brother … that 'you know Noel did the Wallman girl in', that his brother said 'yes I know', or 'I thought so'.

"You said that after seeing him on TV you remembered what Joe had said and that upset you."

Mr Riddel said he could not recall making the comments and had only said that Noel was his cousin.

Unusual not to ride together

Rex Wallman, now 63, was eight when he and his older brother David, then 11, followed 10 minutes behind Marilyn toward the bus.

Mr Wallman recalled a busier-than-usual morning, with Marilyn having trouble with her school uniform and being anxious about missing the bus for sports day.

He said it was unusual for them not to ride to the bus together.

A childhood photo of David, Rex and Marilyn Wallman, taken in Mackay. (Supplied: Rex Wallman)

"Marilyn had a sports day and didn't want to miss the bus, so she took off. David and I were still cleaning our teeth, getting ready to go."

After riding down a dip in the road, he saw Marilyn's bike on the side of the road and the carry-all at the front of the bike holding her bag on the ground.

"At that stage, David and I didn't know what had happened, so we looked around. David said: 'I'm faster than you on the bike; I'll whip home and get mum and you stay here.'"

Mr Wallman said he felt scared being on his own and moved to the centre of the narrow bitumen road, sitting down and hugging his bicycle.

He said no other vehicles passed as there were only two cane farms on the road and a quarry infrequently used by council.

He said he heard voices coming from the cane field.

"A girl's voice saying things like 'my leg hurts', then another voice which sounded more like a man's voice or another voice a bit more, such a loud tone, I guess you could say.

"I heard it a couple of times; to me, it appeared not far over the other side of the cane field.

"They only appeared for a short time and then silence."

'I didn't lie'

Rex Wallman recalled being interviewed by detectives as a child and questioned about a statement in which he agreed with police that he did not hear any noises from the cane.

"At the time it felt like no one believed me, no one wanted to listen to me or take any notice of what I needed to say … the badgering made it easier to say no," he said.

"I don't recall saying I was telling lies. I don't agree with the statement that said I was telling lies."

He told the inquest he did not doubt what he heard.

'Something doesn't seem right'

David Wallman, now 65, said he first thought Marilyn had come off her bike, bumped her head and wandered off into the cane.

"Rex and I called out looking for her; I thought something doesn't seem right here … she's hurt, we need to find her and get Mum on the job," he said.

"I said to Mum, 'Marilyn's had a buster, and we can't find her'. Mum jumped in the car and went back, and we started calling out.

"We walked down the headland again, in the cane paddock a little bit and Mum drove around to the end of the paddock."

Marilyn and mum were close

Rex Wallman said his mother had always felt Marilyn had wanted to tell her something before she disappeared, but the family had visitors that weekend.

In the years after her disappearance, Mrs Wallman drove her sons to school.

"Mum would continually tell us she was upset she didn't give Marilyn the time. We had a lot of people in the house that weekend, and she had a feeling Marilyn wanted to sit down and have a chat with her.

"They had an extraordinary relationship, more like they were best friends rather than mum and daughter."

Former detective

Retired detective Andre Wijtenburg was Mackay's cold case officer from 1993 and interviewed Noel Morris in about 2009 after speaking to his estranged wife Ann.

He said Mr Morris was not willing to discuss Marilyn's disappearance.

Retired detective Andre Wijtenburg. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

Mr Wijtenburg said Ann Morris, who was related to the Wallmans, had suspicions about her former husband's involvement.

"Initially she was scared of Noel and didn't want to talk to police because of that," Mr Wijtenburg said.

Under cross-examination from barrister Scott McLennan, Mr Wijtenburg agreed he had emailed a detective after his retirement, saying Ann was "a little unreliable and perhaps unstable".

Other suspects

Mr McLennan also questioned Mr Wijtenburg about a trip to Victoria to interview another suspect, Michael Anthony Francis, who had been convicted and jailed for sexual violence offences in Mackay and interstate.

Mr Wijtenburg said Mr Francis refused to be interviewed but did not deny his involvement.

Mr McLennan said Mr Francis had admitted to stealing women's underwear in Mackay and had collected more than 400 garments.

He said Mrs Wallman had reported underwear disappearing from her bedroom drawer in the 12 months before Marilyn disappeared; however, she was never shown the underwear Mr Francis was found with.

Noel Morris's barrister also raised another suspect who was convicted of indecently treating his niece and great-niece at the time.

World.title: Rottnest Island bus stop redevelopment over after bones found
World.content:
WARNING: Some Indigenous readers may find the content of this story distressing.

A project to redevelop the main bus stop at tourist destination Rottnest Island — Wadjemup — has officially stopped six months after Aboriginal remains were found at the site.

The decision to cease works was made following advice from the Whadjuk Aboriginal Corporation (WAC), the Wadjemup Aboriginal Reference Group (WARG) and the Wadjemup Whadjuk Cultural Authority (WWCA).

The ancestral remains, referred to as Baalang, were discovered in early April on the grounds of the Holy Trinity Church during the construction works.

Works to upgrade the precinct, which began in March, were then suspended as the bones were brought to the mainland for testing.

A culturally appropriate burial was conducted in May. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

In early May the remains were brought back to Rottnest Island for a culturally appropriate burial.

The Rottnest Island Authority (RIA) said it had collaborated with the WAC since the remains were found and that a ground-penetrating radar survey found there were no more human remains at the site.

"RIA will not proceed with the main bus stop project at its current location," a joint statement released by the island authority and the WAC read.

"The project may be revisited if an alternative suitable site becomes available in the future."

The site where the bones were discovered. (ABC News)

The release stated a new pathway to the church would proceed because "it improves access to the building without impacting the burial site".

The authority's release said the remains would tie into larger memorialisation works.

"Future memorialisation of the Baalang site will be developed in consultation with Whadjuk Traditional Owners and will have regard to the broader memorialisation work being undertaken through the Wadjemup Project," it said.

Dark history

Rottnest Island was used as an Aboriginal prison between 1838 and 1931.

According to state records, more than 3,700 men and boys from across WA were imprisoned there.

An Aboriginal elder holds the remains during the burial. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Hundreds of prisoners are estimated to have died on the island, many of them buried in unmarked graves.

A separate location was found to be the site of 373 unmarked graves, now referred to as the Wadjemup Aboriginal Burial Ground.

The RIA said memorial works at the burial grounds were expected to finish early next year, and works at the Quod, a former prison building, were expected to be completed later this year.

World.title: Israelis mourn on October 7 as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
World.content:
Israelis have gathered to commemorate the 2023 October 7 Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, resulted in 251 being taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its 2 million people living in dire conditions.

In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters, and the site of a music festival that the militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel.

It is the first anniversary since all the hostages were home, marking a new stage of grief.

For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of life of misery and difficulties after an Israeli retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people.

Most of the population of about 2 million people live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip's cities reduced to rubble. More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military. Despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.

Palestinians inspect the site of an early morning Israeli air strike in Gaza. (AP Photo: Jehad Alshrafi)

For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years.

Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with the Hezbollah militant group, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas. Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has resulted in attacks across Gulf Arab countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for, even if they weren't directly connected.

Families mourn at the Nova Festival site

In Reim, the town where the music festival was underway on the day of the attack, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. They hugged at 6:29am, the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago, as booms from explosions in nearby Gaza were heard.

Anya Davitashili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she came to the site every Saturday because it was where she felt closest to him.

Raz Zarfati attends a memorial at the Nova music festival site near Kibbutz Reim. (AP Photo: Ohad Zwigenberg)

"I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning, it's in front of my eyes all the time," she said.

" Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing. "

Hundreds of people came to pay their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site.

Released hostage marks his first October 7

Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time after being released from 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 meters underground in a dark, damp tunnel.

Mr Bohbot, who was abducted from the festival, was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food, and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.

Elkana Bohbot is marking the October 7 anniversary in Israel for the first time. (AP Photo: Ariel Schalit)

In the 11 months since his release, Mr Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation. In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a promise that Mr Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his 5-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.

The newborn Michele was "not a symbol for my people; she is more of a symbol for the enemy", Bohbot told The Associated Press.

"So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever."

Palestinians struggle to recover

No events are expected on Wednesday in Gaza, where Israel's offensive has devastated the territory and displaced about 90 per cent of its population, often multiple times. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a severe hunger crisis.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says about half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by UN agencies and independent experts.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry. (AP Photo: Jehad Alshrafi)

While a ceasefire that took effect on October 10, 2025, has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period.

Hamas portrayed the October 7 attack as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians' dream of an independent state appears even more distant.

A radically altered Middle East

A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government's official memorial services took place on October 5, closer to the Hebrew calendar's anniversary of the attack.

The separate commemorations reflected deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.

Three years after October 7, a big decision looms Israelis are still trying to contend with the October 7 attacks as the country heads to the polls.

Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who is hoping to unseat Netanyahu in Israel's upcoming elections, looked at the photos of the dead in Reim and spoke with sobbing family members.

Gadi Eisenkot, the head of the opposition Yashar party, met with families at a bomb shelter in southern Israel where many were killed as they tried to flee.

The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced.

The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran's military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and up-ending global markets far from the battlefield.

Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel's far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.

AP

World.title: 'Special' moment for researchers as rare fin whales photographed
World.content:
Two separate sightings of rare fin whales has delighted researchers and ocean lovers alike on Western Australia's South West coast.

Drone pilots have photographed two separate whales in Geographe Bay, 220 kilometres south of Perth.

Fin whale numbers are still recovering from the impacts of the whaling industry, which hunted the species to near extinction in the 20th century, killing about 700,000 fin whales.

Fin whales can live to about 70 or 80 years old when left alone, and they have just one calf at a time — making repopulating the dwindling numbers a slow process.

They are second only to blue whales in length, with slender bodies that help them glide through the water at high speed, and tend to remain below the surface, making sightings uncommon.

Loading Instagram content

'Incredibly unusual' sighting

Geographe Marine Research chair Capri Jolliffe said one of the sightings was very close to shore.

Capri Jolliffe says the sightings in the South West's Geographe Bay were unusually close to shore for the species. (ABC News)

"It passed within 50 metres of the land-based observation platform … in really shallow water," she said.

"That one was incredibly unusual.

"And then the second one was a bit further out, close to 2 kilometres offshore."

Loading Instagram content

Recorded sightings are so rare that much of what is known about fin whales comes from passive acoustic data, which is recorded by submerging hydrophones in the ocean, rather than observation.

"We basically eavesdrop on all the whales that are out there," Dr Jolliffe said.

"They all make different sounds that are species- and population-specific.

"It's quite an efficient and effective way of monitoring where whales go and when they're there."

Fin whale populations are still recovering from the impacts of the whaling industry, which hunted them to near extinction in the 20th century. (Supplied: Alfred-Wegener-Institut)

Drones bring a whole new perspective

In Australia, drone pilots are subject to strict regulations when it comes to how close they can fly to marine mammals.

In WA, drones must stay at least 60 metres away, while in New South Wales and Queensland, the limit is 100m. In South Australia and Tasmania, it's 300m; in Victoria, it's 500m.

Macquarie University marine scientist Vanessa Pirotta said citizen scientists who followed the rules when using their drones were making valuable contributions to ocean research.

Throughout Australia, there are legal limits on how close a drone can fly above a marine mammal. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

"When documenting a whale that we know so little about and a threatened species at that, it supports our Australian understanding of these species," she said.

" It's incredibly special because we can share this information through the scientific communities. "

Dr Pirotta said for researchers the footage was much more than "just a sighting".

"For many of us it's a wonderful sighting, and it may be indicative of potential movements that we hadn't really observed, but only acoustically documented," she said.

Vanessa Pirotta says excitement over the footage is quickly spreading throughout the marine research community. (ABC News)

Drone pilot and South West local Scott Baxter had taken his family out for a coastal drive on Monday afternoon when he spotted a spray of water out on the horizon.

He said he initially thought he was capturing footage of a different species.

"As I was filming it, the whole time I just thought it was a small blue whale," Mr Baxter said.

"I had no idea that the fin whales existed in Geograph Bay.

World.title: How Perry’s marketability triggered a revolution, and what’s next for the sporting icon
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket How Perry’s marketability triggered a revolution, and what’s next for the sporting icon Nick Wright October 7, 2026 — 10:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket icon Ellyse Perry concedes there will come a time soon when she needs to think about life beyond the pitch, but she has refused to put a definitive timeline on when she will draw the curtain on her decorated career. “I haven’t thought about it,” the 35-year-old declared in Brisbane. “I still love waking up every day and having the opportunity to hopefully get better, to work with the teams and look forward to a new challenge. While that’s the case, I don’t really want to change my mindset. Ellyse Perry will take to Allan Border Field as one of Australia’s most recognisable athletes. Getty Images “I’m incredibly grateful I’ve had this amount of time doing it. Nothing will last forever, but as long as that’s the case, I just want to make the absolute most of it.”



Speaking ahead of the three-game one-day series against Bangladesh – beginning on Friday at Allan Border Field – Perry was asked to reflect on a looming milestone that will occur during next year’s Ashes series in England. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot The campaign, beginning in late June, will mark the star all-rounder’s 20th year as an international athlete – a tenure that began in July 2007 when she debuted for both the nation’s ODI side and the Matildas within two weeks. “It’s been an incredible privilege to be part of such an amazing period of growth and development in women’s sport, and to have the opportunity when I was younger to play a few sports and have some amazing experiences around the world,” Perry said. “To see over the last 20 years how much has changed in the landscape and the opportunities now for young girls and female athletes wanting to play their sport as a profession, and do that around the world, I just can’t believe that’s happened.”



Throughout Perry’s career, she has become one of the country’s most marketable faces – both for her exploits on the field and for the way she has become a role model to the next generation. Endorsement, sponsorship and ambassador opportunities with adidas and Weet-Bix, among others, have followed, while her franchise cricket in India and England have all culminated in making her one of the world’s most lucrative female cricketers. “Brands are looking to partner with an athlete who showcases authenticity, and authenticity is what drives brand responses from consumers,” marketing expert Dr Monica Chien said.



“Consumers want to see brands being authentic, and the way they show authenticity is to partner with someone they feel authentically brings certain values. “She’s approachable, has the community connection, she’s relatable. That relatability and accessibility enhances the marketability in the eyes of stakeholders.” Loading While Chien stressed that Cathy Freeman’s impact at the 2000 Olympics could not be underestimated, Perry’s dual-sport exploits and how she captured audiences changed industry perceptions of how to source brand ambassadors. Chien said what had changed was collective female sporting bodies were being given greater exposure opportunities due to the values they showcased while attracting stronger family audiences and positive brand associations. This proved appealing to businesses.



The University of Queensland associate professor anticipated that with more broadcast exposure, marketability would continue to rise as some sports fought to become professional. Related Article Australian cricket Is South Africa Steve Smith’s last Test tour? Not even Cummins knows “When Perry debuted for both the cricket and football, she was largely seen as an abnormal case or a success story. There was a novelty at that time when a female athlete succeeded in a male-dominated sporting culture, so she became an inspirational role model,” Chien said. “Now, we’re looking at not just Perry or other athletes, but it’s the collective brand of women’s cricket or the Matildas that actually changed that marketability of women’s sport. “Sponsors started to realise the value of women’s sport, which allowed them to access audiences that were difficult to reach through traditional media. What they are showcasing is not just sports excellence, but their social values, and it’s the social values that partially drive their marketability.”



The Matildas’ historic 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup campaign further proved the marketability of women’s sport, when the semi-final clash with England generated the largest television audience in Australia (11.15 million viewers). Loading Those athletes have become household names, with the shock withdrawal of Mary Fowler – who boasts more than 500,000 Instagram followers and inked a lucrative partnership with adidas this year – from the squad to take on Germany and Haiti triggering extensive engagement. “The interest being paid to female athletes and the sports they’re playing, the competitions they’re involved in, that’s because it is just genuinely such an entertaining product to watch,” Perry said. “The way sports are now covered, there’s so much more critical analysis, where we get into the weeds of how female athletes are performing and the teams are going, and various competitions.



“There’s still so much upside in terms of the growth and development of that. Uniquely, I think it’s starting to present its own landscape; it doesn’t follow men’s sport as much as it probably used to.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Direct line between October 7 and Bondi’: Vigils remember Jewish massacre
World.content:
The coarse wail of the shofar – a ceremonial ram’s horn trumpet – echoed across the Bondi Pavilion courtyard at 6.29am on Wednesday as about 700 people gathered to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane, federal Liberal senator Dave Sharma and Israel’s ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman spoke at the event, metres away from the site of December’s Bondi terrorist attack. A man sounds the shofar, a ceremonial trumpet, at the Bondi Pavilion during a vigil on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel. Audrey Richardson They all drew a link between the events of October 7, 2023, when thousands of militants crossed from Gaza to assault Israel, killing more than 1200 and taking 250 people captive, and the Bondi attack, in which 15 people were killed by gunmen at a Jewish festival. “There is a direct line between the shooting at Nova and the shooting at Bondi,” said Newman.



“We have witnessed verbal violence and bullying which led to vandalism, arson and culminated in the murder of 15 people right here … It is not the actions of Israel, it is the hatred of Jews.” Among the speakers was 11-year-old Ben Carasso, the grandson of a Holocaust survivor who became a child influencer on social media after the father of his friend went missing from the Nova festival in Israel and was later found to have been killed. Ben Carasso, 11, poses for a portrait as people gather at Bondi Pavilion to commemorate the three-year anniversary of the October 7th attack on Israel. Audrey Richardson “I’m very glad we began the connection in Bondi with the Israel children and the Jewish children, they’ve both suffered since October 7,” said Carasso, who lives in Tel Aviv but has travelled widely among the global Jewish diaspora. “We don’t have a normal childhood for three years now. I want to get to speak for the children. We didn’t get a chance to grow up.



Related Article Analysis

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘The world will never be the same again’: How October 7 changed Israel, Gaza and Australia “Since October 7, I saw what the children of Israel were going through. My friend lost his father. They didn’t know where he was for months, he was at the Nova festival. “Israeli children are forced to learn what to do in a rocket attack. It’s a side that is not talked about. For three years we have had this, and I want the world to know.” Sloane told those at the vigil that vision of the October 7 attacks had moved her deeply. “Little boys running from a shelter after their father was attacked, a woman on the back of a ute, kids slaughtered. It was brutality at its worst,” she said.



“What was done to them deserved to be seen, and it can never be denied.” Sloane said people who chose today to protest Israel’s action in Gaza should be ashamed of themselves. Leader of the NSW Opposition Kellie Sloane, whose electorate lies in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, attended the event. Audrey Richardson “On this day, can I just say ‘shame on you’ to the people that have held protests.” Pro-Palestine vigils were due to take place in the Sydney CBD and Wollongong on Wednesday.



Sharma called the Hamas attacks on October 7 “an organised and systematic massacre of Jews … a pogrom”, and said it had created the conditions for the Bondi attack. “It was the terrible tragic result of a culture that took root in Australia after the Hamas terror attack and the war that followed,” Sharma said. Senator Dave Sharma at the Bondi Pavilion to commemorate the third anniversary of the October 7 attack. Audrey Richardson “This was a culture where vilification was permitted to go unchecked, where antisemitism was excused, or tolerated, or met with moral equivocation and where Australian leaders went missing in action and lost their moral compass.” While the Jewish community in Australia is united in grief by the October 7 atrocities, there are diverse views on the way forward.



Alex Ryvchin of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry said the event had exposed antisemitism in sections of the community. “We saw it in Lakemba and the Opera House,” he said. “We saw it among religious fanatics, the far-left and the resurgent neo-Nazis. It made everything clear at once. It exposed the rank hypocrisy of human-rights advocates who lined up to explain why rape and murder were resistance in certain cases.” People gather at Bondi Pavilion to commemorate the three-year anniversary of the October 7 attack, in which about 1200 people were killed, and 250 taken hostage. Audrey Richardson The progressive Jewish Council of Australia used the date to call for sanctions against Israel. “Every life lost is a whole universe, both Palestinian and Israeli,” said the group’s executive director Sarah Schwartz. “But as Jews, we refuse to allow our identities to be weaponised to enable further killing and the silencing of advocacy for Palestinian rights.”



There was a huge police presence at the Central Synagogue in Sydney’s east on Wednesday night, where about 2000 people gathered at a second event to commemorate the lives lost on October 7. Israel responded with attacks on Gaza that are estimated to have killed over 70,000 people. Former prime minister Tony Abbott during the candle-lighting vigil at the Central Synagogue in Sydney. George Chan Opposition Leader Angus Taylor arriving at the Central Synagogue in Sydney on Wednesday, October 7. George Chan Several high-profile parliamentarians joined the nighttime vigil, including Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Jewish Liberal MP Julian Leeser, and opposition spokesman for foreign affairs Ted O’Brien. Former prime minister Tony Abbott was also present.



NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane and NSW Minister for Multiculturalism Steve Kamper both spoke at the commemoration. Despite reminders to refrain from applause during the memorial, Sloane was applauded twice: once at the end of her address and again after she was commended by former AFL player Gerard Healy during his speech later in the evening. “I just wish other politicians would speak with such clarity and authority on antisemitism as Kellie has done,” Healy said. Leader of the Opposition Kellie Sloane speaks during the candle-lighting vigil at the Central Synagogue, Sydney. George Chan In his address, Kamper said that the “passage of time does not lessen the significance of that day... for the families who lost loved ones, for those who have survived.”



He paid homage to Galit Carbone, the 66-year-old Sydneysider and grandmother killed on October 7, and said the Bondi terror attack in December “brought painfully to light the dangers of antisemitism”. Ben Carasso, who addressed Wednesday’s dawn service, spoke again at the evening vigil. He was joined onstage by Matilda Bee’s younger sister, six-year-old Summer. Matilda was killed during last year’s terror attack at Bondi. Matilda’s mother during Wednesday night’s commemoration event. George Chan A small gathering turned up at Town Hall on Wednesday evening for the planned pro-Palestinian vigil. They were almost outnumbered by the contingent of police and TV crews who kept a watchful eye over the proceedings. Palestine Action Group spokesperson Josh Lees was in attendance, but no state MPs joined the protest.

World.title: Richard E. Grant has given us the most chaotic TV moment of the year
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Richard E. Grant has given us the most chaotic TV moment of the year Meg Watson October 7, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Celebrity Traitors UK (season two) ★★★★ When host Claudia Winkleman and the producers of this smash-hit reality series picked Richard E. Grant to play a traitor this season, it would have seemed like a slam dunk. The famed actor is the first Oscar-nominated participant to appear on any version of the international franchise. And what’s more – from his villainous roles in everything from Logan to Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker – he’s renowned for his Machiavellian glee. Richard E. Grant in the second season of The Celebrity Traitors UK. BBC No one would have expected it, then, when this legend of stage and screen proudly outed himself as a traitor literally five minutes after being recruited. It might have entirely cooked his game and ruined the premise of the show, but we’re all the richer for it. This was the best reality-TV moment of the year and we’re not even halfway through the first episode.



If you’re yet to discover the utter joys of Celebrity Traitors and are wondering why someone of Richard E. Grant’s stature is doing reality TV at all, you’re in an ever-shrinking minority. This variant of the hugely popular competition series – essentially a game of Mafia set in a Scottish castle – has transfixed audiences around the world, bringing together a mix of musicians, authors, journalists, comedians, actors and a handful of people famous for being famous. The first celebrity season was the most popular show in the UK for 2025, buoying producers’ hopes for the very future of broadcast TV with a live audience of more than 11 million. Related Article ★★★★

Review Australia, I’m begging you: give this bonkers show a chance The highlight of that season was the ridiculous giggling mischief of comedian Alan Carr, offset by the deadpan investigative efforts of Stephen Fry, Ted Lasso’s Nick Mohammed and former rugby player Joe Marler. The returning season looks set to recreate the magic. Grant is an obvious delight, not just for his epic gaffe but his complete elation with the role he’s been given. (“My wife said to me, four days before she died: ‘Richard, try to find a pocketful of happiness in each day. And I feel like I’ve got a wheelbarrow-full and then some’,” he says, deliriously.) And the faithful – including James Blunt, Michael Sheen, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and Miranda Hart – so far offer a good mix of strategic insight and comedic relief.



Comedian James Acaster is poised for greatness (anyone who’s watched Bake Off knows the incredible TV he can make when put under pressure). And Ross Kemp is another standout after the first episode. The renowned hard man, who has filmed in active war zones and come face-to-face with terrorists, immediately unravels with paranoia because pint-sized Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey popped a sailor’s hat on his head, and Leigh-Anne Pinnock from Little Mix touched his arm. The new cast of Celebrity Traitors UK includes Rob Beckett, James Blunt, Michael Sheen, Myha’la, James Acaster, Hannah Fry and Miranda Hart. BBC There are tweaks to the usual formula in these opening episodes that work to varying degrees of success. As in the recently premiered US series The Traitors: New Blood, this season begins with just two traitors, who are quickly tasked with appointing a third. It’s a move that gives the players added agency and provides further intrigue to the game. Without spoiling the results of that pick (revealed in episode two), it also results in further comedy. The ending of that episode, however, is a real disappointment. While every instalment of this twisty reality show is structured around cliffhangers, the decision to end an episode before a single vote is cast at the round table is excruciating. I suspect, however, it’s a move made to keep the ludicrous Richard E. Grant on our screens for as long as possible. So, hey, I can’t be too mad. The Celebrity Traitors UK airs at 7.30pm, Wednesdays and Thursdays on Ten. New episodes are available on 10Play the Saturday and Sunday before broadcast.

World.title: How a mother’s search for a fresh start in Perth ended in tragedy
World.content:
NationalWACourts How a mother’s search for a fresh start in Perth ended in tragedy Rebecca Peppiatt October 7, 2026 — 8:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eva was 14 years old when her mother took her on a trip through Western Australia in the Christmas school holidays of 2024. It was just the two of them visiting “many famous spots”, taking “countless photos” and eating “lots of delicious food”. They went to the beach and collected seashells together. The new case is now the second involving the family before the Supreme Court of Western Australia. Erin Jonasson “I told her I would one day buy her a big house by the ocean,” recalls Eva. But she never got the chance. Weeks later, her mum was dead, murdered in a hotel room by a man they had trusted to help them start a new life in a country where neither of them knew the language or had any family or friends.



Nongyu Peng was 42 years old and had made the ultimate sacrifice for her daughter by immigrating to Perth to give her a fresh start after she was bullied in school back home in China. Peng left behind a second daughter, just three years old, to stay with her parents while she established a life for herself and Eva. They were going to join them later. Peng wanted to be a lawyer and was studying English and law, but fell into sex work in a desperate attempt to finance the life she wanted for her family. That life never eventuated. Peng was killed by an overdose of GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) by 27-year-old Ruihong Nie in February 2024, having lured her to a hotel room and feeding her the drug without her knowledge.



Nie was not a stranger. He had signed a statutory declaration to support her immigration into the country and Peng lived with his mother at her massage shop. Related Article Updated

Courts Australia’s most senior Catholic convicted of sexual abuse jailed for more than six years On Wednesday, as he was sentenced over her death – as well as on charges for the rape, drugging, and stealing from a second woman three weeks later – the WA’s Supreme Court heard how Peng and Nie’s mother had a disagreement over money. His mother believed she was owed money, and Nie’s plan was drug Peng in the hotel room by luring her there under the pretence that she was meeting a client. Instead, he wanted to go through her phone and transfer the money to his mother that he believed she was owed.



But the court was told the amount of GHB Peng ingested was “significant” and killed her. In the hours before her death, Peng texted her daughter, whom she had left at home. Scared she would be scolded for being on her phone so late at night, Eva did not reply. It is a moment she said would haunt her forever. She broke down as she read out her victim impact statement on Wednesday in the Supreme Court of WA after travelling back to Perth from China for the hearing. “After I got out of the car, Stephen told me my mum had died,” she said, recalling the day she was picked up from school to be told her mother was dead.



“I could not believe it. I could not breathe, and I thought I was going to die as well. I was 14 years old, in a foreign country where we only had each other. No words can express how I felt then or how I feel now. Now I had no one but myself.” She said she was filled with “pain, despair and utter devastation” at having to see her mother’s dead body, before adding that she “lent in close” in case the hospital made a mistake and her mother would start talking to her. “I now fear for my own safety,” she said. “I fear that one day another person will come out and kill me too.” On Wednesday, Nie was sentenced to life in prison for the death of Peng with a non-parole period of 17 years, backdated to March 2024 when he was first remanded in custody.



He was also sentenced separately to five, seven and two years for drugging, raping and stealing from a separate woman which will be served concurrently with the murder sentence. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Luxury homes offer an unmatched lifestyle, with perks including comfort and long-term value. With rare or high-end materials, advanced home automation and technology, resort-style amenities, and layouts designed for entertaining, here are five of our favourite luxury homes priced at $9 million or more. 7 Montalto Avenue, Toorak VIC This Toorak home is set within one of the suburb’s most esteemed precincts, on the cusp of Toorak Village, offering prestige and convenience. It has a price guide of $9,500,000 to $10,400,000.



It sits within approximately 779 square metres of landscaped, north-facing gardens and includes a five-car basement garage with a turntable, a gym, a workshop and a cellar. Wayne Gillespie designed the home, which features expansive living and dining areas on the lower level and five bedrooms on the upper level, two of which open onto a terrace and offer city views. High-end materials and features run throughout, including marble flooring, bespoke cabinetry, stone benchtops and Gaggenau kitchen appliances. 79 Fletcher Street, Tamarama NSW



With a buyer’s guide of $9 million, this Tamarama luxury home offers spectacular water views stretching from Bondi Beach to Ben Buckler, then south over Tamarama and Bronte to the South Maroubra Headland. Related Article Queensland residential property Daisy Hill vendors ‘got more than they wanted’ with $1.47m sale Located approximately 500 metres from both Bondi and Tamarama beaches, the residence’s position is one of its highlights. The property was conceived as a beachside resort with a north-facing travertine courtyard, a mosaic-tiled pool, a Finnish-style cedar sauna, and a built-in BBQ. Another highlight is the top-level bedroom sanctuary, featuring a walk-in robe, an en suite, dual decks, an outdoor bath and a rooftop barbecue.



7 Lascelles Avenue, Toorak VIC Nicholas Day designed this brand-new residence, with landscaping by Jack Merlo. It is priced between $16 million and $17 million. The home spans four levels, each serviced by a lift. The basement level not only houses up to six cars but also serves as the home’s entertainment precinct. It includes a gym, a recreation zone with a marble bar and a soundproofed home theatre, and a glass-encased six-car garage with LED display lighting.



Outside, a travertine al fresco, with a Wolf barbecue and a second fridge, overlooks the private landscaped surrounds and the self-cleaning, heated pool. Other features include high-end materials such as Calacatta Antica marble, full-height glazing, and a top floor with an entirely self-contained guest or entertaining domain, complete with a bedroom and en suite, a marble bar, a dining island and a wraparound outdoor setting with panoramic skyline views. 69-71 Louisa Road, Birchgrove NSW Offered for the first time in over a century, these two 1905 Federation residences are available together on one title.



The double-storey, side-by-side homes have a rich history, originally built by the Commonwealth Naval Dockyard’s dockmaster. They feature period details, including marble fireplaces and balconies with harbour and city views. Backing onto Birchgrove Oval, the residences are close to city-bound ferries, parks, cafes, restaurants, and schools. The price guide is $9.8 million. 13 Haverbrack Avenue, Malvern VIC



Set along a tree-lined avenue in Malvern, this home is in a desirable position, within walking distance of Glenferrie Road, High Street and some of Melbourne’s finest private schools. The approximately 1491 square metre allotment features a 15-metre heated indoor-outdoor pool with a sauna, landscaped feature gardens and a courtyard. Inside, double glazing and a hallway with expansive glass capture natural light and create an indoor-outdoor connection. Other features include a fully renovated V-Zug granite kitchen, a second butler’s kitchen, a self-contained guest suite, a fitted study, soaring 3.1-metre ceilings and a built-in lift. 13 Haverbrack Avenue has a price guide of $13, 000,000 - $14,300,000.

World.title: How Perry’s marketability triggered a revolution, and what’s next for the sporting icon
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket How Perry’s marketability triggered a revolution, and what’s next for the sporting icon Nick Wright October 7, 2026 — 10:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket icon Ellyse Perry concedes there will come a time soon when she needs to think about life beyond the pitch, but she has refused to put a definitive timeline on when she will draw the curtain on her decorated career. “I haven’t thought about it,” the 35-year-old declared in Brisbane. “I still love waking up every day and having the opportunity to hopefully get better, to work with the teams and look forward to a new challenge. While that’s the case, I don’t really want to change my mindset. Ellyse Perry will take to Allan Border Field as one of Australia’s most recognisable athletes. Getty Images “I’m incredibly grateful I’ve had this amount of time doing it. Nothing will last forever, but as long as that’s the case, I just want to make the absolute most of it.”



Speaking ahead of the three-game one-day series against Bangladesh – beginning on Friday at Allan Border Field – Perry was asked to reflect on a looming milestone that will occur during next year’s Ashes series in England. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot The campaign, beginning in late June, will mark the star all-rounder’s 20th year as an international athlete – a tenure that began in July 2007 when she debuted for both the nation’s ODI side and the Matildas within two weeks. “It’s been an incredible privilege to be part of such an amazing period of growth and development in women’s sport, and to have the opportunity when I was younger to play a few sports and have some amazing experiences around the world,” Perry said. “To see over the last 20 years how much has changed in the landscape and the opportunities now for young girls and female athletes wanting to play their sport as a profession, and do that around the world, I just can’t believe that’s happened.”



Throughout Perry’s career, she has become one of the country’s most marketable faces – both for her exploits on the field and for the way she has become a role model to the next generation. Endorsement, sponsorship and ambassador opportunities with adidas and Weet-Bix, among others, have followed, while her franchise cricket in India and England have all culminated in making her one of the world’s most lucrative female cricketers. “Brands are looking to partner with an athlete who showcases authenticity, and authenticity is what drives brand responses from consumers,” marketing expert Dr Monica Chien said.



“Consumers want to see brands being authentic, and the way they show authenticity is to partner with someone they feel authentically brings certain values. “She’s approachable, has the community connection, she’s relatable. That relatability and accessibility enhances the marketability in the eyes of stakeholders.” Loading While Chien stressed that Cathy Freeman’s impact at the 2000 Olympics could not be underestimated, Perry’s dual-sport exploits and how she captured audiences changed industry perceptions of how to source brand ambassadors. Chien said what had changed was collective female sporting bodies were being given greater exposure opportunities due to the values they showcased while attracting stronger family audiences and positive brand associations. This proved appealing to businesses.



The University of Queensland associate professor anticipated that with more broadcast exposure, marketability would continue to rise as some sports fought to become professional. Related Article Australian cricket Is South Africa Steve Smith’s last Test tour? Not even Cummins knows “When Perry debuted for both the cricket and football, she was largely seen as an abnormal case or a success story. There was a novelty at that time when a female athlete succeeded in a male-dominated sporting culture, so she became an inspirational role model,” Chien said. “Now, we’re looking at not just Perry or other athletes, but it’s the collective brand of women’s cricket or the Matildas that actually changed that marketability of women’s sport. “Sponsors started to realise the value of women’s sport, which allowed them to access audiences that were difficult to reach through traditional media. What they are showcasing is not just sports excellence, but their social values, and it’s the social values that partially drive their marketability.”



The Matildas’ historic 2023 FIFA Women’s World Cup campaign further proved the marketability of women’s sport, when the semi-final clash with England generated the largest television audience in Australia (11.15 million viewers). Loading Those athletes have become household names, with the shock withdrawal of Mary Fowler – who boasts more than 500,000 Instagram followers and inked a lucrative partnership with adidas this year – from the squad to take on Germany and Haiti triggering extensive engagement. “The interest being paid to female athletes and the sports they’re playing, the competitions they’re involved in, that’s because it is just genuinely such an entertaining product to watch,” Perry said. “The way sports are now covered, there’s so much more critical analysis, where we get into the weeds of how female athletes are performing and the teams are going, and various competitions.



“There’s still so much upside in terms of the growth and development of that. Uniquely, I think it’s starting to present its own landscape; it doesn’t follow men’s sport as much as it probably used to.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Matilda was killed during last year’s terror attack at Bondi. Matilda’s mother during Wednesday night’s commemoration event. George Chan A small gathering turned up at Town Hall on Wednesday evening for the planned pro-Palestinian vigil. They were almost outnumbered by the contingent of police and TV crews who kept a watchful eye over the proceedings. Palestine Action Group spokesperson Josh Lees was in attendance, but no state MPs joined the protest.
