World.title: Richard E. Grant has given us the most chaotic TV moment of the year
World.content:
★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview Richard E. Grant has given us the most chaotic TV moment of the year Meg Watson October 7, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Celebrity Traitors UK (season two) ★★★★ When host Claudia Winkleman and the producers of this smash-hit reality series picked Richard E. Grant to play a traitor this season, it would have seemed like a slam dunk. The famed actor is the first Oscar-nominated participant to appear on any version of the international franchise. And what’s more – from his villainous roles in everything from Logan to Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker – he’s renowned for his Machiavellian glee. Richard E. Grant in the second season of The Celebrity Traitors UK. BBC No one would have expected it, then, when this legend of stage and screen proudly outed himself as a traitor literally five minutes after being recruited. It might have entirely cooked his game and ruined the premise of the show, but we’re all the richer for it. This was the best reality-TV moment of the year and we’re not even halfway through the first episode.



If you’re yet to discover the utter joys of Celebrity Traitors and are wondering why someone of Richard E. Grant’s stature is doing reality TV at all, you’re in an ever-shrinking minority. This variant of the hugely popular competition series – essentially a game of Mafia set in a Scottish castle – has transfixed audiences around the world, bringing together a mix of musicians, authors, journalists, comedians, actors and a handful of people famous for being famous. The first celebrity season was the most popular show in the UK for 2025, buoying producers’ hopes for the very future of broadcast TV with a live audience of more than 11 million. Related Article ★★★★

Review Australia, I’m begging you: give this bonkers show a chance The highlight of that season was the ridiculous giggling mischief of comedian Alan Carr, offset by the deadpan investigative efforts of Stephen Fry, Ted Lasso’s Nick Mohammed and former rugby player Joe Marler. The returning season looks set to recreate the magic. Grant is an obvious delight, not just for his epic gaffe but his complete elation with the role he’s been given. (“My wife said to me, four days before she died: ‘Richard, try to find a pocketful of happiness in each day. And I feel like I’ve got a wheelbarrow-full and then some’,” he says, deliriously.) And the faithful – including James Blunt, Michael Sheen, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and Miranda Hart – so far offer a good mix of strategic insight and comedic relief.



Comedian James Acaster is poised for greatness (anyone who’s watched Bake Off knows the incredible TV he can make when put under pressure). And Ross Kemp is another standout after the first episode. The renowned hard man, who has filmed in active war zones and come face-to-face with terrorists, immediately unravels with paranoia because pint-sized Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey popped a sailor’s hat on his head, and Leigh-Anne Pinnock from Little Mix touched his arm. The new cast of Celebrity Traitors UK includes Rob Beckett, James Blunt, Michael Sheen, Myha’la, James Acaster, Hannah Fry and Miranda Hart. BBC There are tweaks to the usual formula in these opening episodes that work to varying degrees of success. As in the recently premiered US series The Traitors: New Blood, this season begins with just two traitors, who are quickly tasked with appointing a third. It’s a move that gives the players added agency and provides further intrigue to the game. Without spoiling the results of that pick (revealed in episode two), it also results in further comedy. The ending of that episode, however, is a real disappointment. While every instalment of this twisty reality show is structured around cliffhangers, the decision to end an episode before a single vote is cast at the round table is excruciating. I suspect, however, it’s a move made to keep the ludicrous Richard E. Grant on our screens for as long as possible. So, hey, I can’t be too mad. The Celebrity Traitors UK airs at 7.30pm, Wednesdays and Thursdays on Ten. New episodes are available on 10Play the Saturday and Sunday before broadcast.

World.title: Porridge producer’s oat to joy
World.content:
Brian Lucas from Bundanoon also watched the Golden Spurtle Championship (C8) in Scotland and was thrilled to see Australia’s Robert Reid win the specialty championship with a cannoli filled with sieved porridge, and wondered, “What next? A porridge cheesecake?”

Readers will recall that Ron Polgaze was wondering which spoon to use, so, the great man himself has taken time out from his spurtling commitments to oblige: “Dear Ron. From my memory growing up eating porridge at my Granny’s house, for our porridge, we were always supplied a traditional Scottish horn spoon and told to eat from the edges in. Always salty with a splash of cream. I’m sure this will enhance your couth clout. The last person I heard use the word couth in common vernacular was my Grandad. Robert Reid - Reigning Pearly Spurtle Champion and Golden Spurtle Specialty Dish Champion.”

Another champion, Garry Champion of Jamisontown writes: “Like many, I’ve been catching moths (C8) in the house and taking them outside and releasing them. One caught my eye. Unlike the rest, it appeared to be sporting a mullet. I believe it was a rare Bogan Moth.”

Shout out to Maurice Collins (C8) from Caz Willis of Bowral, who agrees that “clarification of species is important. Tawny Frogmouths are serene, strong observers of the world. I entered an indigenous garden in Gloucester, and was stopped by some presence, looking around, I could see nothing. Then those eyes showed me who ‘it’ was. A tawny, surveying the interloper! A remarkable creature. Bless those who do all they can to protect their habitat.”

Talk of “the trendiest restaurant in Kings Cross” (C8) jogged the warm memories and hunger pangs of Col Begg of Orange who asks: “Who remembers The Chelsea and those much sought-after Chelsea Pots?”

World.title: How a mother’s search for a fresh start in Perth ended in tragedy
World.content:
NationalWACourts How a mother’s search for a fresh start in Perth ended in tragedy Rebecca Peppiatt October 7, 2026 — 8:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eva was 14 years old when her mother took her on a trip through Western Australia in the Christmas school holidays of 2024. It was just the two of them visiting “many famous spots”, taking “countless photos” and eating “lots of delicious food”. They went to the beach and collected seashells together. The new case is now the second involving the family before the Supreme Court of Western Australia. Erin Jonasson “I told her I would one day buy her a big house by the ocean,” recalls Eva. But she never got the chance. Weeks later, her mum was dead, murdered in a hotel room by a man they had trusted to help them start a new life in a country where neither of them knew the language or had any family or friends.



Nongyu Peng was 42 years old and had made the ultimate sacrifice for her daughter by immigrating to Perth to give her a fresh start after she was bullied in school back home in China. Peng left behind a second daughter, just three years old, to stay with her parents while she established a life for herself and Eva. They were going to join them later. Peng wanted to be a lawyer and was studying English and law, but fell into sex work in a desperate attempt to finance the life she wanted for her family. That life never eventuated. Peng was killed by an overdose of GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) by 27-year-old Ruihong Nie in February 2024, having lured her to a hotel room and feeding her the drug without her knowledge.



Nie was not a stranger. He had signed a statutory declaration to support her immigration into the country and Peng lived with his mother at her massage shop. Related Article Updated

Courts Australia’s most senior Catholic convicted of sexual abuse jailed for more than six years On Wednesday, as he was sentenced over her death – as well as on charges for the rape, drugging, and stealing from a second woman three weeks later – the WA’s Supreme Court heard how Peng and Nie’s mother had a disagreement over money. His mother believed she was owed money, and Nie’s plan was drug Peng in the hotel room by luring her there under the pretence that she was meeting a client. Instead, he wanted to go through her phone and transfer the money to his mother that he believed she was owed.



But the court was told the amount of GHB Peng ingested was “significant” and killed her. In the hours before her death, Peng texted her daughter, whom she had left at home. Scared she would be scolded for being on her phone so late at night, Eva did not reply. It is a moment she said would haunt her forever. She broke down as she read out her victim impact statement on Wednesday in the Supreme Court of WA after travelling back to Perth from China for the hearing. “After I got out of the car, Stephen told me my mum had died,” she said, recalling the day she was picked up from school to be told her mother was dead.



“I could not believe it. I could not breathe, and I thought I was going to die as well. I was 14 years old, in a foreign country where we only had each other. No words can express how I felt then or how I feel now. Now I had no one but myself.” She said she was filled with “pain, despair and utter devastation” at having to see her mother’s dead body, before adding that she “lent in close” in case the hospital made a mistake and her mother would start talking to her. “I now fear for my own safety,” she said. “I fear that one day another person will come out and kill me too.” On Wednesday, Nie was sentenced to life in prison for the death of Peng with a non-parole period of 17 years, backdated to March 2024 when he was first remanded in custody.



He was also sentenced separately to five, seven and two years for drugging, raping and stealing from a separate woman which will be served concurrently with the murder sentence. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Kilkenny’s move could cost Labor at polls
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Kilkenny’s move could cost Labor at polls October 7, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Photo: Megan Herbert PLANNING Why on earth would Planning Minister Sonia Kilkenny even bother to approve controversial developments just before Victoria goes to an election? (“Kilkenny green-lights controversial projects”, 7/10) After all, it could cost Labor votes.

Throughout this state government’s term, Kilkenny has consistently approved developments of “excessive height” against the concerns of local communities. Her approach has served the interests of developers, and it is one of the reasons Labor has become unpopular.

Bill O’Connor, Beechworth Only one winner from development decision

Why have all these planning laws in place for councils when the planning minister just overrides them and fast-tracks developments? The only winners are the builders and their hip-pockets. They now go to the minister, and they will win with their original plans every time.

Christine Hammett, Richmond



Plea to protect existing classic structures

The Melbourne Assembly project to discuss the future of our city is about to begin, and an early item on the agenda should be the protection of our existing classic structures. Approval has been given for an eight-storey construction on the corner of Swanston and Flinders streets, and now the developer has requested a height increase which would result in a 16-storey monstrosity that would overshadow the iconic structures at the gateway into our city.

Surely, before the government enters into caretaker mode, this application must be refused and this irreplaceable vista be preserved for our and future generations.

Bill Pimm, Mentone Red gum trees will be a casualty of call

What an appalling decision supporting a housing developer in Nagambie (“Kilkenny green-lights controversial projects”, 7/10). The consequence will be the removal of 50 magnificent river red gum trees. This substantial shaded habitat for hundreds of birds and native animals does not have to be sacrificed for housing.

Does Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny know how much cleared land is available to the east and north of the town, suitable for housing without touching a single tree?

A gratuitous tip for Labor: Don’t waste time, energy and money campaigning in the seat of Euroa, which includes Nagambie. You may not attract a single vote.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff It’s tough to please everyone

Us: “Councils are too slow – they never approve anything!” Also us: “The minister is too fast – she approves everything!”

Steve Melzer, Hughesdale Nervous wait until November

Perhaps the planning minister herself will be disempowered in November, after overriding local council objections to over-height buildings. Shame, minister.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Preserve the character of market

As a lifelong resident of Melbourne’s northern suburbs, I have shopped at Preston Market for more than 20 years. Last week, the state government released a call for submissions on a proposed redevelopment with a speedy two-week deadline.

My concern is that the proposed redevelopment will fundamentally change the market’s character. Large retail outlets risk turning a beloved community market into another commercial shopping precinct. The proposed high-rise towers would dramatically alter the site’s character.

We already have Northland. We don’t need another one. Preston Market’s stallholders and community atmosphere are precisely what make it special.

Any redevelopment of the market should prioritise protecting its heritage, culture, independent traders and community atmosphere, not maximising profit. Once its unique character is lost, it cannot be recreated.

Sophia Tipping, Coburg



THE FORUM We should be so lucky

All political parties have now released their immigration policies (“Taylor in three-way migration battle”, 7/10). They are all coming out with motherhood statements, but it goes without saying that we need the right people coming into the country. The question should be asked who decides who are the right people?

History shows even with some bad elements, our immigration regime has been a success. Without it, Australia would not be the rich country it is.

It should be remembered that when Donald Horne wrote The Lucky Country, it was used as a term of irony not a celebration of greatness.

Peter Roche, Carlton Increasing trauma

Buried in its migration policy, the Coalition proposes a halving of the number of people coming to Australia under the humanitarian program. Further, it will require applicants to lodge applications

for protection within 30 days of arrival.

Experience demonstrates applicants are at their most traumatised at the point of arrival.

Other changes are proposed, and the common factor is to hurt the most traumatised.

It’s time for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor to think again.

Andrew Hewett, Brunswick Aged need migrants

Those of us who are aged 70 and above are not impressed by the Liberal and One Nation proposal to slash immigrant numbers.

There is a shortage of suitable aged care workers – the majority of whom are immigrants.

The media need to query Angus Taylor and Pauline Hanson as to how our ageing population will be suitably cared for without these wonderful support staff.

Barry James, Lilydale Reversing course difficult

Commentators lament that reductions in migration may lead to labour shortages and other negative effects on the economy. Here is a key point that everyone misses. We can always increase migration again. Whereas, once you have granted too many visas, it is very difficult legally or practically to reverse course.

Chris J. Lloyd, Professor of Business Statistics, Melbourne Business School



UK backpackers let loose

I find it infuriating that among the proposed changes to the migration program, limiting the uncapped numbers of UK backpackers to Australia is not one of them. International students and skilled migrants contribute so much more to this country than British holidaymakers who are not required to work in the primary industries to earn their stay. Thanks to Scott Morrison, everyone else gets punished.

James O’Keefe, Prahran Tearing up Treaty

I share your correspondent’s concern (Letters, 7/10) about the Victorian Coalition’s plan to tear up our Treaty.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson mentions the money that will be “saved” by abolishing the Treaty, but fails to ask, “At what cost?”

In place of the Treaty, the Victorian Liberals have pledged to create a whole new government department, First Nations Victoria. What will that cost?

Governments have repeatedly failed to improve the health, social, and educational outcomes for Australia’s First Peoples.

Under the Treaty, we finally have a mechanism with a good chance of achieving positive change. It was developed through a decade of goodwill and bi-partisan collaboration with democratically elected First Nations representatives. Surely, an approach that has the backing of the group it applies to has the best chance of success.

Why would Wilson risk undoing all that good work, wasting all the resources that went into its creation, and repeat the same old failed approach of “we know best”?

Julia Croatto, Kew Tram hazards

My wife and I were appalled to read of the tragic outcome for Pauline following a fall on a tram in September 2022 (“Pauline died after a tram fall. Her family still waits on answers”, 6/10). We could not believe that Yarra Trams’ protocol “required the immediate evacuation of the tram” leaving Pauline on the footpath.

The article raises other safety concerns for us as 80-year-olds who regularly use trams. Firstly, the older trams, in particular, often take off with quite a lurch before one has time to touch on one’s myki and find a seat.

Secondly, seats on crowded trams are often taken by young people with headphones on and eyes glued to their phones. While there are exceptions, many young people make no attempt to offer us a seat, even those designated for the disabled. The hazards of public transport use need to be addressed.

Robert Adler, Albert Park Anger at treatment

I witnessed an older gentleman collapse on a tram. I put him in the recovery position, and called my father (a doctor) who talked me through steps to monitor his welfare. Bystanders alerted the driver and requested an ambulance. It was 20 minutes later that the tram stopped. The driver came and asked the man to get up off the floor and sit on a seat. The man – semi-conscious – did not clear the aisle as requested. The driver then ordered everyone off, including me. I left the man lying on the floor in an empty tram. After reading the experience shared by Pauline’s family, I feel my anger from that day rise again.

Ripeka Walker, Carlton North US response killed millions

Matthew Knott acknowledges the casualty figures resulting from Hamas’ terrorist attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, were in per capita terms, 13 times greater than the fatalities of 9/11 (“Why October 7 changed everything”, 7/10). He also acknowledges Israel’s response resulted in accusations of it committing genocide, a charge that has been repeatedly levelled at Israel in wars that it didn’t initiate since its creation in 1948.

What also needs to be acknowledged is that the United States’ response to 9/11 was estimated to have resulted in about 4.5 million deaths, and the displacement of 38 million people, but no charges of genocide, nor the level of opprobrium that was promptly meted out to Israel as it yet again was forced to respond to those who sought its elimination.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East



Climate hypocrisy

If I were Sitiveni Rabuka, Prime Minister of Fiji, I would be tempted to send Anthony Albanese to The Hague to answer to a higher court for the hypocrisy of Australia’s climate policies (“Pacific leaders demand an end to global fossil fuel addiction”, 7/10).

In 2025, the International Court of Justice said states had legal obligations to protect the climate system and prevent significant transboundary environmental harm. It also recognised that climate impacts such as sea-level rise could impair fundamental human rights.

Surely, you cannot stand on the front line of the climate crisis, express concern for nations facing rising seas, and then continue backing a fossil-fuel industry that is a main driver of the problem?

The Pacific deserves more than sympathetic words and photo opportunities. It deserves action.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Action not words

Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen said the Pacific region was “unified not uniform on climate issues” (“Pacific leaders demand an end to global fossil fuel addiction”, 7/10). Clever words, but, our atmosphere needs united, uniform phasing-out of burning coal and gas now.

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton Related Article Note From The Editor How The Age chooses which letters to publish Growth not sustainable

The concept that Australia needs to produce more babies and there should be incentives for Australians to have more children (“My ovaries are nearly at extinction point, but I’m open to bribes”, 7/10) is consistent with mainstream economics that is based on continual growth including of humans. The perpetual growth model, however, is not consistent with a sustainable world. The planet has limited resources.

But economic models do not incorporate this fact. Despite the overwhelming evidence of humanity’s increasing adverse effects on our planet, overall, it receives insufficient attention in our finance-driven economy.

It is clearly in our interests to remedy this situation that drives us to grow, possibly to extinction.

Leigh Ackland, Deepdene Where is empathy?

As avid reader of the Letters section, I am increasingly in despair. “Stop the world, I want to get off” comes to mind.

Have we gone completely mad? Where is the empathy, the compassion, the care, the will to stand for the greater good? Where have the responsible adults gone?

We all need to take a long, hard look at ourselves and stop this selfish, inward looking behaviour.

Julie Perry, Highton



Resist AI threats

Let’s straighten out the definitions. AI “agents” are computers or machines. They are not being “trained” with someone else’s intellectual property – they are using, borrowing or stealing that content. There must be some guts shown in resisting this imposition.

Any threats of a reduction in investment in Australia if the AI giants don’t get their way should be treated with the disdain they deserve.

Neil Falconer, Castlemaine Logistical exercise

It sounds as though the new zones at Melbourne Airport for drop-off and pick-up require travellers to navigate new areas (“Travellers up in air over departure of ’70s era drop-off ramp”, 7/10). Surprisingly, the new zones do not align with the arrival and departure halls, plus only the first five minutes are free.

What a joke! Now travelling requires a logistical exercise.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East Good exercise

So you are going to fly off somewhere, sitting still for perhaps six hours or more on your journey. Your body will now appreciate the extra walk to the check-in counters from the new drop-off area at the airport.

John Hart, Bright AND ANOTHER THING ...



Politics

Sussan Ley was Liberal leader for 276 days before being dumped for Angus Taylor, who has been in the job for 236 days. According to my calculations, he has 40 days to prove he’s worth keeping. I don’t like his chances.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Photo: Matt Golding Juggling immigration and housing stats is a lot easier than facing up to the elephant in the room: One Nation’s “monoculture” agenda.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Without immigrants, who’ll do all the work?

Peter Rooke, Hawthorn Plague

Is this the way the world ends? Not with a bang but a whimper of thousands of sufferers from pneumonic plague leaked out from a Russian laboratory.

Sandra Torpey, Hawthorn



I suppose Russian transparency about the death of a young lady from pneumonic plague will be much the same as China’s about the COVID-19 pandemic.

Marie Nash, Balwyn State election

What happens if One Nation wins a sizeable number of seats in the election, and neither the ALP nor the Liberals can form a government in their own right? Surely, the best option for Victorians would be for Labor and Liberals to work together to provide a sensible government.

Russ Newton, Black Rock One Nation seems to be offering gullible voters a chance to ramp up fiscal irresponsibility in Victoria, as if it isn’t sky-high already.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills The election choice is like a rainbow – red and blue along with green and orange – but oh, for some sense.

Bruce Dudon, Woodend Furthermore

The Liberal Party finally found a loophole to bump Hughesy from their campaign strategy.

Paul Custance, Highett

World.title: Large bush fire burns through 1400 hectares in high country above Lake Whakatipu
World.content:
Audio player for " Latest from scene of fire near Queenstown " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/emergencies_local/1774948%2Flarge-bush-fire-burns-through-1400-hectares-in-high-country-above-lake-whakatipu

Latest from scene of fire near Queenstown Midday Report Download MP3 3m

Firefighters tackling a large bush blaze in the high country above Lake Whakatipu have stood down for the night.

The fire was estimated to have burnt 1400 hectares of mainly tussock and scrub, with areas of trees, Fire and Emergency NZ (FENZ) said.

It was not yet controlled or contained.

The fire had spread from Walter Peak station along the McKinley's Creek area and had also affected parts of adjoining conservation estate and Cecil Peak station.

No homes or buildings were damaged, and there were no structures or livestock at immediate risk

Five helicopters with monsoon buckets had been dropping water on the fire, targeting the most active fire edges, FENZ said.

"Ground crews are continuing structure protection work around the homestead, creating defensible space and strengthening containment lines. An Incident Management Team is directing operations and planning further ahead.

"Firefighting operations will be suspended overnight for safety, with helicopters standing down at last light. A ground crew will remain at Walter Peak to monitor the fire and maintain readiness, enabling crews to resume operations at first light tomorrow," FENZ said.

District Commander Blair Kiely said the fire's behaviour continued to be influenced by steep terrain, the vegetation and changing wind conditions.

There would be five aircraft supporting 23 firefighters, with incident management and support personnel all active on Thursday.

Crews from the Department of Conservation (DOC) were working alongside Fire and Emergency volunteer firefighters.

The fire at Lake Wakatipu as seen on Wednesday morning. SUPPLIED

Earlier, Kiely said Wednesday's efforts were focused on extending the contained area and protecting livestock in the vicinity, while maintaining the ability to protect the Walter Peak homestead and associated buildings if wind changes drove the fire nearer.

He said forecast rain could assist suppression efforts but could also create additional operational challenges.

Drifting smoke would continue to be seen and smelled in a wide area, with exact locations changing as the wind shifts, Kiely said.

Air quality around affected areas might be impacted by smoke. Health NZ encouraged at-risk people to:

Keep windows and doors closed.

Set air conditioning systems to recirculate or turn them off.

Air out homes once smoke conditions have improved.

Check on children, older people, and others who may be more vulnerable to smoke.

Keep pets indoors where possible and ensure they have access to clean water and food.

The fire on Tuesday. Supplied / FENZ

Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said it would be working with fire investigators to determine how a controlled burn on its land reignited.

Chief executive Dave Beeche said he had been on site today talking to fire crews.

"We had a controlled burn last Wednesday and had an appropriate plan, and FENZ were on site and that all was successful and went well at the time. FENZ believes that that has somehow reignited - so we'll obviously work closely with them to understand how that might have happened," he said.

The fire came within 300 metres of the historic Walter Peak homestead on Tuesday, prompting the evacuation of 350 guests and staff, he said.

It had since moved up towards the McKinlays Creek area, but there had been no stock or property damage on RealNZ's land, he said.

"There's no further immediate risk to property at our station at the moment," he said.

Beeche said he was grateful for the "hard tireless work" of fire crews and pilots.

Barring any changes overnight, he said RealNZ was hoping to resume tours on Thursday.

Queenstown's mayor John Glover said the blaze was "confronting".

"It's very large, very visible, and the fact that we haven't been able to contain it is top of mind for everyone involved in the response."

Glover said it was normal for high country stations in the area to have burns this time of year to renew land for Spring - but these could get out of control.

"It's a real stark reminder of the fact that our hillsides can be dry and if we get a wild fire it can spread quite easily."

Glover understood the historic Walter Peak homestead had not been damaged, which he was relieved about.

He advised locals to keep boats away from the area, which was across the lake from the central city.

Members of the public on the lake should stay at least 500 metres offshore to keep clear of where helicopters were operating.

Supplied / Kevin Pilbrow

This exclusion zone would be monitored by the Harbourmaster and Coastguard throughout the day to ensure public and firefighter safety, FENZ said.

Queenstown locals and visitors flocked to the lakeside to watch as the fire smouldered.

There was a steady stream of people coming by with their binoculars and cameras.

Thomas Ah Chee said it was sad to see how much land had been blackened by the blaze.

"[It's] pretty devastating to watch and quite a spectacle at night last night. It was glowing red and you could see the fires clear as day," he said.

Demi-Ann Klocek, who was visiting from Brisbane, was surprised to see the scale of the fire while driving towards Glenorchy on Wednesday morning.

"I wasn't expecting to experience bush fires here in Queenstown," she said.

World.title: Everything that happened on the campaign trail on 7 October
World.content:
National and Labour's finance spokespeople went head-to-head in a debate on RNZ, NZ First revealed its revamped party list, and major party leaders met voters as campaigning ramped up on 7 October.

Willis v Edmonds

The day began with National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis taking on Labour's Barbara Edmonds on RNZ's Morning Report.

Willis said some households were better off than three years ago, and the country needed to stay on track to grow the economy, create jobs and lift incomes.

Edmonds said Labour was offering a package of solutions to try to help New Zealanders with the cost of living.

Where money was coming from to pay for election promises was up for debate - but both agreed addressing supermarket prices was a priority.

Neither was keen to see house prices increase quickly. Edmonds said they had to be stable and Willis said she wanted to see moderate price rises over time with incomes rising more quickly.

Both parties committed to renewable energy, including encouraging households to put solar power systems on their roofs.

Labour's Barbara Edmonds (L) and National's Nicola Willis (R) with RNZ's John Cambell after the economic debate on Morning Report. RNZ

National's huge plan for small businesses revealed

Following the debate, the National Party unveiled a plan to support small businesses by cutting compliance costs.

Leader Christopher Luxon visited Book Hero in Hobsonville to announce the plan, which includes a new 'tell government once' service, faster disputes processing, and a minimum support threshold for collective bargaining.

Spokesperson Cameron Brewer said the plan was focused on practical changes that would give business owners their time back.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon campaigning at Book Hero in Hobsonville, October 2026. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

Te Pāti Māori electorate gamble might be paying off

As the morning progressed, new polls by Te Ao Māori News revealed Te Pāti Māori candidates Rawiri Waititi and Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke were well in the lead in their electorate battlefields.

The party has urged supporters to give them their electorate votes, and give their party vote to other parties, in an effort to take advantage of MMP's overhang rules.

The strategy is a divisive one.

A few weeks ago, Waititi said the party's plan could see up to 13 Māori MPs get into power.

However, Labour's Māori campaign chair Willie Jackson said the strategy threatened a backlash against the Māori seats that could lead to their abolition.

Hana Maipi-Clarke and Rawiri Waititi announcing a kohanga reo and kura policy in Rotorua. RNZ / Rachel Moore

Voting locations unveiled

Shortly before noon, the campaign took a big step forward, with more than 2300 voting places for the election confirmed.

"Our voting places are in locations people go in their daily lives including community halls, schools, shopping malls, places of worship, tertiary education providers and marae," chief electoral officer Karl Le Quesne said.

There are more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori voting places, including 67 bilingual (reo rua) voting places.

Accessible services include 1679 fully accessible voting places, sign language interpreters at six locations and three voting places with quiet times.

Locations can be found at vote.nz.

Chief electoral officer Karl Le Quesne. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Labour targets big banks

Next it was Labour's turn to make an announcement, with the party vowing to put the big banks in its sights to combat the rising cost of living.

Labour vowed to make it easier for new banking and payment companies to compete with ANZ, ASB, BNZ and Westpac.

Leader Chris Hipkins said more competition would give customers more choice and force banks to offer better prices and services.

"Almost every Kiwi relies on a bank to get paid, pay the bills, buy a home or grow a business," he said.

Under Labour's plan, smaller financial companies would face simpler rules if they wanted to offer services such as digital wallets, prepaid cards or payments.

The big banks would also have to give smaller competitors fair access to important payment systems and banking information.

Chris Hipkins at Sephora, Sylvia Park, October 2026. RNZ / Tu Natanahira

ACT pushes to scrap donations tax benefit cap

Next it was ACT's turn to make a big announcement, with the party promising to scrap a cap on charitable donations being able to receive tax benefits.

Leader David Seymour said the tax system should encourage charitable generosity rather than imposing an arbitrary ceiling on it.

"ACT's plan for New Zealand's first comprehensive cancer centre will also be achieved by partnering with New Zealand's leading philanthropists, families, businesses, charitable trusts, community organisations and successful Kiwis, we can build something extraordinary.

"If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity."

Seymour said the party's fiscal plan would be unveiled on Sunday, promising it would "remove locks on New Zealand's potential" and "will get rid of the waste that prevents us from growing the economy".

ACT leader David Seymour promises to scrap a cap on charitable donations being able to receive tax benefits. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

NZ First reveals party list

One of the day's major announcements came from New Zealand First, which revealed a dramatically reshaped party list.

It's given high placements to former MPs Alfred Ngaro, Michael Laws and Harete Hipango-Brownlie.

Former FMA chair Craig Stobo and former All Blacks captain Taine Randell are also ranked high - beating out several current MPs including Jenny Marcroft, Andy Foster, David Wilson, and Jamie Arbuckle.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters campaigning at Albany Mall in Auckland on 6 October 2026. RNZ / Nick Monro

The Chrises meet their constituents

National and Labour's leaders spent the afternoon getting some face time with potential voters, with National leader Christopher Luxon and Labour leader Chris Hipkins both visiting malls in Auckland.

Luxon visited NorthWest mall, stopping to chat with anyone who wanted to do so.

Children discussed what they liked at school, young adults discussed their jobs and those a bit older weighed in on marriage and how to make it work with National's leader.

Hipkins made his way to Sylvia Park, where he was mobbed by a mix of supporters and shoppers.

One young boy told Hipkins he watched the leaders' debate on TVNZ on Tuesday night and was impressed by Hipkins' performance.

During his mall walkabout, Luxon made what appeared to be a surprise visit to a nail salon.

Hipkins' walkabout took a glamorous turn too, with the Labour leader somehow being corralled into a Sephora beauty shop before he said goodbye to supporters.

World.title: 'Half surprised, half pissed-off': David Tamihere still processing freedom news
World.content:
For nearly 36 years, David Tamihere was at the centre of one of the country's most infamous murder cases.

He was the man convicted of murdering Swedish backpackers Heidi Paakkonen and Urban Höglin, before his convictions were quashed by the Supreme Court in early 2026.

After all that time, Justice Simon Mount KC took less than nine minutes on Wednesday morning to tell Tamihere he was free.

"You are discharged on the two charges of murder in the indictment before the court which was filed in 1990," he said.

"You may stand down and you are free to go."

It had been up to the Crown to decide whether to hold another trial, but on Wednesday the court heard they did not have sufficient evidence to go forward.

Over the decades the case has been fraught by controversy.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406377913112

Jailhouse snitch Roberto Conchie Harris was convicted of perjury having made up evidence that Tamihere had killed the Swedes; Höglin's body was found after the trial, some 70 kilometres from where police claimed the murders occurred; while a watch police claimed Tamihere had stolen from him was found with his remains.

Speaking to media outside court, David Tamihere said he was still processing the news.

"[I'm] kind of half surprised half pissed-off about it," he said.

"I was quite happy to go to a re-trial, and I thought that's what they were gearing up for too."

It was Crown Prosecutor Claire Paterson who said there wasn't sufficient evidence to go proceed with a prosecution.

"As a result of the passage of time, some 36 years, significant pieces of evidence that the Crown adduced in the 1990 trial are no longer available, or if available will likely be subject to reliability challenge," She said.

"The evidential test for prosecution is no longer met."

That was despite pointing to uncontested but circumstantial evidence against Tamihere.

"In the victims were seen in Thames, Coromandel, on the 7th of April, 1989," Paterson said.

"Mr Tamihere was living in that area at the relevant time and was in the Wentworth Valley in the first week of April 1989, close to where Mr Höglin's remains were later found."

Paterson said Tamihere had the victims' car, and had stayed at the a lodge where toiletries belonging to Paakkonen had been found.

Höglin's jacket was also found in the home of Tamihere's partner on 10 July 1989, she said.

But for David Tamihere, there was still the question of compensation, something he said hadn't been decided.

"I'd like to do it at the level that was around when I first got convicted," Tamihere said.

"It's quite huge."

David Tamihere in court in July 2026. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

A range of factors are considered in compensation for wrongful conviction or detention.

The Ministry of Justice website stated an annual amount of $150,000 for each year in custody could be included.

An additional amount of $75,000 a year for time spent on restrictive bail or parole may also be considered.

David Tamihere told reporters his sympathy was with Paakkonen and Höglin's family.

"You've got to admit you've got a hole in the family, there's a huge hole, and it's always going to be there until you die." he said.

"There's some things you will carry for the rest of your life."

Defence lawyer Murray Gibson said he was very pleased with the outcome.

"David's had this accusation hovering over him for about 35 years, and now it's finished and it's been established that he's innocent of these charges," he said.

Police told RNZ they will retain the investigation file into the deaths of Urban Höglin and Heidi Paakkonen.

Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell acknowledged the impact Wednesday's decision would have on the families of the backpackers.

"Given today's decision by the Crown, Police will ensure the investigation file is retained, he said.

World.title: RNZ board member Richard Dellabarca steps in following unexpected resignation of CFO
World.content:
RNZ has taken the step of appointing a board member to complete its end of year accounts after the unexpected resignation of its Chief Financial Officer.

The public broadcaster told staff earlier this week that CFO Hilary Parker had resigned.

"We wish Hilary well," said a spokesperson in a statement.

RNZ said board member Richard Dellabarca, a chartered accountant, is now acting as Chief Financial Officer.

A spokesperson said Dellabarca's appointment would ensure financial leadership during the annual reporting period.

RNZ said it expected to meet the timeframe for reporting its accounts. Last year, the annual report was signed on September 30 and published on October 21.

"As is standard, the accounts are subject to audit before they are finalised."

A spokesperson said all RNZ's key stakeholders had been informed.

A spokesperson for Broadcasting Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed his office had been notified of the CFO's departure under the no surprises convention.

The change in CFO comes six months after the government spelled out financial expectations for the organisation.

Goldsmith highlighted the public broadcaster's financial performance as the top item in the Letter of Expectation to the Board on March 18, 2026. Improving audience reach and growing trust levels were the other main items.

The Letter noted: "It is a vital, ongoing expectation that RNZ delivers improved performance and represents a value-for-money investment for the Crown as owner. This includes right-sizing operations and increasing efficiency to mitigate reliance on cash reserves and the sale of land to fund operations."

Dellabarca, a Chartered Accountant with a Bachelor of Laws, is currently working out of the RNZ Auckland offices it shares with TVNZ.

Dellabarca is a director of RNZ, North Harbour Rugby Union and commercial vehicle group Keith Andrews, and chair of bio-technology distributor Epic Char.

World.title: Loafers Lodge fire trial: Charred remnants of building shown to jury
World.content:
The jury for the Loafers Lodge manslaughter trial have viewed the remnants of the budget accommodation building on Wellington's Adelaide Road.

Five people died when a fire lit by Esarona Lologa tore through the building - with nearly 100 hundred residents inside - in May 2023.

The manslaughter trial of Gregory Bruce Mein, Barry Charles Collins, Glenn Brendan McAllister, and Marie Louise Murphy, for their roles in the maintenance and operation of the building, is in its third day in the High Court at Wellington.

During the tour on Wednesday, court staff pointed out to the jury parts of the building in relation to how they were described in evidential documents.

More than three years on from the fatal fire, the site is boarded up with plywood, spattered with graffiti and in varying states of decay.

Through the building's upper windows, the sky is visible where the fourth floor mezzanine once was.

Here was where victims of the fire; Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings all lived.

Outdated floor plans hamper rescue attempts

Back in the High Court, Fire and Emergency senior station officer Clark Townsley said he was the first senior officer to arrive at the fire and co-ordinated the initial response.

He told the court that, prior to the fire, firefighters' discussions on how best to approach fires in dense, low socio-economic housing in Wellington used the Loafers Lodge site as an example.

On the night of the fire, Townsley and his crew were alerted to "smoke logging in a building" at 12:26am.

They left the Newtown Fire station about a minute and a half later.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Townsley said they could see smoke, but no flames, when they arrived at the scene at 12:30am.

He said he expected there were many people inside, and he called for more support.

Fire crews jostled by panicked residents

While fire-fighters were setting up breathing equipment, Townsley said he saw people streaming out of the entrance on the northern side of the building.

Panicked residents "abused, jostled and accosted" firefighters telling them the fire was on the third floor and there were people still inside.

Townsley called for police to help with the growing number of agitated people gathering outside the building.

Once inside, Townsley said he did not hear any main alarms and other fire-fighters commented as to how quiet it was on the top floors.

Heading up to the third floor, Townsley told the court he saw thick black smoke and determined that survivability for people on the level was "low but not impossible".

He made the decision to attack the fire on that level "to give those residents the best chance".

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Back on the street, he encountered a man who said he had responsibilities relating to the building, he had access keys and warned him there could be up to 148 people staying in the hostel. That man would turn out to be accused, Glen McAllister.

"He wanted to go back in the building. I said 'no way' but I do need your keys," Townsley said.

He told the jury the building's alarm panels indicated fire was present in multiple areas that, in hindsight, were every where but where the fire actually was.

Another light indicated a potential defect in the system.

Firefighters unaware of the addition of mezzanine level to the building

Shortly before 1am, Townsley received a report that someone was trapped on the mezzanine level but said his crews didn't know where that level was, or how to get there.

Soon after, he was told a person had jumped from the building and had landed on the roof of Zip Electrical next door, suffering a broken leg.

He said he assigned an aerial unit to reach people on the building's roof and, seeing a person signalling from with a flashing light, directed crews to their location as well.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"I was still receiving radio messages from the comms centre that people were trapped in the building and making calls to 111," he said.

Crews inside reported deteriorating conditions and the potential for flashover and withdrew from the building.

"Flashover refers to the heat in area reaching such a temperature that all combustible materials can spontaneously combust. The heat could've been upwards of 1000 degrees. The survivability in these sorts of conditions is very low. Within a matter of seconds it can be fatal for even a fully kitted fire-fighter," Townsley said.

He said a firefighter on the ladder of an aerial appliance reported "intense fire and structural collapse" inside the building.

Having avoided the flashover, fire-fighters targeted the blaze from outside - attempting to cool the building until a crew could be prepped to re-enter the structure to assess conditions.

On re-entering, a team of four firefighters found three bodies on the third floor.

Under cross examination from counsel for Greg Mein, Christopher Stevenson KC, Townsley acknowledged that the plans firefighters could see on their systems were actually from 2005 and contained no indication of the mezzanine floor.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

This lead to confusion when residents told 111 dispatchers they were stuck in that part of the building.

"If you had accurate plans showing the mezzanine and how you get up to it, that would've assisted you but you just didn't have that info," Stevenson said.

Stevenson said three people had broken through the mezzanine level's skylight windows to escape the fire, while Liam Hockings had been trapped in a room on the mezzanine.

Stevenson put to Townsley that had firefighters known where the trapped people were, they would have attempted to rescue those people.

"If I had known they were there? Absolutely," Townsley said.

Only centimetres on clear air on the fire floor

Senior firefighter Brady Cutting and firefighter Noel Wellington were tasked with fighting the fire at its source on level three.

Cutting said he had to crawl along the floor towards the fire source due to the low, hot smoke which burnt his ears through his protective equipment when he tried to stand.

Cutting said there was only a matter of about three centimetres of clear air above the floor.

"It was as if you were blind folded. Everything's done by touch," he said.

He said he received reports through his radio that there were people trapped in the building but did not know how to find them.

"Immediately after that an orange flame pulsed through the air behind us.

"The conditions were changing rapidly. The heat was unbearable we were lying on the floor simply to protect ourselves."

As debris began to fall about them, they withdrew from the floor and told other firefighters not to enter.

Appearing by video link, Noel Wellington told the court he had attended a callout at Loafers Lodge before the fatal fire.

Having seen the nature of the building and its tenancy, Wellington told the court he was expecting a "worst case scenario" as his crew travelled towards the blaze.

World.title: Slink skin factory manager takes on regional council in the Environment Court
World.content:
A Southland slink skin factory manager facing environmental charges has taken on the regional council in the Environment Court, arguing restrictions on his business are unjustified.

Da Cheng "Eddie" Zhi and his Tuturau business NZAgri Development are facing six charges brought by the Southland Regional Council over discharges of blood, leachate and/or contaminants to land in circumstances where they could enter water.

A seventh charge alleges they failed to comply with abatement notices issued in August and September 2025.

The Environment Court granted interim enforcement orders on 9 September that meant the business could not receive or process carcasses.

Neighbours had complained about offensive smells and piles of carcasses in NZAgri Development's yard.

Representing himself and his company before Judge Kelvin Reid on Wednesday, Zhi argued the business was being unfairly restricted and wanted the court to revoke the enforcement orders.

The regional council maintained regulatory action was necessary to prevent ongoing environmental harm.

During cross-examination, Zhi intensely questioned several council staff members about their qualifications, scientific training and experience collecting environmental samples.

He sought to introduce his own water samples as evidence and at one point asked a witness to test a glass of water in court.

At times Zhi became visibly frustrated.

"We are facing a bunch of people who have never been trained scientifically, who have no idea how to take samples," he told the court.

"We have never, ever discharged any single drop of wastewater to the creek, to the environment."

Judge Reid repeatedly interrupted, saying parts of Zhi's questioning were irrelevant to the issues before the court.

"The court has in front of it affidavit evidence from various council staff, some of whom have taken samples that have been analysed, and there's evidence about what the analysis means and what the discharges that were occurring on the site are doing to the environment," he said.

"The council is not relying on some other samples that you have."

Following the court action in September, Zhi staged protests outside the Southland Regional Council's office, including carrying dead lambs to the council car park.

The company is also facing legal action from the Southland District Council which holds interim enforcement orders.

In a separate application before the Environment Court the district council is seeking to revoke the factory's resource consent.

World.title: Race for vaccine to save hoiho/yellow eyed penguin
World.content:
The hoiho/yellow eyed penguin could be extinct in less than a decade as a respiratory disease continues to wipe out a significant proportion of the chick population on the mainland.

The hunt is on for a vaccine for the disease, and with fewer than 115 hoiho breeding pairs on mainland New Zealand and Rakiura/Stewart Island, it is a race against time to save the birds.

Scientists have recently discovered there are three "deeply distinct" subspecies of the penguin, and that could have major implications for conservation efforts.

Evolutionary virologist professor Jemma Geoghan told Checkpoint that every year for the past three years, about a quarter or a third of the chicks that hatch on the mainland have died from respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

"And this is really compounded by everything else that they are dealing with, other factors such as fisheries and climate change and predation and things like that, so it's had a really significant impact on the population."

After studying the disease for a number of years and trying to understand its origins, Geoghan and her team discovered a virus that might be responsible for causing the disease.

"Now what is puzzling about this virus is that sometimes chicks can be infected with this virus without disease and sometimes they can be infected with the virus and it causes this really severe disease and death... If they develop symptoms or clinical signs that they have this respiratory disease then most of the time they end up dying within a really short timeframe - 24 hours of showing symptoms.

"So it's a puzzle, that's why we've taken the past couple of years to better understand whether or not this virus is causing the disease."

The scientists also discovered something interesting about the birds themselves.

They found the different populations - the northern ones found around Banks Peninsula and down to Rakiura, and the two southern populations living on sub-Antarctic islands - have actually been not breeding or mixing for thousands of years, with this divergence between their genome suggesting that they were actually sub-species.

"They have the virus in the sub-Antarctic, but don't seem to have the disease, so we're really interested in whether or not the northern population was somehow predisposed to this disease genetically," Geoghan said.

They need to be thought of as sub-species with different lineages that are genetically diverse, Geoghan said.

Understanding more about the northern population and its critical decline in numbers is important so the focus can be on its conservation, she said.

After sequencing the genome of the hoiho from the north and south, they found some genetic markers on the northern birds that were predisposing these hoiho to contract the disease.

Geoghan said they were hopeful this would lead to a vaccine, but time was running out.

World.title: Free mental health support launched for sextortion victims as cases reach record high
World.content:
Audio player for " Netsafe offers free counselling as sextortion at highest level ever " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/crime-and-justice/1783883%2Ffree-mental-health-support-launched-for-sextortion-victims-as-cases-reach-record-high

Netsafe offers free counselling as sextortion at highest level ever Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Online safety organisation Netsafe says sextortion is at its highest ever level in Aotearoa, and the number of people falling victim to the online harm is rising rapidly.

Sextortion is a form of blackmail in which someone is tricked or pressured into sharing intimate images, then threatened with having them posted online unless they pay a ransom or send more.

Netsafe said cases have gone up nearly 25 percent in the last year, but many aren't reported.

From today, they have partnered with counselling service Ignite, to offer free support to victims.

For many people what may have begun as a friend request online, or a message from a friendly stranger, quickly spiralled into something much more sinister.

Netsafe CEO Brent Carey said sextortion is a rapidly growing issue, with nearly one in ten people having reported it to them.

"Netsafe's been getting on average 50 sextortion reports a week, and it's growing. And we've taken more than 16,000 reports of this harm type."

While the harmful practice is rapidly making its way to our shores, Carey said it is a global phenomenon.

All the way in Michigan, John DeMay's 17-year-old son Jordan fell victim to one of those scams, and in 2022 and took his own life hours after a sextortion scam rapidly escalated.

"He just checked his phone, saw the Instagram message come in, accepted the friend request and started having the conversation with her. He was having this conversation casually with Dani Roberts, and that conversation started to turn a little bit sexual.

"She ended up sending him nude images of herself and enticed him to do the same, and he eventually caved."

Netsafe CEO Brent Carey. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

DeMay said that within about 15 minutes "the switch was flipped", with Roberts demanding money, and threatening to send his nude image to everyone he knew.

But Roberts wasn't a teenage girl like she claimed, Jordan was talking to an organised crime group in Nigeria.

In 2023, a Christchurch teen took his own life just hours after he was sexually extorted online, in very similar circumstances.

Despite his reluctance, he exchanged intimate images with a woman on Facebook, who he thought was from Timaru.

After doing so, she demanded he pay $5000 or she would share the images to his contacts.

In reality, she didn't exist, and the account was also traced back to West Africa.

Carey said people in Aotearoa are being targeted from all over the world.

"In terms of blackmail and extortion, we know that there's organised crime targeting New Zealanders, and they're using social media accounts to socially engineer us and target us.

"But we also know [it's happening] through school communities, we know that there also can be a personal relationship to sextortion, and some people know who the perpetrator of this is."

While victims can report the online harm to Netsafe, Carey said they have been lacking services which provide ongoing support.

Today, Netsafe, alongside counselling service Ignite, have begun offering three free counselling sessions for people affected by sextortion.

Director of Ignite, Sarina Finucane said the stigma around sextortion often makes it difficult for victims to find the help they need.

Ignite director Sarina Finucane. Supplied

"Sometimes going locally for support can be a real challenge. There can be stigma and embarrassment attached to this. You might go into your GP to access some primary mental health support, and the GP may not even recognise what image-based abuse or sextortion is.

"This is why it's been really important to have that recovery pathway direct from Netsafe and to support providers that understand the impact of online harm."

Finucane said that mental health services needed to keep up with the rapidly evolving digital landscape.

"I think there's actually a real need for mental health services in New Zealand to meet the need of the modern problems that are arising for Kiwis. Sextortion is a huge issue, online harm is a huge issue, not just for young people, as we tend to think, but for a lot of New Zealanders and adults as well experiencing this."

Carey said they had seen the issue affecting people as young as eight, and as old at 80.

While counselling is key for victims to move forward, Carey said much more needs to be done to tackle the issue, starting with a review to the Harmful Digital Communications Act.

"We want to keep sextortion a live issue to try and tackle it. It's going to take banks, it's going to take platforms, civil society. therapy providers all working together to tackle this. We'd love for the government to review the act. That's a bottom line, and we also want to make sure that it's staying relevant for new harms."

Carey and Finucane said they hope to expand the pilot programme to offer more counselling sessions in the future.

Anyone who has been a victim of sextortion should report the offending to police on 105 (non-emergency) or 111 (emergency), and Netsafe by calling on 0508 NETSAFE (0508 638 723), or reporting online at netsafe.org.nz/report.

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

World.title: 'One of the greats' signs off after fourth Roosters premiership
World.content:
Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson has hailed Daniel Tupou as one of the NRL club's all-time greats after the four-time premiership-winning winger announced his retirement.

Tupou is ending his 15-year career on a high after helping the Roosters win Sunday's grand final against Newcastle.

The 35-year-old, who had been coy about his future all season, became just the sixth player in Roosters history to win four premierships with the club.

Across a 307-game, one-club career, the winger scored 198 tries, the third most of any player in premiership history behind Ken Irvine and Alex Johnston.

"When you look at what Daniel Tupou has achieved over 15 seasons, he will stand as one of the greats," Robinson said in a statement.

"But those numbers only tell part of the story of Toops and what he means to this club.

Tupou a Roosters grand final specialist Daniel Tupou is edging closer to becoming the first Roosters player in more than 80 years to win four premierships because he always finds his best on the biggest day of the season.

"Since he made his debut, he has represented what we want a Rooster to be.

"He has been incredibly consistent, selfless and dependable, and whenever there has been a big moment or a tough moment, he has been present.

"Toops revolutionised the aerial game at the Sydney Roosters and became the greatest high-ball specialist of all time."

Tupou's exit comes as the Roosters prepare for a big off-season exodus over the coming weeks.

Fellow winger Mark Nawaqanitawase and second rower Angus Crichton are moving to rugby union, playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans is heading to Super League side Hull FC, and Connor Watson is joining St George Illawarra.

But none of them gets close to having the impact the towering winger has had on the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2012.

As well as four premierships (2013, 2018, 2019, 2026), Tupou has won three World Club Challenges and played Test matches for both Tonga and Australia.

He was part of the Tongan side that defeated the Kangaroos in 2019 in one of the biggest upsets in international rugby league history.

Tupou played 10 times for NSW at State of Origin level between 2014 and 2022.

"We love Toops, we're incredibly proud of him, and his name will always hold a very special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters," Robinson said.

Tupou retires as the greatest try-scorer in Roosters history after surpassing Anthony Minichiello in 2023.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Lionel Messi scores final goal in emotional farewell to Argentina
World.content:
Lionel Messi has delivered one last masterclass in blue and white as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international ​career by scoring a goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium was less about football ​and more a national ‌celebration of Messi's service to Argentina.

Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team's sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans ‌poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem.

Messi's family watched proudly ⁠from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of ‌1978, 1986 and 2022.

"Even through the worst moments we went through, I never stopped fighting, battling, giving everything I had, wanting to always be here," Messi told the crowd after full-time.

Lionel Messi was emotional as he signed off from international duty. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

"I love all of you, and I will miss all of you. I am proud to be Argentine."

Hours earlier, a ​massive number 10 shirt ‌emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's home town.

As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route.

When the teams took the pitch, Benin captain Sessi D'Almeida looked lost ​for ‌words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake.

The crowd rose for applause and more fireworks erupted in the stadium as the clock ticked past the 10th minute of the match.

After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home ⁠Argentina's opener.

Otamendi shared 17 years with ‌Messi in the national team, including ‌four World Cups, and was also ending his international career.

Messi then set up Nico Paz, one ‌of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's number 10 shirt, to score the second goal.

In a fairytale ending, Messi converted ‌a penalty ​for 3-0, his 126th ⁠international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd.

At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent ⁠Argentina career.

Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international ‌stage into a ‌story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.

For years, Argentina asked ​Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say thank you.

Reuters

World.title: Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
World.content:
Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.

With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.

Marnus Labuschagne picked a good time to score a century ahead of the first Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).

Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.

Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.

Darren Lehmann sees clear reasons for the decline in Test batting, with serious consequences for the game (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.

The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.

ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.

Steve Smith, Travis Head and Alex Carey have all averaged more than 40 over the past 18 Tests. Marnus Labuschagne is in the 20s. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.

We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.

To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.

Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.

It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.

The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.

This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.

Ricky Ponting was at his peak in the early 2000s. (ABC News)

The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.

To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.

The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.

Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.

But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.

Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.

In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.

From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.

It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.

The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.

In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.

The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.

Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.

The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.

The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.

But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26

That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.

To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.

So, why is this happening?

Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.

Darren Lehmann (right) as coach of Australia in 2014, with the current head of selectors, George Bailey, and the late Rod Marsh. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.

"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.

"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"

"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."

The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.

"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.

Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.

"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.

The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.

"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.

"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."

Mitchell Starc can be relied on to take wickets. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."

Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.

Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.

Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.

"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."

Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.
