World.title: Athletes drive to make table tennis a smash at national Special Olympics debut
World.content:
The repetitive click-clack of a small white ball paddling back and forth over a net may seem like a simple game of ping pong, but for these three teammates, it could be their ticket to the world stage.

The Bundaberg athletes are gearing up to compete in the Special Olympics Australia in Melbourne later this month, where table tennis is making its competitive debut.

Oscar Quarrell, 16, is diligently working to perfect his pendulum — a serve with a bit of side and back spin.

Oscar Quarrell (right) talks with coach Ha Bui as he prepares to play in his first Special Olympics. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Oscar is one of three from his regional club, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, to be selected as part of the 14-strong Queensland table tennis team.

"I love table tennis because it's something that takes my mind off thinking and gives me a break," he said.

"It's also very fun to do with people that actually enjoy hanging around you."

Celebrating 50 years

The Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities, cognitive delays or autism. It is also an organisation that supports community-based clubs and participation.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Special Olympics movement in Australia.

Oscar Quarrell, Taylah Sim and Nicholas Jefferson train with coach Ha Bui. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Special Olympics Australia CEO Jamie O'Connor said 850 athletes across 13 sports would compete at the 2026 games.

"Special Olympics provides programs at a grassroots level week in, week out, at a community level," he said.

"But it also has the path that goes through local competitions to state events, to national events, to international events.

"Our Special Olympics is more about participation opportunities than it is about winning gold medals."

Mr O'Connor said that, in addition to the inclusion of table tennis, dance sport would be a demonstration sport for the first time this year.

Oscar Quarrell practises with Taylah Sim. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

"As sport evolves, and the demand for different sports evolves, then we try and provide options for people with intellectual disability and the sports that they want to compete in," he said.

About 60 athletes who are successful in the national games will go on to compete at the Special Olympics World Games in Santiago, Chile, next October.

Trio take on games

As the excitement builds towards the national games alongside his backhand, Oscar was also preparing for a big leap in independence.

"I'm excited to do something different, and it's also the first time I haven't had my parents with me, so they are going to come and watch, but I'm not allowed to speak to them," he said.

Clubmates Taylah and Nicholas will be joining Oscar in Melbourne.

Taylah Sim has been putting in the hours to prepare for her Special Olympics debut. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Taylah has her eyes firmly on the prize, saying she looks forward to winning then going on to compete at the world games.

Nicholas is also hoping to win a medal, having played the game for 13 years.

His mum, Margaret, said table tennis had opened doors for her son and she enjoyed watching the competition.

"They all want to do their best but, at the end of the day, whoever gets first, second or last, they're all rewarded, and they are happy for them," Ms Jefferson said.

"There's cheering, there's no jealousy, they're here to support each other."

Table tennis has opened doors for Nicholas Jefferson. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Queensland table tennis head coach Kim Hammermeister had high hopes for her Queensland team when they competed at the national level for the first time.

"Bundaberg has always been very strong with their school program for people with an intellectual impairment," she said.

Ms Hammermeister said any Special Olympics sport provided opportunities for friendship.

"People with an intellectual impairment can become very isolated, especially after school," she said.

"Of course, the physical benefits of being active are amazing; you can't put a price on that."

World.title: Bombers call draft 'a priority' after Ridley deal amid Blakey link
World.content:
Essendon has once again headlined the trade period after sending veteran defender Jordan Ridley to Geelong in a bumper deal involving the exchange of four draft picks.

Essendon acquired Jack Bowes, who had requested a move to the club, a 2027 first-round selection and a 2028 second-round selection in exchange for Ridley, a fourth-round selection in this year's draft (currently No.60) and 2028 fourth-round pick.

The move comes as the Bombers and Cats were two of three clubs reported to have canvassed a move for Sydney's Nick Blakey, with St Kilda the third.

Blakey is contracted through 2031 with Sydney and there is no indication thus far that the Swans will agree to a trade this summer.

Nick Blakey could be seeking a move away from Sydney. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

While Essendon may be interested in Blakey, given its Sydney links through Mark McVeigh and John Longmire, the Bombers maintain that "bringing in young talent is the priority". It is unclear how the 26-year-old Blakey would fit into that equation.

Geelong and St Kilda also remain at an impasse over a deal for Saints ruckman Rowan Marshall, who wants to join the Cats for the second straight year.

The Cats will likely have to part ways with players if they are successful in luring Marshall and Blakey, with Gryan Miers's name continuing to be linked with a move away.

Miers's agent, Liam Pickering, said on Wednesday that the 27-year-old will not be joining West Coast, but left the door open to another rival club.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all of Wednesday's trade action.

World.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after China Open incident
World.content:
Coco Gauff says she received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after beating local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open.

The ‌American won 7-5, 6-1 on Monday to reach the fourth round but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set.

She raised her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.

After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff won the replayed point and held serve ⁠for 5-5 before cruising to victory against her 16-year-old opponent.

De Minaur retires from China Open with injury Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

The two-time major singles champion said she received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.

"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur.

"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.

"Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."

The WTA has made efforts to ‌tackle ⁠online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.

A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.

Gauff explained she was ⁠following the rules when she challenged the point.

Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.

Gauff said she spoke to Sun about the ⁠point at the end of the match.

"I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff wrote.

"I didn't like to see ⁠her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career.

"It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

Reuters

World.title: Aussies dealt major injury blow ahead of first South Africa Test
World.content:
Cameron Green has been ruled out of the first Test against South Africa in Durban after succumbing to an abdominal strain.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald said Green failed to overcome the injury, which he suffered in the final one-day international (ODI) played in Potchefstroom last week.

McDonald said it was "highly unlikely" Green would bowl later in the series, should he prove his fitness for the remaining two Tests.

The injury blow is likely to leave Australia with a choice to make between Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson at number five in the batting order for the first Test, which begins on Friday night, AEST.

Travis Head is expected to remain as opener, with Alex Carey to bat at six.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Green appeared to be finding some rhythm with the bat, having scored a century against Bangladesh in Darwin in August.

"He is progressing pretty well, all things considered … he is still here for a reason, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel," McDonald said

"It will just be a matter of going through the rehab. He has a pretty demanding week as he reintroduced some activities.

"It's a bit of an unknown, but there is still optimism that he will take part in the series at some stage."

Green had been managing a shoulder injury that stopped him bowling in the white-ball matches against the Proteas.

His planned bowling return in the final ODI was aborted due to the abdominal injury.

"We would be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter. We wouldn't be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler," McDonald said.

"That would be too high-risk, is the information I have."

Maddinson has not played a Test for Australia since 2016 but was a surprise addition to the squad last week when Josh Inglis suffered a fractured finger.

Australia is also weighing up whether a dry Durban surface pushes them towards picking Connolly, with an expectation the Kingsmead wicket will turn later in the match.

Matt Kuhnemann is also on the tour as a second spinner, but it would appear unlikely Australia will opt to play him ahead of one of the three frontline quicks.

Green's injury also increases the chances of Beau Webster holding his spot as a fourth seamer, after he played in the last three Tests batting at number seven.

AAP

World.title: Geelong scores major coup with Matildas-Colombia clash
World.content:
The Matildas will return to Victoria this year, with Geelong's Kardinia Park named as the venue for the second leg of a two-match series against Colombia.

The Victorian government today announced the December 2 fixture, two years after 30,000 fans packed out the regional stadium to see the "Tillies" beat Chinese Taipei 6-0.

The announcement is a major coup for Geelong, which will be the only Victorian city to host the Matildas this year.

The national team last played in Victoria in May 2025.

"This blockbuster clash will drive visitation across the Geelong region, support local businesses and showcase Victoria's unmatched ability to host world-class sporting events," Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements said.

Football Australia deputy chief executive Heather Garriock said Victorians' support of the Matildas was "always outstanding".

"We're delighted to bring the CommBank Matildas back to Victoria for what promises to be a special occasion for football fans, as our FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 preparations intensify," Ms Garriock said.

The first leg of the Colombia series will be played at Canberra Stadium on November 28, with the games expected to serve as a valuable test ahead of the World Cup in Brazil in June.

Both Australia and Colombia have already qualified for the World Cup.

Matildas fans were out in force in 2023, and will be raring to go in Brazil (AAP Image)

The Matildas finished fourth in the 2023 World Cup, and earlier this year were runners up in the AFC Women's Asian Cup.

Ms Garriock, who is also Football Australia's executive director of football, in August said the Colombia series would be an opportunity to give younger talent a chance to impress.

"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Ms Garriock said.

"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.

"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well."

Tech.title: Ring’s first smart lock can be charged by turning a dial when the battery unexpectedly dies
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon announced its first smart lock that eliminates the need for a physical backup key should its rechargeable battery die while you’re away from home. While other smart locks lean on hidden USB ports or metal contacts for connecting a 9-volt battery to replenish a dead battery, the new Ring Smart Lock incorporates a more convenient charger right into its thumb-turn dial. Amazon doesn’t specify how many turns are needed but claims just “a few times” can generate enough power to unlock the door so you can gain access to your home and fully recharge the lock’s battery.

The Ring Smart Lock is expected to be available in the US sometime in early 2027 (pending FCC approval) and will be offered in black, silver, and brass finishes for $249. Unlocking options include a fingerprint reader and a backlit touchscreen keypad with the option to register multiple users and schedule when they have access to your home. This includes setting up temporary access codes that automatically expire after a set amount of time. The Ring Smart Lock can also be opened, locked, and monitored using the Ring mobile app or controlled using voice commands through Alexa-compatible devices like Echo smart speakers.

Installation doesn’t require any wiring since the Smart Lock uses Ring’s replaceable Quick Release Ultra Battery Pack, and instead of relying on your home’s Wi-Fi, the lock wirelessly connects to other devices using Amazon’s low-power, low-bandwidth, long-range Sidewalk network. Assuming you live somewhere with adequate Sidewalk coverage, you won’t have to worry about Wi-Fi outages preventing you from granting remote access or getting alerts about who’s just entered your home.

From left: The $150 Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, the $200 Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, the $220 Floodlight Cam 4K Plus, and the $100 Indoor Cam 4K. Image: Amazon

The Ring Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K can be mounted to a wall or used self-standing, but tethered access to a power source is required. Image: Amazon

Alongside all the new 4K options, Amazon is also introducing a new entry-level 2K indoor camera that’s available starting today for $69.99. The Ring Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K uses “computer vision–based motion detection” to track subjects like pets moving around a room. The camera can rotate a full 360 degrees while tilting 175 degrees to keep subjects in frame, and like Ring’s new 4K indoor camera, the 2K version incorporates a physical privacy shutter that disables both the camera and its microphone when it’s closed.

Tech.title: My cats hate to see this great upright carpet cleaner coming
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For a while, I swore by Bissell’s Little Green carpet cleaner. I liked the sub-$100 price, the fact that it was small enough to fit on a closet shelf, and that it does a good job of cleaning up little messes. However, after you clean enough spots around the place, eventually the entire carpet needs a cleaning because the cleaned spots appear in stark contrast. It looks bad!

For a job that big, I upgraded (after doing a lot of research) to Bissell’s ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro Plus. It’s a great upright machine with more power, though I wish I had waited, having paid $279.99 about a month ago. You can currently get one for $209.99 during October Prime Day at Amazon and Bissell (discount reflects at checkout).

While the Little Green leaves the scrubbing up to you (it handles the sucking), the ProHeat 2X has plenty of deep-cleaning brushes, large reservoirs for dirty water and for cleaning fluid, plus an accessory port that lets you connect a brush-equipped hose for spot cleaning, essentially duplicating every feature I liked of the smaller model.

You’ll need to pony up for some cleaning solution after a handful of large-scale cleaning efforts, and it’s about $23 for a big bottle. I’ve found that you don’t need to use as much of the solution per gallon of water as Bissell notes on the bottle.

Unfortunately, one of my cats threw up at various places around our apartment last night (why can’t cats just do it all in one place?), so I’ll be using this carpet cleaner today. Wish me luck.

Tech.title: Amazon uses its tracking data to guess whether shoppers have a flat butt and no friends
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Most people know that Amazon collects data about your shopping history to serve up personalized product recommendations. But what some of us didn’t realize is that you can check exactly what Amazon knows — or thinks it knows — about you in your settings menu. One user’s findings went viral on Threads after she discovered that Amazon assumed she “has flat buttocks” based on her purchases, resulting in a flood of other posts with users sharing the oddly specific information Amazon uses to describe them.

While some of these descriptions seem like a roast from Amazon, most of them are pretty generic. For example, mine says I “maintain active aquarium systems,” “regularly consume coffee,” and “play video games regularly,” all of which are accurate.

If you want to see what Amazon may have learned about you, you can find out by selecting your account icon in the top-right corner of your screen, scrolling down to the “Your Account” section, and hitting “Your Shopping preferences.” From there, scroll down the page and select “About You.” You’ll then see a list of details Amazon uses to personalize your account, which you can edit or delete.

Tech.title: Windows and Surface event: how to watch and what to expect
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft is heading to San Francisco this morning to reveal what’s coming next for Windows and Surface and a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.” That conversation will include Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri.

I’m expecting to hear a lot more about Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform and Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra that uses Nvidia’s new Arm-based chips.

When Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event will happen and where you can watch it

Microsoft’s keynote will start at 10AM PT / 1PM ET on Wednesday October 7th. The full presentation should run for around an hour. You can watch it live on YouTube, but the best way to follow along is through our live blog.

What to expect from Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event

Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft already unveiled its MacBook Pro competitor earlier this year, but we’re still waiting on pricing, release dates, and full specs. I’d expect we’ll get all of these details and lots more. Microsoft already unveiled its MacBook Pro competitor earlier this year, but we’re still waiting on pricing, release dates, and full specs. I’d expect we’ll get all of these details and lots more. Rumors suggest Microsoft will release multi configurations of the Laptop Ultra, with 18-core and 20-core CPU variants and RAM configurations all the way up to 128GB.

RTX Spark platform. Jensen Huang will appear on stage, so we’re likely to get even more details on Nvidia’s effort to shake-up the Windows laptop market. Microsoft might have the hero device, but there are plenty of OEMs also preparing to launch RTX Spark-powered laptops.

Windows AI agent news. I expect we’ll hear a lot more about Microsoft’s plans to have AI agents running locally on Windows. The Surface Laptop Ultra supercharges these kind of agents thanks to Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips, and Microsoft has already been laying the groundwork for AI agents in Windows for I expect we’ll hear a lot more about Microsoft’s plans to have AI agents running locally on Windows. The Surface Laptop Ultra supercharges these kind of agents thanks to Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips, and Microsoft has already been laying the groundwork for AI agents in Windows for nearly a year now

Windows 11 improvements. Microsoft has been working to improve lots of parts of Windows 11, including performance on 8GB of RAM devices. I’d expect we’ll hear more about these ongoing efforts, as well as some new Windows features designed for developers and creatives.

Tech.title: The Social Reckoning is a tepid thriller that reminds us of how we got here
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

When David Fincher’s The Social Network premiered in 2010, many people still thought of Mark Zuckerberg as a genius who had revolutionized the world by creating Facebook. Writer Aaron Sorkin’s script was critical of Zuckerberg’s character and his ruthless approach to doing business, but it also helped mythologize the co-founder at a time when the general public was much more enchanted by Silicon Valley. When Zuckerberg said in 2014 that he’d been hurt by the film’s depiction of him, Fincher said he was “sorry that it did” and admitted that he “wouldn’t want a movie made about the things I did when I was 19 years old,” either. Fincher’s apology was a reflection of how much grace the public was willing to extend to the world’s (then) youngest billionaire. But in 2026, it is hard to imagine anyone having all that much sympathy for the man running Meta.

The film lacks the propulsive energy that made The Social Network feel operatic.

Similar to the way The Social Network spun details from Ben Mezrich’s book The Accidental Billionaires into a riveting drama, writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoningweaves a narrative around The Wall Street Journal’s bombshell reporting with Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen. Billed as a companion piece rather than a direct sequel, The Social Reckoning chronicles Haugen’s time within Facebook and uses her story to illustrate how the company’s focus on exponential growth turned it into a societal threat. Zuckerberg looms large in the movie, but Sorkin feels far more interested in focusing on the friction that exists between traditional media and tech giants.

Though The Social Reckoning’s core messages about how our lives have been negatively impacted by the rise of social media algorithms are potent, the film lacks the propulsive, thrilling energy that made The Social Network feel operatic. The film does an excellent job of presenting our present day reality as the end result of events Zuckerberg and Facebook helped facilitate. But for all of its insight, The Social Reckoning still feels like a feature that’s arriving a little too late to have a meaningful impact.

The Social Reckoning spends much of its 112 minute runtime ping ponging back and forth through the years when Haugen (Mikey Madison) worked as a product manager on Facebook’s civic integrity team. As the film opens in 2019, Haugen’s just beginning to understand how hate speech and misinformation are being amplified by the platform’s algorithms. Haugen genuinely believes that Facebook could take steps to mitigate these harms if any of her colleagues would take them seriously. But when she realizes that no one else in the company is willing to speak up about Mark Zuckerberg’s (Jeremy Strong) single-minded focus on boosting Facebook’s engagement at all costs, she turns to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White).

Sorkin presents Haugen and Horwitz as uneasy allies. The duo both understand that Facebook is the news for millions of people, but the only way they can report the truth about what’s happening within the company is by doing things the old fashioned way. You can hear echoes of Sorkin’s The Newsroom in Horwitz’s quippy exchanges with taciturn bureau chief Christina (Betty Gilpin) and overworked interns (Aidan Laprete, Kelley Pereira) about the importance of their work. The film frames its reporter characters as competent heroes who are trying to do the public an important service. It does not consistently do the same for the whistleblower, and Sorkin writes Haugen’s dialog with a degree of levity that often feels at odds with the gravity of the larger story.

Madison and White try their best to turn Sorkin’s script into dialog that sounds like it might be spoken by regular humans.

The Social Reckoning feels most like a proper thriller in tense moments when Haugen and Horwitz are secretly meeting in parks and hotel rooms to pore over damning internal documents detailing how Facebook was well aware of its products’ potential to do harm. The movie effectively depicts Facebook — in its pursuit for growth — knowingly becoming a place where conspiracy groups could thrive and radicalize people. Sorkin doesn’t go so far as to solely blame Facebook for turning the modern internet into a nightmare that’s flooded with ragebait and intentionally deceptive information. But The Social Reckoning does make the implicit argument that things might not be so bad today if Zuckerberg had acted more conscientiously in his quest to stay one step ahead of his competitors.

Image: Sony

Though Madison and White try their best to turn Sorkin’s script into dialog that sounds like it might be spoken by regular humans, the writer-director’s penchant for rapidfire back-and-forths gets the better of him here. Sorkin clearly wanted to make The Social Reckoning as dense with information as he possibly could, but in doing so, he made it harder for the movie to work as an entertaining drama. The Social Reckoning truly shines in its handful of scenes that zoom in on an older, more calculating Zuckerberg as he’s preparing to speak at Congressional hearings. Whereas Jesse Eisenberg played Zuckerberg in The Social Network with a quiet vulnerability, Strong leans into an unsettlingly robotic aura that makes his performance feel studied. Strong’s Zuckerberg gives you the distinct sense that he is a man whose success is a testament to his willingness to prioritize profit over people’s well-being.

Especially for those who didn’t follow the Wall Street Journal’s Facebook reporting in real time, The Social Reckoning may serve as a useful recollection of how the company was — at one point, at least — held somewhat accountable for its actions. But the movie also serves as a bleak reminder of how there still hasn’t really been a substantive reckoning that fundamentally changed the way people interact with Meta’s (née Facebook) products. Sorkin seems to believe that a day may come when the public decides that companies like Meta can’t be trusted with the power to shape our perceptions of reality. It’s a hopeful thought, but in 2026, it feels like a dream that has already gotten away from us.

The Social Reckoning also stars Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen, Patrick Fischler, and Nelson Franklin. The movie hits theaters on October 9th.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Buds update will put them to sleep along with you
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google has detailed an update bringing a slew of new features to its Pixel Buds 2A and Pro 2, which the company says are rolling out now. The new features were first teased in August.

The biggest update is Pixel Watch-powered sleep detection, rolling out to both pairs of earbuds. If you’re wearing a Pixel Watch, the buds will now react when you fall asleep, by pausing music, silencing notifications, and turning off touch controls.

Several other updates are also coming to both the Buds 2A and Pro. Tap-to-mute allows you to mute or unmute your microphone with a quick tap during calls, though only when also using a Pixel phone, and you can now activate live translation with a single tap. New Gemini voice commands will allow you to control active noise cancellation (ANC), adjust the EQ, or turn on touch controls.

The final new feature is Dynamic ANC, which will adjust audio and ANC levels based on the quality of the buds’ seal in your ears. This is exclusive to the Buds Pro 2.

Google announced the update rollout in a Pixel Buds community forum post. The original version of the announcement, posted yesterday, said that all the features except Dynamic ANC would also be coming to the original Pixel Buds Pro, but all mention of those earbuds has now been removed from the post. We’ve reached out to Google for comment on the change.

Tech.title: AI could upend food delivery
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

DoorDash, the leading food delivery app, processed 970 million orders in its second quarter this year and generated $4.5 billion in revenue. A 10-person startup called Bites is a blip in comparison: It has just around 300 restaurants signed up in the Bay Area, where it’s operating as a pre-seed startup. But this summer, Bites caught DoorDash’s attention.

In August, a slew of restaurants in the Bay Area received a strange email from DoorDash, warning businesses that they may be listed without their consent on Bites.

The form letter, copies of which were seen by The Verge, said that DoorDash had heard from “several partners” that were added to the third-party platform without their knowledge. DoorDash warned restaurants that they may not have agreed to Bites’ “terms, pricing structures, or service standards”; that they may not have control over the accuracy of their menu or hours of operation on Bites; and that, depending on the state, “such practices could be illegal.” The email included instructions on how to contact Bites to request removal.

One way to look at the warning is DoorDash proactively alerting its restaurant partners. But DoorDash going on the offense over a relatively small peer hints at a battle taking shape between established apps and newer, leaner startups looking to upend business in the age of AI.

Tech companies have promised that the future of AI is that ordinary people will have “agents” completing tasks: scheduling meetings, looking for deals on socks, sifting through their inbox and replying to emails, and yes, ordering food on their behalf. If this really does come to bear — if billions of people shift to interact with the internet not through search engines, webpages, and apps, but through large language models — those websites and services will lose control of the relationship with consumers as they stop visiting webpages and apps. What happens to Amazon when it can’t show shoppers boosted item listings because they don’t come to the site? What happens when Uber can’t entice riders with a free subscription trial? What happens when a food delivery service can upsell you to throw in a bottle of wine with dinner? The Verge has coined this brewing fight “the DoorDash problem.” Bites is now the literal embodiment of the term.

Bites’ pitch is simple: Companies like DoorDash are the middleman, forcing restaurants to raise prices to cover the commission the platforms take, leaving customers paying more to make up the difference. DoorDash fees for restaurants range anywhere from 15 to 30 percent per delivery order — the more in commission fees a restaurant forks over, the more diners they are visible to on the platform. Bites, on the other hand, touts simplified delivery and service fees and a flat $1 surcharge per order, which it says allows partners to keep item prices lower. (Diners typically pay the $1 fee, but some restaurants will cover it on a customer’s behalf.) Bites has a traditional app, but it bills itself as “AI native”: Diners can place orders from Bites restaurants directly in ChatGPT, which go not to a third-party platform like DoorDash, but directly to the restaurant.

Bites founder and CEO Bala Subramaniam says the company heard from 14 restaurant partners who had received a letter from DoorDash, and a handful of businesses who were not listed on Bites but now — having been made aware of the company — wanted to join. (Bites also acknowledges some restaurants did request to be removed from the platform; the company says they were listed on Bites from old demos.) Others got emails despite not being listed at all. One of the emails went to Jay Jayaraman, who has 13 restaurants listed on Bites and considers himself an early adopter of the platform.

Before being on Bites, Jayaraman says 80 percent of orders came from DoorDash; now, 65 percent come in through Bites, he estimates, with 25 percent from DoorDash and the remaining sliver from Uber Eats and Grubhub. Jayaraman says his margins are higher with Bites orders than with DoorDash orders.

“We are seeing a huge drop or a huge shift away from DoorDash, which I personally welcome because it’s adding to my bottom line,” Jayaraman says.

LLMs becoming the portal to the web threatens app- and website-based businesses in myriad ways. A shift away from visiting websites and using individual apps means those companies can’t do things like show consumers similar products, offer deals and free trials, and, significantly, monetize via ads and boosted listings. (DoorDash doesn’t only make money via subscriptions and commission fees — its ads business hit $1 billion in 2024.) The most prominent instance of the LLM-service provider tension materializing is the ongoing legal fight between AI company Perplexity and Amazon, in which Amazon sued Perplexity in 2025 to block agents from browsing and shopping on its site. Amazon has also recently blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from shopping on its site and removed product details from order emails — data that is potentially very valuable for Google’s own agentic shopping features. Amazon’s ad business generated $19.8 billion in revenue in the second quarter of this year, driven by sponsored product listings.

“All of that investment does not have to be made anymore, and yet the pricing has stayed the same.”

Bites can keep prices lower for customers and restaurants because the pricing structure on bigger platforms is outdated, says Matt Maloney, who cofounded both Bites and Grubhub. (Maloney left Grubhub in 2021 after the company was acquired. His involvement with Bites hasn’t been previously reported.) Delivery services spent billions of dollars to build online ordering infrastructure, as well as courting restaurants, diners, and drivers onto their platforms — restaurants raising item prices on delivery apps to offset the high commissions and fees are a relic of that era, Maloney argues. But post-covid lockdown, nobody needs to be convinced of the convenience of delivery.

“All of that investment does not have to be made anymore, and yet the pricing has stayed the same,” Maloney says. Bites partners with point-of-sale systems — companies like Toast and Square that process orders — to pull digitized menus into LLMs and send orders directly to restaurants, instead of through an intermediary like DoorDash. Once a point-of-sale company is partnered with Bites, restaurants click a button to opt in. The Verge tested the service by ordering a pizza and beverage for delivery through ChatGPT using the Bites plugin, which came to a total of $56.73 including tip, tax, and delivery fees. The same order on DoorDash totaled $70.29, which had higher service fees and the same pizza priced $11 more.

“People think it’s the delivery apps that are egregious, [but] it’s actually the model that has made the restaurants actually increase the prices,” Subramaniam, who previously worked at Instacart, says. “And they are actually hungry for a new model.”

Subramaniam says Bites is especially geared toward the diners who already know where they want to eat and don’t need a third-party platform like DoorDash to find them.

“It may not become the discovery platform,” he says. “We don’t need to have sponsored ads … but if you know where you want to eat, we will get you to the place that you want to eat, with the best pricing.”

The explosion of food delivery during the pandemic helped many restaurants stay afloat, but complaints from owners about the platforms are just as common — the high commission fees, the need to buy ads and boost listings, and the wedge that third-party apps create between the people making the food and the people eating it. Platforms like DoorDash withhold most data from the restaurants, typically only sharing a customer’s first name, last initial, and what they ordered. That data is valuable to restaurants: A business could use direct contact information to send discounts or notices to customers, develop loyalty programs, or offer customer support if there are problems with the food that’s delivered. Instead, delivery apps hold on to that information. This has spilled into the courtroom, too: A New York City law attempted to compel third-party platforms to share customer information with restaurants upon request, but was struck down by a judge. Jayaraman, the restaurateur, says he gets “absolutely nothing” from DoorDash when it comes to customer data; with Bites he is able to contact customers directly because the orders (and customer contact information) come straight to him.

Platforms like DoorDash withhold most customer data from restaurants

DoorDash didn’t respond to specific questions around its pricing structure, what data it shares with restaurants, or how AI might disrupt the app-based model of ordering takeout. Spokesperson Lisa Singh told The Verge that “some restaurant partners raised concerns” about appearing on Bites without their consent. “The information shared with partners made clear that no action was needed if they had opted in,” Singh said.

DoorDash itself has signaled agentic ordering is a priority: The company announced in September it was working on a way for diners to place orders within iMessage using prompts like “reorder my usual from [restaurant].” Even this upends the business model — if an agent does the ordering for diners who already know what they want, what does a restaurant get for spending money boosting its business on the DoorDash app? A major benefit that delivery platforms provide is discovery. It’s still not clear what that looks like in an agentic future.

For Jayaraman, there is no love lost for the current business model of delivery apps — but even as the portion of takeout that comes through DoorDash dwindles, he plans to stay on the platform to serve those customers. The AI industry has made lofty promises to the public — automating chores and tasks, saving time and money while shopping, and providing endlessly compliant, personalized virtual assistants at humans’ beck and call. Whether that becomes a reality depends on both customers and goods and service providers agreeing that it’s the future. Jayaraman has not yet turned on ChatGPT ordering, saying he wants to see a live demo from Bites first and hear its pitch.

Subramaniam and Maloney see the emails sent by DoorDash as proof that they’re on the right track. Jayaraman, too, took the email as a sign that the market leader was worried.

“I didn’t respond,” Jayaraman says of receiving the email from DoorDash. “I was very happy when I received the letter, because DoorDash is feeling the pain.”

Tech.title: At $1,279, Google’s Xreal Aura will go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two weeks ago, journalists in the San Francisco Bay Area got to try two hot new wearables that weigh only around 100 grams: the just-revealed Meta VR Glasses, and the long-awaited transparent Google XR glasses built in partnership with Xreal. It turns out they’re going head-to-head. Xreal has just opened Aura pre-orders starting at $1,279, $20 less than the Meta VR Glasses.

That’s for the Xreal Aura with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage; there’ll also be a 16GB / 512GB config for $1,499. (Xreal couldn’t tell us whether the 16GB of RAM would be important for some apps by publish time.)

Both the Google / Xreal Aura and Meta’s VR Glasses let you overlay virtual objects and desktops on the real world. Both are relatively lightweight because they’ve got a cord — their Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chips and batteries both live in a compute puck, which runs either Meta’s Horizon OS or Android XR. Both greet you with a grid of floating app icons to choose from.

Image: Xreal

But they’re very different experiences in practice, primarily because the Google / Xreal Aura has transparent lenses, while the Meta VR Glasses use passthrough vision to let you see the real world and offers more immersion. While the Xreal Aura has one of the largest transparent fields of view yet at 70 degrees diagonal, it’s still smaller than Meta’s passthrough glasses. I wrote all about it in this story, and it’s just one of many differences.

The Meta VR Glasses also have eye tracking, like the Apple Vision Pro, so you can select things just by looking at them and pinching fingers resting on your lap; the Google / Xreal Aura has a touchpad built into the compute puck and hand-tracking to give you virtual laser pointers. (Both let you connect to other peripherals and display other devices too — and you can plug devices with USB-C DisplayPort video right in.)

And, of course, you’ve got your Android apps inside the Xreal Aura, or your Quest games inside the VR Glasses.

I don’t think any journalist can tell you which is better yet; you may want to wait for reviews. We also have yet to test Android XR extensively: while Samsung and Google did technically ship the $1,799 Galaxy XR with Android XR last year, they didn’t send one to The Verge for review.

The Meta VR Glasses aren’t due until spring 2027, but Xreal isn’t necessarily shipping lots of pairs before then. Today, the only people who can preorder the Xreal glasses are those who already put in a reservation, and only the first 2,000 “Founder’s Edition” pairs are necessarily coming at “launch.” Those will ship this year, Xreal CEO and co-founder Chi Xu tells The Verge.

Image: Xreal

It might not take till the end of the year. Xreal’s press release does say they “will begin shipping soon” and that the “launch” is “now just weeks away,” but those are wiggly, and again, those timeframes are just for early adopters. If you don’t have a preorder, “Orders will open to the general public in the coming weeks.” The glasses will also only ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea to start, before expanding to other regions in 2027.

I’m already a fan of Xreal’s glasses and how they let me watch my 3D movies with a 57-degree field of view, and I’m intrigued by the puck. I’d love to see how much more useful these glasses are with a 70-degree view.

Tech.title: Google’s new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media
Tech.content:
In Brief

Google on Tuesday launched a new site that lets anyone verify whether a piece of media, be it an image, a video or an audio clip, is generated using AI.

The company had made this tool available to select journalists, media professionals and researchers for testing at Google I/O last year, and is now opening up access to the tool to everyone.

The site supports JPG, JPEG, PNG, BMP, WEBP, AVIF, HEIC, HEIF, TIFF, TIF, and GIF formats for images; MP4, MOV, and WEBM for videos; and WAV, MP3, OGG, FLAC, AAC, and M4A for audio.

Image Credits: Google Image Credits:Google

Google is using SynthID, which it introduced in 2023, to identify whether media is AI-generated. The company’s Nano Banana, Veo and Lyria models, as well as tools with generation capabilities, like Gemini, Flow, ProducerAI and Vids, all use SynthID to watermark any media they generate.

OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao also support SynthID, and OpenAI maintains its own site for checking content. Apple is said to be adding support soon, too.

Google has baked SynthID verification into the Gemini app and Google Chrome. The company said people currently make 1 million requests to verify content every day.

Microsoft and Meta have their own standards for watermarking and verifying content. However, these tools are not infallible, often failing to identify content created by their makers’ models.

Tech.title: Ring’s first smart lock can be hand-cranked when its battery dies
Tech.content:
Ring, the Amazon-owned video doorbell maker, is entering a new market: smart locks.

Ring’s new device isn’t exactly a copy-and-paste of the other locks already on the market, however, as it tackles a big issue that often deters people from embracing this kind of smart home equipment: the fear of the battery dying and getting locked out.

To address this, Ring’s smart lock has added a power dial. If the battery on the device runs out, the homeowner can just turn the dial a few times to power the lock back up and enter their home.

Ring’s founder Jamie Siminoff said the idea to rethink smart locks came to him when he was looking to buy a lock for a vacation home. “I struggled because this particular house will get used very little, and I know the freaking battery will die on it,” he said.

He also worried that family or friends visiting the house might get stuck outside, as the door isn’t connected to a power source, and any smart lock would be dependent on the battery.

“I’m like, well, why don’t we just fix this,” he said. Using AI, he started working on a project to create a lock you could hand-crank just enough to power the lock to open. Once you’re in, you could then take out the rechargeable battery pack and charge it as usual.

Siminoff says the battery on Ring’s new lock will last about a year, and will alert users when it’s time to charge via the Ring app. The app also allows users to configure access for people who may need periodic access, like dog walkers or house cleaners. Eventually, the company wants to allow third-party app makers to design specialized software for the lock so it can be used in other ways — for example, Airbnb owners who may need to regularly change codes.

The Ring lock also offers four different ways to get in, so you won’t have to worry about forgetting a code. You can either use the device’s fingerprint reader, a backlit touchscreen keypad, the Ring app, or Alexa.

Siminoff admitted that the lock may be comparable to others on the market, but he thinks the fact that it addresses the anxiety over being locked out will be its biggest selling point.

“I do think the power thing is a huge limiter of why people are not buying, and why they’re not putting them in, and why they’re worried about them,” he said.

It’s also true that when smart locks do offer some sort of backup method, they usually involve something cumbersome and less secure — like hiding a physical key somewhere on the property.

Ring’s smart lock will fit a standard single-cylinder deadbolt, and will be available to purchase in the U.S. in the first quarter of 2027, after it receives FCC authorization. It will come in three finishes: black, silver, or brass.

Alongside the lock, Ring also introduced four new 4K cameras: the Outdoor Cam 4K Plus, Spotlight Cam 4K Plus, Floodlight Cam 4K Plus, and a pan-tilt Indoor Cam 4K.

Tech.title: Another personal AI assistant has launched — Meet Tab, which emerged from stealth with a $300M valuation
Tech.content:
In Brief

A new personal AI assistant has arrived. Meet Tab, which announced Tuesday that it had officially emerged from stealth at a $300 million valuation. (The company declined to share the exact funding details.) Tab is part of the rising trend of consumer AI assistants, like the breakout hit Instinct and Meta’s Muse, that promise to help people handle everyday tasks like making reservations and booking travel.

Brennan Erbz, Stafford Schlitt, and Ammar Amdani started working on Tab earlier this year. Speaking to TechCrunch, Amdani said the product works like this: Users simply text the Tab assistant on iMessage or WhatsApp whatever they need help with — whether that’s ordering groceries or finding presents for a birthday party — and Tab makes it happen.

“You text it like you’d text someone you trust and it takes the weight off,” Amdani continued. “The bills, the bookings, the calls you keep putting off, remembering the people you love. It has its own phone number, computer, and wallet, so it doesn’t tell you how to do those things. It does them.”

Investors in the round include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit. Amdani said the company is growing mostly by word of mouth right now and plans to launch a new product soon.

He acknowledged that this is now somewhat of a consumer AI race. “Everyone is racing to make AI more capable,” Amdani said.

“Your grandparents had a family doctor, a banker, someone who knew them and looked out for them,” Amdani said. “Most of us don’t have that anymore.” That’s where personalized AI can come in, but he said that the winners of this consumer AI race won’t necessarily be the ones with the best demos.

“We think the harder question is whether you should let it in.” Any AI assistant that can read emails or make phone calls or purchase stuff is “only as good as your trust in it.”

It’s why Tab is built around that idea, he said. “Your data is never used to train AI. Your card lives in a vault Tab itself never sees. Nothing that can be undone happens without your ‘yes.’ Capability is table stakes. Trust is the product.”

Tech.title: Spotify expands audiobooks to over 180 markets
Tech.content:
Spotify announced on Wednesday that it’s expanding audiobook access to over 180 markets worldwide, including regions across Europe, the Americas, the Caribbean, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. The rollout is starting today and will continue over the coming months. With this move, more than 750 million users will be able to access audiobooks, allowing Spotify to better compete with both music streaming providers and audiobook apps like Audible.

Before this, audiobooks were available primarily in English-speaking markets like the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, as well as in Germany.

The audio platform said it has more than 350,000 titles for its new markets and has increased its collection to include over 120 languages. With its launch in Spain, users in the country will have access to over 45,000 titles in Spanish.

Spotify is working with more than 300 publishers worldwide, including Planeta and Mondadori, to increase the number of titles available in different markets.

With a Premium subscription, users can listen to 12 hours of audiobooks in eligible countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Poland, Chile, Norway, and Peru. People across the world can also purchase an Audiobook+ stand-alone subscription to get access to titles with a 15-hour allowance. Alternatively, users can buy individual titles directly.

Spotify is also adding an Audiobook+ add-on for student plans in select regions in November. The company said that since its launch last year, Audiobook+ has gained over 1 million subscribers and has fetched over 100 million in annual recurring revenue for the platform.

In February, the company launched a “Page Match” feature, which lets users scan a page of a physical book and find the corresponding point in the audiobook to listen to. Since the launch, 1 million people have been using the feature monthly, the company noted.

Spotify said that over the last year, monthly listeners of audiobooks grew by 40% and listening hours increased by 30%.

This year, the company introduced Audiobook Charts to let people discover popular titles. It also launched an AI-powered tool for authors to turn their books into audiobooks using models from ElevenLabs. Plus, Spotify started experimenting with physical sales of books through its audiobook platform in select markets like the U.S. and the U.K.

Tech.title: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have ‘flat buttocks’
Tech.content:
It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. If you buy a lot of cat litter, Amazon will probably infer that you have cats, or if you buy a lot of anti-acne skin products, then Amazon might guess you’re prone to breakouts. Even if we know that Amazon customizes our shopping experiences based on our purchase history, it still comes as a surprise to see all of these personal details laid out in a convenient list. Especially when those details get uncomfortably intimate.

One Threads user came across this section of her Amazon settings where you can see who the shopping giant thinks you are, and alongside more benign assumptions like “Shops from women’s departments” and “Probably owns a Shark robot vacuum,” she found that Amazon assumes she “has flat buttocks.”

“I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless,” an Amazon customer, @fangirlinmegan, wrote on Threads. “I mean it ain’t wrong but damn did you have to call me out like that?”

In less than a day, the post garnered over a million views, including many from users who were curious what their own Amazon profiles might reveal. Here’s how you find out.

On desktop, you can find this page by hovering over where Amazon says “Hello, [your name]” in the upper right corner. Then click “Account” under the “Your Account” section. Under the “Ordering and shopping preferences” section, click “Your Shopping preferences.” From here, you can add in information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. But we’re not here to tell Amazon that it should stop selling you beef jerky since you’re a vegetarian. We’re here to see if Amazon thinks you have “flat buttocks.” When you scroll to the bottom of the page, you’ll see a blue hyperlinked option that says “Manage your information.” Once you click that, you’ll see what dirt Amazon has on you.

On the mobile app, you can get here by clicking the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar, then navigating to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.

For me, Amazon has gleaned that I am someone who “practices photography,” “plays collectible card games,” and is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” This is all true. Amazon has even flattered me by noting that I “read diverse non-fiction,” to which I say — why yes, I am indeed an open-minded intellectual with a thirst for knowledge. Thank you for noticing.

Other colleagues of mine found that Amazon correctly noted their interests in vinyl records and ceramics, as well as a penchant for “natural materials” in home decor and clothing that “prioritizes comfort.” None of us had anything as affronting as “has flat buttocks,” but the Threads user noted that this was likely because she had purchased “butt scrunch leggings.”

Tech companies know too much about us, and it’s jarring to realize just how closely they’re paying attention to how we use their platforms. We live in a world of alarming surveillance, but at least I know that Amazon doesn’t think my butt is flat.

Tech.title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Already Feels Irrelevant
Tech.content:
When The Social Network hit theaters in 2010, it was fair to wonder if the film had come too soon. Facebook had been launched from Mark Zuckerberg’s Harvard dorm room just six years earlier, and nobody really knew how it would reshape digital community in the decade to come.

But, with a breakneck screenplay by Aaron Sorkin, a menacingly propulsive soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and a surgical performance from Jesse Eisenberg as Young Zuck, director David Fincher delivered a slick corporate thriller about the major drama to that point: intersecting lawsuits over who owned what percentage of the platform and who could lay claim as a founder. It was an electrifying film that seemed to only lightly fictionalize the newest and perhaps most cutthroat generation of Silicon Valley warlords.

Flash forward 16 years, and Facebook (now Meta) has accumulated more scandals than Hollywood could possibly hope to keep up with. Sorkin tells WIRED that he was approached many times over those years with pitches for a sequel, though he struggled to see an angle of approach. “Before a film can be anything else, before it can be relevant or thought-provoking, it has to be good,” he says. “It has to work as something that you watch while you're eating popcorn.”

Then, Sorkin says, he met Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who leaked damning internal memos to investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz. Horwitz wrote up what became known as the “Facebook Files” in a far-ranging 2021 series of articles for The Wall Street Journal, exposing much of what the company knew regarding harms to users—everything from hate speech and medical misinformation to body image issues and human trafficking—but had largely brushed aside in pursuit of growth.

Sorkin still wasn’t sure he had a film, but one day he asked Haugen why she finally decided to go to the media. “She just told me in kind of an offhand way, ‘Oh, I had this friend who was radicalized by Facebook after spending too many hours on the platform,’” he recalls. “And I began to get the idea for what is now the opening scene of the movie.”

The cold open of The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Sorkin, depicts an intoxicated woman pulled over on the side of the road in San Mateo, California, with an overheated car. Approached by police officers, she turns combative, pulling out her phone to record a video as she hurls racist abuse at the cops and is at last arrested for threatening to kill one of them. The video turns up on a Facebook page for far-right content, which is where Haugen (Mikey Madison) finds it in 2019, recognizing the woman as an acquaintance from her pilates class who used to hold progressive views. She also learns that this woman is a superuser, intensely active on Facebook for many hours each day.

Tech.title: I Put on Meta and Xreal’s XR Glasses. Face Computers Are Finally Getting Good
Tech.content:
I’m sorry to say, but the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses might just be very good.

That's despite the company's well-earned flak over privacy issues with its smart glasses and the general uneasiness people feel about being recorded. But in the 30 to 45 minutes or so I spent wearing the mixed-reality glasses at Meta’s Connect event in September, I was astounded by the video quality and wearability of a device that has for so long come in the form of a heavy, hot headset.

But it’s not the only big dog in the face computer world. Not by a long shot. Xreal, known for its virtual-display glasses, has partnered with Google to build mixed-reality smart glasses on the Android XR platform—the Xreal Aura. On Wednesday, the company announced the official price, starting at $1,279. That’s 20 bucks cheaper than Meta’s VR glasses. Unlike Meta’s option, the Aura glasses come out this year.

The Auras are available for preorder, but only for people who have already placed paid reservations. Preorder options will open up for the general public “in the coming weeks.” The starting price is for a model with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB storage. Xreal says units will ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. It will launch in more regions in 2027.

I tried both. I attended a demo of the Aura glasses, which was deliberately held a day after Meta announced its VR Glasses at Meta Connect. My immediate takeaway was that these glasses are direct competitors, with very similar experiences. Put on a pair, and you can watch videos, play games, or project a multi-monitor workplace setup. Some of those experiences work better on one device or the other.

Courtesy of Xreal

Same but Different

Smart glasses come in several varieties. The simple ones plug into your phone or laptop and project the screen onto the glasses, acting like a portable monitor that doesn’t require you to crane your neck. Then there are glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta, which feature a camera to capture photos and videos and an AI assistant you can talk to. Display versions of these glasses—and ones coming from Google and Samsung—add a visual component so you can see real-time captions when people speak, translations, navigation instructions, and more.

But mixed reality glasses go a step further, bridging the world of virtual and augmented reality. They’re more akin to headsets like the Apple Vision Pro or the Meta Quest, but in slimmer, lighter designs that aren’t as cumbersome to wear. Snap also recently announced a competing pair called Specs, which cost $2,195 and are shipping later this year.

Neither Meta nor Xreal’s glasses can be mistaken for regular everyday glasses. Meta’s futuristic frames fit like the front half of a VR headset. The Xreal frames are more glasses-forward; chunky but nowhere near as thicc as Snap's Specs. Both have an attached wired compute puck (the thing that houses all the memory and processing power) that you'll need to put in your pocket.

Tech.title: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me
Tech.content:
I’m discussing replacement options for our broken couch with my partner when I get a bright idea: Use OpenAI’s recently announced AI agents, called Dots, to buy a couch on our behalf.

My partner is less sure a bot will actually help, but I insist, calling the always-on agent through ChatGPT to get the task started. “Hello, Connor,” it says, getting my name wrong off the bat. I wince as I watch my partner’s face grow even more skeptical. It’s hard to trust an AI agent when it can’t even remember your name.

AI agents are currently leaping from niche software for early adopters to something ordinary people might actually use—might being the operative word here. From Meta’s Muse to OpenAI’s Dots, these tools are built to feel like you’re texting a friend and asking them to complete online tasks, like booking a flight or canceling a dinner reservation. It’s the next evolution of a chatbot: a cuddly persona designed to feel welcoming with the power of a virtual browser it can control.

After a few days with Dots, it’s clear this nascent feature is still rough in some areas. From mistranscribing what I said to offering to solve captchas it couldn’t, my agent's messy actions didn’t instill me with confidence. Even so, what OpenAI released may eventually overhaul how users interact with the internet, as future iterations improve on this initial offering.

While Meta offers Muse for free, OpenAI’s competing product is behind a $100-a-month subscription. It may eventually drop this paywall, as it has for other AI features.

Dots are considered “always-on,” meaning the agents can run recurring tasks while you’re not using ChatGPT and proactively message you with info. Users can use one agent, though the company may let people control multiple agents in the future.

OpenAI nudges users to connect other information sources, like a Gmail account, for more personalized results. It's worth considering the security implications of giving your agent this level of access before getting started, as this style of digital automation remains fairly new, and agents can make privacy gaffes.

AI companies often market these agents as the future of shopping, so I wanted to see how much help it would actually provide for buying a new couch. After correcting my Dot, named Toolie, on my name, I told it the dimensions we need for the new couch to fit through our doorframe. Toolie followed up asking for our budget range. The agent seemed to detect that two people were chatting with it at once and addressed both of us when asking for more details.

Tech.title: My 7 Top Smart Device Picks for Your Desk or Office
Tech.content:
Your home desk or office space can do far more than hold your computer. It’s an excellent spot for home technology that won’t just make your life easier — it’ll also help you save money and get organized faster. I’ve tested the devices you should get started with.

From new types of heaters to energy monitoring and smart lamps, here’s what your desk needs and why it works.

A smart surge protector to protect all your other devices

Meross has extra cord length if you need to do more positioning with your power strip. Meross/CNET

A strong surge protector is the glue that holds all the other desk devices together — and protects them from dangerous electrical surges. I have a full list of recommendations, but consider a smart surge protector like this Tapo model ($42) to make a bigger difference.

More from CNET

These smart power strips let you name each included plug and port based on what you plug into them, and control them remotely, including through common apps like Google Home or Apple Home. You can also turn them on or off with voice commands when they are properly labeled in the app, which is neat if you have connected lights (more on that later) or fans.

Tapo’s version even allows you to track energy costs, which is a huge plus if you’re worried your desk equipment is sapping too much power.



A smart speaker for music and voice commands

Google’s new speaker does a lot right, especially when it comes to audio. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Yes, I like using my smart speaker for basic things like asking it about the weather and traffic, or setting a timer to remember to get up and stretch. But smart speakers can really put the “assistant” in voice assistant when you use them at a desk.

I cover this in more detail in guides like tricks for using Google Home and Nest, but you can use smart speakers to set reminders, add events to your calendar while you’re responding to an email or create a to-do list. Many also have other abilities that make them ready to help out. And they can connect to your streaming services to play music whenever you like.

These desk-friendly speakers are small but have very good audio for their size. Versions like the Echo Dot 5 are small and around $50, but for a big sound upgrade, consider something like the Echo Dot Max, Apple HomePod Mini or Google’s new Home Speaker.

That’s without getting into all the AI features of upgraded voice assistants like Gemini for Home or Alexa Plus. Alexa Plus is especially notable here because it’s free with an Amazon Prime subscription, and you can connect it with third-party services like Uber/Uber Eats, Ticketmaster, TaskRabbit and more for quick ordering while making plans.

A smart display for multitasking and dual-screen use

A Google control hub is great, especially when you get creative. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Think of a smart display as a smart speaker with a touchscreen. That can be surprisingly helpful, especially as a desktop companion. You get all the advantages of a smart speaker, plus the ability to check its work when it’s creating events or to-do lists — plus the option of watching videos, doing a quick internet search or even glancing through your video doorbell.

This second screen at the side of your computer can serve many in-depth purposes, too. You can get caught up in a show, view how-to videos or consult a gaming walkthrough while you’re playing. I’ve found smart displays a bit slower to react than tablets, but the sound is far better, so these displays are much easier to use as a music source or possibly a video chat.

Check out options like the Echo Show 11 ($220) and Nest Hub Max to see what I’m talking about.

Best Desktop Computer for 2026: Top Picks for Macs and PCs See at CNET

A smart heater for programmable, cost-saving heat

Radiant speakers are especially useful near home desks and offices. Boldr

Normal heaters are nice to have near your desk, but they can be fire hazards and energy hogs, and they aren’t always easy to operate. I suggest a smart upgrade. This radiant heater from Boldr ($400) is a high-end example, but you can see how it uses less electricity, poses fewer fire hazards and can be mounted on the wall to fit right by a desk without needing much space.

Also, don’t discount the ability to control a space heater via app. That allows you to set schedules to ensure your desk area is warm before you get there or make sure the heater is turned off no matter where you are.

A smart lamp to set the mood and send reminders

Ikea’s lamp is smart, stylish and feels at home. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Lamps fit well on a computer desk, especially if you don’t have nearby lights or windows and need extra illumination. But a smart light version, like those in my guide, offers greater versatility and utility.

You can set a smart light to any brightness and color you want, letting you adjust the color temperature and make the light as easy on your eyes as you want. You can even connect these lights to other smart devices in the house to serve as visual notifications.

For example, you program the light to turn blue when a smart lock is unlocked, green when a door sensor is activated or red when a TV is turned on in another room.

You have a couple of options to adopt these smart lights. Depending on the size of the bulb, you may be able to upgrade an existing desk lamp with a smart bulb without changing anything else. Or you could replace a light with something like Ikea’s Varmblixt smart lamp if you have the room.

Light strips for fun and entertainment

For extra flair, today’s powerful lighting strips and panels offer many creative options. Govee

If you use your desk more for gaming, watching movies or other entertainment, consider a different kind of upgrade. Light strips set around the edges of your desk or monitor (or floor, etc.) can shift colors, flash along with music and match the theme of whatever you’re playing or watching. They typically need only one available outlet to get started and some can even be cut to size.

One of my favorite options for this is the Govee Gaming Light Rope, which lets you set scenes, sync to music and program it exactly how you want with the highly capable Govee app (which now includes an AI assistant you can give prompts to). In fact, you may want to take a look at Govee’s entire gaming and desk section, because there’s a lot there you can play with.

A nearby smart fan to help cool down

SwitchBot’s fan is a smart evolution for a bedroom or office fan, but not everyone needs so many features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

A large computer setup can grow hot, and there’s nothing like a fan to help cool things down, especially in summer heat waves. However, putting a fan directly on the desk takes up a lot of room and is too annoying for many people. I suggest putting fans at a distance in the same room instead. Our list of the best smart tower fans is an excellent place to get started. It’s surprisingly pleasant to be able to control your fan speed and direction at a distance with your phone (or smart display), but we have other, less complicated options, too.

If you have a nearby shelf or you prefer your fan up close and personal, you may also consider SwitchBot’s smart desk fan, which is the most advanced model I’ve ever tested.
